段.文: 夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生早上一向起得很晚，只有通宵不睡的时候例外，而这种时候并不少见。这天早上，他正坐在桌边吃早饭。我站在壁炉前的地毯上，拾起昨晚那位客人落下的手杖。这是根结实的好木杖，杖头膨大成球形，是人们叫作“槟榔屿律师”的那一种。紧挨杖头下面，箍着一圈将近一英寸宽的银箍，上面刻着：“赠詹姆斯·莫蒂默，皇家外科医学会会员，C.C.H.的朋友们敬赠”，还刻着年份“1884”。老派的家庭医生常拿的正是这种手杖——庄重、厚实，让人看着就安心。
段.en: Mr. Sherlock Holmes, who was usually very late in the mornings, save upon those not infrequent occasions when he was up all night, was seated at the breakfast table. I stood upon the hearth-rug and picked up the stick which our visitor had left behind him the night before. It was a fine, thick piece of wood, bulbous-headed, of the sort which is known as a “Penang lawyer.” Just under the head was a broad silver band nearly an inch across. “To James Mortimer, M.R.C.S., from his friends of the C.C.H.,” was engraved upon it, with the date “1884.” It was just such a stick as the old-fashioned family practitioner used to carry—dignified, solid, and reassuring.

段.文: “喂，华生，你看出什么来了？”
段.en: “Well, Watson, what do you make of it?”

段.文: 福尔摩斯背对着我坐着，我手上在做什么，一点也没让他知道。
段.en: Holmes was sitting with his back to me, and I had given him no sign of my occupation.

段.文: “你怎么知道我在干什么？我看你后脑勺上也长了眼睛。”
段.en: “How did you know what I was doing? I believe you have eyes in the back of your head.”

段.文: “至少我面前有一把擦得锃亮的镀银咖啡壶，”他说，“不过，华生，跟我说说，你从客人的手杖上看出了什么？可惜我们没碰上他，也不知道他来干什么，这件无意中留下的纪念品就变得要紧了。让我听听，你怎么凭这根手杖把这个人还原出来。”
段.en: “I have, at least, a well-polished, silver-plated coffee-pot in front of me,” said he. “But, tell me, Watson, what do you make of our visitor’s stick? Since we have been so unfortunate as to miss him and have no notion of his errand, this accidental souvenir becomes of importance. Let me hear you reconstruct the man by an examination of it.”

段.文: “我想，”我尽量学着我这位朋友的办法说，“莫蒂默医生是个事业有成、上了年纪的医生，很受人敬重，因为认识他的人送了他这件东西，表示对他的感激。”
段.en: “I think,” said I, following as far as I could the methods of my companion, “that Dr. Mortimer is a successful, elderly medical man, well-esteemed since those who know him give him this mark of their appreciation.”

段.文: “好！”福尔摩斯说，“妙极了！”
段.en: “Good!” said Holmes. “Excellent!”

段.文: “我还认为，他多半是个乡村医生，出诊大多靠两条腿走路。”
段.en: “I think also that the probability is in favour of his being a country practitioner who does a great deal of his visiting on foot.”

段.文: “为什么这么说？”
段.en: “Why so?”

段.文: “因为这根手杖原本很漂亮，现在却磕碰得厉害，我很难想象城里的医生会拿着它。杖底包的厚铁头已经磨平了，可见他拄着它走过很多路。”
段.en: “Because this stick, though originally a very handsome one has been so knocked about that I can hardly imagine a town practitioner carrying it. The thick-iron ferrule is worn down, so it is evident that he has done a great amount of walking with it.”

段.文: “完全说得通！”福尔摩斯说。
段.en: “Perfectly sound!” said Holmes.

段.文: “还有那句‘C.C.H.的朋友们’。我猜那是某某狩猎会，当地的一个狩猎会。他大概给会里的人做过些外科救治，所以他们送了他一件小礼物作为答谢。”
段.en: “And then again, there is the ‘friends of the C.C.H.’ I should guess that to be the Something Hunt, the local hunt to whose members he has possibly given some surgical assistance, and which has made him a small presentation in return.”

段.文: “说真的，华生，你这回超常发挥了，”福尔摩斯说着，把椅子往后一推，点上一支香烟，“我得说，你好心替我那些小小的成绩写了不少记述，可在这些记述里，你总是低估自己的本事。也许你自己不会发光，但你能传导光。有些人本身没有天才，却有一种了不起的能力，能把别人的天才激发出来。老朋友，我承认，我欠你的情可不少。”
段.en: “Really, Watson, you excel yourself,” said Holmes, pushing back his chair and lighting a cigarette. “I am bound to say that in all the accounts which you have been so good as to give of my own small achievements you have habitually underrated your own abilities. It may be that you are not yourself luminous, but you are a conductor of light. Some people without possessing genius have a remarkable power of stimulating it. I confess, my dear fellow, that I am very much in your debt.”

段.文: 他以前从没说过这样的话。说实话，这番话让我十分高兴。我仰慕他，也尽力把他的方法公之于众，可他对这些一向无动于衷，这常常让我有些不快。想到自己已经把他的那套方法学到了家，用起来还能得到他的赞许，我也很自豪。这时他从我手里接过手杖，用肉眼端详了几分钟。接着，他露出感兴趣的神情，放下香烟，拿着手杖走到窗前，又用一个凸透镜从头到尾看了一遍。
段.en: He had never said as much before, and I must admit that his words gave me keen pleasure, for I had often been piqued by his indifference to my admiration and to the attempts which I had made to give publicity to his methods. I was proud, too, to think that I had so far mastered his system as to apply it in a way which earned his approval. He now took the stick from my hands and examined it for a few minutes with his naked eyes. Then with an expression of interest he laid down his cigarette, and carrying the cane to the window, he looked over it again with a convex lens.

段.文: “有意思，不过很简单，”他说着，回到长沙发上他最喜欢的那个角落，“这根手杖上确实有一两处迹象，够我们做出好几个推断。”
段.en: “Interesting, though elementary,” said he as he returned to his favourite corner of the settee. “There are certainly one or two indications upon the stick. It gives us the basis for several deductions.”

段.文: “我漏掉什么了吗？”我有点自负地问，“我想，总不至于漏掉什么要紧的吧？”
段.en: “Has anything escaped me?” I asked with some self-importance. “I trust that there is nothing of consequence which I have overlooked?”

段.文: “亲爱的华生，恐怕你的结论大部分都错了。我说你能激发我，坦白讲，意思是我在留意你的错误时，偶尔会被引到真相上去。倒不是说你这回全错了。这人肯定是个乡村医生，也确实常常走路。”
段.en: “I am afraid, my dear Watson, that most of your conclusions were erroneous. When I said that you stimulated me I meant, to be frank, that in noting your fallacies I was occasionally guided towards the truth. Not that you are entirely wrong in this instance. The man is certainly a country practitioner. And he walks a good deal.”

段.文: “那我说对了。”
段.en: “Then I was right.”

段.文: “就这一点而言。”
段.en: “To that extent.”

段.文: “可我说的也就这些。”
段.en: “But that was all.”

段.文: “不，不，亲爱的华生，不止这些——远远不止。比方说，我认为送给医生的礼物，更可能来自医院，而不是狩猎会。医院名字前面既然是‘C.C.’两个字母，自然就会让人想到‘查令十字’。”
段.en: “No, no, my dear Watson, not all—by no means all. I would suggest, for example, that a presentation to a doctor is more likely to come from a hospital than from a hunt, and that when the initials ‘C.C.’ are placed before that hospital the words ‘Charing Cross’ very naturally suggest themselves.”

段.文: “也许你说得对。”
段.en: “You may be right.”

段.文: “可能性在这一边。我们把这个当作一个可行的假设，就有了新的起点，可以重新勾勒这位陌生客人了。”
段.en: “The probability lies in that direction. And if we take this as a working hypothesis we have a fresh basis from which to start our construction of this unknown visitor.”

段.文: “好吧，假定‘C.C.H.’确实代表‘查令十字医院’，我们还能推出什么来？”
段.en: “Well, then, supposing that ‘C.C.H.’ does stand for ‘Charing Cross Hospital,’ what further inferences may we draw?”

段.文: “你想不到吗？你知道我的方法，用上啊！”
段.en: “Do none suggest themselves? You know my methods. Apply them!”

段.文: “我只能想到一个显而易见的结论：这人下乡之前，在城里行过医。”
段.en: “I can only think of the obvious conclusion that the man has practised in town before going to the country.”

段.文: “我想我们还可以再大胆往前推一步。换个角度看：什么时候最可能送这样一件礼物？他的朋友们会在什么时候凑到一起，向他表示好意？显然是莫蒂默医生离开医院、自己开业的时候。我们知道确实送过礼物；我们也相信他从城里的医院转到了乡下行医。那么，说这件礼物是在他转行的时候送的，算是推得太远吗？”
段.en: “I think that we might venture a little farther than this. Look at it in this light. On what occasion would it be most probable that such a presentation would be made? When would his friends unite to give him a pledge of their good will? Obviously at the moment when Dr. Mortimer withdrew from the service of the hospital in order to start a practice for himself. We know there has been a presentation. We believe there has been a change from a town hospital to a country practice. Is it, then, stretching our inference too far to say that the presentation was on the occasion of the change?”

段.文: “看来确实很有可能。”
段.en: “It certainly seems probable.”

段.文: “你再看，他不可能是医院的正式医师，因为只有在伦敦行医、地位稳固的人才能担任那种职位，而这样的人是不会跑到乡下去的。那他是什么人呢？如果他在医院里工作，却不是正式医师，那就只能是住院外科医生或住院内科医生——比高年级医学生强不了多少。他是五年前离开的——手杖上刻着年份。所以，亲爱的华生，你那位庄重的中年家庭医生就烟消云散了，冒出来的是一个不到三十岁的年轻人，和蔼可亲，没什么野心，有点心不在焉，还养着一条心爱的狗。照我粗略的说法，那条狗比㹴犬大，比獒犬小。”
段.en: “Now, you will observe that he could not have been on the staff of the hospital, since only a man well-established in a London practice could hold such a position, and such a one would not drift into the country. What was he, then? If he was in the hospital and yet not on the staff he could only have been a house-surgeon or a house-physician—little more than a senior student. And he left five years ago—the date is on the stick. So your grave, middle-aged family practitioner vanishes into thin air, my dear Watson, and there emerges a young fellow under thirty, amiable, unambitious, absent-minded, and the possessor of a favourite dog, which I should describe roughly as being larger than a terrier and smaller than a mastiff.”

段.文: 我不相信地笑了起来。夏洛克·福尔摩斯往长沙发上一靠，朝天花板吐出一个个摇摇晃晃的小烟圈。
段.en: I laughed incredulously as Sherlock Holmes leaned back in his settee and blew little wavering rings of smoke up to the ceiling.

段.文: “后半截我没法核对，”我说，“不过，这人的年龄和行医经历，查起来倒不难。”我从我那小小的医书架上取下《医生名录》，翻到这个名字。姓莫蒂默的有好几个，可只有一个可能是我们的客人。我把他的条目念了出来。
段.en: “As to the latter part, I have no means of checking you,” said I, “but at least it is not difficult to find out a few particulars about the man’s age and professional career.” From my small medical shelf I took down the Medical Directory and turned up the name. There were several Mortimers, but only one who could be our visitor. I read his record aloud.

段.文: “莫蒂默，詹姆斯，皇家外科医学会会员，1882年入会，住德文郡达特穆尔格林彭。1882年至1884年任查令十字医院住院外科医生。以论文《疾病是一种返祖现象吗？》获比较病理学杰克逊奖。瑞典病理学会通讯会员。著有《若干返祖畸变》（《柳叶刀》，1882年）、《我们在进步吗？》（《心理学杂志》，1883年3月）。格林彭、索斯利和海巴罗三个教区的医疗官。”
段.en: “Mortimer, James, M.R.C.S., 1882, Grimpen, Dartmoor, Devon. House-surgeon, from 1882 to 1884, at Charing Cross Hospital. Winner of the Jackson prize for Comparative Pathology, with essay entitled ‘Is Disease a Reversion?’ Corresponding member of the Swedish Pathological Society. Author of ‘Some Freaks of Atavism’ (Lancet 1882). ‘Do We Progress?’ (Journal of Psychology, March, 1883). Medical Officer for the parishes of Grimpen, Thorsley, and High Barrow.”

段.文: “没提那个当地狩猎会，华生，”福尔摩斯带着一丝调皮的笑容说，“不过正像你敏锐地指出的，是个乡村医生。我想我的推断还算站得住。至于那几个形容词，没记错的话，我说的是和蔼可亲、没什么野心、心不在焉。依我的经验，这世上只有和蔼可亲的人才会收到纪念品，只有没野心的人才会放弃伦敦的前程跑到乡下去，也只有心不在焉的人，才会在你屋里等了一个钟头之后，不留名片，倒把手杖落下了。”
段.en: “No mention of that local hunt, Watson,” said Holmes with a mischievous smile, “but a country doctor, as you very astutely observed. I think that I am fairly justified in my inferences. As to the adjectives, I said, if I remember right, amiable, unambitious, and absent-minded. It is my experience that it is only an amiable man in this world who receives testimonials, only an unambitious one who abandons a London career for the country, and only an absent-minded one who leaves his stick and not his visiting-card after waiting an hour in your room.”

段.文: “那狗呢？”
段.en: “And the dog?”

段.文: “它习惯叼着这根手杖跟在主人后面。手杖很沉，狗只好紧紧咬住中间，所以牙印清清楚楚。从这些牙印之间的距离看，这条狗的嘴，在我看来，对㹴犬来说太宽，对獒犬来说又不够宽。它可能是——对了，没错，是一条卷毛西班牙猎犬。”
段.en: “Has been in the habit of carrying this stick behind his master. Being a heavy stick the dog has held it tightly by the middle, and the marks of his teeth are very plainly visible. The dog’s jaw, as shown in the space between these marks, is too broad in my opinion for a terrier and not broad enough for a mastiff. It may have been—yes, by Jove, it is a curly-haired spaniel.”

段.文: 他一边说，一边站起身来在屋里踱步，这时停在了窗口的凹处。他的语气是那样笃定，我不由得吃惊地抬起头来。
段.en: He had risen and paced the room as he spoke. Now he halted in the recess of the window. There was such a ring of conviction in his voice that I glanced up in surprise.

段.文: “老朋友，你怎么可能这么有把握？”
段.en: “My dear fellow, how can you possibly be so sure of that?”

段.文: “理由很简单：我看见那条狗本身就在我们门口台阶上，它的主人也在按门铃了。别动，华生，拜托你。他是你的同行，你在场也许能帮上我。华生，这正是命运的戏剧性时刻：你听见楼梯上的脚步声，它正一步步走进你的生活，你却不知道是福是祸。詹姆斯·莫蒂默医生这位科学家，要找犯罪专家夏洛克·福尔摩斯做什么呢？请进！”
段.en: “For the very simple reason that I see the dog himself on our very door-step, and there is the ring of its owner. Don’t move, I beg you, Watson. He is a professional brother of yours, and your presence may be of assistance to me. Now is the dramatic moment of fate, Watson, when you hear a step upon the stair which is walking into your life, and you know not whether for good or ill. What does Dr. James Mortimer, the man of science, ask of Sherlock Holmes, the specialist in crime? Come in!”

段.文: 客人的样子让我吃了一惊，我原以为会是个典型的乡村医生。他个子很高，很瘦，长长的鼻子像鸟喙一样突出来，两只锐利的灰眼睛靠得很近，在一副金边眼镜后面闪闪发亮。他穿着医生常穿的衣服，却相当邋遢：礼服大衣颜色发暗，裤脚也磨破了。他虽然年轻，长长的背却已经驼了。走路时脑袋往前探，整个人带着一种眯眼细看、和和气气的神气。一进门，他的目光就落在福尔摩斯手里的手杖上，欢叫一声朝它奔过去。“太好了，”他说，“我拿不准是落在这儿了，还是落在船运公司办事处了。这根手杖我说什么也不能丢。”
段.en: The appearance of our visitor was a surprise to me, since I had expected a typical country practitioner. He was a very tall, thin man, with a long nose like a beak, which jutted out between two keen, grey eyes, set closely together and sparkling brightly from behind a pair of gold-rimmed glasses. He was clad in a professional but rather slovenly fashion, for his frock-coat was dingy and his trousers frayed. Though young, his long back was already bowed, and he walked with a forward thrust of his head and a general air of peering benevolence. As he entered his eyes fell upon the stick in Holmes’s hand, and he ran towards it with an exclamation of joy. “I am so very glad,” said he. “I was not sure whether I had left it here or in the Shipping Office. I would not lose that stick for the world.”

段.文: “我看，是别人送的礼物吧，”福尔摩斯说。
段.en: “A presentation, I see,” said Holmes.

段.文: “是的，先生。”
段.en: “Yes, sir.”

段.文: “查令十字医院送的？”
段.en: “From Charing Cross Hospital?”

段.文: “是那儿的一两个朋友在我结婚的时候送的。”
段.en: “From one or two friends there on the occasion of my marriage.”

段.文: “哎呀，哎呀，这可糟了！”福尔摩斯摇着头说。
段.en: “Dear, dear, that’s bad!” said Holmes, shaking his head.

段.文: 莫蒂默医生在眼镜后面眨了眨眼，有点惊讶：“怎么就糟了？”
段.en: Dr. Mortimer blinked through his glasses in mild astonishment. “Why was it bad?”

段.文: “只不过是打乱了我们的几个小推断而已。您说，是结婚的时候？”
段.en: “Only that you have disarranged our little deductions. Your marriage, you say?”

段.文: “是的，先生。我结了婚，就离开了医院，也就断了当会诊医师的念想。我得自己成个家。”
段.en: “Yes, sir. I married, and so left the hospital, and with it all hopes of a consulting practice. It was necessary to make a home of my own.”

段.文: “好了，好了，说到底我们也没错得太离谱，”福尔摩斯说，“那么，詹姆斯·莫蒂默医生——”
段.en: “Come, come, we are not so far wrong, after all,” said Holmes. “And now, Dr. James Mortimer—”

段.文: “是先生，先生，叫先生就好——我只是个小小的皇家外科医学会会员。”
段.en: “Mister, sir, Mister—a humble M.R.C.S.”

段.文: “看得出来，还是个一丝不苟的人。”
段.en: “And a man of precise mind, evidently.”

段.文: “我不过是科学上的一个票友，福尔摩斯先生，一个在未知的大洋岸边捡贝壳的人。我想，我是在跟夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生说话，而不是——”
段.en: “A dabbler in science, Mr. Holmes, a picker up of shells on the shores of the great unknown ocean. I presume that it is Mr. Sherlock Holmes whom I am addressing and not—”

段.文: “不，这位是我的朋友华生医生。”
段.en: “No, this is my friend Dr. Watson.”

段.文: “很高兴见到您，先生。我听人提起过您的名字，总是跟您这位朋友的名字连在一起。福尔摩斯先生，您让我非常感兴趣。我真没想到会见到这么长的头颅，眉骨也这么突出。您介意我用手指摸一摸您的顶骨缝吗？先生，在您的头骨本身到手之前，能有一个您头骨的模型，也足以给任何一家人类学博物馆增光了。我不是有意奉承，可我承认，我真眼馋您的头骨。”
段.en: “Glad to meet you, sir. I have heard your name mentioned in connection with that of your friend. You interest me very much, Mr. Holmes. I had hardly expected so dolichocephalic a skull or such well-marked supra-orbital development. Would you have any objection to my running my finger along your parietal fissure? A cast of your skull, sir, until the original is available, would be an ornament to any anthropological museum. It is not my intention to be fulsome, but I confess that I covet your skull.”

段.文: 夏洛克·福尔摩斯招手请这位古怪的客人坐下。“先生，我看您对自己那一行很着迷，就像我对我这一行一样，”他说，“我从您的食指看出您自己卷烟抽。请不必客气，点一支吧。”
段.en: Sherlock Holmes waved our strange visitor into a chair. “You are an enthusiast in your line of thought, I perceive, sir, as I am in mine,” said he. “I observe from your forefinger that you make your own cigarettes. Have no hesitation in lighting one.”

段.文: 那人掏出烟纸和烟丝，用烟纸把烟丝一卷，手法灵巧得惊人。他的手指又长又抖，像昆虫的触须一样灵活，一刻也不停。
段.en: The man drew out paper and tobacco and twirled the one up in the other with surprising dexterity. He had long, quivering fingers as agile and restless as the antennæ of an insect.

段.文: 福尔摩斯没有作声，可他那一下一下飞快的目光让我看出，他对这位古怪的客人很感兴趣。“先生，”他终于开口说，“我想，您昨晚光临，今天又来，总不会只是为了研究我的头骨吧？”
段.en: Holmes was silent, but his little darting glances showed me the interest which he took in our curious companion. “I presume, sir,” said he at last, “that it was not merely for the purpose of examining my skull that you have done me the honour to call here last night and again today?”

段.文: “不，先生，不是的，虽然能顺便研究一下我也很高兴。福尔摩斯先生，我来找您，是因为我知道自己不是个讲求实际的人，又突然碰上了一个极其严重、极不寻常的难题。我知道，您是欧洲排名第二的专家——”
段.en: “No, sir, no; though I am happy to have had the opportunity of doing that as well. I came to you, Mr. Holmes, because I recognized that I am myself an unpractical man and because I am suddenly confronted with a most serious and extraordinary problem. Recognizing, as I do, that you are the second highest expert in Europe—”

段.文: “是吗，先生！请问排第一的是哪位？”福尔摩斯有点不客气地问。
段.en: “Indeed, sir! May I inquire who has the honour to be the first?” asked Holmes with some asperity.

段.文: “对一个讲究严格科学的头脑来说，贝蒂荣先生的工作总是特别有吸引力。”
段.en: “To the man of precisely scientific mind the work of Monsieur Bertillon must always appeal strongly.”

段.文: “那您何不去找他呢？”
段.en: “Then had you not better consult him?”

段.文: “先生，我说的是对讲究严格科学的头脑而言。可要说处理实际事务，大家都承认您独一无二。先生，我希望我没有无意中——”
段.en: “I said, sir, to the precisely scientific mind. But as a practical man of affairs it is acknowledged that you stand alone. I trust, sir, that I have not inadvertently—”

段.文: “只是有一点点，”福尔摩斯说，“莫蒂默医生，我想您最好别再绕弯子，痛痛快快告诉我，您要我帮忙的到底是个什么问题。”
段.en: “Just a little,” said Holmes. “I think, Dr. Mortimer, you would do wisely if without more ado you would kindly tell me plainly what the exact nature of the problem is in which you demand my assistance.”

段.文: “我口袋里有一份手稿，”詹姆斯·莫蒂默医生说。
段.en: “I have in my pocket a manuscript,” said Dr. James Mortimer.

段.文: “您一进屋我就注意到了，”福尔摩斯说。
段.en: “I observed it as you entered the room,” said Holmes.

段.文: “是份古老的手稿。”
段.en: “It is an old manuscript.”

段.文: “18世纪初的，除非是伪造的。”
段.en: “Early eighteenth century, unless it is a forgery.”

段.文: “先生，您怎么知道？”
段.en: “How can you say that, sir?”

段.文: “您说话的时候，一直有一两英寸露在外面让我看。一份文件的年代要是连误差十年左右都断不出来，这个专家也太差劲了。您也许读过我那本谈这个问题的小专论。我判断它是1730年的。”
段.en: “You have presented an inch or two of it to my examination all the time that you have been talking. It would be a poor expert who could not give the date of a document within a decade or so. You may possibly have read my little monograph upon the subject. I put that at 1730.”

段.文: “确切的年份是1742年。”莫蒂默医生从胸前口袋里把它掏了出来，“这份家族文件是查尔斯·巴斯克维尔爵士托我保管的。大约三个月前，他突然惨死，在德文郡闹得沸沸扬扬。我可以说，我既是他的私人朋友，也是他的医生。先生，他是个意志坚强的人，精明，务实，和我一样不爱胡思乱想。可他对这份文件看得非常认真，最后落到他头上的那种结局，他心里早有准备。”
段.en: “The exact date is 1742.” Dr. Mortimer drew it from his breast-pocket. “This family paper was committed to my care by Sir Charles Baskerville, whose sudden and tragic death some three months ago created so much excitement in Devonshire. I may say that I was his personal friend as well as his medical attendant. He was a strong-minded man, sir, shrewd, practical, and as unimaginative as I am myself. Yet he took this document very seriously, and his mind was prepared for just such an end as did eventually overtake him.”

段.文: 福尔摩斯伸手接过手稿，在膝盖上摊平。“华生，你看，长s和短s交替着用。我就是靠这一点和别的几处迹象断定年代的。”
段.en: Holmes stretched out his hand for the manuscript and flattened it upon his knee. “You will observe, Watson, the alternative use of the long s and the short. It is one of several indications which enabled me to fix the date.”

段.文: 我从他肩膀后面看过去，只见纸已发黄，字迹也褪了色。顶上写着“巴斯克维尔庄园”，下面是潦草的大字：“1742”。
段.en: I looked over his shoulder at the yellow paper and the faded script. At the head was written: “Baskerville Hall,” and below in large, scrawling figures: “1742.”

段.文: “看起来像是某种陈述。”
段.en: “It appears to be a statement of some sort.”

段.文: “是的，记述的是巴斯克维尔家族流传的一个传说。”
段.en: “Yes, it is a statement of a certain legend which runs in the Baskerville family.”

段.文: “可我知道，您想跟我商量的，是件更眼下、更实际的事吧？”
段.en: “But I understand that it is something more modern and practical upon which you wish to consult me?”

段.文: “是最眼下的事。一件极实际、极紧迫的事，二十四小时之内就得拿主意。不过这份手稿不长，跟这件事又关系极深。您要是允许，我就念给您听。”
段.en: “Most modern. A most practical, pressing matter, which must be decided within twenty-four hours. But the manuscript is short and is intimately connected with the affair. With your permission I will read it to you.”

段.文: 福尔摩斯往椅背上一靠，十指指尖相抵，闭上眼睛，一副听天由命的样子。莫蒂默医生把手稿转向亮处，用又高又发颤的嗓音念起下面这段古怪的旧时故事：
段.en: Holmes leaned back in his chair, placed his finger-tips together, and closed his eyes, with an air of resignation. Dr. Mortimer turned the manuscript to the light and read in a high, cracking voice the following curious, old-world narrative:

段.文:
“关于巴斯克维尔猎犬的来历，说法向来很多。我是雨果·巴斯克维尔的嫡系后人，这个故事是我父亲讲给我的，他又是从他父亲那里听来的，所以我把它写下来，深信事情正如这里所记。我儿，我愿你们相信：惩罚罪孽的那位公义之主，也会慈悲地宽恕罪孽；无论多重的诅咒，只要祈祷、悔改，都能解除。所以，你们从这个故事里要学的，不是惧怕往日种下的果，而是往后行事务必谨慎，免得那些让我家族吃尽苦头的邪恶情欲再次放纵出来，叫我们遭殃。
要知道，在大叛乱的年代（博学的克拉伦登勋爵写过那段历史，我恳切地劝你们一读），巴斯克维尔这片庄园归同名的雨果所有。不可否认，他是个极其放荡、亵渎、目无上帝的人。其实单是这些，邻居们也许还能原谅，因为那一带从来出不了什么圣人；可他生性里有一种肆意残忍的脾气，弄得他的名字在整个西部成了恶名的代称。事有凑巧，这位雨果爱上了（如果这样阴暗的情欲也配用这么光明的字眼的话）一个自耕农的女儿，那人的田地就在巴斯克维尔庄园附近。可这位年轻姑娘为人端庄，名声清白，又怕他的恶名，总是躲着他。于是有一年米迦勒节，雨果带着五六个游手好闲的狐朋狗友，偷偷摸到农场，把姑娘抢走了。那时她父亲和兄弟都不在家，这一点雨果心里清楚得很。他们把她带回庄园，关在楼上的一间屋子里，雨果和朋友们就坐下来通宵狂饮，这是他们每晚的惯例。可怜的姑娘在楼上听着楼下传来的唱声、吼声和可怕的咒骂，几乎要吓疯了。据说雨果·巴斯克维尔喝醉了酒，说出的话恶毒得能叫说话的人自己遭天打雷劈。最后，她在极度的恐惧之下，做了一件连最勇敢、最矫健的男子都未必敢做的事：她攀着爬满南墙的常春藤（如今那墙上仍旧爬满常春藤），从屋檐下爬了下去，然后穿过荒原往家跑。从庄园到她父亲的农场，足有三里格远。
过了不多时，雨果撇下客人，给他的俘虏送吃的喝的去——或许还带着别的更不堪的东西——却发现笼子空了，鸟儿飞了。看样子，他当时就像魔鬼附了身，冲下楼梯跑进餐厅，跳上大餐桌，酒壶和木盘被他踢得四处乱飞。他当着满座宾客大喊：只要能追上那丫头，他情愿当晚就把身体和灵魂一齐献给邪恶的力量。那群醉汉被他的狂怒吓呆了，其中一个比旁人更坏，也许是比旁人醉得更厉害，嚷着要放猎犬去追她。雨果一听，冲出门去，吆喝马夫给他的母马备鞍，把一群猎犬放出狗舍。他拿姑娘的一块头巾给猎犬闻过，引它们找准气味，就在月光下狂吠着冲上荒原去了。
那群醉汉张着嘴愣了好一阵，一时弄不明白这仓促之间到底出了什么事。可没过多久，他们糊涂的脑子醒过来了，想到荒原上恐怕要出什么样的事。顿时一片大乱，有人喊着要手枪，有人喊着要马，还有人喊着要再来一瓶酒。最后，他们发狂的头脑总算恢复了几分理智，一共十三个人，全都上了马追去。明月当空，他们并排飞驰，沿着姑娘要回家必定会走的那条路追赶。
跑了一两英里，他们遇见荒原上一个守夜的牧羊人，便冲他大喊，问他看没看见那队追猎的人马。据说那人吓得几乎疯了，话都说不出来，好半天才说，他确实看见了那个不幸的姑娘，猎犬正循着她的踪迹追去。‘可我看见的还不止这些，’他说，‘雨果·巴斯克维尔骑着他那匹黑母马从我身边过去，他身后有一条地狱里出来的猎犬，不声不响地跟着跑。求上帝保佑，千万别让那东西跟在我脚后头！’那几个喝醉的乡绅骂了牧羊人一通，又往前骑去。可不久他们就浑身发凉了：荒原上传来一阵马蹄声，那匹黑母马浑身溅满白沫，拖着缰绳，背着空鞍，从他们身边飞奔而过。这群醉汉吓坏了，紧紧挨在一起骑行，但还是沿着荒原追下去。其实他们每一个人，要是只有自己一个，早就巴不得掉转马头回去了。他们就这样慢慢骑着，终于赶上了那群猎犬。这些猎犬向来以勇猛和血统纯正出名，这时却挤成一团，在荒原上一处深谷——我们管它叫‘深涧’——的入口呜呜哀叫。有的夹着尾巴溜开，有的颈毛倒竖，瞪着眼睛，直勾勾地望着前面那条狭窄的山谷。
一行人停了下来。你们可以想见，这时他们比出发时清醒多了。大多数人说什么也不肯再往前走，可其中三个最大胆的——也许是醉得最厉害的——骑马下了深涧。深涧底下是一片开阔地，立着两块巨石，至今还能看见，是远古时代一些早已被遗忘的民族竖起来的。月光明晃晃地照着这片空地，那个不幸的姑娘就倒在正中间，她是被吓死、累死的。可是，让这三个天不怕地不怕的浪荡子头发都竖起来的，并不是她的尸体，也不是躺在她旁边的雨果·巴斯克维尔的尸体，而是站在雨果身上、正撕咬他喉咙的一个邪恶的东西：一头巨大的黑色野兽，样子像猎犬，可比凡人眼睛见过的任何猎犬都大。就在他们眼睁睁看着的时候，那东西把雨果·巴斯克维尔的喉咙撕了下来。接着，它转过那双冒火的眼睛和滴着血的大嘴朝他们望过来。三个人吓得尖叫，拼命逃命，一路尖叫着穿过荒原。据说其中一个当夜就因为见了那情景死了，另外两个后半辈子也都成了废人。
我儿，那条猎犬的来历就是这样。据说从那以后，它一直苦苦纠缠着我们家族。我之所以把它写下来，是因为明明白白知道的事，总不如那些只有暗示、只能猜测的事可怕。不可否认，家族里有很多人都不得好死，死得突然、血腥，又神秘莫测。但我们可以托庇于上天无穷的恩慈。《圣经》里警告过罪罚要延及三四代，上天不会越过这三四代，永远惩罚无辜的人。我儿，我就此把你们托付给上天，并且劝你们多加小心：在邪恶力量猖獗的黑夜里，不要穿越荒原。
［雨果·巴斯克维尔写给他的儿子罗杰和约翰，嘱咐他们不要把此事告诉他们的姊妹伊丽莎白。］”
段.en: “Of the origin of the Hound of the Baskervilles there have been many statements, yet as I come in a direct line from Hugo Baskerville, and as I had the story from my father, who also had it from his, I have set it down with all belief that it occurred even as is here set forth. And I would have you believe, my sons, that the same Justice which punishes sin may also most graciously forgive it, and that no ban is so heavy but that by prayer and repentance it may be removed. Learn then from this story not to fear the fruits of the past, but rather to be circumspect in the future, that those foul passions whereby our family has suffered so grievously may not again be loosed to our undoing. “Know then that in the time of the Great Rebellion (the history of which by the learned Lord Clarendon I most earnestly commend to your attention) this Manor of Baskerville was held by Hugo of that name, nor can it be gainsaid that he was a most wild, profane, and godless man. This, in truth, his neighbours might have pardoned, seeing that saints have never flourished in those parts, but there was in him a certain wanton and cruel humour which made his name a by-word through the West. It chanced that this Hugo came to love (if, indeed, so dark a passion may be known under so bright a name) the daughter of a yeoman who held lands near the Baskerville estate. But the young maiden, being discreet and of good repute, would ever avoid him, for she feared his evil name. So it came to pass that one Michaelmas this Hugo, with five or six of his idle and wicked companions, stole down upon the farm and carried off the maiden, her father and brothers being from home, as he well knew. When they had brought her to the Hall the maiden was placed in an upper chamber, while Hugo and his friends sat down to a long carouse, as was their nightly custom. Now, the poor lass upstairs was like to have her wits turned at the singing and shouting and terrible oaths which came up to her from below, for they say that the words used by Hugo Baskerville, when he was in wine, were such as might blast the man who said them. At last in the stress of her fear she did that which might have daunted the bravest or most active man, for by the aid of the growth of ivy which covered (and still covers) the south wall she came down from under the eaves, and so homeward across the moor, there being three leagues betwixt the Hall and her father’s farm. “It chanced that some little time later Hugo left his guests to carry food and drink—with other worse things, perchance—to his captive, and so found the cage empty and the bird escaped. Then, as it would seem, he became as one that hath a devil, for, rushing down the stairs into the dining-hall, he sprang upon the great table, flagons and trenchers flying before him, and he cried aloud before all the company that he would that very night render his body and soul to the Powers of Evil if he might but overtake the wench. And while the revellers stood aghast at the fury of the man, one more wicked or, it may be, more drunken than the rest, cried out that they should put the hounds upon her. Whereat Hugo ran from the house, crying to his grooms that they should saddle his mare and unkennel the pack, and giving the hounds a kerchief of the maid’s, he swung them to the line, and so off full cry in the moonlight over the moor. “Now, for some space the revellers stood agape, unable to understand all that had been done in such haste. But anon their bemused wits awoke to the nature of the deed which was like to be done upon the moorlands. Everything was now in an uproar, some calling for their pistols, some for their horses, and some for another flask of wine. But at length some sense came back to their crazed minds, and the whole of them, thirteen in number, took horse and started in pursuit. The moon shone clear above them, and they rode swiftly abreast, taking that course which the maid must needs have taken if she were to reach her own home. “They had gone a mile or two when they passed one of the night shepherds upon the moorlands, and they cried to him to know if he had seen the hunt. And the man, as the story goes, was so crazed with fear that he could scarce speak, but at last he said that he had indeed seen the unhappy maiden, with the hounds upon her track. ‘But I have seen more than that,’ said he, ‘for Hugo Baskerville passed me upon his black mare, and there ran mute behind him such a hound of hell as God forbid should ever be at my heels.’ So the drunken squires cursed the shepherd and rode onward. But soon their skins turned cold, for there came a galloping across the moor, and the black mare, dabbled with white froth, went past with trailing bridle and empty saddle. Then the revellers rode close together, for a great fear was on them, but they still followed over the moor, though each, had he been alone, would have been right glad to have turned his horse’s head. Riding slowly in this fashion they came at last upon the hounds. These, though known for their valour and their breed, were whimpering in a cluster at the head of a deep dip or goyal, as we call it, upon the moor, some slinking away and some, with starting hackles and staring eyes, gazing down the narrow valley before them. “The company had come to a halt, more sober men, as you may guess, than when they started. The most of them would by no means advance, but three of them, the boldest, or it may be the most drunken, rode forward down the goyal. Now, it opened into a broad space in which stood two of those great stones, still to be seen there, which were set by certain forgotten peoples in the days of old. The moon was shining bright upon the clearing, and there in the centre lay the unhappy maid where she had fallen, dead of fear and of fatigue. But it was not the sight of her body, nor yet was it that of the body of Hugo Baskerville lying near her, which raised the hair upon the heads of these three dare-devil roysterers, but it was that, standing over Hugo, and plucking at his throat, there stood a foul thing, a great, black beast, shaped like a hound, yet larger than any hound that ever mortal eye has rested upon. And even as they looked the thing tore the throat out of Hugo Baskerville, on which, as it turned its blazing eyes and dripping jaws upon them, the three shrieked with fear and rode for dear life, still screaming, across the moor. One, it is said, died that very night of what he had seen, and the other twain were but broken men for the rest of their days. “Such is the tale, my sons, of the coming of the hound which is said to have plagued the family so sorely ever since. If I have set it down it is because that which is clearly known hath less terror than that which is but hinted at and guessed. Nor can it be denied that many of the family have been unhappy in their deaths, which have been sudden, bloody, and mysterious. Yet may we shelter ourselves in the infinite goodness of Providence, which would not forever punish the innocent beyond that third or fourth generation which is threatened in Holy Writ. To that Providence, my sons, I hereby commend you, and I counsel you by way of caution to forbear from crossing the moor in those dark hours when the powers of evil are exalted. “[This from Hugo Baskerville to his sons Rodger and John, with instructions that they say nothing thereof to their sister Elizabeth.]”

段.文: 莫蒂默医生念完这段奇特的故事，把眼镜往额头上一推，隔着桌子盯着夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生。福尔摩斯打了个哈欠，把烟头扔进了炉火里。
段.en: When Dr. Mortimer had finished reading this singular narrative he pushed his spectacles up on his forehead and stared across at Mr. Sherlock Holmes. The latter yawned and tossed the end of his cigarette into the fire.

段.文: “怎么样？”他说。
段.en: “Well?” said he.

段.文: “您不觉得有意思吗？”
段.en: “Do you not find it interesting?”

段.文: “对收集童话的人来说有意思。”
段.en: “To a collector of fairy tales.”

段.文: 莫蒂默医生从口袋里掏出一份折好的报纸。
段.en: Dr. Mortimer drew a folded newspaper out of his pocket.

段.文: “好吧，福尔摩斯先生，那我们给您来点新近的东西。这是今年5月14日的《德文郡纪事报》，上面简短地报道了查尔斯·巴斯克维尔爵士死亡一案查明的事实。他就是在这日子前几天去世的。”
段.en: “Now, Mr. Holmes, we will give you something a little more recent. This is the Devon County Chronicle of May 14th of this year. It is a short account of the facts elicited at the death of Sir Charles Baskerville which occurred a few days before that date.”

段.文: 我的朋友身子稍稍前倾，神情专注起来。客人重新扶正眼镜，念道：
段.en: My friend leaned a little forward and his expression became intent. Our visitor readjusted his glasses and began:

段.文:
“查尔斯·巴斯克维尔爵士近日猝然去世，全郡为之黯然。据传，他很可能作为自由党候选人参加下届中德文选区的选举。查尔斯爵士在巴斯克维尔庄园住的时间虽然不算长，但他性情和蔼，慷慨至极，凡是和他打过交道的人，无不对他又敬又爱。在这个暴发户遍地的年代，一个家道中落的郡中世家子弟，能够自己挣下家业，再带着财富回乡，重振家族往日的荣光，实在令人耳目一新。众所周知，查尔斯爵士在南非做投机生意赚了大钱。有些人一直做下去，直到运气转坏；他比这些人明智，及时把收益兑现，带回了英格兰。他住进巴斯克维尔庄园才两年，他那些重建和改良的计划规模有多大，人们至今津津乐道，如今却因他的去世而中断。他自己没有子女，曾公开表示，希望在自己有生之年让整个乡里都分享他的好运。很多人有自己的理由为他的早逝而痛惜。他向本地和本郡慈善事业慷慨捐款，本报曾屡次报道。
查尔斯爵士之死的种种情形，不能说已经由死因调查彻底查清，但至少足以平息当地迷信引出的种种谣言。没有任何理由怀疑有人行凶，也没有理由设想他不是自然死亡。查尔斯爵士是个鳏夫，在某些方面可以说有点古怪。他虽然非常富有，个人的喜好却很简朴，巴斯克维尔庄园里的家仆只有一对姓巴里摩尔的夫妇，丈夫当管家，妻子管家务。他们的证词，加上几位朋友的佐证，表明查尔斯爵士的身体有一段时间以来一直不好，特别是心脏有毛病，表现为脸色变化、呼吸急促，还有严重的神经抑郁发作。死者的朋友兼医生詹姆斯·莫蒂默医生，也作了同样的证明。
案情很简单。查尔斯·巴斯克维尔爵士每晚睡前都习惯到巴斯克维尔庄园那条有名的紫杉小径上散步。巴里摩尔夫妇的证词表明，这是他的老习惯。5月4日，查尔斯爵士宣布第二天要动身去伦敦，并吩咐巴里摩尔给他收拾行李。当天夜里，他照常出去散步，散步时他习惯抽一支雪茄。他再也没有回来。十二点钟，巴里摩尔发现大门还开着，惊慌起来，点上提灯出去找主人。那天下过雨，查尔斯爵士沿小径走下去的脚印很容易辨认。小径走到一半，有一扇门通向荒原。种种迹象表明，查尔斯爵士曾在这里站了一会儿。然后他继续沿小径往前走，尸体就是在小径尽头发现的。有一件事至今没有解释：据巴里摩尔说，他主人走过那扇通荒原的门以后，脚印的样子就变了，从那里往后，他好像是踮着脚尖走的。当时有个叫墨菲的吉卜赛马贩子在不远的荒原上，可据他自己承认，他喝得醉醺醺的。他说他听见了喊叫，却说不出是从哪个方向传来的。查尔斯爵士身上找不到任何暴力痕迹。医生的证词虽然指出死者面部扭曲得几乎令人难以置信——严重到莫蒂默医生起初都不敢相信，躺在面前的真是他的朋友和病人——但有人解释说，呼吸困难和心力衰竭致死的病例中，这种症状并不少见。尸体解剖证实了这个解释，显示死者患有多年的器质性疾病。验尸陪审团根据医学证据作出了裁决。这样很好，因为查尔斯爵士的继承人能在庄园定居下来，把不幸中断的善举继续下去，显然是最要紧的事。要不是验尸官平淡无奇的结论终于平息了围绕此事悄悄流传的种种离奇故事，巴斯克维尔庄园恐怕就很难找到人来住了。据悉，查尔斯爵士最近的亲属是他弟弟的儿子亨利·巴斯克维尔先生，如果他还在世的话。这个年轻人最后一次有消息时人在美洲，现正在多方查询，以便通知他这一好运。”
段.en: “The recent sudden death of Sir Charles Baskerville, whose name has been mentioned as the probable Liberal candidate for Mid-Devon at the next election, has cast a gloom over the county. Though Sir Charles had resided at Baskerville Hall for a comparatively short period his amiability of character and extreme generosity had won the affection and respect of all who had been brought into contact with him. In these days of nouveaux riches it is refreshing to find a case where the scion of an old county family which has fallen upon evil days is able to make his own fortune and to bring it back with him to restore the fallen grandeur of his line. Sir Charles, as is well known, made large sums of money in South African speculation. More wise than those who go on until the wheel turns against them, he realised his gains and returned to England with them. It is only two years since he took up his residence at Baskerville Hall, and it is common talk how large were those schemes of reconstruction and improvement which have been interrupted by his death. Being himself childless, it was his openly expressed desire that the whole countryside should, within his own lifetime, profit by his good fortune, and many will have personal reasons for bewailing his untimely end. His generous donations to local and county charities have been frequently chronicled in these columns. “The circumstances connected with the death of Sir Charles cannot be said to have been entirely cleared up by the inquest, but at least enough has been done to dispose of those rumours to which local superstition has given rise. There is no reason whatever to suspect foul play, or to imagine that death could be from any but natural causes. Sir Charles was a widower, and a man who may be said to have been in some ways of an eccentric habit of mind. In spite of his considerable wealth he was simple in his personal tastes, and his indoor servants at Baskerville Hall consisted of a married couple named Barrymore, the husband acting as butler and the wife as housekeeper. Their evidence, corroborated by that of several friends, tends to show that Sir Charles’s health has for some time been impaired, and points especially to some affection of the heart, manifesting itself in changes of colour, breathlessness, and acute attacks of nervous depression. Dr. James Mortimer, the friend and medical attendant of the deceased, has given evidence to the same effect. “The facts of the case are simple. Sir Charles Baskerville was in the habit every night before going to bed of walking down the famous yew alley of Baskerville Hall. The evidence of the Barrymores shows that this had been his custom. On the fourth of May Sir Charles had declared his intention of starting next day for London, and had ordered Barrymore to prepare his luggage. That night he went out as usual for his nocturnal walk, in the course of which he was in the habit of smoking a cigar. He never returned. At twelve o’clock Barrymore, finding the hall door still open, became alarmed, and, lighting a lantern, went in search of his master. The day had been wet, and Sir Charles’s footmarks were easily traced down the alley. Halfway down this walk there is a gate which leads out on to the moor. There were indications that Sir Charles had stood for some little time here. He then proceeded down the alley, and it was at the far end of it that his body was discovered. One fact which has not been explained is the statement of Barrymore that his master’s footprints altered their character from the time that he passed the moor-gate, and that he appeared from thence onward to have been walking upon his toes. One Murphy, a gipsy horse-dealer, was on the moor at no great distance at the time, but he appears by his own confession to have been the worse for drink. He declares that he heard cries but is unable to state from what direction they came. No signs of violence were to be discovered upon Sir Charles’s person, and though the doctor’s evidence pointed to an almost incredible facial distortion—so great that Dr. Mortimer refused at first to believe that it was indeed his friend and patient who lay before him—it was explained that that is a symptom which is not unusual in cases of dyspnœa and death from cardiac exhaustion. This explanation was borne out by the post-mortem examination, which showed long-standing organic disease, and the coroner’s jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence. It is well that this is so, for it is obviously of the utmost importance that Sir Charles’s heir should settle at the Hall and continue the good work which has been so sadly interrupted. Had the prosaic finding of the coroner not finally put an end to the romantic stories which have been whispered in connection with the affair, it might have been difficult to find a tenant for Baskerville Hall. It is understood that the next of kin is Mr. Henry Baskerville, if he be still alive, the son of Sir Charles Baskerville’s younger brother. The young man when last heard of was in America, and inquiries are being instituted with a view to informing him of his good fortune.”

段.文: 莫蒂默医生把报纸重新折好，放回口袋。“福尔摩斯先生，关于查尔斯·巴斯克维尔爵士之死，公开的事实就是这些。”
段.en: Dr. Mortimer refolded his paper and replaced it in his pocket. “Those are the public facts, Mr. Holmes, in connection with the death of Sir Charles Baskerville.”

段.文: “我得谢谢您，”夏洛克·福尔摩斯说，“让我注意到这个案子，它确实有几处有意思的地方。当时我看到过一些报上的评论，可那阵子我正一门心思忙着梵蒂冈浮雕宝石那件小事，急着给教皇效劳，就错过了国内好几件有意思的案子。您说，这篇文章包括了全部公开的事实？”
段.en: “I must thank you,” said Sherlock Holmes, “for calling my attention to a case which certainly presents some features of interest. I had observed some newspaper comment at the time, but I was exceedingly preoccupied by that little affair of the Vatican cameos, and in my anxiety to oblige the Pope I lost touch with several interesting English cases. This article, you say, contains all the public facts?”

段.文: “是的。”
段.en: “It does.”

段.文: “那就请把不公开的告诉我吧。”他往后一靠，十指指尖相抵，摆出一副最不动声色、最像法官的神情。
段.en: “Then let me have the private ones.” He leaned back, put his finger-tips together, and assumed his most impassive and judicial expression.

段.文: “我要说的这些，”莫蒂默医生说，他已经开始显得很激动，“我还从没对任何人讲过。我在死因调查时没有说出来，是因为一个科学工作者不愿意当众摆出一副赞同民间迷信的样子。我还有一个顾虑：就像报上说的，巴斯克维尔庄园的名声已经够阴森了，要是再做点什么让它更糟，那就肯定没人肯住了。出于这两个原因，我觉得少说一些是有道理的，反正说了也没有实际好处。可是对您，我没有理由不完全坦白。
段.en: “In doing so,” said Dr. Mortimer, who had begun to show signs of some strong emotion, “I am telling that which I have not confided to anyone. My motive for withholding it from the coroner’s inquiry is that a man of science shrinks from placing himself in the public position of seeming to indorse a popular superstition. I had the further motive that Baskerville Hall, as the paper says, would certainly remain untenanted if anything were done to increase its already rather grim reputation. For both these reasons I thought that I was justified in telling rather less than I knew, since no practical good could result from it, but with you there is no reason why I should not be perfectly frank.

段.文: “荒原上人烟稀少，住得近的几户人家来往就格外多。因为这个缘故，我和查尔斯·巴斯克维尔爵士常常见面。方圆好多英里之内，除了拉夫特庄园的弗兰克兰先生和博物学者斯台普顿先生，就再没有别的受过教育的人了。查尔斯爵士不爱交际，可他生病让我们走到了一起，后来对科学的共同爱好又让我们一直来往。他从南非带回来许多科学资料，我们一起度过了许多愉快的夜晚，讨论布须曼人和霍屯督人的比较解剖学。
段.en: “The moor is very sparsely inhabited, and those who live near each other are thrown very much together. For this reason I saw a good deal of Sir Charles Baskerville. With the exception of Mr. Frankland, of Lafter Hall, and Mr. Stapleton, the naturalist, there are no other men of education within many miles. Sir Charles was a retiring man, but the chance of his illness brought us together, and a community of interests in science kept us so. He had brought back much scientific information from South Africa, and many a charming evening we have spent together discussing the comparative anatomy of the Bushman and the Hottentot.

段.文: “最近几个月，我越来越明显地看出，查尔斯爵士的神经已经绷到了快要断的地步。他把我念给您听的那个传说看得极重，重到什么程度呢？他虽然会在自家园子里散步，可无论如何也不肯在夜里走到荒原上去。福尔摩斯先生，您也许难以相信，他真心认定有一种可怕的厄运笼罩着他的家族。说实在的，他讲给我听的那些祖先的事，确实让人宽心不起来。他总觉得有个可怕的东西在附近，这个念头一直缠着他。不止一次，他问我夜里出诊的时候，有没有见过什么怪东西，或者听到过猎犬的嚎叫。后面这个问题他问过我好几次，每次声音都激动得发颤。
段.en: “Within the last few months it became increasingly plain to me that Sir Charles’s nervous system was strained to the breaking point. He had taken this legend which I have read you exceedingly to heart—so much so that, although he would walk in his own grounds, nothing would induce him to go out upon the moor at night. Incredible as it may appear to you, Mr. Holmes, he was honestly convinced that a dreadful fate overhung his family, and certainly the records which he was able to give of his ancestors were not encouraging. The idea of some ghastly presence constantly haunted him, and on more than one occasion he has asked me whether I had on my medical journeys at night ever seen any strange creature or heard the baying of a hound. The latter question he put to me several times, and always with a voice which vibrated with excitement.

段.文: “我还清楚地记得，出事前大约三个星期，有天傍晚我驾车到他家去。他碰巧正站在大门口。我下了马车，站在他面前，忽然看见他的眼睛定定地越过我的肩膀，往我身后望去，脸上是一种极度恐怖的神情。我猛地转过身，刚好瞥见一个东西从车道尽头过去，我当时以为是一头黑色的大牛犊。他又激动又惊慌，我只好走到那东西刚才待的地方，四下找了找。可它已经不见了。这件事好像在他心里留下了极坏的印象。那天晚上我一直陪着他。也就是那一次，为了解释他为什么那么激动，他把我刚来时念给您听的那份手稿交给我保管。我提到这件小事，是因为想到后来发生的惨剧，它显得有些分量了。可当时我深信这完全是件小事，他的激动毫无道理。
段.en: “I can well remember driving up to his house in the evening some three weeks before the fatal event. He chanced to be at his hall door. I had descended from my gig and was standing in front of him, when I saw his eyes fix themselves over my shoulder and stare past me with an expression of the most dreadful horror. I whisked round and had just time to catch a glimpse of something which I took to be a large black calf passing at the head of the drive. So excited and alarmed was he that I was compelled to go down to the spot where the animal had been and look around for it. It was gone, however, and the incident appeared to make the worst impression upon his mind. I stayed with him all the evening, and it was on that occasion, to explain the emotion which he had shown, that he confided to my keeping that narrative which I read to you when first I came. I mention this small episode because it assumes some importance in view of the tragedy which followed, but I was convinced at the time that the matter was entirely trivial and that his excitement had no justification.

段.文: “查尔斯爵士要去伦敦，是我劝的。我知道他心脏有病，而他终日忧心忡忡，不管起因多么荒诞，显然都在严重损害他的健康。我想，让他到城里换换心思，住上几个月，回来就会像换了个人。我们共同的朋友斯台普顿先生很担心他的身体，也是这个意见。谁知到了最后关头，就出了这场可怕的惨祸。
段.en: “It was at my advice that Sir Charles was about to go to London. His heart was, I knew, affected, and the constant anxiety in which he lived, however chimerical the cause of it might be, was evidently having a serious effect upon his health. I thought that a few months among the distractions of town would send him back a new man. Mr. Stapleton, a mutual friend who was much concerned at his state of health, was of the same opinion. At the last instant came this terrible catastrophe.

段.文: “查尔斯爵士死的那天夜里，发现尸体的管家巴里摩尔派马夫珀金斯骑马来找我。我那时还没睡，所以出事后不到一个钟头就赶到了巴斯克维尔庄园。死因调查时提到的事实，我都一一核对、证实过。我沿着紫杉小径一路跟着脚印走，看到了通荒原的门那儿他好像等过的地方，注意到从那里往后脚印形状变了，也注意到松软的沙砾路上除了巴里摩尔的脚印，再没有别人的。最后，我仔细检查了尸体，在我来之前，谁都没碰过它。查尔斯爵士脸朝下趴着，两臂伸开，手指抠进土里，五官因为某种强烈的情绪抽搐变形，我几乎都不敢断定是他本人。身上确实没有任何外伤。可巴里摩尔在死因调查时说了一句假话。他说尸体周围的地上没有任何痕迹。他是没看见。可我看见了——离尸体有一小段距离，但是新鲜、清楚。”
段.en: “On the night of Sir Charles’s death Barrymore the butler, who made the discovery, sent Perkins the groom on horseback to me, and as I was sitting up late I was able to reach Baskerville Hall within an hour of the event. I checked and corroborated all the facts which were mentioned at the inquest. I followed the footsteps down the yew alley, I saw the spot at the moor-gate where he seemed to have waited, I remarked the change in the shape of the prints after that point, I noted that there were no other footsteps save those of Barrymore on the soft gravel, and finally I carefully examined the body, which had not been touched until my arrival. Sir Charles lay on his face, his arms out, his fingers dug into the ground, and his features convulsed with some strong emotion to such an extent that I could hardly have sworn to his identity. There was certainly no physical injury of any kind. But one false statement was made by Barrymore at the inquest. He said that there were no traces upon the ground round the body. He did not observe any. But I did—some little distance off, but fresh and clear.”

段.文: “脚印？”
段.en: “Footprints?”

段.文: “脚印。”
段.en: “Footprints.”

段.文: “男人的还是女人的？”
段.en: “A man’s or a woman’s?”

段.文: 莫蒂默医生古怪地看了我们一眼，回答的时候，声音低得几乎像耳语。
段.en: Dr. Mortimer looked strangely at us for an instant, and his voice sank almost to a whisper as he answered.

段.文: “福尔摩斯先生，那是一条巨大的猎犬的脚印！”
段.en: “Mr. Holmes, they were the footprints of a gigantic hound!”

段.文: 说实话，听到这句话，我浑身一阵发冷。医生的声音在发颤，可见他自己讲起这件事来也深受震动。福尔摩斯激动地向前探着身子，眼睛里闪着那种冷硬、干涩的光——他一对什么产生浓厚兴趣，眼里就会射出这种光来。
段.en: I confess at these words a shudder passed through me. There was a thrill in the doctor’s voice which showed that he was himself deeply moved by that which he told us. Holmes leaned forward in his excitement and his eyes had the hard, dry glitter which shot from them when he was keenly interested.

段.文: “您亲眼看见的？”
段.en: “You saw this?”

段.文: “就像我现在看见您一样清楚。”
段.en: “As clearly as I see you.”

段.文: “您却什么也没说？”
段.en: “And you said nothing?”

段.文: “说了又有什么用？”
段.en: “What was the use?”

段.文: “怎么别人都没看见呢？”
段.en: “How was it that no one else saw it?”

段.文: “那些印子离尸体大约有二十码，谁也没往心里去。我要不是知道那个传说，大概也不会注意。”
段.en: “The marks were some twenty yards from the body and no one gave them a thought. I don’t suppose I should have done so had I not known this legend.”

段.文: “荒原上牧羊犬很多吧？”
段.en: “There are many sheep-dogs on the moor?”

段.文: “当然很多，可那绝不是牧羊犬。”
段.en: “No doubt, but this was no sheep-dog.”

段.文: “您说它很大？”
段.en: “You say it was large?”

段.文: “大极了。”
段.en: “Enormous.”

段.文: “可它没走近尸体？”
段.en: “But it had not approached the body?”

段.文: “没有。”
段.en: “No.”

段.文: “那天夜里天气怎么样？”
段.en: “What sort of night was it?”

段.文: “又潮又冷。”
段.en: “Damp and raw.”

段.文: “但没真下雨？”
段.en: “But not actually raining?”

段.文: “没有。”
段.en: “No.”

段.文: “那条小径是什么样子？”
段.en: “What is the alley like?”

段.文: “两边是两排老紫杉树篱，有十二英尺高，密不透风。中间的小路大约八英尺宽。”
段.en: “There are two lines of old yew hedge, twelve feet high and impenetrable. The walk in the centre is about eight feet across.”

段.文: “树篱和小路之间还有什么吗？”
段.en: “Is there anything between the hedges and the walk?”

段.文: “有，两边各有一条六英尺左右宽的草地。”
段.en: “Yes, there is a strip of grass about six feet broad on either side.”

段.文: “我听说紫杉树篱在一个地方开了一扇门？”
段.en: “I understand that the yew hedge is penetrated at one point by a gate?”

段.文: “是的，就是通荒原的那扇小门。”
段.en: “Yes, the wicket-gate which leads on to the moor.”

段.文: “还有别的出入口吗？”
段.en: “Is there any other opening?”

段.文: “没有。”
段.en: “None.”

段.文: “这么说，要进紫杉小径，要么从宅子那头走下来，要么从通荒原的门进来？”
段.en: “So that to reach the yew alley one either has to come down it from the house or else to enter it by the moor-gate?”

段.文: “小径尽头还有一座凉亭，可以从那里出去。”
段.en: “There is an exit through a summer-house at the far end.”

段.文: “查尔斯爵士走到凉亭了吗？”
段.en: “Had Sir Charles reached this?”

段.文: “没有，他倒下的地方离凉亭大约五十码。”
段.en: “No; he lay about fifty yards from it.”

段.文: “那么，莫蒂默医生，请告诉我——这一点很重要——您看见的印子是在小路上，不是在草地上？”
段.en: “Now, tell me, Dr. Mortimer—and this is important—the marks which you saw were on the path and not on the grass?”

段.文: “草地上留不下印子。”
段.en: “No marks could show on the grass.”

段.文: “印子和通荒原的门在小路的同一边吗？”
段.en: “Were they on the same side of the path as the moor-gate?”

段.文: “是的，就在小路边上，和通荒原的门在同一边。”
段.en: “Yes; they were on the edge of the path on the same side as the moor-gate.”

段.文: “您让我太感兴趣了。还有一点：那扇小门关着吗？”
段.en: “You interest me exceedingly. Another point. Was the wicket-gate closed?”

段.文: “关着，还上了挂锁。”
段.en: “Closed and padlocked.”

段.文: “门有多高？”
段.en: “How high was it?”

段.文: “四英尺左右。”
段.en: “About four feet high.”

段.文: “那谁都能翻过去？”
段.en: “Then anyone could have got over it?”

段.文: “是的。”
段.en: “Yes.”

段.文: “小门旁边您看到了什么痕迹？”
段.en: “And what marks did you see by the wicket-gate?”

段.文: “没什么特别的。”
段.en: “None in particular.”

段.文: “老天！就没人查一查吗？”
段.en: “Good heaven! Did no one examine?”

段.文: “查了，我亲自查的。”
段.en: “Yes, I examined, myself.”

段.文: “什么也没发现？”
段.en: “And found nothing?”

段.文: “那里乱糟糟的。查尔斯爵士显然在那儿站了五到十分钟。”
段.en: “It was all very confused. Sir Charles had evidently stood there for five or ten minutes.”

段.文: “您怎么知道？”
段.en: “How do you know that?”

段.文: “因为他的雪茄落了两回烟灰。”
段.en: “Because the ash had twice dropped from his cigar.”

段.文: “妙极了！华生，这位同行真对我们的脾气。那么痕迹呢？”
段.en: “Excellent! This is a colleague, Watson, after our own heart. But the marks?”

段.文: “那一小片沙砾地上满是他自己的脚印，别的我一个也认不出来。”
段.en: “He had left his own marks all over that small patch of gravel. I could discern no others.”

段.文: 夏洛克·福尔摩斯不耐烦地一拍膝盖。
段.en: Sherlock Holmes struck his hand against his knee with an impatient gesture.

段.文: “我当时要是在场就好了！”他嚷道，“这显然是个极不寻常的案子，对一个科学的侦探来说，本来有大把大把的机会。那片沙砾地就像一页书，我本可以从上面读出许多东西，可如今早被雨水冲糊了，又被好奇的乡下人的木鞋踩得一塌糊涂。唉，莫蒂默医生，莫蒂默医生，您居然没来找我！这您可真得负很大的责任。”
段.en: “If I had only been there!” he cried. “It is evidently a case of extraordinary interest, and one which presented immense opportunities to the scientific expert. That gravel page upon which I might have read so much has been long ere this smudged by the rain and defaced by the clogs of curious peasants. Oh, Dr. Mortimer, Dr. Mortimer, to think that you should not have called me in! You have indeed much to answer for.”

段.文: “福尔摩斯先生，我要找您，就得把这些事公之于众，我已经说过我为什么不愿这样做了。再说，再说——”
段.en: “I could not call you in, Mr. Holmes, without disclosing these facts to the world, and I have already given my reasons for not wishing to do so. Besides, besides—”

段.文: “您为什么吞吞吐吐的？”
段.en: “Why do you hesitate?”

段.文: “有一个领域，就算是最敏锐、最老练的侦探，也无能为力。”
段.en: “There is a realm in which the most acute and most experienced of detectives is helpless.”

段.文: “您是说，这件事是超自然的？”
段.en: “You mean that the thing is supernatural?”

段.文: “我并没有明确这么说。”
段.en: “I did not positively say so.”

段.文: “是没说，可您显然是这么想的。”
段.en: “No, but you evidently think it.”

段.文: “福尔摩斯先生，惨剧发生以后，我听说了好几件事，很难跟自然界的常理对得上。”
段.en: “Since the tragedy, Mr. Holmes, there have come to my ears several incidents which are hard to reconcile with the settled order of Nature.”

段.文: “比如说？”
段.en: “For example?”

段.文: “我发现，在那件可怕的事发生之前，有好几个人在荒原上见过一个怪物，跟巴斯克维尔家传说里的那个魔物一模一样，绝不可能是科学上已知的哪一种动物。他们都说，那是个庞然大物，浑身发光，样子可怕，像个鬼怪。我一个个盘问过这几个人：一个是头脑清醒的乡下人，一个是钉马掌的铁匠，还有一个是荒原上的农夫。他们讲的都是同一个可怕的幽灵，和传说里那条地狱猎犬丝毫不差。我向您保证，这一带已经人人自危，夜里敢穿过荒原的，得是胆子很大的人。”
段.en: “I find that before the terrible event occurred several people had seen a creature upon the moor which corresponds with this Baskerville demon, and which could not possibly be any animal known to science. They all agreed that it was a huge creature, luminous, ghastly, and spectral. I have cross-examined these men, one of them a hard-headed countryman, one a farrier, and one a moorland farmer, who all tell the same story of this dreadful apparition, exactly corresponding to the hell-hound of the legend. I assure you that there is a reign of terror in the district, and that it is a hardy man who will cross the moor at night.”

段.文: “您这样一个受过训练的科学工作者，也相信这是超自然的？”
段.en: “And you, a trained man of science, believe it to be supernatural?”

段.文: “我不知道该信什么。”
段.en: “I do not know what to believe.”

段.文: 福尔摩斯耸了耸肩。“到目前为止，我的调查一直局限在人世间，”他说，“我也算尽了点微薄之力，跟邪恶作过斗争，可要去对付邪恶之父本人，这个任务恐怕就太大了。不过您得承认，脚印可是实实在在的东西。”
段.en: Holmes shrugged his shoulders. “I have hitherto confined my investigations to this world,” said he. “In a modest way I have combated evil, but to take on the Father of Evil himself would, perhaps, be too ambitious a task. Yet you must admit that the footmark is material.”

段.文: “最早那条猎犬也实在得很，能把一个人的喉咙扯出来，可它同样是魔鬼。”
段.en: “The original hound was material enough to tug a man’s throat out, and yet he was diabolical as well.”

段.文: “看来您已经完全倒向相信超自然的那一边了。可是，莫蒂默医生，请您告诉我：您既然这么看，又何必来找我呢？您一边说调查查尔斯爵士的死毫无用处，一边又要我去调查。”
段.en: “I see that you have quite gone over to the supernaturalists. But now, Dr. Mortimer, tell me this. If you hold these views, why have you come to consult me at all? You tell me in the same breath that it is useless to investigate Sir Charles’s death, and that you desire me to do it.”

段.文: “我没说要您去调查。”
段.en: “I did not say that I desired you to do it.”

段.文: “那我能帮您什么？”
段.en: “Then, how can I assist you?”

段.文: “请您给我出个主意，我该拿亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士怎么办。他要到滑铁卢车站——”莫蒂默医生看了看表，“——还有整整一小时一刻钟。”
段.en: “By advising me as to what I should do with Sir Henry Baskerville, who arrives at Waterloo Station”—Dr. Mortimer looked at his watch—“in exactly one hour and a quarter.”

段.文: “他就是继承人？”
段.en: “He being the heir?”

段.文: “是的。查尔斯爵士死后，我们打听这位年轻绅士的下落，得知他一直在加拿大务农。从我们得到的消息看，他各方面都是个出色的小伙子。我现在说话，不是以医生的身份，而是以查尔斯爵士遗嘱的受托人和执行人的身份。”
段.en: “Yes. On the death of Sir Charles we inquired for this young gentleman and found that he had been farming in Canada. From the accounts which have reached us he is an excellent fellow in every way. I speak now not as a medical man but as a trustee and executor of Sir Charles’s will.”

段.文: “我想，没有别人来争继承权吧？”
段.en: “There is no other claimant, I presume?”

段.文: “没有。我们能查到的另一个亲属，只有罗杰·巴斯克维尔。他们一共兄弟三个，可怜的查尔斯爵士是老大，罗杰是老三。老二很年轻就死了，他就是亨利这孩子的父亲。老三罗杰是家里的败类。他继承了巴斯克维尔家祖上那股专横的血统，听人说，长得跟家里老雨果的画像一模一样。他在英格兰闹得待不下去，逃到中美洲，1876年在那里得黄热病死了。亨利是巴斯克维尔家最后一个人了。再过一小时零五分，我就要去滑铁卢车站接他。我收到电报，说他今天早上已经到了南安普敦。福尔摩斯先生，您看我该拿他怎么办？”
段.en: “None. The only other kinsman whom we have been able to trace was Rodger Baskerville, the youngest of three brothers of whom poor Sir Charles was the elder. The second brother, who died young, is the father of this lad Henry. The third, Rodger, was the black sheep of the family. He came of the old masterful Baskerville strain and was the very image, they tell me, of the family picture of old Hugo. He made England too hot to hold him, fled to Central America, and died there in 1876 of yellow fever. Henry is the last of the Baskervilles. In one hour and five minutes I meet him at Waterloo Station. I have had a wire that he arrived at Southampton this morning. Now, Mr. Holmes, what would you advise me to do with him?”

段.文: “他为什么不能回他祖上的家呢？”
段.en: “Why should he not go to the home of his fathers?”

段.文: “这看起来是理所当然的，对吧？可是您想想，每个到那里去的巴斯克维尔家的人，都没有好下场。我敢肯定，查尔斯爵士死前要是能跟我说上几句话，一定会警告我，不要把这个古老家族的最后一个人、这笔巨大财富的继承人，带到那个要命的地方去。可也不能否认，整个贫穷荒凉的乡里能不能兴旺，就全看他来不来了。庄园要是没有主人住，查尔斯爵士做的那些好事就全都要垮掉。我怕自己在这件事上牵涉的利益太明显，会影响判断，所以才把这件事摆到您面前，请您指点。”
段.en: “It seems natural, does it not? And yet, consider that every Baskerville who goes there meets with an evil fate. I feel sure that if Sir Charles could have spoken with me before his death he would have warned me against bringing this, the last of the old race, and the heir to great wealth, to that deadly place. And yet it cannot be denied that the prosperity of the whole poor, bleak countryside depends upon his presence. All the good work which has been done by Sir Charles will crash to the ground if there is no tenant of the Hall. I fear lest I should be swayed too much by my own obvious interest in the matter, and that is why I bring the case before you and ask for your advice.”

段.文: 福尔摩斯想了一会儿。
段.en: Holmes considered for a little time.

段.文: “说白了，事情是这样，”他说，“依您看，有一种魔鬼的力量，让达特穆尔对巴斯克维尔家的人来说成了不安全的地方——您是这么看的吧？”
段.en: “Put into plain words, the matter is this,” said he. “In your opinion there is a diabolical agency which makes Dartmoor an unsafe abode for a Baskerville—that is your opinion?”

段.文: “至少我可以说，有些证据表明可能是这样。”
段.en: “At least I might go the length of saying that there is some evidence that this may be so.”

段.文: “正是。可是，如果您那套超自然的说法是对的，它在伦敦害这个年轻人，肯定也跟在德文郡一样容易。一个魔鬼只在本地有法力，跟教区委员会似的，那也太不可思议了。”
段.en: “Exactly. But surely, if your supernatural theory be correct, it could work the young man evil in London as easily as in Devonshire. A devil with merely local powers like a parish vestry would be too inconceivable a thing.”

段.文: “福尔摩斯先生，您说得这么轻巧，要是您亲身碰上这些事，恐怕就不会这样了。那么照我的理解，您的意见是，这个年轻人在德文郡和在伦敦一样安全。他五十分钟后就到了。您建议我怎么做？”
段.en: “You put the matter more flippantly, Mr. Holmes, than you would probably do if you were brought into personal contact with these things. Your advice, then, as I understand it, is that the young man will be as safe in Devonshire as in London. He comes in fifty minutes. What would you recommend?”

段.文: “先生，我建议您叫一辆马车，把正在挠我家前门的那条长毛垂耳猎犬叫走，然后去滑铁卢车站接亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士。”
段.en: “I recommend, sir, that you take a cab, call off your spaniel who is scratching at my front door, and proceed to Waterloo to meet Sir Henry Baskerville.”

段.文: “然后呢？”
段.en: “And then?”

段.文: “然后，在我对这件事拿定主意之前，您什么也别跟他说。”
段.en: “And then you will say nothing to him at all until I have made up my mind about the matter.”

段.文: “您要多久才能拿定主意？”
段.en: “How long will it take you to make up your mind?”

段.文: “二十四小时。莫蒂默医生，明天上午十点，请您到这里来一趟，我将不胜感激。您要是能把亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士一起带来，对我下一步的安排会很有帮助。”
段.en: “Twenty-four hours. At ten o’clock tomorrow, Dr. Mortimer, I will be much obliged to you if you will call upon me here, and it will be of help to me in my plans for the future if you will bring Sir Henry Baskerville with you.”

段.文: “我一定照办，福尔摩斯先生。”他把约定的时间潦草地记在衬衫袖口上，就匆匆走了，还是那副探着头、眯着眼、心不在焉的古怪样子。福尔摩斯在楼梯口叫住了他。
段.en: “I will do so, Mr. Holmes.” He scribbled the appointment on his shirt-cuff and hurried off in his strange, peering, absent-minded fashion. Holmes stopped him at the head of the stair.

段.文: “还有一个问题，莫蒂默医生。您说查尔斯·巴斯克维尔爵士死前，有好几个人在荒原上见过这个幽灵？”
段.en: “Only one more question, Dr. Mortimer. You say that before Sir Charles Baskerville’s death several people saw this apparition upon the moor?”

段.文: “有三个人见过。”
段.en: “Three people did.”

段.文: “他死后还有人见过吗？”
段.en: “Did any see it after?”

段.文: “我没听说。”
段.en: “I have not heard of any.”

段.文: “谢谢您。再见。”
段.en: “Thank you. Good-morning.”

段.文: 福尔摩斯回到座位上，脸上带着那种暗自满意的平静神情——这表示他眼前有了一件合心意的工作。
段.en: Holmes returned to his seat with that quiet look of inward satisfaction which meant that he had a congenial task before him.

段.文: “要出去吗，华生？”
段.en: “Going out, Watson?”

段.文: “除非我能帮上你的忙。”
段.en: “Unless I can help you.”

段.文: “不用，老朋友，要行动的时候我才会找你帮忙。不过这件事真妙，从某些方面看简直独一无二。你路过布拉德利烟草店的时候，请他送一磅最烈的粗切烟丝上来，好吗？谢谢。你要是方便的话，最好傍晚以前别回来。到时候，我很想跟你交换一下看法，谈谈今天早上送到我们面前的这个极有意思的问题。”
段.en: “No, my dear fellow, it is at the hour of action that I turn to you for aid. But this is splendid, really unique from some points of view. When you pass Bradley’s, would you ask him to send up a pound of the strongest shag tobacco? Thank you. It would be as well if you could make it convenient not to return before evening. Then I should be very glad to compare impressions as to this most interesting problem which has been submitted to us this morning.”

段.文: 我知道，我的朋友在高度集中精神思考的时候，非常需要清静独处。这种时候，他要掂量每一点证据，构想出几种不同的推论，反复权衡，再判定哪些地方要紧、哪些无关紧要。所以那一天我是在俱乐部里度过的，直到傍晚才回贝克街。我重新走进起居室时，已经快九点了。
段.en: I knew that seclusion and solitude were very necessary for my friend in those hours of intense mental concentration during which he weighed every particle of evidence, constructed alternative theories, balanced one against the other, and made up his mind as to which points were essential and which immaterial. I therefore spent the day at my club and did not return to Baker Street until evening. It was nearly nine o’clock when I found myself in the sitting-room once more.

段.文: 我一推开门，头一个念头就是着火了。屋里烟雾弥漫，桌上的灯光都被遮得模模糊糊。可我一进去，就放下心来，原来是浓烈的粗烟丝冒出的呛人烟气，呛得我喉咙发紧，咳个不停。透过烟雾，我隐隐约约看见福尔摩斯穿着睡袍，蜷在一张扶手椅里，嘴里叼着他那只黑色陶土烟斗，身边散放着几卷纸。
段.en: My first impression as I opened the door was that a fire had broken out, for the room was so filled with smoke that the light of the lamp upon the table was blurred by it. As I entered, however, my fears were set at rest, for it was the acrid fumes of strong coarse tobacco which took me by the throat and set me coughing. Through the haze I had a vague vision of Holmes in his dressing-gown coiled up in an armchair with his black clay pipe between his lips. Several rolls of paper lay around him.

段.文: “着凉了吗，华生？”他说。
段.en: “Caught cold, Watson?” said he.

段.文: “没有，是这毒烟熏的。”
段.en: “No, it’s this poisonous atmosphere.”

段.文: “你这么一说，我也觉得是够浓的。”
段.en: “I suppose it is pretty thick, now that you mention it.”

段.文: “够浓！简直受不了。”
段.en: “Thick! It is intolerable.”

段.文: “那就开窗吧！我看你一整天都待在俱乐部里。”
段.en: “Open the window, then! You have been at your club all day, I perceive.”

段.文: “我的好福尔摩斯！”
段.en: “My dear Holmes!”

段.文: “我说对了吧？”
段.en: “Am I right?”

段.文: “当然对，可你怎么知道的？”
段.en: “Certainly, but how?”

段.文: 他看着我一脸困惑的样子，笑了起来。“华生，你身上有一种可爱的天真，所以拿你来施展我那点小本事，真是一种乐趣。一位先生在一个阵雨不断、满地泥泞的日子出门，傍晚回来却干干净净，帽子和靴子还锃光发亮。可见他一整天都待在一个地方没动。他又不是那种有知心朋友的人。那他能去哪儿呢？这不是明摆着的吗？”
段.en: He laughed at my bewildered expression. “There is a delightful freshness about you, Watson, which makes it a pleasure to exercise any small powers which I possess at your expense. A gentleman goes forth on a showery and miry day. He returns immaculate in the evening with the gloss still on his hat and his boots. He has been a fixture therefore all day. He is not a man with intimate friends. Where, then, could he have been? Is it not obvious?”

段.文: “嗯，是挺明显的。”
段.en: “Well, it is rather obvious.”

段.文: “世上满是明摆着的事，偏偏谁也不去留意。你猜我去哪儿了？”
段.en: “The world is full of obvious things which nobody by any chance ever observes. Where do you think that I have been?”

段.文: “也一整天没动地方。”
段.en: “A fixture also.”

段.文: “恰恰相反，我去了一趟德文郡。”
段.en: “On the contrary, I have been to Devonshire.”

段.文: “神游？”
段.en: “In spirit?”

段.文: “正是。我的身体一直留在这张扶手椅里，而且很遗憾，趁我不在的时候，它喝掉了两大壶咖啡，抽掉了多得惊人的烟丝。你走以后，我派人到斯坦福德地图店买来荒原这一带的陆军测绘局地图，我的魂儿就在地图上空飘了一整天。我敢说，到了那里，我自己就能认得路。”
段.en: “Exactly. My body has remained in this armchair and has, I regret to observe, consumed in my absence two large pots of coffee and an incredible amount of tobacco. After you left I sent down to Stamford’s for the Ordnance map of this portion of the moor, and my spirit has hovered over it all day. I flatter myself that I could find my way about.”

段.文: “我想，是张大比例尺的地图吧？”
段.en: “A large-scale map, I presume?”

段.文: “比例尺很大。”
段.en: “Very large.”

段.文: 他展开其中一卷，摊在膝盖上。“这就是跟我们有关的那一片地方。中间是巴斯克维尔庄园。”
段.en: He unrolled one section and held it over his knee. “Here you have the particular district which concerns us. That is Baskerville Hall in the middle.”

段.文: “周围还有一片树林？”
段.en: “With a wood round it?”

段.文: “对。紫杉小径虽然没用这个名字标出来，但我想一定是顺着这条线延伸的。你看，荒原在它右边。这里这一小片房子是格林彭村，我们的朋友莫蒂默医生就住在这儿。你看，方圆五英里之内，只有零零星星几处住宅。这里是拉夫特庄园，那篇报道里提到过。这里标着一所房子，可能是那位博物学者的住处——没记错的话，他叫斯台普顿。这里是荒原上的两座农庄，高岩农庄和福尔迈尔农庄。再往外十四英里，是普林斯敦的大监狱。在这些零散的地点之间和周围，是一片荒凉、死寂的荒原。这就是惨剧上演的舞台，我们说不定还要在这个舞台上帮着再演一场。”
段.en: “Exactly. I fancy the yew alley, though not marked under that name, must stretch along this line, with the moor, as you perceive, upon the right of it. This small clump of buildings here is the hamlet of Grimpen, where our friend Dr. Mortimer has his headquarters. Within a radius of five miles there are, as you see, only a very few scattered dwellings. Here is Lafter Hall, which was mentioned in the narrative. There is a house indicated here which may be the residence of the naturalist—Stapleton, if I remember right, was his name. Here are two moorland farmhouses, High Tor and Foulmire. Then fourteen miles away the great convict prison of Princetown. Between and around these scattered points extends the desolate, lifeless moor. This, then, is the stage upon which tragedy has been played, and upon which we may help to play it again.”

段.文: “那一定是个荒凉的地方。”
段.en: “It must be a wild place.”

段.文: “是啊，这布景配得上这出戏。要是魔鬼真想插手人间的事——”
段.en: “Yes, the setting is a worthy one. If the devil did desire to have a hand in the affairs of men—”

段.文: “这么说，你自己也倾向于超自然的解释了。”
段.en: “Then you are yourself inclining to the supernatural explanation.”

段.文: “魔鬼的爪牙也可以是有血有肉的人，不是吗？一开始，我们面前就摆着两个问题：第一，到底有没有人犯罪；第二，犯的是什么罪，又是怎么犯的？当然，如果莫蒂默医生的猜测是对的，我们面对的是超出自然常规的力量，那我们的调查也就到头了。可是在退到这一步之前，我们必须把其他所有假设都试遍。你要是不介意，我想还是把窗户关上吧。说来奇怪，我发现空气浓了，思想也容易集中。我还没走到钻进箱子里思考的地步，可照我的信条推下去，那就是合乎逻辑的结果。这个案子你琢磨过了吗？”
段.en: “The devil’s agents may be of flesh and blood, may they not? There are two questions waiting for us at the outset. The one is whether any crime has been committed at all; the second is, what is the crime and how was it committed? Of course, if Dr. Mortimer’s surmise should be correct, and we are dealing with forces outside the ordinary laws of Nature, there is an end of our investigation. But we are bound to exhaust all other hypotheses before falling back upon this one. I think we’ll shut that window again, if you don’t mind. It is a singular thing, but I find that a concentrated atmosphere helps a concentration of thought. I have not pushed it to the length of getting into a box to think, but that is the logical outcome of my convictions. Have you turned the case over in your mind?”

段.文: “琢磨过，这一天我想了很多。”
段.en: “Yes, I have thought a good deal of it in the course of the day.”

段.文: “你怎么看？”
段.en: “What do you make of it?”

段.文: “让人摸不着头脑。”
段.en: “It is very bewildering.”

段.文: “这案子确实有它自己的特点，有几处与众不同的地方。比如脚印的变化，你怎么看？”
段.en: “It has certainly a character of its own. There are points of distinction about it. That change in the footprints, for example. What do you make of that?”

段.文: “莫蒂默说，那人在小径的那一段是踮着脚尖走的。”
段.en: “Mortimer said that the man had walked on tiptoe down that portion of the alley.”

段.文: “他只是重复了死因调查时某个蠢人说的话。一个人在小径上走，为什么要踮着脚尖？”
段.en: “He only repeated what some fool had said at the inquest. Why should a man walk on tiptoe down the alley?”

段.文: “那是怎么回事？”
段.en: “What then?”

段.文: “他是在跑，华生——拼命地跑，逃命地跑，一直跑到心脏迸裂，脸朝下倒地死去。”
段.en: “He was running, Watson—running desperately, running for his life, running until he burst his heart—and fell dead upon his face.”

段.文: “他在躲什么？”
段.en: “Running from what?”

段.文: “问题就在这里。有迹象表明，他还没开始跑，就已经吓得发了狂。”
段.en: “There lies our problem. There are indications that the man was crazed with fear before ever he began to run.”

段.文: “你怎么知道？”
段.en: “How can you say that?”

段.文: “我推测，让他害怕的东西是从荒原那边朝他过来的。如果是这样——看来很有可能——那么只有吓昏了头的人，才会不往宅子那边跑，反倒背着宅子跑。如果那个吉卜赛人的证词可信，他是一边呼救一边往最不可能有人救他的方向跑的。还有，那天夜里他在等谁？为什么不在自己家里等，而要在紫杉小径上等？”
段.en: “I am presuming that the cause of his fears came to him across the moor. If that were so, and it seems most probable, only a man who had lost his wits would have run from the house instead of towards it. If the gipsy’s evidence may be taken as true, he ran with cries for help in the direction where help was least likely to be. Then, again, whom was he waiting for that night, and why was he waiting for him in the yew alley rather than in his own house?”

段.文: “你认为他在等人？”
段.en: “You think that he was waiting for someone?”

段.文: “他上了年纪，身体又弱。他傍晚出去散散步，我们能理解；可那天地上潮湿，夜里天气又坏。他在那儿站了五到十分钟——莫蒂默医生从雪茄烟灰推断出这一点，比我原先以为的要有实际头脑得多——这合乎常情吗？”
段.en: “The man was elderly and infirm. We can understand his taking an evening stroll, but the ground was damp and the night inclement. Is it natural that he should stand for five or ten minutes, as Dr. Mortimer, with more practical sense than I should have given him credit for, deduced from the cigar ash?”

段.文: “可他每天晚上都出去的。”
段.en: “But he went out every evening.”

段.文: “我看他不太可能每天晚上都在通荒原的门口等着。恰恰相反，证据表明他一直躲着荒原。那天夜里他却在那里等着。那是他动身去伦敦的前一夜。事情有了眉目了，华生，前后连得起来了。麻烦你把我的小提琴递给我，等明天上午见过莫蒂默医生和亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士之后，我们再接着想这件事。”
段.en: “I think it unlikely that he waited at the moor-gate every evening. On the contrary, the evidence is that he avoided the moor. That night he waited there. It was the night before he made his departure for London. The thing takes shape, Watson. It becomes coherent. Might I ask you to hand me my violin, and we will postpone all further thought upon this business until we have had the advantage of meeting Dr. Mortimer and Sir Henry Baskerville in the morning.”

段.文: 早餐桌收拾得很早，福尔摩斯穿着睡袍，等着约好的会面。两位委托人很守时，钟刚敲十点，莫蒂默医生就被领上楼来，年轻的准男爵跟在后面。这位准男爵个子不高，三十岁上下，机灵，黑眼睛，身板非常结实，两道浓黑的眉毛，一张刚毅好斗的脸。他穿一套红褐色的花呢西装，脸上饱经风吹日晒，一看就是大半辈子待在户外的人。可他目光沉稳，举止从容自信，又透出一股绅士气度。
段.en: Our breakfast table was cleared early, and Holmes waited in his dressing-gown for the promised interview. Our clients were punctual to their appointment, for the clock had just struck ten when Dr. Mortimer was shown up, followed by the young baronet. The latter was a small, alert, dark-eyed man about thirty years of age, very sturdily built, with thick black eyebrows and a strong, pugnacious face. He wore a ruddy-tinted tweed suit and had the weather-beaten appearance of one who has spent most of his time in the open air, and yet there was something in his steady eye and the quiet assurance of his bearing which indicated the gentleman.

段.文: “这位是亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士。”莫蒂默医生说。
段.en: “This is Sir Henry Baskerville,” said Dr. Mortimer.

段.文: “是啊，”他说，“奇怪的是，夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生，就算我这位朋友今天早上没提议来找您，我自己也会来的。听说您擅长琢磨小谜题，我今天早上就碰上一个，我自己想不明白。”
段.en: “Why, yes,” said he, “and the strange thing is, Mr. Sherlock Holmes, that if my friend here had not proposed coming round to you this morning I should have come on my own account. I understand that you think out little puzzles, and I’ve had one this morning which wants more thinking out than I am able to give it.”

段.文: “请坐，亨利爵士。您的意思是，您到伦敦以后，自己就遇上了什么怪事？”
段.en: “Pray take a seat, Sir Henry. Do I understand you to say that you have yourself had some remarkable experience since you arrived in London?”

段.文: “也不算什么大事，福尔摩斯先生。多半只是个玩笑。就是这封信——如果这也能叫信的话——今天早上送到我手上的。”
段.en: “Nothing of much importance, Mr. Holmes. Only a joke, as like as not. It was this letter, if you can call it a letter, which reached me this morning.”

段.文: 他把一个信封放在桌上，我们都俯身去看。信封质地普通，灰扑扑的颜色。地址“诺森伯兰旅馆，亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士收”是用粗糙的印刷体字母写的；邮戳是“查令十字”，寄出时间是前一天晚上。
段.en: He laid an envelope upon the table, and we all bent over it. It was of common quality, greyish in colour. The address, “Sir Henry Baskerville, Northumberland Hotel,” was printed in rough characters; the post-mark “Charing Cross,” and the date of posting the preceding evening.

段.文: “谁知道您要住诺森伯兰旅馆？”福尔摩斯问，目光锐利地看着客人。
段.en: “Who knew that you were going to the Northumberland Hotel?” asked Holmes, glancing keenly across at our visitor.

段.文: “谁也不可能知道。我们是在我见了莫蒂默医生之后才定下来的。”
段.en: “No one could have known. We only decided after I met Dr. Mortimer.”

段.文: “不过，莫蒂默医生想必早就住在那里了吧？”
段.en: “But Dr. Mortimer was no doubt already stopping there?”

段.文: “不是，我之前一直住在一位朋友家。”医生说。
段.en: “No, I had been staying with a friend,” said the doctor.

段.文: “我们要去这家旅馆，事先不可能有任何迹象。”
段.en: “There was no possible indication that we intended to go to this hotel.”

段.文: “嗯！看来有人对您的行踪非常关心。”他从信封里抽出半张大页纸，叠成了四折。他把纸打开，平铺在桌上。纸的中间有一句话，是把印好的字一个个剪下来贴成的。上面写着：
段.en: “Hum! Someone seems to be very deeply interested in your movements.” Out of the envelope he took a half-sheet of foolscap paper folded into four. This he opened and spread flat upon the table. Across the middle of it a single sentence had been formed by the expedient of pasting printed words upon it. It ran:

段.文: 如果你珍惜自己的性命或理智，就离荒原远一点。
段.en: As you value your life or your reason keep away from the moor.

段.文: 只有“荒原”这个词是用墨水写上去的。
段.en: The word “moor” only was printed in ink.

段.文: “好了，”亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士说，“福尔摩斯先生，也许您能告诉我，这到底是什么鬼意思？又是谁对我的事这么上心？”
段.en: “Now,” said Sir Henry Baskerville, “perhaps you will tell me, Mr. Holmes, what in thunder is the meaning of that, and who it is that takes so much interest in my affairs?”

段.文: “您怎么看，莫蒂默医生？至少您得承认，这件事里没什么超自然的东西吧？”
段.en: “What do you make of it, Dr. Mortimer? You must allow that there is nothing supernatural about this, at any rate?”

段.文: “是没有，先生。不过，写信的人很可能就认定这件事是超自然的。”
段.en: “No, sir, but it might very well come from someone who was convinced that the business is supernatural.”

段.文: “什么事？”亨利爵士厉声问，“我看你们几位先生对我自己的事，知道得比我多得多。”
段.en: “What business?” asked Sir Henry sharply. “It seems to me that all you gentlemen know a great deal more than I do about my own affairs.”

段.文: “您离开这间屋子之前，我们知道的您都会知道，亨利爵士。这一点我向您保证。”夏洛克·福尔摩斯说，“如果您允许，眼下我们先只谈这份非常有意思的文件。它一定是昨天晚上拼好、寄出的。华生，有昨天的《泰晤士报》吗？”
段.en: “You shall share our knowledge before you leave this room, Sir Henry. I promise you that,” said Sherlock Holmes. “We will confine ourselves for the present with your permission to this very interesting document, which must have been put together and posted yesterday evening. Have you yesterday’s Times, Watson?”

段.文: “就在角落里。”
段.en: “It is here in the corner.”

段.文: “麻烦你递给我——要里面登社论的那一版。”他飞快地扫了一遍，目光在各栏之间上下移动，“这篇谈自由贸易的文章写得好极了。让我给你们念一段。
段.en: “Might I trouble you for it—the inside page, please, with the leading articles?” He glanced swiftly over it, running his eyes up and down the columns. “Capital article this on free trade. Permit me to give you an extract from it.

段.文: ‘你也许会被哄骗，以为保护性关税会扶持你自己的行业或产业。但道理很明白：从长远看，这样的立法必然会使财富远离这个国家，降低我们进口货物的价值，并使这个岛国的整体生活水平下降。’
段.en: ‘You may be cajoled into imagining that your own special trade or your own industry will be encouraged by a protective tariff, but it stands to reason that such legislation must in the long run keep away wealth from the country, diminish the value of our imports, and lower the general conditions of life in this island.’

段.文: “你觉得怎么样，华生？”福尔摩斯兴高采烈地大声说，满意地搓着双手，“你不觉得这观点非常精彩吗？”
段.en: “What do you think of that, Watson?” cried Holmes in high glee, rubbing his hands together with satisfaction. “Don’t you think that is an admirable sentiment?”

段.文: 莫蒂默医生带着一种职业性的兴趣看着福尔摩斯，亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士则把一双困惑的黑眼睛转向了我。
段.en: Dr. Mortimer looked at Holmes with an air of professional interest, and Sir Henry Baskerville turned a pair of puzzled dark eyes upon me.

段.文: “关税这类事我不太懂，”他说，“不过就那张字条来说，我们好像有点跑题了。”
段.en: “I don’t know much about the tariff and things of that kind,” said he, “but it seems to me we’ve got a bit off the trail so far as that note is concerned.”

段.文: “恰恰相反，亨利爵士，我觉得我们正紧紧咬着线索。华生比您更了解我的方法，但恐怕连他也没完全看出这句话的意义。”
段.en: “On the contrary, I think we are particularly hot upon the trail, Sir Henry. Watson here knows more about my methods than you do, but I fear that even he has not quite grasped the significance of this sentence.”

段.文: “没错，我承认，我看不出两者有什么联系。”
段.en: “No, I confess that I see no connection.”

段.文: “可是，亲爱的华生，两者的联系紧密得很，一个就是从另一个里摘出来的。‘你’‘你的’‘自己的’‘性命’‘理智’‘珍惜’‘远一点’‘离’。现在你还看不出这些字是从哪儿来的吗？”
段.en: “And yet, my dear Watson, there is so very close a connection that the one is extracted out of the other. ‘You,’ ‘your,’ ‘your,’ ‘life,’ ‘reason,’ ‘value,’ ‘keep away,’ ‘from the.’ Don’t you see now whence these words have been taken?”

段.文: “天哪，您说对了！嘿，这可真够聪明的！”亨利爵士叫道。
段.en: “By thunder, you’re right! Well, if that isn’t smart!” cried Sir Henry.

段.文: “就算还有什么疑问，也可以由这一点打消：‘远一点’和‘离’是连在一起剪下来的。”
段.en: “If any possible doubt remained it is settled by the fact that ‘keep away’ and ‘from the’ are cut out in one piece.”

段.文: “哎呀，还真是！”
段.en: “Well, now—so it is!”

段.文: “说真的，福尔摩斯先生，这完全超出了我的想象。”莫蒂默医生惊奇地盯着我的朋友，“有人说这些字来自报纸，我能理解；可您竟能说出是哪份报纸，还说出自社论，这真是我见过的最了不起的事情之一。您是怎么做到的？”
段.en: “Really, Mr. Holmes, this exceeds anything which I could have imagined,” said Dr. Mortimer, gazing at my friend in amazement. “I could understand anyone saying that the words were from a newspaper; but that you should name which, and add that it came from the leading article, is really one of the most remarkable things which I have ever known. How did you do it?”

段.文: “医生，我想您能分辨黑人的头骨和爱斯基摩人的头骨吧？”
段.en: “I presume, Doctor, that you could tell the skull of a negro from that of an Esquimau?”

段.文: “当然能。”
段.en: “Most certainly.”

段.文: “怎么分辨的呢？”
段.en: “But how?”

段.文: “因为那是我特别的爱好。区别很明显。眶上嵴、面角、上颌的弧度，还有——”
段.en: “Because that is my special hobby. The differences are obvious. The supra-orbital crest, the facial angle, the maxillary curve, the—”

段.文: “这也是我特别的爱好，区别也同样明显。在我眼里，《泰晤士报》文章所用的那种加了铅条间距的小号字，和一份半便士晚报上邋里邋遢的印刷，差别就像您说的黑人和爱斯基摩人一样大。对研究犯罪的专家来说，辨认字体是最基本的学问之一。不过我承认，我很年轻的时候，有一回把《利兹信使报》和《西部晨报》弄混了。但《泰晤士报》的社论非常有特色，这些字不可能出自别处。既然信是昨天拼的，那么十有八九能在昨天的报纸上找到这些字。”
段.en: “But this is my special hobby, and the differences are equally obvious. There is as much difference to my eyes between the leaded bourgeois type of a Times article and the slovenly print of an evening half-penny paper as there could be between your negro and your Esquimau. The detection of types is one of the most elementary branches of knowledge to the special expert in crime, though I confess that once when I was very young I confused the Leeds Mercury with the Western Morning News. But a Times leader is entirely distinctive, and these words could have been taken from nothing else. As it was done yesterday the strong probability was that we should find the words in yesterday’s issue.”

段.文: “照您这么说，福尔摩斯先生，”亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士说，“有人用剪刀剪下了这些字——”
段.en: “So far as I can follow you, then, Mr. Holmes,” said Sir Henry Baskerville, “someone cut out this message with a scissors—”

段.文: “指甲剪。”福尔摩斯说，“您看得出来，那把剪刀刃很短，因为剪‘远一点’的时候剪了两下。”
段.en: “Nail-scissors,” said Holmes. “You can see that it was a very short-bladed scissors, since the cutter had to take two snips over ‘keep away.’”

段.文: “是这样。那么，有人用一把短刃剪刀剪下这些字，用糨糊贴——”
段.en: “That is so. Someone, then, cut out the message with a pair of short-bladed scissors, pasted it with paste—”

段.文: “胶水。”福尔摩斯说。
段.en: “Gum,” said Holmes.

段.文: “用胶水贴到纸上。可我想知道，‘荒原’这个词为什么是手写的？”
段.en: “With gum on to the paper. But I want to know why the word ‘moor’ should have been written?”

段.文: “因为他在报上找不到这个词。别的词都很普通，哪一期报纸上都找得到，‘荒原’就没那么常见了。”
段.en: “Because he could not find it in print. The other words were all simple and might be found in any issue, but ‘moor’ would be less common.”

段.文: “哦，当然，这就说得通了。您从这封信里还看出别的什么了吗，福尔摩斯先生？”
段.en: “Why, of course, that would explain it. Have you read anything else in this message, Mr. Holmes?”

段.文: “有一两个迹象，尽管写信的人费尽心思抹掉了一切线索。您看，地址是用粗糙的印刷体写的。可《泰晤士报》很少有人看，看的几乎都是受过高等教育的人。所以我们可以认定，写信的是一个受过教育、却想装成没受过教育的人。他费力掩饰自己的笔迹，说明您可能认得他的笔迹，或者将来会认得。还有，您会注意到，这些字贴得并不整齐，有的比别的高出一大截。比如‘性命’，就完全不在该在的位置。这可能说明剪字的人粗心，也可能说明他慌张匆忙。总的来说，我倾向于后一种看法。因为这件事显然很要紧，写这种信的人不大可能粗心。如果他是匆忙的，那就引出一个有意思的问题：他为什么要匆忙？因为任何信只要在清早之前寄出，都能在亨利爵士离开旅馆前送到他手上。写信的人是怕被人打断吗？怕被谁打断？”
段.en: “There are one or two indications, and yet the utmost pains have been taken to remove all clues. The address, you observe is printed in rough characters. But the Times is a paper which is seldom found in any hands but those of the highly educated. We may take it, therefore, that the letter was composed by an educated man who wished to pose as an uneducated one, and his effort to conceal his own writing suggests that that writing might be known, or come to be known, by you. Again, you will observe that the words are not gummed on in an accurate line, but that some are much higher than others. ‘Life,’ for example is quite out of its proper place. That may point to carelessness or it may point to agitation and hurry upon the part of the cutter. On the whole I incline to the latter view, since the matter was evidently important, and it is unlikely that the composer of such a letter would be careless. If he were in a hurry it opens up the interesting question why he should be in a hurry, since any letter posted up to early morning would reach Sir Henry before he would leave his hotel. Did the composer fear an interruption—and from whom?”

段.文: “我们现在有点进入瞎猜的范围了。”莫蒂默医生说。
段.en: “We are coming now rather into the region of guesswork,” said Dr. Mortimer.

段.文: “不如说，是进入了权衡各种可能、选出最可能那一种的范围。这是科学地运用想象力，而且我们的推测总有一些实际依据作起点。好了，您无疑会说这是猜测，可我几乎可以肯定，这个地址是在旅馆里写的。”
段.en: “Say, rather, into the region where we balance probabilities and choose the most likely. It is the scientific use of the imagination, but we have always some material basis on which to start our speculation. Now, you would call it a guess, no doubt, but I am almost certain that this address has been written in a hotel.”

段.文: “您到底凭什么这么说？”
段.en: “How in the world can you say that?”

段.文: “您仔细看就会发现，笔和墨水都让写字的人很伤脑筋。一个词里笔尖溅了两次墨，一个短短的地址里笔写干了三次，说明墨水瓶里墨水很少。私人的笔和墨水瓶很少会弄成这个样子，两样同时这样就更少见了。可您知道旅馆里的墨水和笔，那里很难碰上别的样子。没错，我可以毫不犹豫地说：只要我们去查查查令十字附近各家旅馆的废纸篓，找到那张被剪坏的《泰晤士报》社论，就能直接抓到寄这封怪信的人。哎呀！哎呀！这是什么？”
段.en: “If you examine it carefully you will see that both the pen and the ink have given the writer trouble. The pen has spluttered twice in a single word and has run dry three times in a short address, showing that there was very little ink in the bottle. Now, a private pen or ink-bottle is seldom allowed to be in such a state, and the combination of the two must be quite rare. But you know the hotel ink and the hotel pen, where it is rare to get anything else.
