Yes, I have very little hesitation in saying that could we examine the waste-paper baskets of the hotels around Charing Cross until we found the remains of the mutilated Times leader we could lay our hands straight upon the person who sent this singular message. Halloa! Halloa! What’s this?”

段.文: 他正仔细检查那张贴着字的大页纸，把它举到离眼睛只有一两英寸的地方。
段.en: He was carefully examining the foolscap, upon which the words were pasted, holding it only an inch or two from his eyes.

段.文: “怎么了？”
段.en: “Well?”

段.文: “没什么。”他说着把纸丢下，“只是半张白纸，连水印都没有。这封古怪的信，能看出来的我想都看出来了。那么，亨利爵士，您到伦敦以后，还碰到过别的什么有意思的事吗？”
段.en: “Nothing,” said he, throwing it down. “It is a blank half-sheet of paper, without even a water-mark upon it. I think we have drawn as much as we can from this curious letter; and now, Sir Henry, has anything else of interest happened to you since you have been in London?”

段.文: “呃，没有，福尔摩斯先生。我想没有。”
段.en: “Why, no, Mr. Holmes. I think not.”

段.文: “您没发现有人跟踪您、监视您吗？”
段.en: “You have not observed anyone follow or watch you?”

段.文: “我好像一头闯进了一本廉价小说里。”我们的客人说，“到底为什么会有人跟踪我、监视我？”
段.en: “I seem to have walked right into the thick of a dime novel,” said our visitor. “Why in thunder should anyone follow or watch me?”

段.文: “这个我们待会儿再谈。在我们深入这件事之前，您还有别的情况要告诉我们吗？”
段.en: “We are coming to that. You have nothing else to report to us before we go into this matter?”

段.文: “嗯，这要看您觉得什么值得说了。”
段.en: “Well, it depends upon what you think worth reporting.”

段.文: “我认为，凡是超出日常生活常规的事，都很值得说。”
段.en: “I think anything out of the ordinary routine of life well worth reporting.”

段.文: 亨利爵士笑了。“我对英国的生活还不太了解，因为我几乎一直待在美国和加拿大。不过我希望，在这边丢一只靴子，不算日常生活的常规吧。”
段.en: Sir Henry smiled. “I don’t know much of British life yet, for I have spent nearly all my time in the States and in Canada. But I hope that to lose one of your boots is not part of the ordinary routine of life over here.”

段.文: “您丢了一只靴子？”
段.en: “You have lost one of your boots?”

段.文: “我亲爱的先生，”莫蒂默医生叫道，“只是放错地方了。等您回旅馆就会找到的。拿这种小事来打扰福尔摩斯先生有什么用呢？”
段.en: “My dear sir,” cried Dr. Mortimer, “it is only mislaid. You will find it when you return to the hotel. What is the use of troubling Mr. Holmes with trifles of this kind?”

段.文: “唉，是他让我说说不寻常的事嘛。”
段.en: “Well, he asked me for anything outside the ordinary routine.”

段.文: “说得对，”福尔摩斯说，“不管这件事看起来多么无聊。您说您丢了一只靴子？”
段.en: “Exactly,” said Holmes, “however foolish the incident may seem. You have lost one of your boots, you say?”

段.文: “嗯，反正是找不着了。昨晚我把两只都放在了房门外，早上就只剩一只。擦鞋的那个家伙什么也说不清楚。最糟糕的是，这双靴子是我昨晚才在斯特兰德街买的，一次都没穿过。”
段.en: “Well, mislaid it, anyhow. I put them both outside my door last night, and there was only one in the morning. I could get no sense out of the chap who cleans them. The worst of it is that I only bought the pair last night in the Strand, and I have never had them on.”

段.文: “既然一次都没穿过，您为什么要把它们放出去擦？”
段.en: “If you have never worn them, why did you put them out to be cleaned?”

段.文: “那是一双浅棕色的靴子，还从没上过油。所以我才放出去的。”
段.en: “They were tan boots and had never been varnished. That was why I put them out.”

段.文: “那么，我理解的是，您昨天一到伦敦，就马上出门买了一双靴子？”
段.en: “Then I understand that on your arrival in London yesterday you went out at once and bought a pair of boots?”

段.文: “我买了不少东西。莫蒂默医生陪我一起去的。您知道，我既然要去那边当乡绅，就得穿得像个样子。再说我在西部待久了，可能有点不修边幅。我买的东西里就有这双棕色靴子——花了六美元——结果还没上脚，就被偷了一只。”
段.en: “I did a good deal of shopping. Dr. Mortimer here went round with me. You see, if I am to be squire down there I must dress the part, and it may be that I have got a little careless in my ways out West. Among other things I bought these brown boots—gave six dollars for them—and had one stolen before ever I had them on my feet.”

段.文: “偷这东西似乎毫无用处。”夏洛克·福尔摩斯说，“我承认，我和莫蒂默医生想的一样：丢的那只靴子用不了多久就会找到的。”
段.en: “It seems a singularly useless thing to steal,” said Sherlock Holmes. “I confess that I share Dr. Mortimer’s belief that it will not be long before the missing boot is found.”

段.文: “好了，先生们，”准男爵果断地说，“我知道的那一点点，我想已经说得够多了。该你们兑现承诺，把我们到底在追查什么，原原本本告诉我了。”
段.en: “And, now, gentlemen,” said the baronet with decision, “it seems to me that I have spoken quite enough about the little that I know. It is time that you kept your promise and gave me a full account of what we are all driving at.”

段.文: “您的要求很合理。”福尔摩斯回答，“莫蒂默医生，我看您最好把讲给我们听的故事，照样再讲一遍。”
段.en: “Your request is a very reasonable one,” Holmes answered. “Dr. Mortimer, I think you could not do better than to tell your story as you told it to us.”

段.文: 得到鼓励，我们这位搞科学的朋友从口袋里掏出文件，把整个案子像前一天早上那样讲了一遍。亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士听得全神贯注，不时惊叹一声。
段.en: Thus encouraged, our scientific friend drew his papers from his pocket and presented the whole case as he had done upon the morning before. Sir Henry Baskerville listened with the deepest attention and with an occasional exclamation of surprise.

段.文: “嘿，看来我继承的这份遗产可真够厉害的。”长长的叙述结束后，他说，“当然，那条猎犬的事，我从小在育儿室里就听说过。那是我们家最爱讲的故事，不过我以前从没当真。可说到我伯父的死——唉，我脑子里一团乱麻，还理不清楚。你们好像还没拿定主意，这件事该找警察，还是该找牧师。”
段.en: “Well, I seem to have come into an inheritance with a vengeance,” said he when the long narrative was finished. “Of course, I’ve heard of the hound ever since I was in the nursery. It’s the pet story of the family, though I never thought of taking it seriously before. But as to my uncle’s death—well, it all seems boiling up in my head, and I can’t get it clear yet. You don’t seem quite to have made up your mind whether it’s a case for a policeman or a clergyman.”

段.文: “正是这样。”
段.en: “Precisely.”

段.文: “现在又有了旅馆里这封寄给我的信。我想它也能对上号。”
段.en: “And now there’s this affair of the letter to me at the hotel. I suppose that fits into its place.”

段.文: “这似乎说明，有人比我们更清楚荒原上发生的事。”莫蒂默医生说。
段.en: “It seems to show that someone knows more than we do about what goes on upon the moor,” said Dr. Mortimer.

段.文: “还说明，”福尔摩斯说，“这个人对您没有恶意，因为他在提醒您有危险。”
段.en: “And also,” said Holmes, “that someone is not ill-disposed towards you, since they warn you of danger.”

段.文: “也可能是他们有自己的目的，想把我吓跑。”
段.en: “Or it may be that they wish, for their own purposes, to scare me away.”

段.文: “嗯，当然，这也有可能。莫蒂默医生，我非常感谢您给我带来这个问题，它有好几种有意思的可能。不过，亨利爵士，我们眼下要决定的实际问题是：您到底该不该去巴斯克维尔庄园。”
段.en: “Well, of course, that is possible also. I am very much indebted to you, Dr. Mortimer, for introducing me to a problem which presents several interesting alternatives. But the practical point which we now have to decide, Sir Henry, is whether it is or is not advisable for you to go to Baskerville Hall.”

段.文: “我为什么不该去？”
段.en: “Why should I not go?”

段.文: “似乎有危险。”
段.en: “There seems to be danger.”

段.文: “您说的危险，是来自这个家族的恶魔，还是来自人？”
段.en: “Do you mean danger from this family fiend or do you mean danger from human beings?”

段.文: “这个嘛，正是我们要查清楚的。”
段.en: “Well, that is what we have to find out.”

段.文: “不管是哪一种，我的回答都不会变。福尔摩斯先生，地狱里没有哪个魔鬼，世上也没有哪个人，能拦着我回自己祖辈的家。您就把这当作我最后的答复吧。”他说话时浓黑的眉头紧锁，脸涨成了暗红色。显然，巴斯克维尔家族的火爆脾气，在这最后一位传人身上并没有熄灭。“不过，”他说，“你们告诉我的这些事，我还没来得及好好想一想。要一个人一下子弄明白、拿定主意，这可是件大事。我想一个人安安静静待一个钟头，好好想想。听我说，福尔摩斯先生，现在是十一点半，我这就回旅馆去。您和您的朋友华生医生两点钟过来，跟我们一起吃午饭怎么样？到时候我能更清楚地告诉你们，我对这件事是怎么看的。”
段.en: “Whichever it is, my answer is fixed. There is no devil in hell, Mr. Holmes, and there is no man upon earth who can prevent me from going to the home of my own people, and you may take that to be my final answer.” His dark brows knitted and his face flushed to a dusky red as he spoke. It was evident that the fiery temper of the Baskervilles was not extinct in this their last representative. “Meanwhile,” said he, “I have hardly had time to think over all that you have told me. It’s a big thing for a man to have to understand and to decide at one sitting. I should like to have a quiet hour by myself to make up my mind. Now, look here, Mr. Holmes, it’s half-past eleven now and I am going back right away to my hotel. Suppose you and your friend, Dr. Watson, come round and lunch with us at two. I’ll be able to tell you more clearly then how this thing strikes me.”

段.文: “你方便吗，华生？”
段.en: “Is that convenient to you, Watson?”

段.文: “完全方便。”
段.en: “Perfectly.”

段.文: “那就等着我们吧。要我叫辆马车吗？”
段.en: “Then you may expect us. Shall I have a cab called?”

段.文: “我宁愿走走，这件事让我心里有点乱。”
段.en: “I’d prefer to walk, for this affair has flurried me rather.”

段.文: “我很乐意陪您走走。”他的同伴说。
段.en: “I’ll join you in a walk, with pleasure,” said his companion.

段.文: “那就两点钟再见。回头见，再会！”
段.en: “Then we meet again at two o’clock. Au revoir, and good-morning!”

段.文: 我们听见客人下楼的脚步声，接着是前门砰的一声关上。转眼之间，福尔摩斯就从一个懒洋洋的空想家变成了一个行动派。
段.en: We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang of the front door. In an instant Holmes had changed from the languid dreamer to the man of action.

段.文: “帽子，靴子，华生，快！一刻也不能耽误！”他穿着睡袍冲进自己的房间，几秒钟后就换上礼服大衣出来了。我们一起匆匆下楼，来到街上。莫蒂默医生和巴斯克维尔还看得见，在我们前面大约两百码，正朝牛津街方向走去。
段.en: “Your hat and boots, Watson, quick! Not a moment to lose!” He rushed into his room in his dressing-gown and was back again in a few seconds in a frock-coat. We hurried together down the stairs and into the street. Dr. Mortimer and Baskerville were still visible about two hundred yards ahead of us in the direction of Oxford Street.

段.文: “要我跑过去叫住他们吗？”
段.en: “Shall I run on and stop them?”

段.文: “千万别，亲爱的华生。只要你不嫌弃我，我有你做伴就心满意足了。我们的朋友很明智，今天早上确实很适合散步。”
段.en: “Not for the world, my dear Watson. I am perfectly satisfied with your company if you will tolerate mine. Our friends are wise, for it is certainly a very fine morning for a walk.”

段.文: 他加快脚步，直到我们和他们的距离缩短了大约一半。然后我们始终保持在一百码之后，跟着他们走进牛津街，又顺着摄政街往下走。有一次，我们的朋友停下来看一家商店的橱窗，福尔摩斯也跟着停下来。片刻之后，他满意地轻呼了一声。我顺着他急切的目光看去，只见一辆双轮马车原先停在街对面，车里坐着一个人，这时又慢慢往前走了。
段.en: He quickened his pace until we had decreased the distance which divided us by about half. Then, still keeping a hundred yards behind, we followed into Oxford Street and so down Regent Street. Once our friends stopped and stared into a shop window, upon which Holmes did the same. An instant afterwards he gave a little cry of satisfaction, and, following the direction of his eager eyes, I saw that a hansom cab with a man inside which had halted on the other side of the street was now proceeding slowly onward again.

段.文: “那就是我们要找的人，华生！快来！就算别的做不了，我们也要好好看看他。”
段.en: “There’s our man, Watson! Come along! We’ll have a good look at him, if we can do no more.”

段.文: 就在这时，我看见了一大把浓密的黑胡子，还有一双锐利的眼睛，正透过马车的侧窗盯着我们。车顶的小窗猛地掀开，有人朝车夫尖声喊了句什么，马车便发疯似的顺着摄政街飞驰而去。福尔摩斯急切地四下张望，想找另一辆马车，可眼前一辆空车也没有。他冲进车流，拼命追赶，但对方领先太多，马车早已不见踪影。
段.en: At that instant I was aware of a bushy black beard and a pair of piercing eyes turned upon us through the side window of the cab. Instantly the trapdoor at the top flew up, something was screamed to the driver, and the cab flew madly off down Regent Street. Holmes looked eagerly round for another, but no empty one was in sight. Then he dashed in wild pursuit amid the stream of the traffic, but the start was too great, and already the cab was out of sight.

段.文: “唉！”福尔摩斯从车流中钻出来，气喘吁吁，脸都气白了，懊恼地说，“哪有这么倒霉、又这么笨的事？华生，华生，你要是个诚实的人，就把这件事也记下来，跟我的那些成功摆在一起！”
段.en: “There now!” said Holmes bitterly as he emerged panting and white with vexation from the tide of vehicles. “Was ever such bad luck and such bad management, too? Watson, Watson, if you are an honest man you will record this also and set it against my successes!”

段.文: “那人是谁？”
段.en: “Who was the man?”

段.文: “我一点也不知道。”
段.en: “I have not an idea.”

段.文: “是个密探？”
段.en: “A spy?”

段.文: “嗯，从我们听到的情况看，很明显，巴斯克维尔进城以后，一直被人紧紧盯着。不然怎么会这么快就知道他选的是诺森伯兰旅馆？我推断，既然他们第一天跟踪他，第二天也会跟。你可能注意到了，莫蒂默医生念那个传说的时候，我两次踱到窗前。”
段.en: “Well, it was evident from what we have heard that Baskerville has been very closely shadowed by someone since he has been in town. How else could it be known so quickly that it was the Northumberland Hotel which he had chosen? If they had followed him the first day I argued that they would follow him also the second. You may have observed that I twice strolled over to the window while Dr. Mortimer was reading his legend.”

段.文: “是的，我记得。”
段.en: “Yes, I remember.”

段.文: “我是在看街上有没有闲逛的人，可一个也没看见。华生，我们对付的是个聪明人。这件事牵涉很深。跟我们打交道的这股力量是善意还是恶意，我还没最后拿定主意，但我始终感到背后有实力、有预谋。我们的朋友一走，我就马上跟了出去，希望能发现那个看不见的跟踪者。他狡猾得很，不敢步行，而是坐了一辆马车，这样他既可以慢慢跟在后面，也可以从他们身边冲过去，不被他们注意。这个办法还有一个好处：如果他们叫马车，他随时可以跟上。不过，它也有一个明显的缺点。”
段.en: “I was looking out for loiterers in the street, but I saw none. We are dealing with a clever man, Watson. This matter cuts very deep, and though I have not finally made up my mind whether it is a benevolent or a malevolent agency which is in touch with us, I am conscious always of power and design. When our friends left I at once followed them in the hopes of marking down their invisible attendant. So wily was he that he had not trusted himself upon foot, but he had availed himself of a cab so that he could loiter behind or dash past them and so escape their notice. His method had the additional advantage that if they were to take a cab he was all ready to follow them. It has, however, one obvious disadvantage.”

段.文: “这就让他落到了车夫手里。”
段.en: “It puts him in the power of the cabman.”

段.文: “正是。”
段.en: “Exactly.”

段.文: “真可惜，我们没记下车号！”
段.en: “What a pity we did not get the number!”

段.文: “亲爱的华生，我虽然笨手笨脚，可你不会真以为我连车号都没记吧？2704号就是我们要找的人。不过眼下这对我们没什么用。”
段.en: “My dear Watson, clumsy as I have been, you surely do not seriously imagine that I neglected to get the number? No. 2704 is our man. But that is no use to us for the moment.”

段.文: “我看不出您还能多做什么。”
段.en: “I fail to see how you could have done more.”

段.文: “一看到那辆马车，我就该马上转身往反方向走。然后我可以从从容容地另雇一辆马车，远远地跟着第一辆；或者更好的办法是，直接坐车去诺森伯兰旅馆，在那里等着。等那个不明身份的人跟着巴斯克维尔回到旅馆，我们就可以用他的办法对付他，看看他往哪儿去。可现在，我太急躁，不够谨慎，对手又出奇地敏捷果断，马上抓住了机会。结果我们暴露了自己，还把人跟丢了。”
段.en: “On observing the cab I should have instantly turned and walked in the other direction. I should then at my leisure have hired a second cab and followed the first at a respectful distance, or, better still, have driven to the Northumberland Hotel and waited there. When our unknown had followed Baskerville home we should have had the opportunity of playing his own game upon himself and seeing where he made for. As it is, by an indiscreet eagerness, which was taken advantage of with extraordinary quickness and energy by our opponent, we have betrayed ourselves and lost our man.”

段.文: 说这些话的时候，我们一直顺着摄政街慢慢溜达。莫蒂默医生和他的同伴早就在前面不见了。
段.en: We had been sauntering slowly down Regent Street during this conversation, and Dr. Mortimer, with his companion, had long vanished in front of us.

段.文: “跟着他们已经没有意义了。”福尔摩斯说，“影子走了，不会再回来。我们得看看手里还有什么牌，然后果断地打出去。车里那个人的脸，你能发誓认得出来吗？”
段.en: “There is no object in our following them,” said Holmes. “The shadow has departed and will not return. We must see what further cards we have in our hands and play them with decision. Could you swear to that man’s face within the cab?”

段.文: “我只能发誓认得那把胡子。”
段.en: “I could swear only to the beard.”

段.文: “我也一样——由此我推断，那胡子十有八九是假的。一个聪明人干这么微妙的差事，留胡子只有一个用处：遮住自己的相貌。进来，华生！”
段.en: “And so could I—from which I gather that in all probability it was a false one. A clever man upon so delicate an errand has no use for a beard save to conceal his features. Come in here, Watson!”

段.文: 他拐进了一家送信公司，经理热情地招呼了他。
段.en: He turned into one of the district messenger offices, where he was warmly greeted by the manager.

段.文: “啊，威尔逊，看来你还没忘记那件小案子，那次我有幸帮了你一把？”
段.en: “Ah, Wilson, I see you have not forgotten the little case in which I had the good fortune to help you?”

段.文: “没忘，先生，当然没忘。您保住了我的名声，说不定还保住了我的命。”
段.en: “No, sir, indeed I have not. You saved my good name, and perhaps my life.”

段.文: “老兄，你言重了。威尔逊，我记得你手下的孩子里有个叫卡特赖特的，在那次调查中表现得挺能干。”
段.en: “My dear fellow, you exaggerate. I have some recollection, Wilson, that you had among your boys a lad named Cartwright, who showed some ability during the investigation.”

段.文: “是的，先生，他还在我们这儿。”
段.en: “Yes, sir, he is still with us.”

段.文: “能叫他来一下吗？——谢谢！另外，请帮我把这张五镑的钞票换开。”
段.en: “Could you ring him up?—thank you! And I should be glad to have change of this five-pound note.”

段.文: 一个十四岁的小伙子应经理的召唤来了，一张脸聪明伶俐。他站在那里，满怀崇敬地望着这位大名鼎鼎的侦探。
段.en: A lad of fourteen, with a bright, keen face, had obeyed the summons of the manager. He stood now gazing with great reverence at the famous detective.

段.文: “把《旅馆名录》给我。”福尔摩斯说，“谢谢！好，卡特赖特，这里有二十三家旅馆的名字，都在查令十字附近。看见了吗？”
段.en: “Let me have the Hotel Directory,” said Holmes. “Thank you! Now, Cartwright, there are the names of twenty-three hotels here, all in the immediate neighbourhood of Charing Cross. Do you see?”

段.文: “看见了，先生。”
段.en: “Yes, sir.”

段.文: “你要一家一家去。”
段.en: “You will visit each of these in turn.”

段.文: “是，先生。”
段.en: “Yes, sir.”

段.文: “每到一家，你先给门外的看门人一先令。这里是二十三先令。”
段.en: “You will begin in each case by giving the outside porter one shilling. Here are twenty-three shillings.”

段.文: “是，先生。”
段.en: “Yes, sir.”

段.文: “你跟他说，你要看看昨天的废纸。就说有一封重要的电报送错了，你正在找。明白吗？”
段.en: “You will tell him that you want to see the waste-paper of yesterday. You will say that an important telegram has miscarried and that you are looking for it. You understand?”

段.文: “明白，先生。”
段.en: “Yes, sir.”

段.文: “可你真正要找的，是一张《泰晤士报》的中间版，上面有几个用剪刀剪出来的洞。这是一份《泰晤士报》，就是这一版。你很容易认出来，对吧？”
段.en: “But what you are really looking for is the centre page of the Times with some holes cut in it with scissors. Here is a copy of the Times. It is this page. You could easily recognize it, could you not?”

段.文: “对，先生。”
段.en: “Yes, sir.”

段.文: “每一家门外的看门人都会去叫门厅的门房来，你也给他一先令。这里又是二十三先令。然后你很可能会发现，二十三家里有二十家，前一天的废纸已经烧掉或运走了。另外三家会给你看一堆废纸，你就在里面找《泰晤士报》的这一版。找到的可能性非常小。这里另外多给你十先令，以备急用。傍晚之前，给贝克街发个电报，告诉我结果。好了，华生，现在只剩下用电报查明2704号马车夫的身份，然后我们去邦德街的哪家画廊逛逛，打发时间，等到点再去旅馆。”
段.en: “In each case the outside porter will send for the hall porter, to whom also you will give a shilling. Here are twenty-three shillings. You will then learn in possibly twenty cases out of the twenty-three that the waste of the day before has been burned or removed. In the three other cases you will be shown a heap of paper and you will look for this page of the Times among it. The odds are enormously against your finding it. There are ten shillings over in case of emergencies. Let me have a report by wire at Baker Street before evening. And now, Watson, it only remains for us to find out by wire the identity of the cabman, No. 2704, and then we will drop into one of the Bond Street picture galleries and fill in the time until we are due at the hotel.”

段.文: 夏洛克·福尔摩斯有一种非常了不起的本领：想把心思从一件事上抽开，就能抽开。整整两个钟头，我们卷进去的那件怪事他好像全忘了，一心一意地欣赏比利时现代名家的画。从我们离开画廊，一直到走进诺森伯兰旅馆，他除了艺术什么也不谈——尽管他对艺术的见解粗浅得很。
段.en: Sherlock Holmes had, in a very remarkable degree, the power of detaching his mind at will. For two hours the strange business in which we had been involved appeared to be forgotten, and he was entirely absorbed in the pictures of the modern Belgian masters. He would talk of nothing but art, of which he had the crudest ideas, from our leaving the gallery until we found ourselves at the Northumberland Hotel.

段.文: “亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士在楼上等您。”旅馆职员说，“他吩咐过，您一来就马上领您上去。”
段.en: “Sir Henry Baskerville is upstairs expecting you,” said the clerk. “He asked me to show you up at once when you came.”

段.文: “我看看你们的旅客登记簿，你不介意吧？”福尔摩斯说。
段.en: “Have you any objection to my looking at your register?” said Holmes.

段.文: “一点也不介意。”
段.en: “Not in the least.”

段.文: 登记簿上，巴斯克维尔的名字后面又添了两个名字。一个是纽卡斯尔的西奥菲勒斯·约翰逊及家人；另一个是奥尔顿海洛奇的奥尔德莫尔太太及女仆。
段.en: The book showed that two names had been added after that of Baskerville. One was Theophilus Johnson and family, of Newcastle; the other Mrs. Oldmore and maid, of High Lodge, Alton.

段.文: “这一定就是我从前认识的那个约翰逊。”福尔摩斯对门房说，“是个律师，对吧？头发灰白，走路有点瘸？”
段.en: “Surely that must be the same Johnson whom I used to know,” said Holmes to the porter. “A lawyer, is he not, grey-headed, and walks with a limp?”

段.文: “不是，先生，这位约翰逊先生是煤矿老板，精神头很足，年纪不比您大。”
段.en: “No, sir, this is Mr. Johnson, the coal-owner, a very active gentleman, not older than yourself.”

段.文: “你肯定没把他的职业弄错吧？”
段.en: “Surely you are mistaken about his trade?”

段.文: “没弄错，先生！他在我们旅馆住了好多年了，我们都很熟。”
段.en: “No, sir! he has used this hotel for many years, and he is very well known to us.”

段.文: “啊，那就没错了。还有奥尔德莫尔太太，这名字我好像也有印象。请原谅我好奇，不过拜访一个朋友时，常常会碰上另一个朋友。”
段.en: “Ah, that settles it. Mrs. Oldmore, too; I seem to remember the name. Excuse my curiosity, but often in calling upon one friend one finds another.”

段.文: “她是位身体不好的太太，先生。她丈夫当过格洛斯特市长。她每次进城都住我们这里。”
段.en: “She is an invalid lady, sir. Her husband was once mayor of Gloucester. She always comes to us when she is in town.”

段.文: “谢谢。恐怕我不能说认识她。华生，这几个问题让我们弄清了一个非常重要的事实。”我们一起上楼时，他压低声音接着说，“我们现在知道，那些对我们的朋友这么感兴趣的人，并没有住进他住的这家旅馆。这就是说，我们已经看到，他们非常急于监视他，可他们同样急于不让他看见自己。这个事实很能说明问题。”
段.en: “Thank you; I am afraid I cannot claim her acquaintance. We have established a most important fact by these questions, Watson,” he continued in a low voice as we went upstairs together. “We know now that the people who are so interested in our friend have not settled down in his own hotel. That means that while they are, as we have seen, very anxious to watch him, they are equally anxious that he should not see them. Now, this is a most suggestive fact.”

段.文: “说明什么？”
段.en: “What does it suggest?”

段.文: “说明——哎呀，老兄，到底出什么事了？”
段.en: “It suggests—halloa, my dear fellow, what on earth is the matter?”

段.文: 我们刚拐过楼梯顶，就和亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士本人撞了个正着。他气得满脸通红，一只手里拿着一只又旧又脏的靴子。他气得话都说不利索了，等他终于开口，口音比早上我们听到的重得多，西部腔浓得多。
段.en: As we came round the top of the stairs we had run up against Sir Henry Baskerville himself. His face was flushed with anger, and he held an old and dusty boot in one of his hands. So furious was he that he was hardly articulate, and when he did speak it was in a much broader and more Western dialect than any which we had heard from him in the morning.

段.文: “我看这家旅馆是把我当傻瓜耍了。”他嚷道，“他们要是不当心，就会发现自己惹错人了。天哪，那家伙要是找不到我丢的靴子，可有他好看的。福尔摩斯先生，开玩笑我比谁都开得起，可这回他们有点过分了。”
段.en: “Seems to me they are playing me for a sucker in this hotel,” he cried. “They’ll find they’ve started in to monkey with the wrong man unless they are careful. By thunder, if that chap can’t find my missing boot there will be trouble. I can take a joke with the best, Mr. Holmes, but they’ve got a bit over the mark this time.”

段.文: “还在找您的靴子？”
段.en: “Still looking for your boot?”

段.文: “是的，先生，而且非找到不可。”
段.en: “Yes, sir, and mean to find it.”

段.文: “可是，您不是说那是一只新的棕色靴子吗？”
段.en: “But, surely, you said that it was a new brown boot?”

段.文: “是啊，先生。可现在丢的是一只旧的黑靴子。”
段.en: “So it was, sir. And now it’s an old black one.”

段.文: “什么！您是说——？”
段.en: “What! you don’t mean to say—?”

段.文: “我正是这个意思。我一共就三双靴子——新的棕色那双，旧的黑色那双，还有我脚上穿的这双漆皮的。昨晚他们拿走了我一只棕色的，今天又偷偷摸走了一只黑色的。喂，找到没有？说话呀，伙计，别光站着发愣！”
段.en: “That’s just what I do mean to say. I only had three pairs in the world—the new brown, the old black, and the patent leathers, which I am wearing. Last night they took one of my brown ones, and today they have sneaked one of the black. Well, have you got it? Speak out, man, and don’t stand staring!”

段.文: 一个慌慌张张的德国侍者出现了。
段.en: An agitated German waiter had appeared upon the scene.

段.文: “没有，先生。整个旅馆我都问遍了，一点消息也没有。”
段.en: “No, sir; I have made inquiry all over the hotel, but I can hear no word of it.”

段.文: “好，要么天黑之前把靴子还回来，要么我就去找经理，告诉他我马上搬出这家旅馆。”
段.en: “Well, either that boot comes back before sundown or I’ll see the manager and tell him that I go right straight out of this hotel.”

段.文: “会找到的，先生——我向您保证，只要您稍微耐心一点，一定会找到的。”
段.en: “It shall be found, sir—I promise you that if you will have a little patience it will be found.”

段.文: “最好是这样，在这个贼窝里，我可不能再丢东西了。好了，好了，福尔摩斯先生，这点小事也来烦您，请您见谅——”
段.en: “Mind it is, for it’s the last thing of mine that I’ll lose in this den of thieves. Well, well, Mr. Holmes, you’ll excuse my troubling you about such a trifle—”

段.文: “我认为这件事很值得一烦。”
段.en: “I think it’s well worth troubling about.”

段.文: “咦，您看起来挺当回事的。”
段.en: “Why, you look very serious over it.”

段.文: “您怎么解释这件事？”
段.en: “How do you explain it?”

段.文: “我压根儿没打算解释。这真是我碰到过的最疯狂、最古怪的事。”
段.en: “I just don’t attempt to explain it. It seems the very maddest, queerest thing that ever happened to me.”

段.文: “最古怪，也许是——”福尔摩斯若有所思地说。
段.en: “The queerest perhaps—” said Holmes thoughtfully.

段.文: “您自己怎么看？”
段.en: “What do you make of it yourself?”

段.文: “嗯，我还不敢说已经弄明白了。亨利爵士，您这个案子非常复杂。要是和您伯父的死联系起来看，我经手过的五百件重大案子里，我都不敢说有哪一件牵涉得这么深。不过我们手里已经握着好几条线索，很可能其中总有一条会把我们引向真相。我们也许会沿着错的那条白白浪费时间，但迟早会找到对的那条。”
段.en: “Well, I don’t profess to understand it yet. This case of yours is very complex, Sir Henry. When taken in conjunction with your uncle’s death I am not sure that of all the five hundred cases of capital importance which I have handled there is one which cuts so deep. But we hold several threads in our hands, and the odds are that one or other of them guides us to the truth. We may waste time in following the wrong one, but sooner or later we must come upon the right.”

段.文: 我们愉快地吃了午饭，席间很少谈起让我们聚到一起的那件事。饭后我们去了私人起居室，福尔摩斯在那里问巴斯克维尔打算怎么办。
段.en: We had a pleasant luncheon in which little was said of the business which had brought us together. It was in the private sitting-room to which we afterwards repaired that Holmes asked Baskerville what were his intentions.

段.文: “去巴斯克维尔庄园。”
段.en: “To go to Baskerville Hall.”

段.文: “什么时候？”
段.en: “And when?”

段.文: “这个周末。”
段.en: “At the end of the week.”

段.文: “总的来说，”福尔摩斯说，“我认为您的决定是明智的。我有充分的证据表明，您在伦敦一直被人跟踪。在这座几百万人的大城市里，很难查出这些人是谁，目的又是什么。如果他们存心不良，就可能伤害您，而我们没办法阻止。莫蒂默医生，您不知道今天早上您从我家出来以后，一直有人跟着吧？”
段.en: “On the whole,” said Holmes, “I think that your decision is a wise one. I have ample evidence that you are being dogged in London, and amid the millions of this great city it is difficult to discover who these people are or what their object can be. If their intentions are evil they might do you a mischief, and we should be powerless to prevent it. You did not know, Dr. Mortimer, that you were followed this morning from my house?”

段.文: 莫蒂默医生吓了一大跳。“跟着！谁？”
段.en: Dr. Mortimer started violently. “Followed! By whom?”

段.文: “可惜，这一点我没法告诉您。在达特穆尔，您的邻居或熟人当中，有没有谁留着一大把黑胡子？”
段.en: “That, unfortunately, is what I cannot tell you. Have you among your neighbours or acquaintances on Dartmoor any man with a black, full beard?”

段.文: “没有——等等，让我想想——哦，有的。查尔斯爵士的管家巴里摩尔，就留着一大把黑胡子。”
段.en: “No—or, let me see—why, yes. Barrymore, Sir Charles’s butler, is a man with a full, black beard.”

段.文: “哈！巴里摩尔在哪儿？”
段.en: “Ha! Where is Barrymore?”

段.文: “他在照管庄园。”
段.en: “He is in charge of the Hall.”

段.文: “我们最好查清楚，他是不是真在那里，会不会有可能在伦敦。”
段.en: “We had best ascertain if he is really there, or if by any possibility he might be in London.”

段.文: “怎么查呢？”
段.en: “How can you do that?”

段.文: “给我一张电报纸。‘迎接亨利爵士的一切都准备好了吗？’这就行了。收报人：巴斯克维尔庄园，巴里摩尔先生。最近的电报局在哪儿？格林彭。很好，我们再给格林彭的邮政局长发一封：‘致巴里摩尔先生的电报须交本人亲收。如本人不在，请回电诺森伯兰旅馆亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士。’这样，天黑之前我们就能知道巴里摩尔到底在不在德文郡守着他的岗位。”
段.en: “Give me a telegraph form. ‘Is all ready for Sir Henry?’ That will do. Address to Mr. Barrymore, Baskerville Hall. What is the nearest telegraph-office? Grimpen. Very good, we will send a second wire to the postmaster, Grimpen: ‘Telegram to Mr. Barrymore to be delivered into his own hand. If absent, please return wire to Sir Henry Baskerville, Northumberland Hotel.’ That should let us know before evening whether Barrymore is at his post in Devonshire or not.”

段.文: “是这样。”巴斯克维尔说，“对了，莫蒂默医生，这个巴里摩尔到底是什么人？”
段.en: “That’s so,” said Baskerville. “By the way, Dr. Mortimer, who is this Barrymore, anyhow?”

段.文: “他是老看守人的儿子，老看守人已经去世了。他们家照管庄园到现在已经四代了。据我所知，他们夫妇俩在全郡都算得上是最正派的一对。”
段.en: “He is the son of the old caretaker, who is dead. They have looked after the Hall for four generations now. So far as I know, he and his wife are as respectable a couple as any in the county.”

段.文: “不过，”巴斯克维尔说，“很清楚，只要庄园里没有家族的人住，这两口子就住着一座好房子，又什么事都不用干。”
段.en: “At the same time,” said Baskerville, “it’s clear enough that so long as there are none of the family at the Hall these people have a mighty fine home and nothing to do.”

段.文: “这倒是真的。”
段.en: “That is true.”

段.文: “查尔斯爵士的遗嘱里，巴里摩尔得到什么好处没有？”福尔摩斯问。
段.en: “Did Barrymore profit at all by Sir Charles’s will?” asked Holmes.

段.文: “他和他妻子各得了五百镑。”
段.en: “He and his wife had five hundred pounds each.”

段.文: “哈！他们事先知道会得到这笔钱吗？”
段.en: “Ha! Did they know that they would receive this?”

段.文: “知道。查尔斯爵士很爱谈他遗嘱里的安排。”
段.en: “Yes; Sir Charles was very fond of talking about the provisions of his will.”

段.文: “这很有意思。”
段.en: “That is very interesting.”

段.文: “我希望，”莫蒂默医生说，“您不会怀疑每一个从查尔斯爵士那里得到遗产的人，因为他也给我留了一千镑。”
段.en: “I hope,” said Dr. Mortimer, “that you do not look with suspicious eyes upon everyone who received a legacy from Sir Charles, for I also had a thousand pounds left to me.”

段.文: “是吗！还有别人吗？”
段.en: “Indeed! And anyone else?”

段.文: “有很多给个人的小额款项，还捐给了许多公共慈善机构。剩下的全归亨利爵士。”
段.en: “There were many insignificant sums to individuals, and a large number of public charities. The residue all went to Sir Henry.”

段.文: “剩下的有多少？”
段.en: “And how much was the residue?”

段.文: “七十四万镑。”
段.en: “Seven hundred and forty thousand pounds.”

段.文: 福尔摩斯惊讶地扬起眉毛。“我没想到涉及的金额这么巨大。”他说。
段.en: Holmes raised his eyebrows in surprise. “I had no idea that so gigantic a sum was involved,” said he.

段.文: “查尔斯爵士素有富名，可直到我们清点他的证券，才知道他富到了什么程度。全部财产的总值将近一百万镑。”
段.en: “Sir Charles had the reputation of being rich, but we did not know how very rich he was until we came to examine his securities. The total value of the estate was close on to a million.”

段.文: “天哪！为了这么大一笔赌注，一个人很可能会孤注一掷。还有一个问题，莫蒂默医生。假如我们这位年轻的朋友出了什么事——请原谅我做这种不愉快的假设！——谁会继承这份财产？”
段.en: “Dear me! It is a stake for which a man might well play a desperate game. And one more question, Dr. Mortimer. Supposing that anything happened to our young friend here—you will forgive the unpleasant hypothesis!—who would inherit the estate?”

段.文: “查尔斯爵士的弟弟罗杰·巴斯克维尔没结婚就死了，所以财产会传给德斯蒙德家，他们是远房表亲。詹姆斯·德斯蒙德是威斯特摩兰的一位老牧师。”
段.en: “Since Rodger Baskerville, Sir Charles’s younger brother died unmarried, the estate would descend to the Desmonds, who are distant cousins. James Desmond is an elderly clergyman in Westmoreland.”

段.文: “谢谢。这些细节都很有意思。您见过詹姆斯·德斯蒙德先生吗？”
段.en: “Thank you. These details are all of great interest. Have you met Mr. James Desmond?”

段.文: “见过。他有一次来拜访查尔斯爵士。他相貌庄重，生活像圣徒一样清白。我记得查尔斯爵士一再要给他一笔钱，他却怎么也不肯收。”
段.en: “Yes; he once came down to visit Sir Charles. He is a man of venerable appearance and of saintly life. I remember that he refused to accept any settlement from Sir Charles, though he pressed it upon him.”

段.文: “这位清心寡欲的人，就会成为查尔斯爵士这几十万家产的继承人了。”
段.en: “And this man of simple tastes would be the heir to Sir Charles’s thousands.”

段.文: “他会继承地产，因为地产是限定继承的。他也会继承钱，除非现在的主人另立遗嘱。当然，钱怎么处置，现在的主人想怎样就怎样。”
段.en: “He would be the heir to the estate because that is entailed. He would also be the heir to the money unless it were willed otherwise by the present owner, who can, of course, do what he likes with it.”

段.文: “您立过遗嘱吗，亨利爵士？”
段.en: “And have you made your will, Sir Henry?”

段.文: “没有，福尔摩斯先生，还没有。我没时间，昨天我才弄清楚情况。不过不管怎样，我觉得钱应该跟着爵位和地产走。我可怜的伯父也是这么想的。主人要是没有足够的钱维持这份产业，怎么恢复巴斯克维尔家族的荣光呢？房子、土地和钱，必须放在一起。”
段.en: “No, Mr. Holmes, I have not. I’ve had no time, for it was only yesterday that I learned how matters stood. But in any case I feel that the money should go with the title and estate. That was my poor uncle’s idea. How is the owner going to restore the glories of the Baskervilles if he has not money enough to keep up the property? House, land, and dollars must go together.”

段.文: “说得对。好吧，亨利爵士，您应该马上去德文郡，这一点我和您想法一致。只有一个条件，我必须提出来：您绝对不能一个人去。”
段.en: “Quite so. Well, Sir Henry, I am of one mind with you as to the advisability of your going down to Devonshire without delay. There is only one provision which I must make. You certainly must not go alone.”

段.文: “莫蒂默医生和我一起回去。”
段.en: “Dr. Mortimer returns with me.”

段.文: “可莫蒂默医生要给人看病，他家离您家又有好几英里。就算他一片好心，也可能帮不上您。不行，亨利爵士，您得带上一个人，一个靠得住的人，时时刻刻待在您身边。”
段.en: “But Dr. Mortimer has his practice to attend to, and his house is miles away from yours. With all the goodwill in the world he may be unable to help you. No, Sir Henry, you must take with you someone, a trusty man, who will be always by your side.”

段.文: “福尔摩斯先生，您本人能来吗？”
段.en: “Is it possible that you could come yourself, Mr. Holmes?”

段.文: “如果事情到了紧要关头，我会尽量亲自到场。不过您也能理解，我的咨询业务很多，各方面的求助又源源不断，我不可能无限期地离开伦敦。眼下，英国一个最受尊敬的名字正被一个敲诈者抹黑，只有我能阻止一场灾难性的丑闻。您看得出来，我是不可能去达特穆尔的。”
段.en: “If matters came to a crisis I should endeavour to be present in person; but you can understand that, with my extensive consulting practice and with the constant appeals which reach me from many quarters, it is impossible for me to be absent from London for an indefinite time. At the present instant one of the most revered names in England is being besmirched by a blackmailer, and only I can stop a disastrous scandal. You will see how impossible it is for me to go to Dartmoor.”

段.文: “那您推荐谁呢？”
段.en: “Whom would you recommend, then?”

段.文: 福尔摩斯把手放在我的胳膊上。“如果我的朋友肯接下这件事，那么在您遇到困境时，没有谁比他更值得陪在您身边了。这话没人能比我说得更有把握。”
段.en: Holmes laid his hand upon my arm. “If my friend would undertake it there is no man who is better worth having at your side when you are in a tight place. No one can say so more confidently than I.”

段.文: 这个提议完全出乎我的意料。我还没来得及回答，巴斯克维尔就抓住我的手，热情地使劲握着。
段.en: The proposition took me completely by surprise, but before I had time to answer, Baskerville seized me by the hand and wrung it heartily.

段.文: “哎呀，您真是太好了，华生医生。”他说，“我的处境您都看到了，这件事您知道的和我一样多。要是您肯去巴斯克维尔庄园，帮我渡过这一关，我一辈子都不会忘记。”
段.en: “Well, now, that is real kind of you, Dr. Watson,” said he. “You see how it is with me, and you know just as much about the matter as I do. If you will come down to Baskerville Hall and see me through I’ll never forget it.”

段.文: 冒险的前景对我向来很有吸引力。福尔摩斯的那番话，还有准男爵那样热切地要我做伴，也让我感到很荣幸。
段.en: The promise of adventure had always a fascination for me, and I was complimented by the words of Holmes and by the eagerness with which the baronet hailed me as a companion.

段.文: “我很乐意去。”我说，“我想不出还有什么更好的办法打发我的时间。”
段.en: “I will come, with pleasure,” said I. “I do not know how I could employ my time better.”

段.文: “你要非常仔细地向我报告。”福尔摩斯说，“紧要关头一定会来，到时候我会指点你怎么做。我想，到星期六一切都能准备好吧？”
段.en: “And you will report very carefully to me,” said Holmes. “When a crisis comes, as it will do, I will direct how you shall act. I suppose that by Saturday all might be ready?”

段.文: “华生医生方便吗？”
段.en: “Would that suit Dr. Watson?”

段.文: “完全方便。”
段.en: “Perfectly.”

段.文: “那么星期六，除非另有通知，我们就在帕丁顿车站十点半那班火车上碰头。”
段.en: “Then on Saturday, unless you hear to the contrary, we shall meet at the ten-thirty train from Paddington.”

段.文: 我们起身要走，巴斯克维尔忽然得意地叫了一声，一头扎进房间的一个角落，从柜子底下拽出一只棕色靴子。
段.en: We had risen to depart when Baskerville gave a cry of triumph, and diving into one of the corners of the room he drew a brown boot from under a cabinet.

段.文: “我丢的靴子！”他叫道。
段.en: “My missing boot!” he cried.

段.文: “但愿我们所有的难题都能这么轻易地消失！”夏洛克·福尔摩斯说。
段.en: “May all our difficulties vanish as easily!” said Sherlock Holmes.

段.文: “可这件事很奇怪，”莫蒂默医生说，“午饭前我仔细搜过这个房间。”
段.en: “But it is a very singular thing,” Dr. Mortimer remarked. “I searched this room carefully before lunch.”

段.文: “我也搜过，”巴斯克维尔说，“每一寸都搜过。”
段.en: “And so did I,” said Baskerville. “Every inch of it.”

段.文: “那时候屋里肯定没有靴子。”
段.en: “There was certainly no boot in it then.”

段.文: “这么说，一定是我们吃午饭的时候，侍者把它放在那儿的。”
段.en: “In that case the waiter must have placed it there while we were lunching.”

段.文: 那个德国侍者被叫了来，可他说自己什么也不知道，怎么查问也查不清楚。一连串接连发生、似乎毫无目的的小谜团里，又多了一件。撇开查尔斯爵士之死那整个阴森的故事不谈，短短两天之内，就出了一连串无法解释的事：收到那封用印刷字拼成的信，双轮马车里那个黑胡子密探，新的棕色靴子丢了，旧的黑靴子丢了，现在新的棕色靴子又回来了。坐马车回贝克街的路上，福尔摩斯一言不发。看他紧皱的眉头和专注的神情，我知道他和我一样，正在苦苦思索，想找出一个框架，把这些奇怪的、看似毫不相干的事件都装进去。整个下午直到深夜，他都坐在那里，沉浸在烟雾和思考里。
段.en: The German was sent for but professed to know nothing of the matter, nor could any inquiry clear it up. Another item had been added to that constant and apparently purposeless series of small mysteries which had succeeded each other so rapidly. Setting aside the whole grim story of Sir Charles’s death, we had a line of inexplicable incidents all within the limits of two days, which included the receipt of the printed letter, the black-bearded spy in the hansom, the loss of the new brown boot, the loss of the old black boot, and now the return of the new brown boot. Holmes sat in silence in the cab as we drove back to Baker Street, and I knew from his drawn brows and keen face that his mind, like my own, was busy in endeavouring to frame some scheme into which all these strange and apparently disconnected episodes could be fitted. All afternoon and late into the evening he sat lost in tobacco and thought.

段.文: 快吃晚饭的时候，送来了两封电报。第一封写的是：
段.en: Just before dinner two telegrams were handed in. The first ran:

段.文: 刚得知巴里摩尔在庄园。巴斯克维尔。
段.en: Have just heard that Barrymore is at the Hall. BASKERVILLE.

段.文: 第二封：
段.en: The second:

段.文: 已按吩咐走访二十三家旅馆，很抱歉，未能找到剪过的《泰晤士报》。卡特赖特。
段.en: Visited twenty-three hotels as directed, but sorry to report unable to trace cut sheet of Times. CARTWRIGHT.

段.文: “我的两条线索断了，华生。没有什么比处处碰壁的案子更让人来劲了。我们得四处找找别的气味。”
段.en: “There go two of my threads, Watson. There is nothing more stimulating than a case where everything goes against you. We must cast round for another scent.”

段.文: “我们还有那个给密探赶车的车夫。”
段.en: “We have still the cabman who drove the spy.”

段.文: “正是。我已经发电报给官方登记处，要他的姓名和住址。如果这就是答复，我一点也不奇怪。”
段.en: “Exactly. I have wired to get his name and address from the Official Registry. I should not be surprised if this were an answer to my question.”

段.文: 可是门铃声带来的东西比答复还要令人满意。门开了，进来一个粗里粗气的家伙，显然就是车夫本人。
段.en: The ring at the bell proved to be something even more satisfactory than an answer, however, for the door opened and a rough-looking fellow entered who was evidently the man himself.

段.文: “总公司给我捎了个信，说这个地址有位先生在打听2704号。”他说，“我赶车七年了，从没被人投诉过一句。我从车行直接过来，想当面问问您，我到底哪儿得罪您了。”
段.en: “I got a message from the head office that a gent at this address had been inquiring for No. 2704,” said he. “I’ve driven my cab this seven years and never a word of complaint. I came here straight from the Yard to ask you to your face what you had against me.”

段.文: “我对你一点意见也没有，伙计。”福尔摩斯说，“恰恰相反，只要你把我的问题回答清楚，我还要给你半镑金币。”
段.en: “I have nothing in the world against you, my good man,” said Holmes. “On the contrary, I have half a sovereign for you if you will give me a clear answer to my questions.”

段.文: “哟，今天我可真走运。”车夫咧嘴笑着说，“您想问什么，先生？”
段.en: “Well, I’ve had a good day and no mistake,” said the cabman with a grin. “What was it you wanted to ask, sir?”

段.文: “首先，你的姓名和住址，以防我还要找你。”
段.en: “First of all your name and address, in case I want you again.”

段.文: “约翰·克莱顿，博罗区特皮街3号。我的马车停在滑铁卢车站附近的希普利车行。”
段.en: “John Clayton, 3 Turpey Street, the Borough. My cab is out of Shipley’s Yard, near Waterloo Station.”

段.文: 夏洛克·福尔摩斯把它记了下来。
段.en: Sherlock Holmes made a note of it.

段.文: “好，克莱顿，今天早上十点钟有个乘客来监视这所房子，后来又跟着两位先生顺着摄政街走了。把他的事全告诉我。”
段.en: “Now, Clayton, tell me all about the fare who came and watched this house at ten o’clock this morning and afterwards followed the two gentlemen down Regent Street.”

段.文: 车夫显得很惊讶，还有点不好意思。“哎呀，我跟您说也没什么用，您好像已经知道得跟我一样多了。”他说，“说实话，那位先生告诉我他是侦探，叫我对谁也别提他的事。”
段.en: The man looked surprised and a little embarrassed. “Why, there’s no good my telling you things, for you seem to know as much as I do already,” said he. “The truth is that the gentleman told me that he was a detective and that I was to say nothing about him to anyone.”

段.文: “伙计，这件事非常严重。你要是想对我隐瞒什么，可能会把自己弄得很狼狈。你说你的乘客告诉你，他是侦探？”
段.en: “My good fellow; this is a very serious business, and you may find yourself in a pretty bad position if you try to hide anything from me. You say that your fare told you that he was a detective?”

段.文: “是的，他是这么说的。”
段.en: “Yes, he did.”

段.文: “他什么时候说的？”
段.en: “When did he say this?”

段.文: “他下车的时候。”
段.en: “When he left me.”

段.文: “他还说了别的吗？”
段.en: “Did he say anything more?”

段.文: “他说了他的名字。”
段.en: “He mentioned his name.”

段.文: 福尔摩斯得意地飞快瞥了我一眼。“哦，他说了名字，是吗？这可不够谨慎。他说的名字是什么？”
段.en: Holmes cast a swift glance of triumph at me. “Oh, he mentioned his name, did he? That was imprudent. What was the name that he mentioned?”

段.文: “他的名字，”车夫说，“叫夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生。”
段.en: “His name,” said the cabman, “was Mr. Sherlock Holmes.”

段.文: 我从没见过我的朋友像听到车夫这句回答时那样措手不及。有那么一会儿，他坐在那里，惊得说不出话。接着，他放声大笑起来。
段.en: Never have I seen my friend more completely taken aback than by the cabman’s reply. For an instant he sat in silent amazement. Then he burst into a hearty laugh.

段.文: “一剑刺中，华生——不得不承认，刺中了！”他说，“我遇上了一把和我自己一样快、一样灵活的剑。这一下他刺得真漂亮。这么说，他叫夏洛克·福尔摩斯，是吗？”
段.en: “A touch, Watson—an undeniable touch!” said he. “I feel a foil as quick and supple as my own. He got home upon me very prettily that time. So his name was Sherlock Holmes, was it?”

段.文: “是的，先生，那位先生就叫这个名字。”
段.en: “Yes, sir, that was the gentleman’s name.”

段.文: “好极了！告诉我你是在哪儿让他上车的，还有后来发生的一切。”
段.en: “Excellent! Tell me where you picked him up and all that occurred.”

段.文: “九点半，他在特拉法尔加广场叫住了我。他说他是侦探，只要我一整天完全照他的吩咐办，什么也不问，他就给我两个几尼。我当然乐意答应。我们先去了诺森伯兰旅馆，在那儿等着，直到两位先生出来，在车站叫了辆马车。我们跟着他们的车，一直到它在这附近什么地方停下。”
段.en: “He hailed me at half-past nine in Trafalgar Square. He said that he was a detective, and he offered me two guineas if I would do exactly what he wanted all day and ask no questions. I was glad enough to agree. First we drove down to the Northumberland Hotel and waited there until two gentlemen came out and took a cab from the rank. We followed their cab until it pulled up somewhere near here.”

段.文: “就是这扇门口。”福尔摩斯说。
段.en: “This very door,” said Holmes.

段.文: “这个嘛，我说不准，不过我敢说我的乘客心里一清二楚。我们在这条街中段停下，等了一个半钟头。后来那两位先生走着从我们旁边经过，我们就跟着，顺着贝克街走，又沿着——”
段.en: “Well, I couldn’t be sure of that, but I dare say my fare knew all about it. We pulled up halfway down the street and waited an hour and a half. Then the two gentlemen passed us, walking, and we followed down Baker Street and along—”

段.文: “我知道。”福尔摩斯说。
段.en: “I know,” said Holmes.

段.文: “一直走到摄政街的四分之三处。这时我那位先生掀开车顶小窗，叫我拼命往滑铁卢车站赶。我抽了母马几鞭子，不到十分钟就到了。他很大方，付了两个几尼，就进车站去了。只是在走的时候，他转过身来说：‘你也许会有兴趣知道，你今天拉的是夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生。’我就是这么知道这个名字的。”
段.en: “Until we got three-quarters down Regent Street. Then my gentleman threw up the trap, and he cried that I should drive right away to Waterloo Station as hard as I could go. I whipped up the mare and we were there under the ten minutes. Then he paid up his two guineas, like a good one, and away he went into the station. Only just as he was leaving he turned round and he said: ‘It might interest you to know that you have been driving Mr. Sherlock Holmes.’ That’s how I come to know the name.”

段.文: “明白了。后来你再也没见过他？”
段.en: “I see. And you saw no more of him?”

段.文: “他进了车站以后就没见过了。”
段.en: “Not after he went into the station.”

段.文: “那你说说，这位夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生长什么样？”
段.en: “And how would you describe Mr. Sherlock Holmes?”

段.文: 车夫挠了挠头。“嗯，这位先生可不太好形容。我看他有四十岁，中等个子，比您矮两三英寸，先生。他穿得很阔气，留着黑胡子，下面剪得方方正正，脸色苍白。别的我就说不上来了。”
段.en: The cabman scratched his head. “Well, he wasn’t altogether such an easy gentleman to describe. I’d put him at forty years of age, and he was of a middle height, two or three inches shorter than you, sir. He was dressed like a toff, and he had a black beard, cut square at the end, and a pale face. I don’t know as I could say more than that.”

段.文: “眼睛什么颜色？”
段.en: “Colour of his eyes?”

段.文: “这个我说不上来。”
段.en: “No, I can’t say that.”

段.文: “别的还记得什么吗？”
段.en: “Nothing more that you can remember?”

段.文: “没有了，先生，什么也没有了。”
段.en: “No, sir; nothing.”

段.文: “好吧，这是给你的半镑金币。你要是能再带来什么消息，还有一枚等着你。晚安！”
段.en: “Well, then, here is your half-sovereign. There’s another one waiting for you if you can bring any more information. Good-night!”

段.文: “晚安，先生，谢谢您！”
段.en: “Good-night, sir, and thank you!”

段.文: 约翰·克莱顿咯咯笑着走了。福尔摩斯转向我，耸耸肩，苦笑了一下。
段.en: John Clayton departed chuckling, and Holmes turned to me with a shrug of his shoulders and a rueful smile.

段.文: “第三条线索也断了，我们又回到了起点。”他说，“这个狡猾的流氓！他知道我们的门牌号，知道亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士来找过我，在摄政街认出了我，猜到我记下了车号、会找到车夫，于是就送回来这么一句大胆的话。我告诉你，华生，这一回我们碰上了一个配得上和我们较量的对手。我在伦敦被将死了。我只能祝你在德文郡运气好些。不过我心里不踏实。”
段.en: “Snap goes our third thread, and we end where we began,” said he. “The cunning rascal! He knew our number, knew that Sir Henry Baskerville had consulted me, spotted who I was in Regent Street, conjectured that I had got the number of the cab and would lay my hands on the driver, and so sent back this audacious message. I tell you, Watson, this time we have got a foeman who is worthy of our steel. I’ve been checkmated in London. I can only wish you better luck in Devonshire. But I’m not easy in my mind about it.”

段.文: “对什么不踏实？”
段.en: “About what?”

段.文: “对派你去这件事。华生，这件事很险恶，又险恶又危险，我越看越不喜欢。是的，老兄，你可以笑我，但我向你保证，等你平平安安回到贝克街，我会非常高兴的。”
段.en: “About sending you. It’s an ugly business, Watson, an ugly dangerous business, and the more I see of it the less I like it. Yes, my dear fellow, you may laugh, but I give you my word that I shall be very glad to have you back safe and sound in Baker Street once more.”

段.文: 到了约定的那天，亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士和莫蒂默医生都准备好了，我们按计划动身前往德文郡。夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生和我一起坐车去车站，临别前又给了我最后的嘱咐和建议。
段.en: Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Mortimer were ready upon the appointed day, and we started as arranged for Devonshire. Mr. Sherlock Holmes drove with me to the station and gave me his last parting injunctions and advice.

段.文: “华生，我不想提出什么理论或怀疑，免得让你先入为主。”他说，“我只希望你把事实尽可能详细地报告给我，推理的事交给我就行。”
段.en: “I will not bias your mind by suggesting theories or suspicions, Watson,” said he; “I wish you simply to report facts in the fullest possible manner to me, and you can leave me to do the theorizing.”

段.文: “什么样的事实？”我问。
段.en: “What sort of facts?” I asked.

段.文: “凡是看起来和案子有关的事，哪怕关系再间接都行。尤其是年轻的巴斯克维尔和邻居们的关系，还有查尔斯爵士之死的任何新细节。这几天我自己也做了些调查，可恐怕没什么结果。只有一件事似乎可以肯定：下一位继承人詹姆斯·德斯蒙德先生是一位性情非常和善的老先生，这番迫害不会是他搞的。我真觉得可以把他完全排除在外。剩下的，就是在荒原上实际围在亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士身边的那些人了。”
段.en: “Anything which may seem to have a bearing however indirect upon the case, and especially the relations between young Baskerville and his neighbours or any fresh particulars concerning the death of Sir Charles. I have made some inquiries myself in the last few days, but the results have, I fear, been negative. One thing only appears to be certain, and that is that Mr. James Desmond, who is the next heir, is an elderly gentleman of a very amiable disposition, so that this persecution does not arise from him. I really think that we may eliminate him entirely from our calculations. There remain the people who will actually surround Sir Henry Baskerville upon the moor.”

段.文: “首先把巴里摩尔夫妇打发走，不是更好吗？”
段.en: “Would it not be well in the first place to get rid of this Barrymore couple?”

段.文: “千万不要。那会是你犯的最大错误。如果他们是清白的，这样做就太冤枉人、太残忍了；如果他们有罪，我们就再也没机会给他们定罪了。不，不，我们要把他们留在嫌疑人名单上。另外，我没记错的话，庄园里还有一个马夫。还有两个荒原上的农夫。还有我们的朋友莫蒂默医生，我相信他完全诚实；还有他的妻子，我们对她一无所知。还有那个博物学者斯台普顿，以及他的妹妹，据说是位迷人的年轻小姐。还有拉夫特庄园的弗兰克兰先生，他也是个未知数。另外还有一两位邻居。这些人你都要特别仔细地研究。”
段.en: “By no means. You could not make a greater mistake. If they are innocent it would be a cruel injustice, and if they are guilty we should be giving up all chance of bringing it home to them. No, no, we will preserve them upon our list of suspects. Then there is a groom at the Hall, if I remember right. There are two moorland farmers. There is our friend Dr. Mortimer, whom I believe to be entirely honest, and there is his wife, of whom we know nothing. There is this naturalist, Stapleton, and there is his sister, who is said to be a young lady of attractions. There is Mr. Frankland, of Lafter Hall, who is also an unknown factor, and there are one or two other neighbours. These are the folk who must be your very special study.”

段.文: “我会尽力的。”
段.en: “I will do my best.”

段.文: “我想你带了武器吧？”
段.en: “You have arms, I suppose?”

段.文: “带了，我想还是带上的好。”
段.en: “Yes, I thought it as well to take them.”

段.文: “当然要带。把左轮手枪日夜放在身边，一刻也不要放松警惕。”
段.en: “Most certainly. Keep your revolver near you night and day, and never relax your precautions.”

段.文: 我们的朋友已经订好了一节头等车厢，正在站台上等我们。
段.en: Our friends had already secured a first-class carriage and were waiting for us upon the platform.

段.文: “没有，什么消息也没有。”莫蒂默医生回答我朋友的问题，“有一点我可以发誓：这两天没人跟踪我们。我们每次出门都严加留意，谁也逃不过我们的眼睛。”
段.en: “No, we have no news of any kind,” said Dr. Mortimer in answer to my friend’s questions. “I can swear to one thing, and that is that we have not been shadowed during the last two days. We have never gone out without keeping a sharp watch, and no one could have escaped our notice.”

段.文: “我想你们一直在一起吧？”
段.en: “You have always kept together, I presume?”

段.文: “除了昨天下午。我每次进城，通常都留出一天专门消遣，所以昨天下午我去了外科医学会的博物馆。”
段.en: “Except yesterday afternoon. I usually give up one day to pure amusement when I come to town, so I spent it at the Museum of the College of Surgeons.”

段.文: “我去公园看人了。”巴斯克维尔说。
段.en: “And I went to look at the folk in the park,” said Baskerville.

段.文: “不过我们什么麻烦也没碰上。”
段.en: “But we had no trouble of any kind.”

段.文: “可还是太大意了。”福尔摩斯摇着头，神情非常严肃，“亨利爵士，我求您别一个人到处走。不然您会遭大难的。您另一只靴子找到了吗？”
段.en: “It was imprudent, all the same,” said Holmes, shaking his head and looking very grave. “I beg, Sir Henry, that you will not go about alone. Some great misfortune will befall you if you do. Did you get your other boot?”

段.文: “没有，先生，再也找不回来了。”
段.en: “No, sir, it is gone forever.”

段.文: “是吗。这很有意思。好了，再见。”火车开始沿着站台缓缓滑动，他又说，“亨利爵士，请记住莫蒂默医生给我们念的那个古怪的老传说里的一句话：在邪恶势力猖獗的黑夜里，不要走上荒原。”
段.en: “Indeed. That is very interesting. Well, good-bye,” he added as the train began to glide down the platform. “Bear in mind, Sir Henry, one of the phrases in that queer old legend which Dr. Mortimer has read to us, and avoid the moor in those hours of darkness when the powers of evil are exalted.”

段.文: 火车把站台远远甩在身后时，我回头望去，看见福尔摩斯高高的、严峻的身影一动不动地站在那里，目送着我们。
段.en: I looked back at the platform when we had left it far behind and saw the tall, austere figure of Holmes standing motionless and gazing after us.

段.文: 旅途又快又愉快。我一路上和两位旅伴熟络起来，还逗着莫蒂默医生的长毛垂耳猎犬玩。没过几个钟头，褐色的土地变成了红色，砖房变成了花岗岩房子，红色的牛在篱笆整齐的田里吃草。那里青草茂盛，草木葱茏，说明这里的气候更温润，虽然也更潮湿。年轻的巴斯克维尔热切地望着窗外，认出德文郡风景里熟悉的样子时，高兴得大声叫起来。
段.en: The journey was a swift and pleasant one, and I spent it in making the more intimate acquaintance of my two companions and in playing with Dr. Mortimer’s spaniel. In a very few hours the brown earth had become ruddy, the brick had changed to granite, and red cows grazed in well-hedged fields where the lush grasses and more luxuriant vegetation spoke of a richer, if a damper, climate. Young Baskerville stared eagerly out of the window and cried aloud with delight as he recognized the familiar features of the Devon scenery.

段.文: “华生医生，离开这儿以后，我走过世界上不少地方，”他说，“可从没见过哪儿能比得上这里。”
段.en: “I’ve been over a good part of the world since I left it, Dr. Watson,” said he; “but I have never seen a place to compare with it.”

段.文: “我从没见过哪个德文郡人不夸自己家乡的。”我说。
段.en: “I never saw a Devonshire man who did not swear by his county,” I remarked.

段.文: “这既取决于郡，也同样取决于人的血统。”莫蒂默医生说，“看看我们这位朋友，就能看出他长着凯尔特人的圆脑袋，里面装着凯尔特人的热情和依恋之心。可怜的查尔斯爵士的头型就非常少见，特征一半是盖尔人的，一半是伊弗尼亚人的。不过，您上次见到巴斯克维尔庄园的时候还很小，对吧？”
段.en: “It depends upon the breed of men quite as much as on the county,” said Dr. Mortimer. “A glance at our friend here reveals the rounded head of the Celt, which carries inside it the Celtic enthusiasm and power of attachment. Poor Sir Charles’s head was of a very rare type, half Gaelic, half Ivernian in its characteristics. But you were very young when you last saw Baskerville Hall, were you not?”

段.文: “我父亲去世时，我才十几岁，那时我还从没见过庄园，因为他住在南海岸的一座小屋里。后来我直接去了美洲，投奔一个朋友。我跟您说，这一切对我和对华生医生一样新鲜。我特别想看看荒原。”
段.en: “I was a boy in my teens at the time of my father’s death and had never seen the Hall, for he lived in a little cottage on the South Coast. Thence I went straight to a friend in America. I tell you it is all as new to me as it is to Dr. Watson, and I’m as keen as possible to see the moor.”

段.文: “是吗？那您的愿望很容易满足，因为您第一眼就能看到荒原了。”莫蒂默医生指着车窗外说。
段.en: “Are you? Then your wish is easily granted, for there is your first sight of the moor,” said Dr. Mortimer, pointing out of the carriage window.

段.文: 越过一块块绿色的田地和一片低低起伏的树林，远处升起一座灰暗、阴郁的山，山顶参差古怪，远远望去模模糊糊，就像梦里的奇幻风景。巴斯克维尔坐在那里，久久地盯着它。从他急切的脸上，我看得出这第一眼对他有多么重要——在那个奇异的地方，他的祖辈统治了那么久，留下了那么深的印记。他就坐在那里，穿着花呢西装，一口美国口音，待在一节平淡无奇的火车车厢角落里。可是，当我看着他那张黝黑而富于表情的脸，我比任何时候都更强烈地感到，他确实是那一长串血统高贵、性情火爆、生来就要发号施令的人的真正后裔。他浓密的眉毛、敏感的鼻翼、一双大大的淡褐色眼睛里，都透着骄傲、勇敢和力量。如果在那片令人生畏的荒原上，等着我们的是一场艰难而危险的追查，那么至少有这样一位同伴，你可以放心为他冒险，并且确信他会勇敢地和你同担。
段.en: Over the green squares of the fields and the low curve of a wood there rose in the distance a grey, melancholy hill, with a strange jagged summit, dim and vague in the distance, like some fantastic landscape in a dream. Baskerville sat for a long time, his eyes fixed upon it, and I read upon his eager face how much it meant to him, this first sight of that strange spot where the men of his blood had held sway so long and left their mark so deep. There he sat, with his tweed suit and his American accent, in the corner of a prosaic railway-carriage, and yet as I looked at his dark and expressive face I felt more than ever how true a descendant he was of that long line of high-blooded, fiery, and masterful men. There were pride, valour, and strength in his thick brows, his sensitive nostrils, and his large hazel eyes. If on that forbidding moor a difficult and dangerous quest should lie before us, this was at least a comrade for whom one might venture to take a risk with the certainty that he would bravely share it.

段.文: 火车在路边一个小站停下，我们都下了车。站外，低矮的白栅栏那边，一辆四轮游览马车已经套好两匹矮脚马在等着。我们的到来显然是件大事，站长和脚夫们都围上来帮我们搬行李。这是个可爱、朴素的乡间小站，可我惊讶地发现，大门边站着两个军人模样的人，穿着深色制服，倚着短步枪，在我们走过时用锐利的目光打量我们。车夫是个面相冷硬、身材矮小、骨节粗大的家伙，他向亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士行了个礼。几分钟后，我们就沿着宽阔的白色大路飞驰而去。道路两旁，起伏的牧场向上延伸，古老的山墙房屋从浓密的绿叶间露出来。可是在这片洒满阳光的宁静乡野后面，始终耸立着荒原那道漫长而阴沉的曲线，在暮色里黑沉沉的，中间点缀着参差不齐、阴森可怕的山丘。
段.en: The train pulled up at a small wayside station and we all descended. Outside, beyond the low, white fence, a wagonette with a pair of cobs was waiting. Our coming was evidently a great event, for station-master and porters clustered round us to carry out our luggage. It was a sweet, simple country spot, but I was surprised to observe that by the gate there stood two soldierly men in dark uniforms who leaned upon their short rifles and glanced keenly at us as we passed. The coachman, a hard-faced, gnarled little fellow, saluted Sir Henry Baskerville, and in a few minutes we were flying swiftly down the broad, white road. Rolling pasture lands curved upward on either side of us, and old gabled houses peeped out from amid the thick green foliage, but behind the peaceful and sunlit countryside there rose ever, dark against the evening sky, the long, gloomy curve of the moor, broken by the jagged and sinister hills.

段.文: 马车拐上一条岔路，我们沿着深深的小路盘旋而上。这些小路被几百年的车轮碾得很深，两边是高高的土坡，上面长满了湿漉漉的青苔和肥厚的鹿舌蕨。渐渐变成古铜色的蕨菜和斑驳的荆棘，在落日的余晖里闪着光。我们一路稳稳地往上走，过了一座窄窄的花岗岩桥，又沿着一条喧闹的溪流前进。溪水湍急地奔流而下，在灰色的巨石间翻着白沫，哗哗作响。路和溪水一起蜿蜒穿过一道山谷，谷里长满了矮栎树和冷杉。每到一个转弯，巴斯克维尔都会高兴地惊叹一声，急切地四处张望，问个没完。在他眼里，一切都很美，可在我看来，这片乡野笼罩着一层忧郁，处处清清楚楚地带着秋残岁暮的印记。黄叶铺满了小路，我们经过时，又纷纷飘落到我们身上。马车驶过一堆堆腐烂的落叶，车轮的辘辘声也消失了——在我看来，这是大自然抛在巴斯克维尔家族归来的继承人车前的一份凄凉的礼物。
段.en: The wagonette swung round into a side road, and we curved upward through deep lanes worn by centuries of wheels, high banks on either side, heavy with dripping moss and fleshy hart’s-tongue ferns. Bronzing bracken and mottled bramble gleamed in the light of the sinking sun. Still steadily rising, we passed over a narrow granite bridge and skirted a noisy stream which gushed swiftly down, foaming and roaring amid the grey boulders. Both road and stream wound up through a valley dense with scrub oak and fir. At every turn Baskerville gave an exclamation of delight, looking eagerly about him and asking countless questions. To his eyes all seemed beautiful, but to me a tinge of melancholy lay upon the countryside, which bore so clearly the mark of the waning year. Yellow leaves carpeted the lanes and fluttered down upon us as we passed. The rattle of our wheels died away as we drove through drifts of rotting vegetation—sad gifts, as it seemed to me, for Nature to throw before the carriage of the returning heir of the Baskervilles.

段.文: “哎呀！”莫蒂默医生叫道，“这是怎么回事？”
段.en: “Halloa!” cried Dr. Mortimer, “what is this?”

段.文: 我们面前是一片陡峭的、长满石南的坡地，那是荒原伸出来的一道山梁。坡顶上，一个骑马的士兵轮廓分明，就像基座上的一座骑马雕像。他黑沉沉的，神情严峻，步枪平端在前臂上，随时准备开火。他在监视我们走的这条路。
段.en: A steep curve of heath-clad land, an outlying spur of the moor, lay in front of us. On the summit, hard and clear like an equestrian statue upon its pedestal, was a mounted soldier, dark and stern, his rifle poised ready over his forearm. He was watching the road along which we travelled.

段.文: “这是怎么回事，珀金斯？”莫蒂默医生问。
段.en: “What is this, Perkins?” asked Dr. Mortimer.

段.文: 车夫在座位上半转过身来。“普林斯敦有个囚犯逃出来了，先生。已经逃了三天了，看守们守着每一条路、每一个车站，可到现在还没见到他的影子。这附近的农夫都很不安，先生，这是实话。”
段.en: Our driver half turned in his seat. “There’s a convict escaped from Princetown, sir. He’s been out three days now, and the warders watch every road and every station, but they’ve had no sight of him yet. The farmers about here don’t like it, sir, and that’s a fact.”

段.文: “嗯，我听说谁要是能提供消息，就能得五镑赏钱。”
段.en: “Well, I understand that they get five pounds if they can give information.”

段.文: “是的，先生，可是比起被人割断喉咙的危险，有机会得五镑又算得了什么。您知道，这可不是一般的囚犯。这个人什么事都干得出来。”
段.en: “Yes, sir, but the chance of five pounds is but a poor thing compared to the chance of having your throat cut. You see, it isn’t like any ordinary convict. This is a man that would stick at nothing.”

段.文: “那他是谁？”
段.en: “Who is he, then?”

段.文: “是塞尔登，诺丁山那个杀人犯。”
段.en: “It is Selden, the Notting Hill murderer.”

段.文: 我对那个案子记得很清楚。罪行异常凶残，凶手的一举一动都残暴得毫无人性，福尔摩斯因此对它很感兴趣。他的行为实在太残暴，人们怀疑他神志是否完全正常，所以他的死刑才被减了刑。我们的马车爬上了一道坡，眼前展现出一大片辽阔的荒原，上面散布着嶙峋的石堆和突岩。一阵寒风从那里扫下来，吹得我们直打哆嗦。就在那片荒凉的原野上，某个地方，这个恶魔一样的人正潜伏着，像野兽一样躲在洞里，心里充满了对整个抛弃了他的人类的恶毒仇恨。有了这一点，那片不毛之地、刺骨的寒风和渐渐昏暗的天空所带来的阴森之感，就更完整了。连巴斯克维尔也沉默下来，把大衣裹得更紧了。
段.en: I remembered the case well, for it was one in which Holmes had taken an interest on account of the peculiar ferocity of the crime and the wanton brutality which had marked all the actions of the assassin. The commutation of his death sentence had been due to some doubts as to his complete sanity, so atrocious was his conduct. Our wagonette had topped a rise and in front of us rose the huge expanse of the moor, mottled with gnarled and craggy cairns and tors. A cold wind swept down from it and set us shivering. Somewhere there, on that desolate plain, was lurking this fiendish man, hiding in a burrow like a wild beast, his heart full of malignancy against the whole race which had cast him out. It needed but this to complete the grim suggestiveness of the barren waste, the chilling wind, and the darkling sky. Even Baskerville fell silent and pulled his overcoat more closely around him.

段.文: 我们已经把肥沃的田野抛在身后、留在下面了。这时我们回头望去，西沉的太阳斜照过来，把溪流染成一条条金线，照亮了刚被犁翻过的红土和大片纠缠的林地。前面的路越来越荒凉、越来越蛮野，穿过一道道巨大的赤褐色和橄榄色的山坡，坡上散落着一块块巨石。我们不时经过一间荒原上的农舍，墙和屋顶都是石头的，没有一根藤蔓来柔化它生硬的轮廓。忽然，我们俯视着一处杯子形状的洼地，里面零零星星长着矮小的栎树和冷杉，它们被多年的狂风暴雨吹得扭曲变形。两座又高又窄的塔楼耸立在树梢之上。车夫用鞭子指了指。
段.en: We had left the fertile country behind and beneath us. We looked back on it now, the slanting rays of a low sun turning the streams to threads of gold and glowing on the red earth new turned by the plough and the broad tangle of the woodlands. The road in front of us grew bleaker and wilder over huge russet and olive slopes, sprinkled with giant boulders. Now and then we passed a moorland cottage, walled and roofed with stone, with no creeper to break its harsh outline. Suddenly we looked down into a cuplike depression, patched with stunted oaks and firs which had been twisted and bent by the fury of years of storm. Two high, narrow towers rose over the trees. The driver pointed with his whip.

段.文: “巴斯克维尔庄园。”他说。
段.en: “Baskerville Hall,” said he.

段.文: 庄园的主人已经站了起来，两颊通红，眼睛发亮，凝神望着。几分钟后，我们来到了门房的大门前。大门是熟铁铸的，花纹繁复奇特，两边的柱子饱经风雨，长满了斑斑点点的地衣，柱顶是巴斯克维尔家族的野猪头。门房已成了一片废墟，只剩下黑色的花岗岩和光秃秃的椽子。它对面是一座新房子，才盖了一半，那是查尔斯爵士用南非的金子结出的第一个果实。
段.en: Its master had risen and was staring with flushed cheeks and shining eyes. A few minutes later we had reached the lodge-gates, a maze of fantastic tracery in wrought iron, with weather-bitten pillars on either side, blotched with lichens, and surmounted by the boars’ heads of the Baskervilles. The lodge was a ruin of black granite and bared ribs of rafters, but facing it was a new building, half constructed, the first fruit of Sir Charles’s South African gold.

段.文: 穿过大门，我们驶上林荫道。车轮又一次在落叶中悄无声息，老树的枝条在我们头顶交织成一条阴暗的隧道。巴斯克维尔望着这条长长的、黑黝黝的车道，看到尽头那座宅子像幽灵一样隐隐发光，不由得打了个寒战。
段.en: Through the gateway we passed into the avenue, where the wheels were again hushed amid the leaves, and the old trees shot their branches in a sombre tunnel over our heads. Baskerville shuddered as he looked up the long, dark drive to where the house glimmered like a ghost at the farther end.

段.文: “就是在这里吗？”他低声问。
段.en: “Was it here?” he asked in a low voice.

段.文: “不，不是，紫杉小径在另一边。”
段.en: “No, no, the yew alley is on the other side.”

段.文: 年轻的继承人阴沉着脸四下看了看。
段.en: The young heir glanced round with a gloomy face.

段.文: “难怪我伯父住在这种地方，会觉得要大祸临头。”他说，“谁都会被吓着的。不出六个月，我就要在这儿装上一排电灯。到时候，大门口亮着一千烛光的斯旺和爱迪生电灯，你们就认不出这地方了。”
段.en: “It’s no wonder my uncle felt as if trouble were coming on him in such a place as this,” said he. “It’s enough to scare any man. I’ll have a row of electric lamps up here inside of six months, and you won’t know it again, with a thousand candle-power Swan and Edison right here in front of the hall door.”

段.文: 林荫道尽头是一大片开阔的草坪，宅子就在我们眼前。在渐暗的天光里，我看见宅子中央是一座厚重的主楼，前面伸出一道门廊。整个正面爬满了常春藤，只在窗户或族徽露出来的地方，东一块西一块地剪掉了，在这层黑色的帷幕上开出口子。主楼上耸立着两座古老的塔楼，顶上筑着城垛，墙上开着许多射击孔。塔楼左右两边，是较新的黑色花岗岩侧翼。沉重的竖框窗里透出昏暗的灯光，陡峭的高屋顶上竖着高高的烟囱，其中一根冒出一股黑烟。
段.en: The avenue opened into a broad expanse of turf, and the house lay before us. In the fading light I could see that the centre was a heavy block of building from which a porch projected. The whole front was draped in ivy, with a patch clipped bare here and there where a window or a coat of arms broke through the dark veil. From this central block rose the twin towers, ancient, crenelated, and pierced with many loopholes. To right and left of the turrets were more modern wings of black granite. A dull light shone through heavy mullioned windows, and from the high chimneys which rose from the steep, high-angled roof there sprang a single black column of smoke.

段.文: “欢迎您，亨利爵士！欢迎来到巴斯克维尔庄园！”
段.en: “Welcome, Sir Henry! Welcome to Baskerville Hall!”

段.文: 一个高个子男人从门廊的阴影里走出来，打开了马车门。门厅黄色的灯光映出一个女人的身影。她走出来，帮那男人把我们的包递下来。
段.en: A tall man had stepped from the shadow of the porch to open the door of the wagonette. The figure of a woman was silhouetted against the yellow light of the hall. She came out and helped the man to hand down our bags.

段.文: “亨利爵士，我直接回家，您不介意吧？”莫蒂默医生说，“我妻子在等我。”
段.en: “You don’t mind my driving straight home, Sir Henry?” said Dr. Mortimer. “My wife is expecting me.”

段.文: “您不留下来吃顿晚饭吗？”
段.en: “Surely you will stay and have some dinner?”

段.文: “不了，我得走了。家里大概有活儿等着我。我本想留下来带您看看宅子，不过巴里摩尔会是比我更好的向导。再见。只要用得着我，不管白天黑夜，千万别犹豫，派人来叫我。”
段.en: “No, I must go. I shall probably find some work awaiting me. I would stay to show you over the house, but Barrymore will be a better guide than I. Good-bye, and never hesitate night or day to send for me if I can be of service.”

段.文: 车轮声沿着车道渐渐远去，亨利爵士和我转身走进门厅，大门在我们身后沉重地哐当一声关上了。这是一间很气派的大厅，宽敞，高大，屋顶架着一根根巨大的橡木梁，年深日久，已经变黑了。老式的大壁炉里，高高的铁柴架后面，木柴烧得噼啪作响。我们坐了这么久的车，都冻僵了，亨利爵士和我便伸手去烤火。然后我们环顾四周：高而窄的老式彩色玻璃窗，橡木护墙板，鹿头，墙上的族徽，在中央那盏灯柔和的光线下，一切都显得昏暗而阴沉。
段.en: The wheels died away down the drive while Sir Henry and I turned into the hall, and the door clanged heavily behind us. It was a fine apartment in which we found ourselves, large, lofty, and heavily raftered with huge baulks of age-blackened oak. In the great old-fashioned fireplace behind the high iron dogs a log-fire crackled and snapped. Sir Henry and I held out our hands to it, for we were numb from our long drive. Then we gazed round us at the high, thin window of old stained glass, the oak panelling, the stags’ heads, the coats of arms upon the walls, all dim and sombre in the subdued light of the central lamp.

段.文: “跟我想象的一模一样。”亨利爵士说，“这不正是一座古老家族宅邸的样子吗？想想看，五百年来，我的祖辈就住在这同一座大厅里。一想到这个，我就感到肃然起敬。”
段.en: “It’s just as I imagined it,” said Sir Henry. “Is it not the very picture of an old family home? To think that this should be the same hall in which for five hundred years my people have lived. It strikes me solemn to think of it.”

段.文: 他环顾四周，我看见他黝黑的脸上焕发出孩子般的热情。灯光照在他站着的地方，可长长的影子沿着墙壁垂下来，像一顶黑色的华盖悬在他头上。巴里摩尔把我们的行李送进房间，回来了。这时他站在我们面前，举止恭谨，是个训练有素的仆人。他的相貌很引人注目，高个子，长得英俊，留着方方正正的黑胡子，脸色苍白，五官很有气度。
段.en: I saw his dark face lit up with a boyish enthusiasm as he gazed about him. The light beat upon him where he stood, but long shadows trailed down the walls and hung like a black canopy above him. Barrymore had returned from taking our luggage to our rooms. He stood in front of us now with the subdued manner of a well-trained servant. He was a remarkable-looking man, tall, handsome, with a square black beard and pale, distinguished features.

段.文: “您想现在就开晚饭吗，先生？”
段.en: “Would you wish dinner to be served at once, sir?”

段.文: “准备好了吗？”
段.en: “Is it ready?”

段.文: “再过几分钟就好，先生。您房间里有热水。亨利爵士，在您重新做好安排之前，我和我妻子很乐意留下来伺候您。不过您也明白，在新的情况下，这所宅子需要相当多的仆人。”
段.en: “In a very few minutes, sir. You will find hot water in your rooms. My wife and I will be happy, Sir Henry, to stay with you until you have made your fresh arrangements, but you will understand that under the new conditions this house will require a considerable staff.”

段.文: “什么新的情况？”
段.en: “What new conditions?”

段.文: “我只是说，先生，查尔斯爵士过的是隐居生活，我们两个就能照顾好他的起居。您自然会希望多些交际，所以家里需要做些调整。”
段.en: “I only meant, sir, that Sir Charles led a very retired life, and we were able to look after his wants. You would, naturally, wish to have more company, and so you will need changes in your household.”

段.文: “你是说，你和你妻子想走？”
段.en: “Do you mean that your wife and you wish to leave?”

段.文: “只等您完全方便的时候，先生。”
段.en: “Only when it is quite convenient to you, sir.”

段.文: “可你们家已经跟着我们好几代了，不是吗？我一来就断了这么一段老交情，我会很遗憾的。”
段.en: “But your family have been with us for several generations, have they not? I should be sorry to begin my life here by breaking an old family connection.”

段.文: 我好像在管家苍白的脸上看到了一丝激动。
段.en: I seemed to discern some signs of emotion upon the butler’s white face.

段.文: “我也这么觉得，先生，我妻子也是。可是说实话，先生，我们俩都非常爱戴查尔斯爵士。他的死让我们受了很大的打击，这里的一切都让我们非常难过。恐怕我们在巴斯克维尔庄园再也不会安心了。”
段.en: “I feel that also, sir, and so does my wife. But to tell the truth, sir, we were both very much attached to Sir Charles, and his death gave us a shock and made these surroundings very painful to us. I fear that we shall never again be easy in our minds at Baskerville Hall.”

段.文: “那你们打算做什么？”
段.en: “But what do you intend to do?”

段.文: “先生，我相信我们能做点小生意，自己立足。查尔斯爵士很慷慨，给了我们这么做的本钱。好了，先生，我还是先带您去您的房间吧。”
段.en: “I have no doubt, sir, that we shall succeed in establishing ourselves in some business. Sir Charles’s generosity has given us the means to do so. And now, sir, perhaps I had best show you to your rooms.”

段.文: 古老大厅的上方，围着一圈方形的回廊，装着栏杆，有两道楼梯通上去。从这个中心点，两条长长的走廊贯穿整座建筑，所有卧室都朝走廊开门。我的房间和巴斯克维尔的在同一侧，差不多就在隔壁。这些房间比宅子的中央部分新得多，明亮的墙纸和许多蜡烛，多少冲淡了我们刚到时留在我心里的阴沉印象。
段.en: A square balustraded gallery ran round the top of the old hall, approached by a double stair. From this central point two long corridors extended the whole length of the building, from which all the bedrooms opened. My own was in the same wing as Baskerville’s and almost next door to it. These rooms appeared to be much more modern than the central part of the house, and the bright paper and numerous candles did something to remove the sombre impression which our arrival had left upon my mind.

段.文: 可是，从大厅通出去的餐厅却是个阴影重重、阴森沉闷的地方。那是一间长长的屋子，有一级台阶把屋子分成两部分：高处是主人一家坐的，低处留给他们的仆从。屋子一头有一道乐师廊台俯临下方。头顶上，黑色的横梁纵横交错，横梁上方是被烟熏黑的天花板。要是点起一排排熊熊的火把，再有旧时宴会的五光十色和粗豪欢闹，这里也许会柔和一些。可现在，只有两位穿黑衣的绅士坐在一盏带罩的灯投下的一小圈光里，人说话不由得放低了声音，心情也变得压抑。一排模模糊糊的祖先画像，衣着五花八门，从伊丽莎白时代的骑士到摄政时期的花花公子，都从墙上俯视着我们，默默地陪着我们，叫人心里发怵。我们没怎么说话。至少我很高兴，饭总算吃完了，我们可以躲进那间新式的台球室，抽一支香烟。
段.en: But the dining-room which opened out of the hall was a place of shadow and gloom. It was a long chamber with a step separating the daïs where the family sat from the lower portion reserved for their dependents. At one end a minstrel’s gallery overlooked it. Black beams shot across above our heads, with a smoke-darkened ceiling beyond them. With rows of flaring torches to light it up, and the colour and rude hilarity of an old-time banquet, it might have softened; but now, when two black-clothed gentlemen sat in the little circle of light thrown by a shaded lamp, one’s voice became hushed and one’s spirit subdued. A dim line of ancestors, in every variety of dress, from the Elizabethan knight to the buck of the Regency, stared down upon us and daunted us by their silent company. We talked little, and I for one was glad when the meal was over and we were able to retire into the modern billiard-room and smoke a cigarette.

段.文: “说真的，这地方可不怎么让人高兴。”亨利爵士说，“我想人慢慢会习惯的，可眼下我觉得自己有点格格不入。我伯父要是一个人住在这样一座宅子里，难怪会变得有点神经兮兮的。好了，如果你不介意，我们今晚早点睡吧，也许到了早上，一切会显得愉快些。”
段.en: “My word, it isn’t a very cheerful place,” said Sir Henry. “I suppose one can tone down to it, but I feel a bit out of the picture at present. I don’t wonder that my uncle got a little jumpy if he lived all alone in such a house as this. However, if it suits you, we will retire early tonight, and perhaps things may seem more cheerful in the morning.”

段.文: 上床之前，我拉开窗帘，往窗外看了看。窗户正对着大门前的那片草地。草地那边，两丛树在渐起的风中摇摆，发出呜呜的声音。半个月亮从飞驰的云缝里钻了出来。借着清冷的月光，我看见树林那边有一排参差不齐的岩石，还有荒原那道又长又低的阴郁曲线。我拉上窗帘，觉得这最后的印象和之前的一切倒是很协调。
段.en: I drew aside my curtains before I went to bed and looked out from my window. It opened upon the grassy space which lay in front of the hall door. Beyond, two copses of trees moaned and swung in a rising wind. A half moon broke through the rifts of racing clouds. In its cold light I saw beyond the trees a broken fringe of rocks, and the long, low curve of the melancholy moor. I closed the curtain, feeling that my last impression was in keeping with the rest.

段.文: 可这还不完全是最后的印象。我觉得很累，却又睡不着，在床上辗转反侧，想睡又睡不着。远处有一座钟，每过一刻钟就敲一次，除此之外，这座古老的宅子里一片死寂。然后，就在深更半夜，突然有一个声音传进我耳朵里，清晰、响亮，绝不会听错。那是一个女人的抽泣声，是一个被无法抑制的悲伤撕扯着的人发出的、压抑而哽咽的喘息。我从床上坐起来，凝神细听。声音不可能离得很远，而且肯定是在宅子里。我每根神经都绷得紧紧的，等了半个钟头，可除了那座钟的报时声和墙上常春藤的沙沙声，再也没有别的声音了。
段.en: And yet it was not quite the last. I found myself weary and yet wakeful, tossing restlessly from side to side, seeking for the sleep which would not come. Far away a chiming clock struck out the quarters of the hours, but otherwise a deathly silence lay upon the old house. And then suddenly, in the very dead of the night, there came a sound to my ears, clear, resonant, and unmistakable. It was the sob of a woman, the muffled, strangling gasp of one who is torn by an uncontrollable sorrow. I sat up in bed and listened intently. The noise could not have been far away and was certainly in the house. For half an hour I waited with every nerve on the alert, but there came no other sound save the chiming clock and the rustle of the ivy on the wall.

章.标题: 梅里皮特宅的斯台普顿一家

段.文: 第二天早晨天气清新明媚，多少冲淡了巴斯克维尔庄园初次给我们俩留下的阴森灰暗的印象。亨利爵士和我坐下吃早饭时，阳光从高高的直棂窗里涌进来，窗上满是彩绘的纹章，在屋里投下一块块水汪汪的彩色光斑。深色的护墙板在金色的光线里像青铜一样发亮。很难相信，这就是昨天晚上让我们心头那么沉重的那间屋子。
段.en: The fresh beauty of the following morning did something to efface from our minds the grim and grey impression which had been left upon both of us by our first experience of Baskerville Hall. As Sir Henry and I sat at breakfast the sunlight flooded in through the high mullioned windows, throwing watery patches of colour from the coats of arms which covered them. The dark panelling glowed like bronze in the golden rays, and it was hard to realise that this was indeed the chamber which had struck such a gloom into our souls upon the evening before.

段.文: “我看该怪的是咱们自己，不是这房子！”准男爵说，“咱们一路坐车，又累又冷，所以把这地方看得灰溜溜的。现在精神养足了，一切就又显得挺愉快了。”
段.en: “I guess it is ourselves and not the house that we have to blame!” said the baronet. “We were tired with our journey and chilled by our drive, so we took a grey view of the place. Now we are fresh and well, so it is all cheerful once more.”

段.文: “不过也不全是心理作用，”我说，“比如说，夜里你有没有听见有人在哭？我觉得是个女人。”
段.en: “And yet it was not entirely a question of imagination,” I answered. “Did you, for example, happen to hear someone, a woman I think, sobbing in the night?”

段.文: “这就怪了，我迷迷糊糊快睡着的时候，好像也听见了这么个声音。我等了好一阵，没再听见，就以为是做梦。”
段.en: “That is curious, for I did when I was half asleep fancy that I heard something of the sort. I waited quite a time, but there was no more of it, so I concluded that it was all a dream.”

段.文: “我听得清清楚楚，敢肯定那确实是女人的哭声。”
段.en: “I heard it distinctly, and I am sure that it was really the sob of a woman.”

段.文: “这事得马上问问。”他摇铃把巴里摩尔叫来，问他能不能解释我们听到的声音。我觉得，管家听主人问话的时候，那张苍白的脸又白了几分。
段.en: “We must ask about this right away.” He rang the bell and asked Barrymore whether he could account for our experience. It seemed to me that the pallid features of the butler turned a shade paler still as he listened to his master’s question.

段.文: “亨利爵士，这房子里只有两个女人，”他答道，“一个是洗碗的女仆，睡在另一边的厢房。另一个是我妻子。我可以担保，那声音不会是她发出来的。”
段.en: “There are only two women in the house, Sir Henry,” he answered. “One is the scullery-maid, who sleeps in the other wing. The other is my wife, and I can answer for it that the sound could not have come from her.”

段.文: 可他这话是在撒谎。凑巧的是，早饭后我在长廊里碰见了巴里摩尔太太，阳光正照在她脸上。她是个高大的女人，五官粗重，神情木然，嘴角紧绷，显得很严厉。可她那双眼睛泄露了秘密：眼圈通红，从肿起的眼皮缝里瞟了我一眼。这么说，夜里哭的正是她。既然如此，她丈夫一定知道。可他偏偏冒着明摆着会被拆穿的风险，一口否认。他为什么要这样？她又为什么哭得那么伤心？这个脸色苍白、相貌英俊、留着黑胡子的男人身上，已经开始笼罩着一层神秘而阴郁的气氛。最先发现查尔斯爵士尸体的就是他；老人死前的种种情形，我们也只听过他一个人的说法。难道我们在摄政街那辆马车上看见的，归根到底就是巴里摩尔？胡子倒很可能是一样的。车夫说那人个子稍矮些，可这种印象很容易出错。我怎样才能把这一点彻底弄清楚？显然，第一步是去找格林彭的邮政局长，问问那封试探的电报是不是真的交到了巴里摩尔本人手里。不管答案如何，我至少有点东西可以向夏洛克·福尔摩斯汇报了。
段.en: And yet he lied as he said it, for it chanced that after breakfast I met Mrs. Barrymore in the long corridor with the sun full upon her face. She was a large, impassive, heavy-featured woman with a stern set expression of mouth. But her telltale eyes were red and glanced at me from between swollen lids. It was she, then, who wept in the night, and if she did so her husband must know it. Yet he had taken the obvious risk of discovery in declaring that it was not so. Why had he done this? And why did she weep so bitterly? Already round this pale-faced, handsome, black-bearded man there was gathering an atmosphere of mystery and of gloom. It was he who had been the first to discover the body of Sir Charles, and we had only his word for all the circumstances which led up to the old man’s death. Was it possible that it was Barrymore, after all, whom we had seen in the cab in Regent Street? The beard might well have been the same. The cabman had described a somewhat shorter man, but such an impression might easily have been erroneous. How could I settle the point forever? Obviously the first thing to do was to see the Grimpen postmaster and find whether the test telegram had really been placed in Barrymore’s own hands. Be the answer what it might, I should at least have something to report to Sherlock Holmes.

段.文: 早饭后，亨利爵士有一大堆文件要看，正好是我出门的好时机。我沿着荒原边上走了四英里，一路很惬意，最后来到一个灰扑扑的小村子。村里有两座比较大的房子，比别的房子高出一截，原来一座是客栈，一座是莫蒂默医生的家。邮政局长同时也是村里的杂货店老板，他对那封电报记得很清楚。
段.en: Sir Henry had numerous papers to examine after breakfast, so that the time was propitious for my excursion. It was a pleasant walk of four miles along the edge of the moor, leading me at last to a small grey hamlet, in which two larger buildings, which proved to be the inn and the house of Dr. Mortimer, stood high above the rest. The postmaster, who was also the village grocer, had a clear recollection of the telegram.

段.文: “当然，先生，”他说，“我完全照吩咐，叫人把电报送到了巴里摩尔先生手上。”
段.en: “Certainly, sir,” said he, “I had the telegram delivered to Mr. Barrymore exactly as directed.”

段.文: “谁送的？”
段.en: “Who delivered it?”

段.文: “我这孩子。詹姆斯，上星期你把那封电报送到庄园交给巴里摩尔先生了，是不是？”
段.en: “My boy here. James, you delivered that telegram to Mr. Barrymore at the Hall last week, did you not?”

段.文: “是的，爸爸，我送去了。”
段.en: “Yes, father, I delivered it.”

段.文: “交到他本人手里了吗？”我问。
段.en: “Into his own hands?” I asked.

段.文: “呃，他那会儿在阁楼上，所以我没法亲手交给他。不过我交给了巴里摩尔太太，她答应马上转交。”
段.en: “Well, he was up in the loft at the time, so that I could not put it into his own hands, but I gave it into Mrs. Barrymore’s hands, and she promised to deliver it at once.”

段.文: “你看见巴里摩尔先生了吗？”
段.en: “Did you see Mr. Barrymore?”

段.文: “没有，先生。我跟您说了，他在阁楼上。”
段.en: “No, sir; I tell you he was in the loft.”

段.文: “你既然没看见他，怎么知道他在阁楼上？”
段.en: “If you didn’t see him, how do you know he was in the loft?”

段.文: “哎，他自己的老婆总该知道他在哪儿吧，”邮政局长不耐烦地说，“难道他没收到电报？要是出了什么差错，也该由巴里摩尔先生自己来抱怨。”
段.en: “Well, surely his own wife ought to know where he is,” said the postmaster testily. “Didn’t he get the telegram? If there is any mistake it is for Mr. Barrymore himself to complain.”

段.文: 看来再追问下去也没用了。但有一点很清楚：尽管福尔摩斯用了计，我们还是没法证明巴里摩尔这段时间一直不在伦敦。假如他就在伦敦呢？假如最后见到活着的查尔斯爵士的人，和新继承人一回英格兰就跟踪他的人，是同一个人呢？那又说明什么？他是受人指使，还是自己另有什么阴谋？他迫害巴斯克维尔家族能有什么好处？我想起那封古怪的警告信，字是从《泰晤士报》社论上剪下来的。那是他干的吗？还是另有人一心要破坏他的计划？唯一说得通的动机，就是亨利爵士提过的那个：要是能把这家人吓跑，巴里摩尔夫妇就能一直舒舒服服地住下去。可是，这样的解释远远不足以说明眼前这个深沉而巧妙的阴谋——它就像一张看不见的网，正在年轻的准男爵四周慢慢收紧。福尔摩斯自己也说过，他经手过那么多轰动一时的案子，还没有哪一件比这件更复杂。我沿着那条灰暗冷清的路往回走，心里暗暗祈祷，盼我的朋友早点忙完手头的事，赶来这里，卸下压在我肩上的这副重担。
段.en: It seemed hopeless to pursue the inquiry any farther, but it was clear that in spite of Holmes’s ruse we had no proof that Barrymore had not been in London all the time. Suppose that it were so—suppose that the same man had been the last who had seen Sir Charles alive, and the first to dog the new heir when he returned to England. What then? Was he the agent of others or had he some sinister design of his own? What interest could he have in persecuting the Baskerville family? I thought of the strange warning clipped out of the leading article of the Times. Was that his work or was it possibly the doing of someone who was bent upon counteracting his schemes? The only conceivable motive was that which had been suggested by Sir Henry, that if the family could be scared away a comfortable and permanent home would be secured for the Barrymores. But surely such an explanation as that would be quite inadequate to account for the deep and subtle scheming which seemed to be weaving an invisible net round the young baronet. Holmes himself had said that no more complex case had come to him in all the long series of his sensational investigations. I prayed, as I walked back along the grey, lonely road, that my friend might soon be freed from his preoccupations and able to come down to take this heavy burden of responsibility from my shoulders.

段.文: 忽然，身后传来一阵奔跑的脚步声，还有人在喊我的名字，打断了我的思绪。我转过身，以为是莫蒂默医生，没想到追上来的是个陌生人。他个子不高，身材瘦削，胡子刮得干干净净，面容拘谨，淡黄色的头发，下巴瘦长，年纪在三十到四十岁之间，穿一身灰色衣服，戴着草帽。他肩上挎着一个装植物标本的铁皮盒子，一只手里拿着绿色的捕蝶网。
段.en: Suddenly my thoughts were interrupted by the sound of running feet behind me and by a voice which called me by name. I turned, expecting to see Dr. Mortimer, but to my surprise it was a stranger who was pursuing me. He was a small, slim, clean-shaven, prim-faced man, flaxen-haired and lean-jawed, between thirty and forty years of age, dressed in a grey suit and wearing a straw hat. A tin box for botanical specimens hung over his shoulder and he carried a green butterfly-net in one of his hands.

段.文: “华生医生，我这样冒昧，想必您会原谅，”他气喘吁吁地跑到我跟前，说道，“我们荒原上的人都随便惯了，用不着等别人正式介绍。您也许听我们共同的朋友莫蒂默提起过我。我是斯台普顿，住在梅里皮特宅。”
段.en: “You will, I am sure, excuse my presumption, Dr. Watson,” said he as he came panting up to where I stood. “Here on the moor we are homely folk and do not wait for formal introductions. You may possibly have heard my name from our mutual friend, Mortimer. I am Stapleton, of Merripit House.”

段.文: “看您的网和盒子，我也猜得出来，”我说，“因为我知道斯台普顿先生是位博物学家。可您怎么认得我？”
段.en: “Your net and box would have told me as much,” said I, “for I knew that Mr. Stapleton was a naturalist. But how did you know me?”

段.文: “我刚才去拜访莫蒂默，您从他诊所窗前经过，他指给我看了。我们正好同路，我想不如追上来自我介绍一下。亨利爵士一路上没累着吧？”
段.en: “I have been calling on Mortimer, and he pointed you out to me from the window of his surgery as you passed. As our road lay the same way I thought that I would overtake you and introduce myself. I trust that Sir Henry is none the worse for his journey?”

段.文: “他很好，谢谢。”
段.en: “He is very well, thank you.”

段.文: “查尔斯爵士不幸去世以后，我们都有点担心新来的准男爵不肯住在这儿。要一个有钱人到这种地方来隐居，确实是强人所难。不过不用我说您也知道，这对周围一带关系太大了。我想，亨利爵士对这件事没有什么迷信的顾虑吧？”
段.en: “We were all rather afraid that after the sad death of Sir Charles the new baronet might refuse to live here. It is asking much of a wealthy man to come down and bury himself in a place of this kind, but I need not tell you that it means a very great deal to the countryside. Sir Henry has, I suppose, no superstitious fears in the matter?”

段.文: “我看不大会有。”
段.en: “I do not think that it is likely.”

段.文: “您当然知道那个缠着这家人的魔犬传说吧？”
段.en: “Of course you know the legend of the fiend dog which haunts the family?”

段.文: “听说过。”
段.en: “I have heard it.”

段.文: “这一带的乡下人真是轻信得出奇！好多人都敢赌咒发誓，说在荒原上见过那样一个怪物。”他说这话时带着笑，可我好像从他眼里看出，他把这件事看得更认真。“这个故事在查尔斯爵士的脑子里扎了根，我毫不怀疑，正是它导致了他的惨死。”
段.en: “It is extraordinary how credulous the peasants are about here! Any number of them are ready to swear that they have seen such a creature upon the moor.” He spoke with a smile, but I seemed to read in his eyes that he took the matter more seriously. “The story took a great hold upon the imagination of Sir Charles, and I have no doubt that it led to his tragic end.”
