段.文: “怎么会呢？”
段.en: “But how?”

段.文: “他的神经绷得太紧了，随便出现一条什么狗，都可能让他那颗有病的心脏受不了。我猜，那天晚上他在紫杉小径上，真的看见了这类东西。我早就担心会出事，因为我很喜欢这位老人，也知道他心脏不好。”
段.en: “His nerves were so worked up that the appearance of any dog might have had a fatal effect upon his diseased heart. I fancy that he really did see something of the kind upon that last night in the yew alley. I feared that some disaster might occur, for I was very fond of the old man, and I knew that his heart was weak.”

段.文: “您怎么知道的？”
段.en: “How did you know that?”

段.文: “我的朋友莫蒂默告诉我的。”
段.en: “My friend Mortimer told me.”

段.文: “那么您认为，是有条狗追赶查尔斯爵士，他因此吓死了？”
段.en: “You think, then, that some dog pursued Sir Charles, and that he died of fright in consequence?”

段.文: “您还有更好的解释吗？”
段.en: “Have you any better explanation?”

段.文: “我还没有得出什么结论。”
段.en: “I have not come to any conclusion.”

段.文: “夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生呢？”
段.en: “Has Mr. Sherlock Holmes?”

段.文: 这句话让我一时喘不过气来。可我看了一眼同伴，他神色平静，目光坦然，显然并不是有意要吓我一跳。
段.en: The words took away my breath for an instant but a glance at the placid face and steadfast eyes of my companion showed that no surprise was intended.

段.文: “华生医生，我们装作不认识您是没用的，”他说，“您写的那位侦探的故事，已经传到我们这儿来了。您颂扬他，自己也就出了名。莫蒂默告诉我您的名字时，也没法否认您的身份。既然您来了，那就说明夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生也在关注这件事。我自然很想知道他是怎么看的。”
段.en: “It is useless for us to pretend that we do not know you, Dr. Watson,” said he. “The records of your detective have reached us here, and you could not celebrate him without being known yourself. When Mortimer told me your name he could not deny your identity. If you are here, then it follows that Mr. Sherlock Holmes is interesting himself in the matter, and I am naturally curious to know what view he may take.”

段.文: “这个问题，恐怕我没法回答。”
段.en: “I am afraid that I cannot answer that question.”

段.文: “那我能不能问一句，他会不会亲自光临？”
段.en: “May I ask if he is going to honour us with a visit himself?”

段.文: “他目前离不开伦敦，有别的案子要办。”
段.en: “He cannot leave town at present. He has other cases which engage his attention.”

段.文: “太可惜了！我们觉得一团漆黑的事，他也许能照亮一些。不过说到您自己的调查，只要有什么地方用得着我，请尽管吩咐。要是我知道您怀疑什么，或者打算怎么调查，说不定现在就能给您出点力，提点建议。”
段.en: “What a pity! He might throw some light on that which is so dark to us. But as to your own researches, if there is any possible way in which I can be of service to you I trust that you will command me. If I had any indication of the nature of your suspicions or how you propose to investigate the case, I might perhaps even now give you some aid or advice.”

段.文: “我向您保证，我只是来看望我的朋友亨利爵士的，什么帮助都不需要。”
段.en: “I assure you that I am simply here upon a visit to my friend, Sir Henry, and that I need no help of any kind.”

段.文: “好极了！”斯台普顿说，“您小心谨慎，完全正确。我刚才多管闲事，确实不该，受您这番责备是应当的。我保证不再提这件事了。”
段.en: “Excellent!” said Stapleton. “You are perfectly right to be wary and discreet. I am justly reproved for what I feel was an unjustifiable intrusion, and I promise you that I will not mention the matter again.”

段.文: 我们走到一个地方，一条长满青草的窄路从大路岔出去，弯弯曲曲地穿过荒原。右边是一座陡峭的小山，到处散落着大石头，从前曾被开凿成花岗岩采石场。朝着我们的一面是一道黑黢黢的峭壁，石缝里长着蕨草和荆棘。远处一道坡后面，飘起一缕灰色的炊烟。
段.en: We had come to a point where a narrow grassy path struck off from the road and wound away across the moor. A steep, boulder-sprinkled hill lay upon the right which had in bygone days been cut into a granite quarry. The face which was turned towards us formed a dark cliff, with ferns and brambles growing in its niches. From over a distant rise there floated a grey plume of smoke.

段.文: “顺着这条荒原小路走一会儿，就到梅里皮特宅了，”他说，“您能不能抽出一个钟头，让我有幸把您介绍给我妹妹？”
段.en: “A moderate walk along this moor-path brings us to Merripit House,” said he. “Perhaps you will spare an hour that I may have the pleasure of introducing you to my sister.”

段.文: 我头一个念头是，我应该守在亨利爵士身边。可我又想起他书桌上堆得乱七八糟的那些文件和账单，那些事我肯定帮不上忙。何况福尔摩斯明明白白交代过，要我留心荒原上的邻居。于是我接受了斯台普顿的邀请，和他一起拐上了那条小路。
段.en: My first thought was that I should be by Sir Henry’s side. But then I remembered the pile of papers and bills with which his study table was littered. It was certain that I could not help with those. And Holmes had expressly said that I should study the neighbours upon the moor. I accepted Stapleton’s invitation, and we turned together down the path.

段.文: “荒原真是个奇妙的地方，”他说着，环顾四周起伏的丘陵。那些丘陵像一道道绿色的长浪，浪尖上是参差的花岗岩，翻腾成各种奇形怪状的浪头。“荒原永远看不厌。您想象不到它藏着多少奇妙的秘密。它那么辽阔，那么荒凉，又那么神秘。”
段.en: “It is a wonderful place, the moor,” said he, looking round over the undulating downs, long green rollers, with crests of jagged granite foaming up into fantastic surges. “You never tire of the moor. You cannot think the wonderful secrets which it contains. It is so vast, and so barren, and so mysterious.”

段.文: “这么说，您对它很熟了？”
段.en: “You know it well, then?”

段.文: “我在这儿才住了两年，本地人会说我是新来的。我们是在查尔斯爵士定居后不久搬来的。不过我的爱好让我把周围每一处都走遍了。我想，比我更熟悉这一带的人恐怕不多。”
段.en: “I have only been here two years. The residents would call me a newcomer. We came shortly after Sir Charles settled. But my tastes led me to explore every part of the country round, and I should think that there are few men who know it better than I do.”

段.文: “要熟悉它很难吗？”
段.en: “Is it hard to know?”

段.文: “很难。比如说，您看北边这片大平原，中间突兀地冒出几座古怪的小山。您看出它有什么特别的地方吗？”
段.en: “Very hard. You see, for example, this great plain to the north here with the queer hills breaking out of it. Do you observe anything remarkable about that?”

段.文: “在这儿纵马飞奔倒是难得的好地方。”
段.en: “It would be a rare place for a gallop.”

段.文: “您自然会这么想，可这个念头已经要了好几个人的命。您注意到上面密密麻麻散布着的那些鲜绿的斑点了吗？”
段.en: “You would naturally think so and the thought has cost several their lives before now. You notice those bright green spots scattered thickly over it?”

段.文: “看到了，那些地方好像比别处肥沃。”
段.en: “Yes, they seem more fertile than the rest.”

段.文: 斯台普顿笑了起来。“那就是格林彭大泥沼，”他说，“在那儿走错一步，人也好，牲口也好，都是死路一条。就在昨天，我还看见一匹荒原小马跑了进去，再也没出来。好长一段时间，我都看见它的脑袋从沼地的泥坑里伸出来，可最后还是被吸下去了。就算在干燥的季节，穿过它也很危险；秋雨过后，那里更是可怕。可我却能找到路，一直走到它的中心，再活着回来。天哪，又有一匹倒霉的小马！”
段.en: Stapleton laughed. “That is the great Grimpen Mire,” said he. “A false step yonder means death to man or beast. Only yesterday I saw one of the moor ponies wander into it. He never came out. I saw his head for quite a long time craning out of the bog-hole, but it sucked him down at last. Even in dry seasons it is a danger to cross it, but after these autumn rains it is an awful place. And yet I can find my way to the very heart of it and return alive. By George, there is another of those miserable ponies!”

段.文: 有个棕色的东西在绿色的莎草丛里翻滚挣扎。接着，一条长长的脖子猛地向上一伸，痛苦地扭动着，一声凄厉的嘶叫在荒原上回荡。我吓得浑身发冷，可我同伴的神经似乎比我坚强。
段.en: Something brown was rolling and tossing among the green sedges. Then a long, agonised, writhing neck shot upward and a dreadful cry echoed over the moor. It turned me cold with horror, but my companion’s nerves seemed to be stronger than mine.

段.文: “没了！”他说，“泥沼把它吞了。两天两匹，说不定还不止。天干的时候，它们习惯了往那儿跑，等到被泥沼抓住，才知道情况变了。格林彭大泥沼，真是个凶险的地方。”
段.en: “It’s gone!” said he. “The mire has him. Two in two days, and many more, perhaps, for they get in the way of going there in the dry weather and never know the difference until the mire has them in its clutches. It’s a bad place, the great Grimpen Mire.”

段.文: “您说您能走进去？”
段.en: “And you say you can penetrate it?”

段.文: “是的，有一两条路，身手非常敏捷的人可以走。我把它们找出来了。”
段.en: “Yes, there are one or two paths which a very active man can take. I have found them out.”

段.文: “可您为什么要到那么可怕的地方去？”
段.en: “But why should you wish to go into so horrible a place?”

段.文: “嗯，您看见那边的小山了吗？它们其实是一座座孤岛，四面都被走不过去的泥沼隔断了，那是泥沼多年来慢慢爬过去围住的。稀有的植物和蝴蝶就在那儿，就看您有没有本事过去。”
段.en: “Well, you see the hills beyond? They are really islands cut off on all sides by the impassable mire, which has crawled round them in the course of years. That is where the rare plants and the butterflies are, if you have the wit to reach them.”

段.文: “哪天我也去碰碰运气。”
段.en: “I shall try my luck some day.”

段.文: 他一脸吃惊地看着我。“看在上帝分上，千万别打这种主意，”他说，“那样您的命就要算在我头上了。我向您保证，您绝对没有一点活着回来的机会。我自己也是靠记住几处复杂的标志才走得通。”
段.en: He looked at me with a surprised face. “For God’s sake put such an idea out of your mind,” said he. “Your blood would be upon my head. I assure you that there would not be the least chance of your coming back alive. It is only by remembering certain complex landmarks that I am able to do it.”

段.文: “哎！”我叫道，“那是什么声音？”
段.en: “Halloa!” I cried. “What is that?”

段.文: 一声低沉悠长的哀号掠过荒原，说不出地凄凉。它充满了整个天地，却根本听不出是从哪儿来的。声音从低沉的呜咽渐渐涨成深沉的吼叫，接着又落回一阵忧郁的、一起一伏的呜咽。斯台普顿看着我，脸上的神情很古怪。
段.en: A long, low moan, indescribably sad, swept over the moor. It filled the whole air, and yet it was impossible to say whence it came. From a dull murmur it swelled into a deep roar, and then sank back into a melancholy, throbbing murmur once again. Stapleton looked at me with a curious expression in his face.

段.文: “荒原真是个怪地方！”他说。
段.en: “Queer place, the moor!” said he.

段.文: “可那到底是什么？”
段.en: “But what is it?”

段.文: “乡下人说，那是巴斯克维尔的猎犬在呼唤它的猎物。我以前也听到过一两次，可从来没这么响。”
段.en: “The peasants say it is the Hound of the Baskervilles calling for its prey. I’ve heard it once or twice before, but never quite so loud.”

段.文: 我心里发冷，环顾四周。巨大的平原起起伏伏，上面点缀着一块块绿色的灯芯草。在这片辽阔的土地上，除了一对渡鸦在我们身后的一座突岩上呱呱大叫，什么东西都没有动静。
段.en: I looked round, with a chill of fear in my heart, at the huge swelling plain, mottled with the green patches of rushes. Nothing stirred over the vast expanse save a pair of ravens, which croaked loudly from a tor behind us.

段.文: “您是有学问的人，总不会相信那种无稽之谈吧？”我说，“您认为这么奇怪的声音是怎么来的？”
段.en: “You are an educated man. You don’t believe such nonsense as that?” said I. “What do you think is the cause of so strange a sound?”

段.文: “沼地有时候会发出奇怪的声音。可能是泥浆下沉，或者是水往上涌，诸如此类。”
段.en: “Bogs make queer noises sometimes. It’s the mud settling, or the water rising, or something.”

段.文: “不，不，那是活物的叫声。”
段.en: “No, no, that was a living voice.”

段.文: “嗯，也许是吧。您听过麻鳽叫吗？”
段.en: “Well, perhaps it was. Did you ever hear a bittern booming?”

段.文: “没有，从来没听过。”
段.en: “No, I never did.”

段.文: “那是一种很稀有的鸟，在英格兰差不多已经绝迹了。不过在荒原上，什么事都有可能。是啊，就算我们刚才听到的是最后一只麻鳽的叫声，我也不会觉得奇怪。”
段.en: “It’s a very rare bird—practically extinct—in England now, but all things are possible upon the moor. Yes, I should not be surprised to learn that what we have heard is the cry of the last of the bitterns.”

段.文: “这是我这辈子听过的最怪异、最离奇的声音。”
段.en: “It’s the weirdest, strangest thing that ever I heard in my life.”

段.文: “是啊，总的说来，这是个有点阴森的地方。您看那边的山坡，您觉得那些是什么？”
段.en: “Yes, it’s rather an uncanny place altogether. Look at the hillside yonder. What do you make of those?”

段.文: 整片陡坡上布满了灰色的环形石圈，至少有二十来个。
段.en: The whole steep slope was covered with grey circular rings of stone, a score of them at least.

段.文: “那是什么？羊圈吗？”
段.en: “What are they? Sheep-pens?”

段.文: “不，那是我们可敬的祖先的家。史前人类曾经密密地住在荒原上。后来就没什么人在那儿住过，所以他们留下的那些小摆设，我们发现还原封不动。这些是他们的棚屋，只是屋顶没了。您要是好奇，走进去还能看见他们的炉灶和睡铺。”
段.en: “No, they are the homes of our worthy ancestors. Prehistoric man lived thickly on the moor, and as no one in particular has lived there since, we find all his little arrangements exactly as he left them. These are his wigwams with the roofs off. You can even see his hearth and his couch if you have the curiosity to go inside.”

段.文: “这简直是座小城了。是什么时候有人住的？”
段.en: “But it is quite a town. When was it inhabited?”

段.文: “新石器时代人，年代不详。”
段.en: “Neolithic man—no date.”

段.文: “他们靠什么过活？”
段.en: “What did he do?”

段.文: “他们在这些山坡上放牛。等到青铜剑开始取代石斧，他们又学会了挖锡。您看对面山上那道大沟，那就是他们留下的痕迹。是啊，华生医生，您会发现荒原上有些非常奇特的地方。哎呀，请原谅，失陪一下！那一定是弄蝶。”
段.en: “He grazed his cattle on these slopes, and he learned to dig for tin when the bronze sword began to supersede the stone axe. Look at the great trench in the opposite hill. That is his mark. Yes, you will find some very singular points about the moor, Dr. Watson. Oh, excuse me an instant! It is surely Cyclopides.”

段.文: 一只小飞虫或者小蛾子飞过我们面前的小路。一转眼，斯台普顿就以惊人的劲头和速度追了过去。让我惊慌的是，那小东西径直朝大泥沼飞去，而我这位新相识一刻也没停，从一簇草丛跳到另一簇草丛，紧追不舍，绿色的网在空中挥舞。他穿着灰衣服，一蹦一跳，东拐西拐，毫无章法，自己倒有点像一只大蛾子。我站在那儿看他追蝴蝶，一面佩服他身手非凡，一面又怕他在那片暗藏凶险的泥沼里失足。就在这时，我听见脚步声，转身一看，小路上离我不远站着一个女人。她是从那缕炊烟的方向过来的——炊烟那里就是梅里皮特宅——只是荒原上地势低洼，把她挡住了，直到走近才看见。
段.en: A small fly or moth had fluttered across our path, and in an instant Stapleton was rushing with extraordinary energy and speed in pursuit of it. To my dismay the creature flew straight for the great mire, and my acquaintance never paused for an instant, bounding from tuft to tuft behind it, his green net waving in the air. His grey clothes and jerky, zigzag, irregular progress made him not unlike some huge moth himself. I was standing watching his pursuit with a mixture of admiration for his extraordinary activity and fear lest he should lose his footing in the treacherous mire, when I heard the sound of steps and, turning round, found a woman near me upon the path. She had come from the direction in which the plume of smoke indicated the position of Merripit House, but the dip of the moor had hid her until she was quite close.

段.文: 我毫不怀疑，这就是别人跟我提过的斯台普顿小姐。荒原上的女士本来就少，而且我记得听人说过她是个美人。走过来的这位女子确实很美，而且美得非常少见。兄妹俩真是再不相像不过了：斯台普顿颜色浅淡，头发淡黄，眼睛灰色；她却比我在英格兰见过的任何一位黑发女子都要黝黑，身材修长，苗条优雅。她的脸高傲而清秀，五官十分端正，要不是那张敏感的嘴和那双热切的、美丽的黑眼睛，简直会显得毫无表情。她身段完美，衣着雅致，出现在这条冷清的荒原小路上，真像一个奇异的幻影。我转身的时候，她正望着她哥哥，随后就加快脚步朝我走来。我已经举起帽子，正要解释几句，她开口说的话却让我的思绪一下子转到了别处。
段.en: I could not doubt that this was the Miss Stapleton of whom I had been told, since ladies of any sort must be few upon the moor, and I remembered that I had heard someone describe her as being a beauty. The woman who approached me was certainly that, and of a most uncommon type. There could not have been a greater contrast between brother and sister, for Stapleton was neutral tinted, with light hair and grey eyes, while she was darker than any brunette whom I have seen in England—slim, elegant, and tall. She had a proud, finely cut face, so regular that it might have seemed impassive were it not for the sensitive mouth and the beautiful dark, eager eyes. With her perfect figure and elegant dress she was, indeed, a strange apparition upon a lonely moorland path. Her eyes were on her brother as I turned, and then she quickened her pace towards me. I had raised my hat and was about to make some explanatory remark when her own words turned all my thoughts into a new channel.

段.文: “回去！”她说，“马上直接回伦敦去。”
段.en: “Go back!” she said. “Go straight back to London, instantly.”

段.文: 我只能傻愣愣地盯着她。她的眼睛像在冒火，脚不耐烦地在地上轻轻跺着。
段.en: I could only stare at her in stupid surprise. Her eyes blazed at me, and she tapped the ground impatiently with her foot.

段.文: “我为什么要回去？”我问。
段.en: “Why should I go back?” I asked.

段.文: “我没法解释。”她声音很低，又很急切，说话有点奇怪的咬舌。“可是看在上帝分上，照我说的做吧。回去，永远别再踏上荒原一步。”
段.en: “I cannot explain.” She spoke in a low, eager voice, with a curious lisp in her utterance. “But for God’s sake do what I ask you. Go back and never set foot upon the moor again.”

段.文: “可我才刚来。”
段.en: “But I have only just come.”

段.文: “哎呀，你这人！”她叫道，“别人警告你是为你好，你还听不出来吗？回伦敦去！今晚就走！不管怎样都要离开这个地方！嘘，我哥哥来了！我说的话一个字也别提。能不能请你帮我把那边木贼草丛里的那朵兰花摘来？我们荒原上兰花多得很，不过当然了，你来得有点晚，看不到这地方最美的时候了。”
段.en: “Man, man!” she cried. “Can you not tell when a warning is for your own good? Go back to London! Start tonight! Get away from this place at all costs! Hush, my brother is coming! Not a word of what I have said. Would you mind getting that orchid for me among the mare’s-tails yonder? We are very rich in orchids on the moor, though, of course, you are rather late to see the beauties of the place.”

段.文: 斯台普顿已经放弃了追捕，回到我们这边，气喘吁吁，累得满脸通红。
段.en: Stapleton had abandoned the chase and came back to us breathing hard and flushed with his exertions.

段.文: “嗨，贝丽尔！”他说。我觉得他打招呼的口气并不怎么亲热。
段.en: “Halloa, Beryl!” said he, and it seemed to me that the tone of his greeting was not altogether a cordial one.

段.文: “哎，杰克，你热坏了吧。”
段.en: “Well, Jack, you are very hot.”

段.文: “是啊，我在追一只弄蝶。这种蝴蝶很稀有，深秋时节很少见。真可惜让它跑了！”他说得满不在乎，可那双浅色的小眼睛却不停地在姑娘和我之间来回打量。
段.en: “Yes, I was chasing a Cyclopides. He is very rare and seldom found in the late autumn. What a pity that I should have missed him!” He spoke unconcernedly, but his small light eyes glanced incessantly from the girl to me.

段.文: “我看你们已经自我介绍过了。”
段.en: “You have introduced yourselves, I can see.”

段.文: “是的。我正跟亨利爵士说，他来得有点晚，看不到荒原真正美的时候了。”
段.en: “Yes. I was telling Sir Henry that it was rather late for him to see the true beauties of the moor.”

段.文: “咦，你以为这位是谁？”
段.en: “Why, who do you think this is?”

段.文: “我想一定是亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士吧。”
段.en: “I imagine that it must be Sir Henry Baskerville.”

段.文: “不，不，”我说，“我只是个普通平民，不过是他的朋友。我是华生医生。”
段.en: “No, no,” said I. “Only a humble commoner, but his friend. My name is Dr. Watson.”

段.文: 她那张表情丰富的脸上掠过一丝懊恼的红晕。“我们刚才说岔了。”她说。
段.en: A flush of vexation passed over her expressive face. “We have been talking at cross purposes,” said she.

段.文: “咦，你们也没多少时间说话呀。”她哥哥说，眼神里还是带着同样的疑问。
段.en: “Why, you had not very much time for talk,” her brother remarked with the same questioning eyes.

段.文: “我把华生医生当成了常住这儿的人，其实他只是来做客的，”她说，“兰花开得早还是晚，对他来说没什么关系。不过您会去看看梅里皮特宅的，对吧？”
段.en: “I talked as if Dr. Watson were a resident instead of being merely a visitor,” said she. “It cannot much matter to him whether it is early or late for the orchids. But you will come on, will you not, and see Merripit House?”

段.文: 没走多远就到了。这是一座荒凉的荒原房子，从前日子兴旺的时候是哪个牧场主的农舍，如今修缮过，改成了一座新式住宅。房子四周围着果园，可荒原上的树向来如此，都长得又矮又秃，整个地方看上去寒酸而凄凉。给我们开门的是一个古怪的老男仆，干瘪瘦小，穿着一件褪了色的外衣，和这座房子倒挺相称。不过屋里的房间都很宽敞，布置得十分雅致，我似乎看出这是那位女士的品位。我从窗口望出去，荒原上点缀着花岗岩，一望无际，连绵不断地伸向天边。我不禁纳闷：是什么让这位学识渊博的男子和这位美丽的女子住到这种地方来的？
段.en: A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the farm of some grazier in the old prosperous days, but now put into repair and turned into a modern dwelling. An orchard surrounded it, but the trees, as is usual upon the moor, were stunted and nipped, and the effect of the whole place was mean and melancholy. We were admitted by a strange, wizened, rusty-coated old manservant, who seemed in keeping with the house. Inside, however, there were large rooms furnished with an elegance in which I seemed to recognize the taste of the lady. As I looked from their windows at the interminable granite-flecked moor rolling unbroken to the farthest horizon I could not but marvel at what could have brought this highly educated man and this beautiful woman to live in such a place.

段.文: “选了个古怪的地方，是不是？”他说，好像在回答我心里的疑问，“不过我们过得还挺快活，对吧，贝丽尔？”
段.en: “Queer spot to choose, is it not?” said he as if in answer to my thought. “And yet we manage to make ourselves fairly happy, do we not, Beryl?”

段.文: “很快活。”她说，可话里听不出一点真心。
段.en: “Quite happy,” said she, but there was no ring of conviction in her words.

段.文: “我以前办过一所学校，”斯台普顿说，“在北方。对我这种性情的人来说，那份工作刻板乏味。可是能和年轻人生活在一起，帮着塑造那些年轻的心灵，把自己的品格和理想传给他们，这对我来说非常可贵。可惜命运和我们作对。学校里爆发了一场严重的传染病，死了三个孩子。学校从此一蹶不振，我的大部分资本也赔得一干二净。不过，要不是失去了和孩子们相处的那份乐趣，我倒可以为自己的不幸感到庆幸。因为我特别爱好植物学和动物学，在这里有无穷无尽的事情可做，我妹妹也和我一样热爱大自然。华生医生，我说了这么一大通，都怪您刚才从窗口眺望荒原时的那副表情。”
段.en: “I had a school,” said Stapleton. “It was in the north country. The work to a man of my temperament was mechanical and uninteresting, but the privilege of living with youth, of helping to mould those young minds, and of impressing them with one’s own character and ideals was very dear to me. However, the fates were against us. A serious epidemic broke out in the school and three of the boys died. It never recovered from the blow, and much of my capital was irretrievably swallowed up. And yet, if it were not for the loss of the charming companionship of the boys, I could rejoice over my own misfortune, for, with my strong tastes for botany and zoology, I find an unlimited field of work here, and my sister is as devoted to Nature as I am. All this, Dr. Watson, has been brought upon your head by your expression as you surveyed the moor out of our window.”

段.文: “我确实想过，这里也许有点沉闷——对您也许还好，对令妹恐怕就难说了。”
段.en: “It certainly did cross my mind that it might be a little dull—less for you, perhaps, than for your sister.”

段.文: “不，不，我从来不觉得沉闷。”她连忙说。
段.en: “No, no, I am never dull,” said she quickly.

段.文: “我们有书，有研究，还有有趣的邻居。莫蒂默医生在他那一行里是个非常有学问的人。可怜的查尔斯爵士也是个很好的伙伴。我们和他很熟，他走了，我们心里的怀念简直说不出来。您看，我今天下午去拜访亨利爵士，和他认识一下，会不会太冒昧？”
段.en: “We have books, we have our studies, and we have interesting neighbours. Dr. Mortimer is a most learned man in his own line. Poor Sir Charles was also an admirable companion. We knew him well and miss him more than I can tell. Do you think that I should intrude if I were to call this afternoon and make the acquaintance of Sir Henry?”

段.文: “我相信他一定会很高兴的。”
段.en: “I am sure that he would be delighted.”

段.文: “那就请您跟他说一声，我打算去拜访。在他适应新环境之前，我们也许能尽一点微薄之力，让他过得方便些。华生医生，您要不要上楼看看我收集的鳞翅目标本？我想那是英格兰西南部最齐全的一套。等您看完，午饭也差不多好了。”
段.en: “Then perhaps you would mention that I propose to do so. We may in our humble way do something to make things more easy for him until he becomes accustomed to his new surroundings. Will you come upstairs, Dr. Watson, and inspect my collection of Lepidoptera? I think it is the most complete one in the south-west of England. By the time that you have looked through them lunch will be almost ready.”

段.文: 可我急着回去照看我要保护的人。荒原的凄凉，那匹可怜的小马的死，那和巴斯克维尔家族可怕传说联系在一起的怪声，这一切都让我心情阴沉。在这些多少有些模糊的印象之上，又加上了斯台普顿小姐那明明白白的警告。她说得那么恳切，我毫不怀疑背后一定有什么严重而深刻的原因。他们再三留我吃午饭，我都谢绝了，立刻沿着来时那条长满青草的小路往回走。
段.en: But I was eager to get back to my charge. The melancholy of the moor, the death of the unfortunate pony, the weird sound which had been associated with the grim legend of the Baskervilles, all these things tinged my thoughts with sadness. Then on the top of these more or less vague impressions there had come the definite and distinct warning of Miss Stapleton, delivered with such intense earnestness that I could not doubt that some grave and deep reason lay behind it. I resisted all pressure to stay for lunch, and I set off at once upon my return journey, taking the grass-grown path by which we had come.

段.文: 不过，熟悉地形的人似乎一定有条近路。因为我还没走到大路，就惊讶地看见斯台普顿小姐坐在路边的一块石头上。她跑得满脸红晕，显得格外好看，一只手按着腰侧。
段.en: It seems, however, that there must have been some short cut for those who knew it, for before I had reached the road I was astounded to see Miss Stapleton sitting upon a rock by the side of the track. Her face was beautifully flushed with her exertions and she held her hand to her side.

段.文: “华生医生，我一路跑过来，就是为了在这儿拦住您，”她说，“我连帽子都来不及戴。我不能久留，不然我哥哥会发现我不见了。我想跟您说，我把您错当成亨利爵士，犯了个愚蠢的错误，真是很抱歉。请您忘了我说的那些话，那跟您完全没有关系。”
段.en: “I have run all the way in order to cut you off, Dr. Watson,” said she. “I had not even time to put on my hat. I must not stop, or my brother may miss me. I wanted to say to you how sorry I am about the stupid mistake I made in thinking that you were Sir Henry. Please forget the words I said, which have no application whatever to you.”

段.文: “可我忘不了，斯台普顿小姐，”我说，“我是亨利爵士的朋友，他的安危和我关系很密切。请告诉我，您为什么那么急着要亨利爵士回伦敦去？”
段.en: “But I can’t forget them, Miss Stapleton,” said I. “I am Sir Henry’s friend, and his welfare is a very close concern of mine. Tell me why it was that you were so eager that Sir Henry should return to London.”

段.文: “女人一时心血来潮罢了，华生医生。等您跟我熟了就会明白，我说什么、做什么，并不总能讲出道理来。”
段.en: “A woman’s whim, Dr. Watson. When you know me better you will understand that I cannot always give reasons for what I say or do.”

段.文: “不，不。我记得您声音里的那种颤抖，记得您那时的眼神。请您，请您跟我说实话吧，斯台普顿小姐。自从来到这里，我就觉得四周全是阴影。生活变得就像那片格林彭大泥沼，到处都是绿色的小斑点，一不留神就会陷进去，又没有人指路。那就请告诉我，您到底是什么意思，我保证把您的警告转告亨利爵士。”
段.en: “No, no. I remember the thrill in your voice. I remember the look in your eyes. Please, please, be frank with me, Miss Stapleton, for ever since I have been here I have been conscious of shadows all round me. Life has become like that great Grimpen Mire, with little green patches everywhere into which one may sink and with no guide to point the track. Tell me then what it was that you meant, and I will promise to convey your warning to Sir Henry.”

段.文: 她脸上闪过一丝犹豫，可回答我的时候，目光又变得冷硬了。
段.en: An expression of irresolution passed for an instant over her face, but her eyes had hardened again when she answered me.

段.文: “您把这件事看得太严重了，华生医生，”她说，“查尔斯爵士的死让我哥哥和我非常震惊。我们和他很亲近，他最喜欢散步穿过荒原到我们家来。那个笼罩着他们家族的诅咒，在他心里留下了很深的印象。所以这场悲剧发生以后，我自然觉得他那些担忧一定有些根据。因此，当这个家族又有人搬来住的时候，我心里很不安，觉得应该提醒他，他将面临危险。我想说的就是这些。”
段.en: “You make too much of it, Dr. Watson,” said she. “My brother and I were very much shocked by the death of Sir Charles. We knew him very intimately, for his favourite walk was over the moor to our house. He was deeply impressed with the curse which hung over the family, and when this tragedy came I naturally felt that there must be some grounds for the fears which he had expressed. I was distressed therefore when another member of the family came down to live here, and I felt that he should be warned of the danger which he will run. That was all which I intended to convey.”

段.文: “可那是什么危险？”
段.en: “But what is the danger?”

段.文: “您知道那条猎犬的故事吗？”
段.en: “You know the story of the hound?”

段.文: “我不相信那种无稽之谈。”
段.en: “I do not believe in such nonsense.”

段.文: “可我相信。要是您说得动亨利爵士，就带他离开这个地方吧，这里对他们家向来是凶地。天下那么大，他为什么偏要住在危险的地方？”
段.en: “But I do. If you have any influence with Sir Henry, take him away from a place which has always been fatal to his family. The world is wide. Why should he wish to live at the place of danger?”

段.文: “正因为这里危险，他才要住。亨利爵士就是这种性子。恐怕除非您能给我更确切的消息，否则没法劝他离开。”
段.en: “Because it is the place of danger. That is Sir Henry’s nature. I fear that unless you can give me some more definite information than this it would be impossible to get him to move.”

段.文: “我说不出什么确切的事，因为我什么确切的事也不知道。”
段.en: “I cannot say anything definite, for I do not know anything definite.”

段.文: “我再问您一个问题，斯台普顿小姐。如果您最初跟我说话时只是这个意思，为什么不愿意让您哥哥听见呢？这些话，他也好，别人也好，都挑不出什么毛病。”
段.en: “I would ask you one more question, Miss Stapleton. If you meant no more than this when you first spoke to me, why should you not wish your brother to overhear what you said? There is nothing to which he, or anyone else, could object.”

段.文: “我哥哥非常希望庄园里有人住，他认为这对荒原上的穷苦人有好处。要是他知道我说了什么可能让亨利爵士离开的话，他会非常生气的。不过我已经尽到了责任，不会再多说了。我得回去了，不然他会发现我不见了，怀疑我来见过您。再见！”她转身走了，几分钟后就消失在零零散散的大石头之间。而我满怀着说不清的恐惧，继续朝巴斯克维尔庄园走去。
段.en: “My brother is very anxious to have the Hall inhabited, for he thinks it is for the good of the poor folk upon the moor. He would be very angry if he knew that I have said anything which might induce Sir Henry to go away. But I have done my duty now and I will say no more. I must go back, or he will miss me and suspect that I have seen you. Good-bye!” She turned and had disappeared in a few minutes among the scattered boulders, while I, with my soul full of vague fears, pursued my way to Baskerville Hall.

章.标题: 华生医生的第一份报告

段.文: 从这里开始，我把自己写给夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生的几封信照抄下来，按事情发展的顺序讲下去。这些信此刻就摆在我面前的桌上。其中缺了一页，其余都和当初写的一模一样。这些悲惨的事我虽然记得很清楚，可要说我当时的感受和怀疑，还是这些信比我的记忆更准确。
段.en: From this point onward I will follow the course of events by transcribing my own letters to Mr. Sherlock Holmes which lie before me on the table. One page is missing, but otherwise they are exactly as written and show my feelings and suspicions of the moment more accurately than my memory, clear as it is upon these tragic events, can possibly do.

段.文: 巴斯克维尔庄园，10月13日
段.en: Baskerville Hall, October 13th.

段.文: 亲爱的福尔摩斯：
段.en: MY DEAR HOLMES,

段.文: 我前几封信和电报，已经把这个被上帝遗弃的角落里发生的一切，差不多都告诉你了。在这里待得越久，荒原的气息就越深地渗进人的心里——它的辽阔，还有它那种阴森的魅力。一旦走进荒原深处，现代英格兰的痕迹就全被抛在身后了；可另一方面，你又处处感觉得到史前人类的居所和他们留下的劳作痕迹。你走到哪里，四周都是这些被遗忘的人的房屋，还有他们的坟墓，以及据说是标记神庙的巨大石柱。你看着满是伤痕的山坡上那些灰色的石屋，就仿佛离开了自己的时代。这时候，假如你看见一个披着兽皮、浑身毛发的人从矮门里爬出来，正把一支燧石箭头的箭搭上弓弦，你会觉得他出现在那里比你自己还要自然。奇怪的是，这片土地想必向来十分贫瘠，他们却在这里住得那么密。我不是考古学家，不过我能想象，他们大概是一个不善打仗、饱受欺压的民族，只好接受别人谁也不愿占的地方。
段.en: My previous letters and telegrams have kept you pretty well up to date as to all that has occurred in this most God-forsaken corner of the world. The longer one stays here the more does the spirit of the moor sink into one’s soul, its vastness, and also its grim charm. When you are once out upon its bosom you have left all traces of modern England behind you, but, on the other hand, you are conscious everywhere of the homes and the work of the prehistoric people. On all sides of you as you walk are the houses of these forgotten folk, with their graves and the huge monoliths which are supposed to have marked their temples. As you look at their grey stone huts against the scarred hillsides you leave your own age behind you, and if you were to see a skin-clad, hairy man crawl out from the low door fitting a flint-tipped arrow on to the string of his bow, you would feel that his presence there was more natural than your own. The strange thing is that they should have lived so thickly on what must always have been most unfruitful soil. I am no antiquarian, but I could imagine that they were some unwarlike and harried race who were forced to accept that which none other would occupy.

段.文: 不过这些都和你派我来的任务无关，你那颗极讲实际的头脑大概也会觉得索然无味。我还记得，太阳绕着地球转还是地球绕着太阳转，你完全不在乎。所以，还是让我回到有关亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士的事实上来吧。
段.en: All this, however, is foreign to the mission on which you sent me and will probably be very uninteresting to your severely practical mind. I can still remember your complete indifference as to whether the sun moved round the earth or the earth round the sun. Let me, therefore, return to the facts concerning Sir Henry Baskerville.

段.文: 如果这几天你没收到我的报告，那是因为直到今天，都没有什么要紧的事可说。今天却发生了一件非常出人意料的事，我会在后面慢慢告诉你。不过首先，我得让你了解一下这里的其他一些情况。
段.en: If you have not had any report within the last few days it is because up to today there was nothing of importance to relate. Then a very surprising circumstance occurred, which I shall tell you in due course. But, first of all, I must keep you in touch with some of the other factors in the situation.

段.文: 其中一件，我之前很少提起，就是荒原上那个越狱的逃犯。现在有充分的理由相信，他已经逃远了。这让这一带孤零零的住户大大松了一口气。他逃走已经两个星期了，这期间没人看见过他，也没听到他的任何消息。说他能在荒原上一直熬到现在，实在难以想象。当然，要藏身是一点也不难，随便哪座石屋都能让他躲起来。可是没有东西吃，除非他抓一只荒原上的羊来宰了。所以我们认为他已经走了，偏远农庄的人也因此睡得安稳些了。
段.en: One of these, concerning which I have said little, is the escaped convict upon the moor. There is strong reason now to believe that he has got right away, which is a considerable relief to the lonely householders of this district. A fortnight has passed since his flight, during which he has not been seen and nothing has been heard of him. It is surely inconceivable that he could have held out upon the moor during all that time. Of course, so far as his concealment goes there is no difficulty at all. Any one of these stone huts would give him a hiding-place. But there is nothing to eat unless he were to catch and slaughter one of the moor sheep. We think, therefore, that he has gone, and the outlying farmers sleep the better in consequence.

段.文: 我们这一家有四个身强力壮的男人，足能照顾好自己。可我承认，一想到斯台普顿一家，我就有些不安。他们住的地方离任何能求援的人家都有好几英里。家里只有一个女仆、一个老男仆、妹妹和哥哥，而哥哥身体又不算强壮。像那个诺丁山罪犯那样的亡命之徒，只要能闯进门去，他们就只能任他摆布。亨利爵士和我都替他们担心，提议让马夫珀金斯过去睡在那儿，可斯台普顿怎么也不肯。
段.en: We are four able-bodied men in this household, so that we could take good care of ourselves, but I confess that I have had uneasy moments when I have thought of the Stapletons. They live miles from any help. There are one maid, an old manservant, the sister, and the brother, the latter not a very strong man. They would be helpless in the hands of a desperate fellow like this Notting Hill criminal if he could once effect an entrance. Both Sir Henry and I were concerned at their situation, and it was suggested that Perkins the groom should go over to sleep there, but Stapleton would not hear of it.

段.文: 事实上，我们的朋友准男爵，开始对我们这位漂亮的女邻居大感兴趣了。这也不奇怪：他这样好动的人待在这个冷清的地方，日子过得很慢；而她又是个非常迷人的美人。她身上有种热带的、异国的风情，和她那个冷静淡漠的哥哥形成了奇特的对比。不过她哥哥也给人一种感觉，好像心里藏着火。他对她的影响显然很大，因为我看见她说话时不住地瞟他，好像在看自己说的话合不合他的意。但愿他待她和善。他眼里有一种干冷的光，薄薄的嘴唇抿得很紧，这种人性格专断，也许还很严厉。你会觉得他是个有意思的研究对象。
段.en: The fact is that our friend, the baronet, begins to display a considerable interest in our fair neighbour. It is not to be wondered at, for time hangs heavily in this lonely spot to an active man like him, and she is a very fascinating and beautiful woman. There is something tropical and exotic about her which forms a singular contrast to her cool and unemotional brother. Yet he also gives the idea of hidden fires. He has certainly a very marked influence over her, for I have seen her continually glance at him as she talked as if seeking approbation for what she said. I trust that he is kind to her. There is a dry glitter in his eyes and a firm set of his thin lips, which goes with a positive and possibly a harsh nature. You would find him an interesting study.

段.文: 第一天他就过来拜访了巴斯克维尔。第二天早上，他带我们俩去看据说是那个恶人雨果的传说发源的地方。我们穿过荒原走了几英里，到了一个阴惨惨的去处，那样子简直就像是专为这个故事准备的。我们看到一条夹在嶙峋突岩之间的短短山谷，走出去是一片开阔的草地，上面点缀着白色的羊胡子草。草地中央竖着两块巨石，顶端被磨得尖尖的，看上去就像某种怪兽那正在朽烂的巨大獠牙。这里的一切都和那场古老悲剧的场景吻合。亨利爵士很感兴趣，不止一次地问斯台普顿，他是不是真的相信超自然的力量可能干预人间的事。他说得很轻松，可显然是非常认真的。斯台普顿回答得很谨慎，不过很容易看出，他话只说了一半，是顾及准男爵的感受，才没有把自己的看法全说出来。他给我们讲了一些类似的例子，说有些家族也曾受过某种邪恶力量的祸害。他给我们留下的印象是，他对这件事的看法和一般人一样。
段.en: He came over to call upon Baskerville on that first day, and the very next morning he took us both to show us the spot where the legend of the wicked Hugo is supposed to have had its origin. It was an excursion of some miles across the moor to a place which is so dismal that it might have suggested the story. We found a short valley between rugged tors which led to an open, grassy space flecked over with the white cotton grass. In the middle of it rose two great stones, worn and sharpened at the upper end until they looked like the huge corroding fangs of some monstrous beast. In every way it corresponded with the scene of the old tragedy. Sir Henry was much interested and asked Stapleton more than once whether he did really believe in the possibility of the interference of the supernatural in the affairs of men. He spoke lightly, but it was evident that he was very much in earnest. Stapleton was guarded in his replies, but it was easy to see that he said less than he might, and that he would not express his whole opinion out of consideration for the feelings of the baronet. He told us of similar cases, where families had suffered from some evil influence, and he left us with the impression that he shared the popular view upon the matter.

段.文: 回来的路上，我们在梅里皮特宅吃了午饭。亨利爵士就是在那里认识了斯台普顿小姐。他从第一眼看见她起，似乎就被她深深吸引住了。要是我没看错的话，她对他也是一样。回家路上他一次又一次地提起她。从那以后，我们几乎天天都和这兄妹俩见面。今晚他们来这里吃饭，还说好下星期我们去他们家。按说这样一门亲事，斯台普顿应该很欢迎才对。可是不止一次，亨利爵士向他妹妹献殷勤的时候，我都看见他脸上露出极不赞成的神色。他无疑很依恋妹妹，没有她，他的日子会很孤单。可是她能有这么好的一门婚事，他要是从中阻拦，那就未免太自私了。不过我敢肯定，他不希望他们的亲密发展成爱情。我好几次注意到，他想方设法不让他们俩单独在一起。顺便说一句，你吩咐我绝不能让亨利爵士单独出门，要是在我们别的难处之外再添上一桩恋爱，这个任务可就难办得多了。要是我一字不差地执行你的命令，我很快就要招人嫌了。
段.en: On our way back we stayed for lunch at Merripit House, and it was there that Sir Henry made the acquaintance of Miss Stapleton. From the first moment that he saw her he appeared to be strongly attracted by her, and I am much mistaken if the feeling was not mutual. He referred to her again and again on our walk home, and since then hardly a day has passed that we have not seen something of the brother and sister. They dine here tonight, and there is some talk of our going to them next week. One would imagine that such a match would be very welcome to Stapleton, and yet I have more than once caught a look of the strongest disapprobation in his face when Sir Henry has been paying some attention to his sister. He is much attached to her, no doubt, and would lead a lonely life without her, but it would seem the height of selfishness if he were to stand in the way of her making so brilliant a marriage. Yet I am certain that he does not wish their intimacy to ripen into love, and I have several times observed that he has taken pains to prevent them from being tête-à-tête. By the way, your instructions to me never to allow Sir Henry to go out alone will become very much more onerous if a love affair were to be added to our other difficulties. My popularity would soon suffer if I were to carry out your orders to the letter.

段.文: 前几天——确切地说是星期四——莫蒂默医生来和我们一起吃午饭。他一直在朗唐发掘一座古冢，挖到了一个史前人的头骨，高兴得不得了。从没见过像他这样一门心思的热心人！后来斯台普顿兄妹也来了。在亨利爵士的请求下，这位好医生带我们大家去了紫杉小径，把那个不幸的夜晚发生的一切原原本本地指给我们看。紫杉小径是一条又长又阴沉的路，两边是修剪过的高高的树篱，像两堵墙，墙脚各有一窄条草地。小径尽头是一座破旧的凉亭。走到一半是通荒原的门，老先生就是在那里留下了雪茄烟灰。那是一扇白色的木门，带着门闩，门外就是辽阔的荒原。我想起你对这件事的推断，试着想象当时的情形：老人站在那里，看见有个东西穿过荒原过来，那东西把他吓得魂飞魄散，他拼命地跑啊跑，最后纯粹是吓死、累死的。他逃命时跑过的，就是那条长长的、阴暗的通道。可他是在躲什么呢？荒原上的一条牧羊犬？还是一条幽灵般的猎犬，漆黑、无声、巨大可怖？这件事里有没有人在作祟？那个脸色苍白、处处留神的巴里摩尔，是不是知道得比他肯说的多？一切都模模糊糊，可背后总有罪恶的黑影。
段.en: The other day—Thursday, to be more exact—Dr. Mortimer lunched with us. He has been excavating a barrow at Long Down and has got a prehistoric skull which fills him with great joy. Never was there such a single-minded enthusiast as he! The Stapletons came in afterwards, and the good doctor took us all to the yew alley at Sir Henry’s request to show us exactly how everything occurred upon that fatal night. It is a long, dismal walk, the yew alley, between two high walls of clipped hedge, with a narrow band of grass upon either side. At the far end is an old tumble-down summer-house. Halfway down is the moor-gate, where the old gentleman left his cigar-ash. It is a white wooden gate with a latch. Beyond it lies the wide moor. I remembered your theory of the affair and tried to picture all that had occurred. As the old man stood there he saw something coming across the moor, something which terrified him so that he lost his wits and ran and ran until he died of sheer horror and exhaustion. There was the long, gloomy tunnel down which he fled. And from what? A sheep-dog of the moor? Or a spectral hound, black, silent, and monstrous? Was there a human agency in the matter? Did the pale, watchful Barrymore know more than he cared to say? It was all dim and vague, but always there is the dark shadow of crime behind it.

段.文: 自从上次写信以来，我又认识了一位邻居。他就是拉夫特庄园的弗兰克兰先生，住在我们南边大约四英里的地方。他是个上了年纪的人，红脸膛，白头发，脾气暴躁。他热衷于英国法律，打官司已经花掉了一大笔财产。他打官司纯粹是为了打着好玩，一个问题哪一方他都乐意站，所以难怪这种消遣让他破费不少。有时候他会封住一条公众通行的路，看教区敢不敢逼他打开；有时候他又亲手拆掉别人家的门，宣称那里自古以来就有一条路，看主人敢不敢告他擅闯。他精通古老的庄园权和村社权，有时用这些学问替弗恩沃西的村民说话，有时又用来跟他们作对。所以，看他最近干了什么事，他时而被村民们抬着在村街上游行庆祝，时而又被做成草人烧掉。据说他手头眼下有七桩左右的官司，大概会把他剩下的家产吞个精光，那样他也就没了刺，以后不会再害人了。撇开法律不谈，他倒像是个和蔼厚道的人。我提到他，只是因为你特别嘱咐过，要我把周围的人描述给你听。他眼下正干着一件古怪的事：他是个业余天文爱好者，有一架很好的望远镜，整天趴在自家屋顶上，用它扫视荒原，指望能瞥见那个逃犯。要是他只把精力花在这上面倒也罢了，可有传言说，他打算告莫蒂默医生，理由是莫蒂默在朗唐的古冢里挖出了那个新石器时代的头骨，没有征得死者近亲的同意就开了坟。他让我们的生活不至于单调，在正需要的时候给我们添了一点笑料。
段.en: One other neighbour I have met since I wrote last. This is Mr. Frankland, of Lafter Hall, who lives some four miles to the south of us. He is an elderly man, red-faced, white-haired, and choleric. His passion is for the British law, and he has spent a large fortune in litigation. He fights for the mere pleasure of fighting and is equally ready to take up either side of a question, so that it is no wonder that he has found it a costly amusement. Sometimes he will shut up a right of way and defy the parish to make him open it. At others he will with his own hands tear down some other man’s gate and declare that a path has existed there from time immemorial, defying the owner to prosecute him for trespass. He is learned in old manorial and communal rights, and he applies his knowledge sometimes in favour of the villagers of Fernworthy and sometimes against them, so that he is periodically either carried in triumph down the village street or else burned in effigy, according to his latest exploit. He is said to have about seven lawsuits upon his hands at present, which will probably swallow up the remainder of his fortune and so draw his sting and leave him harmless for the future. Apart from the law he seems a kindly, good-natured person, and I only mention him because you were particular that I should send some description of the people who surround us. He is curiously employed at present, for, being an amateur astronomer, he has an excellent telescope, with which he lies upon the roof of his own house and sweeps the moor all day in the hope of catching a glimpse of the escaped convict. If he would confine his energies to this all would be well, but there are rumours that he intends to prosecute Dr. Mortimer for opening a grave without the consent of the next of kin because he dug up the Neolithic skull in the barrow on Long Down. He helps to keep our lives from being monotonous and gives a little comic relief where it is badly needed.

段.文: 好了，逃犯、斯台普顿一家、莫蒂默医生和拉夫特庄园的弗兰克兰，这些人的近况我都告诉你了。最后让我说说最重要的事：巴里摩尔夫妇的更多情况，特别是昨晚那件出人意料的事。
段.en: And now, having brought you up to date in the escaped convict, the Stapletons, Dr. Mortimer, and Frankland, of Lafter Hall, let me end on that which is most important and tell you more about the Barrymores, and especially about the surprising development of last night.

段.文: 先说那封试探的电报。你从伦敦发来那封电报，是想确认巴里摩尔真的在这里。我已经说过，根据邮政局长的证词，那次试探毫无用处，我们无论哪方面都拿不出证据。我把情况告诉了亨利爵士，他马上照他那直来直去的作风，把巴里摩尔叫上来，问他是不是亲自收到了那封电报。巴里摩尔说是的。
段.en: First of all about the test telegram, which you sent from London in order to make sure that Barrymore was really here. I have already explained that the testimony of the postmaster shows that the test was worthless and that we have no proof one way or the other. I told Sir Henry how the matter stood, and he at once, in his downright fashion, had Barrymore up and asked him whether he had received the telegram himself. Barrymore said that he had.

段.文: “那孩子是把电报交到你本人手里的吗？”亨利爵士问。
段.en: “Did the boy deliver it into your own hands?” asked Sir Henry.

段.文: 巴里摩尔显得有些吃惊，想了一会儿。
段.en: Barrymore looked surprised, and considered for a little time.

段.文: “不是，”他说，“当时我在储藏间，是我妻子拿上来给我的。”
段.en: “No,” said he, “I was in the box-room at the time, and my wife brought it up to me.”

段.文: “是你亲自回的电报吗？”
段.en: “Did you answer it yourself?”

段.文: “不是。我告诉我妻子怎么回，她下楼去写的。”
段.en: “No; I told my wife what to answer and she went down to write it.”

段.文: 到了晚上，他又主动提起了这件事。
段.en: In the evening he recurred to the subject of his own accord.

段.文: “亨利爵士，我不太明白您今天早上问那些话是什么意思，”他说，“我希望那不是说我做了什么事，让您不再信任我了吧？”
段.en: “I could not quite understand the object of your questions this morning, Sir Henry,” said he. “I trust that they do not mean that I have done anything to forfeit your confidence?”

段.文: 亨利爵士只好向他保证没有这回事，又把自己不少旧衣服送给他，这才让他平静下来。这时，在伦敦置办的那些衣物已经全部运到了。
段.en: Sir Henry had to assure him that it was not so and pacify him by giving him a considerable part of his old wardrobe, the London outfit having now all arrived.

段.文: 巴里摩尔太太引起了我的兴趣。她是个身材粗壮、结实的女人，见识很有限，极其规矩体面，还有点清教徒式的古板。你很难想象还有比她更不动感情的人了。可我已经告诉过你，我来这里的头一晚就听见她在伤心地哭，从那以后，我也不止一次看见她脸上有泪痕。有某种深深的悲伤一直啃噬着她的心。有时我怀疑，是不是有什么负罪的往事一直缠着她；有时我又怀疑巴里摩尔在家里是个暴君。我一直觉得这个人的性格有些古怪、可疑。而昨晚的那件事，让我所有的怀疑都到了顶点。
段.en: Mrs. Barrymore is of interest to me. She is a heavy, solid person, very limited, intensely respectable, and inclined to be puritanical. You could hardly conceive a less emotional subject. Yet I have told you how, on the first night here, I heard her sobbing bitterly, and since then I have more than once observed traces of tears upon her face. Some deep sorrow gnaws ever at her heart. Sometimes I wonder if she has a guilty memory which haunts her, and sometimes I suspect Barrymore of being a domestic tyrant. I have always felt that there was something singular and questionable in this man’s character, but the adventure of last night brings all my suspicions to a head.

段.文: 不过这件事本身也许显得微不足道。你知道我睡觉向来不太沉，自从在这座房子里担任警戒以来，我睡得更浅了。昨晚大约凌晨两点，我被一阵从我门前经过的、偷偷摸摸的脚步声惊醒了。我起床打开门，往外偷看。只见一道长长的黑影沿着走廊拖过去。那是一个人的影子，他手里拿着蜡烛，正轻手轻脚地顺着过道往前走。他穿着衬衫和裤子，光着脚。我只看得见一个轮廓，可从个头看出那是巴里摩尔。他走得很慢，很小心，整个样子说不出地心虚、鬼祟。
段.en: And yet it may seem a small matter in itself. You are aware that I am not a very sound sleeper, and since I have been on guard in this house my slumbers have been lighter than ever. Last night, about two in the morning, I was aroused by a stealthy step passing my room. I rose, opened my door, and peeped out. A long black shadow was trailing down the corridor. It was thrown by a man who walked softly down the passage with a candle held in his hand. He was in shirt and trousers, with no covering to his feet. I could merely see the outline, but his height told me that it was Barrymore. He walked very slowly and circumspectly, and there was something indescribably guilty and furtive in his whole appearance.

段.文: 我跟你说过，走廊被环绕大厅的楼廊隔断，到了另一头又接上了。我等他走得看不见了，就跟了上去。等我绕过楼廊，他已经走到另一头走廊的尽头。从一扇开着的门里透出的微光，我看出他进了其中一个房间。那些房间都没有家具，也没人住，所以他这趟行动就显得更加神秘了。烛光一动不动，好像他站在那里没动。我尽量不出声地沿着过道蹑手蹑脚地走过去，从门边偷偷往里看。
段.en: I have told you that the corridor is broken by the balcony which runs round the hall, but that it is resumed upon the farther side. I waited until he had passed out of sight and then I followed him. When I came round the balcony he had reached the end of the farther corridor, and I could see from the glimmer of light through an open door that he had entered one of the rooms. Now, all these rooms are unfurnished and unoccupied so that his expedition became more mysterious than ever. The light shone steadily as if he were standing motionless. I crept down the passage as noiselessly as I could and peeped round the corner of the door.

段.文: 巴里摩尔弯着腰蹲在窗前，把蜡烛贴在玻璃上。他的脸半侧着对着我，凝视着窗外漆黑的荒原，脸上的表情因为期待而显得僵硬。他专注地望了好几分钟，然后深深地叹了一口气，不耐烦地一挥手，把蜡烛灭了。我立刻回到自己房间。过了不久，那偷偷摸摸的脚步声又从门前经过，往回去了。又过了好久，我刚迷迷糊糊睡着，听见不知什么地方有钥匙在锁里转动的声音，可分辨不出是从哪儿传来的。这一切是什么意思，我猜不出来。但这座阴森的房子里一定在进行着什么秘密勾当，我们迟早会把它查个水落石出。我不拿我的种种推测来烦你，因为你只要我给你提供事实。今天早上我和亨利爵士长谈了一次，根据我昨晚观察到的情况，我们定下了一个行动计划。现在我先不说，不过我下一份报告应该会很有看头。
段.en: Barrymore was crouching at the window with the candle held against the glass. His profile was half turned towards me, and his face seemed to be rigid with expectation as he stared out into the blackness of the moor. For some minutes he stood watching intently. Then he gave a deep groan and with an impatient gesture he put out the light. Instantly I made my way back to my room, and very shortly came the stealthy steps passing once more upon their return journey. Long afterwards when I had fallen into a light sleep I heard a key turn somewhere in a lock, but I could not tell whence the sound came. What it all means I cannot guess, but there is some secret business going on in this house of gloom which sooner or later we shall get to the bottom of. I do not trouble you with my theories, for you asked me to furnish you only with facts. I have had a long talk with Sir Henry this morning, and we have made a plan of campaign founded upon my observations of last night. I will not speak about it just now, but it should make my next report interesting reading.

段.文: 巴斯克维尔庄园，10月15日
段.en: Baskerville Hall, Oct. 15th.

段.文: 亲爱的福尔摩斯：
段.en: MY DEAR HOLMES,

段.文: 如果说我刚接手任务的头几天，不得不让你没什么消息可听，那你得承认，我现在正把耽误的时间补回来，因为事情一件接一件，来得又多又快。上一份报告，我是在最紧要的地方停下的——巴里摩尔站在窗前。现在我已经攒了一大堆消息，要是我没想错，这些消息会让你大吃一惊。事情的发展是我没有料到的。在过去这四十八小时里，有些方面变得清楚多了，有些方面却更复杂了。不过我会把一切都告诉你，由你自己来判断。
段.en: If I was compelled to leave you without much news during the early days of my mission you must acknowledge that I am making up for lost time, and that events are now crowding thick and fast upon us. In my last report I ended upon my top note with Barrymore at the window, and now I have quite a budget already which will, unless I am much mistaken, considerably surprise you. Things have taken a turn which I could not have anticipated. In some ways they have within the last forty-eight hours become much clearer and in some ways they have become more complicated. But I will tell you all and you shall judge for yourself.

段.文: 那次夜里的经历之后，第二天早饭前，我顺着走廊过去，查看了巴里摩尔前一晚待过的那个房间。我注意到，他那么专注地向外张望的那扇西窗，和这房子里所有别的窗户相比，有一个特别之处：从这里望荒原，视野最近。两棵树中间有个空隙，从这个位置可以直接俯瞰荒原；从其他窗户望出去，都只能远远地瞥见一点。由此可见，既然只有这扇窗才合用，巴里摩尔一定是在荒原上寻找什么东西或者什么人。那天夜里很黑，我简直想象不出他怎么能指望看见人。我想到，也许他在搞什么私情。这可以解释他为什么鬼鬼祟祟，也能解释他妻子为什么心神不宁。这个男人相貌出众，很有本事俘获乡下姑娘的心，所以这个推测似乎也有些根据。我回房以后听到的那声开门的声音，可能说明他出去赴什么秘密约会了。那天早上我就是这样推想的。我把我怀疑的方向告诉你，尽管后来的结果证明这些怀疑毫无根据。
段.en: Before breakfast on the morning following my adventure I went down the corridor and examined the room in which Barrymore had been on the night before. The western window through which he had stared so intently has, I noticed, one peculiarity above all other windows in the house—it commands the nearest outlook on to the moor. There is an opening between two trees which enables one from this point of view to look right down upon it, while from all the other windows it is only a distant glimpse which can be obtained. It follows, therefore, that Barrymore, since only this window would serve the purpose, must have been looking out for something or somebody upon the moor. The night was very dark, so that I can hardly imagine how he could have hoped to see anyone. It had struck me that it was possible that some love intrigue was on foot. That would have accounted for his stealthy movements and also for the uneasiness of his wife. The man is a striking-looking fellow, very well equipped to steal the heart of a country girl, so that this theory seemed to have something to support it. That opening of the door which I had heard after I had returned to my room might mean that he had gone out to keep some clandestine appointment. So I reasoned with myself in the morning, and I tell you the direction of my suspicions, however much the result may have shown that they were unfounded.

段.文: 不过，不管巴里摩尔的行动真正的原因是什么，我觉得，在弄明白之前一直把这些事藏在自己心里，这份责任太重，我担不起。早饭后，我到书房去见准男爵，把我看到的一切都告诉了他。他倒没有我预料的那么吃惊。
段.en: But whatever the true explanation of Barrymore’s movements might be, I felt that the responsibility of keeping them to myself until I could explain them was more than I could bear. I had an interview with the baronet in his study after breakfast, and I told him all that I had seen. He was less surprised than I had expected.

段.文: “我知道巴里摩尔夜里到处走动，正想找他谈谈这件事，”他说，“有两三次，差不多就在你说的那个钟点，我听见他的脚步声在过道里来来去去。”
段.en: “I knew that Barrymore walked about nights, and I had a mind to speak to him about it,” said he. “Two or three times I have heard his steps in the passage, coming and going, just about the hour you name.”

段.文: “那么，也许他每天夜里都要到那扇窗户那儿去一趟。”我说。
段.en: “Perhaps then he pays a visit every night to that particular window,” I suggested.

段.文: “也许是吧。要是这样，我们就可以跟踪他，看看他到底想干什么。不知道你的朋友福尔摩斯要是在这儿，会怎么做。”
段.en: “Perhaps he does. If so, we should be able to shadow him and see what it is that he is after. I wonder what your friend Holmes would do if he were here.”

段.文: “我相信，他会正好照你现在说的去做，”我说，“他会跟踪巴里摩尔，看他干什么。”
段.en: “I believe that he would do exactly what you now suggest,” said I. “He would follow Barrymore and see what he did.”

段.文: “那咱们就一起干。”
段.en: “Then we shall do it together.”

段.文: “可他一定会听见的。”
段.en: “But surely he would hear us.”

段.文: “这家伙耳朵有点背，再说，不管怎样，我们也只能碰碰运气。今晚咱们就在我屋里熬夜，等他走过去。”亨利爵士高兴地搓着手。显然，他在荒原上的日子有点冷清，所以很欢迎这次冒险，觉得可以换换口味。
段.en: “The man is rather deaf, and in any case we must take our chance of that. We’ll sit up in my room tonight and wait until he passes.” Sir Henry rubbed his hands with pleasure, and it was evident that he hailed the adventure as a relief to his somewhat quiet life upon the moor.

段.文: 准男爵已经和当初给查尔斯爵士画过图纸的建筑师联系上了，还找了一个伦敦的承包商，所以这里不久就会有大变化了。普利茅斯已经有室内装饰和家具商来过。看得出，我们的朋友雄心勃勃，打算不惜花费任何力气和钱财，恢复他家族昔日的气派。等房子翻修一新、重新布置好以后，就只差一位妻子来让它圆满了。我们私下说，种种迹象已经很明显：只要那位女士愿意，这一点是不会缺的。因为我很少见过哪个男人像他迷恋我们的美丽邻居斯台普顿小姐那样，迷恋一个女人。可是，真心相爱的路，并不像在这种情况下人们以为的那样平坦。比如今天，平静的水面上就意外地起了一道涟漪，让我们的朋友大为困惑和恼火。
段.en: The baronet has been in communication with the architect who prepared the plans for Sir Charles, and with a contractor from London, so that we may expect great changes to begin here soon. There have been decorators and furnishers up from Plymouth, and it is evident that our friend has large ideas and means to spare no pains or expense to restore the grandeur of his family. When the house is renovated and refurnished, all that he will need will be a wife to make it complete. Between ourselves there are pretty clear signs that this will not be wanting if the lady is willing, for I have seldom seen a man more infatuated with a woman than he is with our beautiful neighbour, Miss Stapleton. And yet the course of true love does not run quite as smoothly as one would under the circumstances expect. Today, for example, its surface was broken by a very unexpected ripple, which has caused our friend considerable perplexity and annoyance.

段.文: 前面我引述的那番关于巴里摩尔的谈话之后，亨利爵士戴上帽子，准备出门。我当然也照样戴上了帽子。
段.en: After the conversation which I have quoted about Barrymore, Sir Henry put on his hat and prepared to go out. As a matter of course I did the same.

段.文: “怎么，华生，你也要去？”他问，神情有点古怪地看着我。
段.en: “What, are you coming, Watson?” he asked, looking at me in a curious way.

段.文: “那要看你是不是去荒原。”我说。
段.en: “That depends on whether you are going on the moor,” said I.

段.文: “是的，我去荒原。”
段.en: “Yes, I am.”

段.文: “那么，你知道我受了什么嘱托。很抱歉打扰你，可你也听见了，福尔摩斯是多么恳切地坚持要我别离开你，特别是不能让你一个人到荒原上去。”
段.en: “Well, you know what my instructions are. I am sorry to intrude, but you heard how earnestly Holmes insisted that I should not leave you, and especially that you should not go alone upon the moor.”

段.文: 亨利爵士把手搭在我肩上，和气地笑了笑。
段.en: Sir Henry put his hand upon my shoulder with a pleasant smile.

段.文: “我亲爱的朋友，”他说，“福尔摩斯尽管聪明绝顶，可我到了荒原以后发生的有些事，他并没有料到。你明白我的意思吧？我相信，你是世上最不愿意扫别人兴的人。我得一个人出去。”
段.en: “My dear fellow,” said he, “Holmes, with all his wisdom, did not foresee some things which have happened since I have been on the moor. You understand me? I am sure that you are the last man in the world who would wish to be a spoil-sport. I must go out alone.”

段.文: 这下可让我十分为难。我不知道该说什么，该做什么。还没等我拿定主意，他已经拿起手杖走了。
段.en: It put me in a most awkward position. I was at a loss what to say or what to do, and before I had made up my mind he picked up his cane and was gone.

段.文: 可是等我仔细一想，良心就狠狠地责备起我来：不管什么理由，我都不该让他离开我的视线。我想象着，假如我因为没照你的嘱咐办而出了什么不幸，回去向你认错时会是什么滋味。我向你保证，光是想一想，我的脸就发烧了。现在去追他也许还来得及，于是我立刻朝梅里皮特宅的方向出发了。
段.en: But when I came to think the matter over my conscience reproached me bitterly for having on any pretext allowed him to go out of my sight. I imagined what my feelings would be if I had to return to you and to confess that some misfortune had occurred through my disregard for your instructions. I assure you my cheeks flushed at the very thought. It might not even now be too late to overtake him, so I set off at once in the direction of Merripit House.

段.文: 我沿着大路拼命快走，一直没看到亨利爵士的影子，直到走到那条荒原小路岔出去的地方。我担心自己是不是走错了方向，就爬上一座能看得远的小山——就是那座被开成黑黢黢采石场的小山。从那里我一眼就看见了他。他在荒原小路上，离我大约四分之一英里，身边有一位女士，那只能是斯台普顿小姐。显然，他们之间已经有了默契，是约好了见面的。他们一边慢慢走，一边谈得很投入。我看见她的手不停地做着急促的小动作，好像她说的话非常要紧；他专心地听着，有一两次使劲摇头，表示坚决不同意。我站在岩石中间望着他们，不知道下一步该怎么办才好。跟上去打断他们的私密谈话，似乎太过分了；可我的职责明明是一刻也不能让他离开我的视线。暗中监视朋友是件讨厌的差事。不过，我想不出比在山上看着他更好的办法，事后再向他坦白，好让良心过得去。没错，要是他突然遇到什么危险，我离得太远，帮不上忙。可我相信你会同意，我的处境确实非常为难，我也实在做不了更多了。
段.en: I hurried along the road at the top of my speed without seeing anything of Sir Henry, until I came to the point where the moor path branches off. There, fearing that perhaps I had come in the wrong direction after all, I mounted a hill from which I could command a view—the same hill which is cut into the dark quarry. Thence I saw him at once. He was on the moor path about a quarter of a mile off, and a lady was by his side who could only be Miss Stapleton. It was clear that there was already an understanding between them and that they had met by appointment. They were walking slowly along in deep conversation, and I saw her making quick little movements of her hands as if she were very earnest in what she was saying, while he listened intently, and once or twice shook his head in strong dissent. I stood among the rocks watching them, very much puzzled as to what I should do next. To follow them and break into their intimate conversation seemed to be an outrage, and yet my clear duty was never for an instant to let him out of my sight. To act the spy upon a friend was a hateful task. Still, I could see no better course than to observe him from the hill, and to clear my conscience by confessing to him afterwards what I had done. It is true that if any sudden danger had threatened him I was too far away to be of use, and yet I am sure that you will agree with me that the position was very difficult, and that there was nothing more which I could do.

段.文: 我们的朋友亨利爵士和那位女士在小路上停了下来，站在那里谈得入了神。就在这时，我忽然发现，目睹他们会面的不止我一个人。一缕绿色的东西在空中飘动，引起了我的注意。再一看，原来是一个人用竿子挑着，那人正在高低不平的地上走动。那是斯台普顿，拿着他的捕蝶网。他离那两个人比我近得多，而且好像正朝他们走去。就在这一刻，亨利爵士突然把斯台普顿小姐拉到身边。他搂住了她，可我觉得她把脸扭开，正使劲往后挣。他低下头凑近她，她举起一只手，好像在抗拒。紧接着，我看见他们猛地分开，慌忙转过身去。打断他们的正是斯台普顿。他发疯似的朝他们跑过去，那张可笑的网在身后晃荡。他在这对恋人面前比手画脚，激动得几乎要跳起来。我想象不出这是怎么回事，不过在我看来，斯台普顿是在辱骂亨利爵士。亨利爵士在解释，对方不肯接受，他的解释也就越来越带火气。那位女士站在一旁，高傲地一言不发。最后，斯台普顿一转身，专横地朝他妹妹招了招手。她犹豫地看了亨利爵士一眼，就跟在哥哥身边走了。从这位博物学家气冲冲的手势看得出，他连他妹妹也一起怪上了。准男爵站在那里望着他们的背影，过了一会儿，才低着头，慢慢地顺着来路往回走，一副垂头丧气的样子。
段.en: Our friend, Sir Henry, and the lady had halted on the path and were standing deeply absorbed in their conversation, when I was suddenly aware that I was not the only witness of their interview. A wisp of green floating in the air caught my eye, and another glance showed me that it was carried on a stick by a man who was moving among the broken ground. It was Stapleton with his butterfly-net. He was very much closer to the pair than I was, and he appeared to be moving in their direction. At this instant Sir Henry suddenly drew Miss Stapleton to his side. His arm was round her, but it seemed to me that she was straining away from him with her face averted. He stooped his head to hers, and she raised one hand as if in protest. Next moment I saw them spring apart and turn hurriedly round. Stapleton was the cause of the interruption. He was running wildly towards them, his absurd net dangling behind him. He gesticulated and almost danced with excitement in front of the lovers. What the scene meant I could not imagine, but it seemed to me that Stapleton was abusing Sir Henry, who offered explanations, which became more angry as the other refused to accept them. The lady stood by in haughty silence. Finally Stapleton turned upon his heel and beckoned in a peremptory way to his sister, who, after an irresolute glance at Sir Henry, walked off by the side of her brother. The naturalist’s angry gestures showed that the lady was included in his displeasure. The baronet stood for a minute looking after them, and then he walked slowly back the way that he had come, his head hanging, the very picture of dejection.

段.文: 这一切是什么意思，我想象不出。可我在朋友不知情的情况下，目睹了这么私密的一幕，心里深感羞愧。于是我跑下山，在山脚下迎上了准男爵。他气得满脸通红，紧皱着眉头，像是一点办法也没有了。
段.en: What all this meant I could not imagine, but I was deeply ashamed to have witnessed so intimate a scene without my friend’s knowledge. I ran down the hill therefore and met the baronet at the bottom. His face was flushed with anger and his brows were wrinkled, like one who is at his wit’s ends what to do.

段.文: “嗨，华生！你是从哪儿冒出来的？”他说，“你该不会是不管我怎么说，还是跟着我来了吧？”
段.en: “Halloa, Watson! Where have you dropped from?” said he. “You don’t mean to say that you came after me in spite of all?”

段.文: 我把一切都向他说明了：我怎么觉得没法留在家里，怎么跟了出来，又怎么目睹了刚才发生的一切。有那么一瞬间，他的眼睛冲我冒火，可我的坦白平息了他的怒气，最后他苦笑了起来。
段.en: I explained everything to him: how I had found it impossible to remain behind, how I had followed him, and how I had witnessed all that had occurred. For an instant his eyes blazed at me, but my frankness disarmed his anger, and he broke at last into a rather rueful laugh.

段.文: “你会以为，在那片大草原中间，一个人总该能清清静静的吧，”他说，“可是，见鬼，好像全乡的人都跑出来看我求爱了——而且求得那么糟糕！你的座位订在哪儿？”
段.en: “You would have thought the middle of that prairie a fairly safe place for a man to be private,” said he, “but, by thunder, the whole countryside seems to have been out to see me do my wooing—and a mighty poor wooing at that! Where had you engaged a seat?”

段.文: “我在那座山上。”
段.en: “I was on that hill.”

段.文: “最后一排，嗯？可她哥哥坐的倒是前排。你看见他冲我们跑过来了吗？”
段.en: “Quite in the back row, eh? But her brother was well up to the front. Did you see him come out on us?”

段.文: “看见了。”
段.en: “Yes, I did.”

段.文: “你有没有觉得，她这个哥哥是个疯子？”
段.en: “Did he ever strike you as being crazy—this brother of hers?”

段.文: “我不能说我这样觉得过。”
段.en: “I can’t say that he ever did.”

段.文: “我想也是。直到今天以前，我一直觉得他神志挺正常。可你听我说，要么是他，要么是我，该穿上拘束衣了。我到底有什么毛病？华生，你在我身边住了几个星期了。你老实告诉我！有什么会妨碍我给一个我爱的女人当个好丈夫吗？”
段.en: “I dare say not. I always thought him sane enough until today, but you can take it from me that either he or I ought to be in a straitjacket. What’s the matter with me, anyhow? You’ve lived near me for some weeks, Watson. Tell me straight, now! Is there anything that would prevent me from making a good husband to a woman that I loved?”

段.文: “我看没有。”
段.en: “I should say not.”

段.文: “他不可能嫌弃我的地位，那他一定是看不上我这个人了。他对我有什么不满？据我所知，我这辈子从来没伤害过谁，不管男人女人。可他连她的指尖都不让我碰一下。”
段.en: “He can’t object to my worldly position, so it must be myself that he has this down on. What has he against me? I never hurt man or woman in my life that I know of. And yet he would not so much as let me touch the tips of her fingers.”

段.文: “他这么说了？”
段.en: “Did he say so?”

段.文: “说了，还说了一大堆别的。我跟你说，华生，我认识她才这么几个星期，可从一开始我就觉得她是为我而生的。她也一样——她和我在一起时很快活，这我敢发誓。女人眼睛里有一种光，比说什么都清楚。可他从来不让我们单独在一块儿。直到今天，我才头一回找到机会，能和她单独说几句话。她很高兴见到我，可见了面，她却不肯谈爱情；要是她拦得住，也不会让我谈。她一个劲儿地说，这是个危险的地方，不等我离开这里，她永远不会安心。我对她说，自从见了她，我就一点也不急着走了；要是她真心希望我走，唯一的办法就是她安排好和我一起走。说着，我就明明白白地向她求婚了。可她还没来得及回答，她这个哥哥就冲了过来，朝我们跑来，那张脸像个疯子。他气得脸都白了，那双浅色的眼睛里怒火直冒。我在对这位女士做什么？她不喜欢我献殷勤，我怎么敢纠缠她？我是不是以为自己是个准男爵，就可以为所欲为？要不是他是她哥哥，我就知道该怎么回敬他了。可既然如此，我只能告诉他，我对他妹妹的感情没有什么可羞愧的，我希望她肯赏脸做我的妻子。这话好像也没让事情好转，于是我也发火了，回他的话恐怕比该说的冲了些，毕竟她就站在旁边。结果，就像你看到的，他带着她走了。现在我在这个郡里，比谁都更摸不着头脑。华生，你只要告诉我这到底是怎么回事，我欠你的情就一辈子也还不清。”
段.en: “That, and a deal more. I tell you, Watson, I’ve only known her these few weeks, but from the first I just felt that she was made for me, and she, too—she was happy when she was with me, and that I’ll swear. There’s a light in a woman’s eyes that speaks louder than words. But he has never let us get together and it was only today for the first time that I saw a chance of having a few words with her alone. She was glad to meet me, but when she did it was not love that she would talk about, and she wouldn’t have let me talk about it either if she could have stopped it. She kept coming back to it that this was a place of danger, and that she would never be happy until I had left it. I told her that since I had seen her I was in no hurry to leave it, and that if she really wanted me to go, the only way to work it was for her to arrange to go with me. With that I offered in as many words to marry her, but before she could answer, down came this brother of hers, running at us with a face on him like a madman. He was just white with rage, and those light eyes of his were blazing with fury. What was I doing with the lady? How dared I offer her attentions which were distasteful to her? Did I think that because I was a baronet I could do what I liked? If he had not been her brother I should have known better how to answer him. As it was I told him that my feelings towards his sister were such as I was not ashamed of, and that I hoped that she might honour me by becoming my wife. That seemed to make the matter no better, so then I lost my temper too, and I answered him rather more hotly than I should perhaps, considering that she was standing by. So it ended by his going off with her, as you saw, and here am I as badly puzzled a man as any in this county. Just tell me what it all means, Watson, and I’ll owe you more than ever I can hope to pay.”

段.文: 我试着给出一两种解释，可说实话，我自己也完全糊涂了。我们这位朋友的爵位、财产、年龄、品格和相貌，样样都对他有利。除了他家族里那个阴暗的厄运之外，我想不出他有什么不好。他的求爱竟然这样被粗暴地拒绝，根本不问那位女士自己愿不愿意，而那位女士也一声不吭地接受了，真是叫人惊讶。不过，当天下午斯台普顿亲自来访，我们的种种猜测也就告一段落了。他是来为早上的无礼道歉的。他和亨利爵士在书房里单独谈了很久，结果是两人的嫌隙完全弥合了。作为和好的表示，我们下星期五要去梅里皮特宅吃饭。
段.en: I tried one or two explanations, but, indeed, I was completely puzzled myself. Our friend’s title, his fortune, his age, his character, and his appearance are all in his favour, and I know nothing against him unless it be this dark fate which runs in his family. That his advances should be rejected so brusquely without any reference to the lady’s own wishes and that the lady should accept the situation without protest is very amazing. However, our conjectures were set at rest by a visit from Stapleton himself that very afternoon. He had come to offer apologies for his rudeness of the morning, and after a long private interview with Sir Henry in his study the upshot of their conversation was that the breach is quite healed, and that we are to dine at Merripit House next Friday as a sign of it.

段.文: “我现在也不敢说他不是疯子，”亨利爵士说，“今天早上他冲我跑过来时那种眼神，我忘不了。不过我得承认，没有谁的道歉能比他的更体面了。”
段.en: “I don’t say now that he isn’t a crazy man,” said Sir Henry; “I can’t forget the look in his eyes when he ran at me this morning, but I must allow that no man could make a more handsome apology than he has done.”

段.文: “他对自己的举动有什么解释吗？”
段.en: “Did he give any explanation of his conduct?”

段.文: “他说，他妹妹就是他生活的全部。这倒很自然，他懂得她的可贵，我也高兴。他们一直在一起。照他的说法，他是个很孤独的人，只有她这一个伴儿，所以一想到要失去她，他就觉得实在可怕。他说他原先没看出我对她有了感情，等他亲眼看见确实如此，看见她可能会被人从他身边带走，他受的打击太大，一时之间说的话、做的事都由不得自己了。他对发生的一切非常抱歉。他也承认，以为自己能把像他妹妹这样一个美丽的女人一辈子留在身边，是多么愚蠢、多么自私。如果她非离开他不可，他宁愿她嫁给像我这样的邻居，而不是别人。不过无论如何，这对他是个打击，他需要一些时间才能做好准备去面对。只要我答应三个月内不提这件事，这段时间里只和那位女士培养友谊，不要求她的爱情，他这方面就不再反对。我答应了，事情就这么定了。”
段.en: “His sister is everything in his life, he says. That is natural enough, and I am glad that he should understand her value. They have always been together, and according to his account he has been a very lonely man with only her as a companion, so that the thought of losing her was really terrible to him. He had not understood, he said, that I was becoming attached to her, but when he saw with his own eyes that it was really so, and that she might be taken away from him, it gave him such a shock that for a time he was not responsible for what he said or did. He was very sorry for all that had passed, and he recognized how foolish and how selfish it was that he should imagine that he could hold a beautiful woman like his sister to himself for her whole life. If she had to leave him he had rather it was to a neighbour like myself than to anyone else. But in any case it was a blow to him and it would take him some time before he could prepare himself to meet it. He would withdraw all opposition upon his part if I would promise for three months to let the matter rest and to be content with cultivating the lady’s friendship during that time without claiming her love. This I promised, and so the matter rests.”

段.文: 这样，我们的一个小谜团算是解开了。我们在这片沼地里挣扎，能在某个地方踩到底，总算是有点收获。现在我们知道斯台普顿为什么看不惯他妹妹的追求者了——哪怕这个追求者是亨利爵士这样般配的人选。下面我要谈另一条线索，那是我从这团乱麻里理出来的：夜里的哭声，巴里摩尔太太满是泪痕的脸，还有管家悄悄走到西边格子窗前的秘密。祝贺我吧，亲爱的福尔摩斯，告诉我，我这个助手没有让你失望，你派我来时对我的信任没有让你后悔。所有这些事，一个晚上的工夫就彻底弄清楚了。
段.en: So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is something to have touched bottom anywhere in this bog in which we are floundering. We know now why Stapleton looked with disfavour upon his sister’s suitor—even when that suitor was so eligible a one as Sir Henry. And now I pass on to another thread which I have extricated out of the tangled skein, the mystery of the sobs in the night, of the tear-stained face of Mrs. Barrymore, of the secret journey of the butler to the western lattice window. Congratulate me, my dear Holmes, and tell me that I have not disappointed you as an agent—that you do not regret the confidence which you showed in me when you sent me down. All these things have by one night’s work been thoroughly cleared.

段.文: 我说“一个晚上的工夫”，其实是两个晚上，因为第一晚我们一无所获。我和亨利爵士在他房里一直坐到将近凌晨三点，除了楼梯上的钟报时的声音，什么动静也没听见。那次守夜真是凄凉透顶，最后我们俩都在椅子上睡着了。幸好我们没有灰心，决定再试一次。第二天夜里，我们把灯拧暗，坐着抽烟，一点声音也不出。时间过得慢得叫人难以置信。不过，支撑我们熬下去的，是一种耐心的兴致，就像猎人守着陷阱、盼着猎物走进去时的那种心情。钟敲了一点，又敲了两点。我们第二次几乎要绝望地放弃了，就在这时，我们俩一下子在椅子上坐得笔直，疲倦的感官又全都警觉起来。我们听见过道里有脚步踩得地板嘎吱一响。
段.en: I have said “by one night’s work,” but, in truth, it was by two nights’ work, for on the first we drew entirely blank. I sat up with Sir Henry in his rooms until nearly three o’clock in the morning, but no sound of any sort did we hear except the chiming clock upon the stairs. It was a most melancholy vigil and ended by each of us falling asleep in our chairs. Fortunately we were not discouraged, and we determined to try again. The next night we lowered the lamp and sat smoking cigarettes without making the least sound. It was incredible how slowly the hours crawled by, and yet we were helped through it by the same sort of patient interest which the hunter must feel as he watches the trap into which he hopes the game may wander. One struck, and two, and we had almost for the second time given it up in despair when in an instant we both sat bolt upright in our chairs with all our weary senses keenly on the alert once more. We had heard the creak of a step in the passage.

段.文: 我们听着那脚步声偷偷摸摸地过去，渐渐消失在远处。于是准男爵轻轻打开房门，我们跟了出去。那人已经绕过了楼廊，走廊里一片漆黑。我们悄悄地往前走，一直走到另一边的厢房。正好来得及瞥见那个高个子、留黑胡子的身影，他弓着背，踮着脚尖沿着过道走。接着他走进了上次那扇门。烛光在黑暗中映出门框，一道黄色的光柱射过阴暗的走廊。我们小心翼翼地朝那里挪过去，每块地板都先试一试，才敢把全身的重量放上去。我们事先留了心，把靴子脱在了屋里。即使这样，旧地板在我们脚下还是噼啪作响，嘎吱嘎吱。有时候，简直不可能想象他会听不见我们走近。不过幸好这人耳朵有点背，而且他全神贯注在自己干的事情上。我们终于走到门口，往里一看，只见他蹲在窗前，手里拿着蜡烛，那张苍白而专注的脸紧贴着窗玻璃，和我两天前看到的一模一样。
段.en: Very stealthily we heard it pass along until it died away in the distance. Then the baronet gently opened his door and we set out in pursuit. Already our man had gone round the gallery and the corridor was all in darkness. Softly we stole along until we had come into the other wing. We were just in time to catch a glimpse of the tall, black-bearded figure, his shoulders rounded as he tiptoed down the passage. Then he passed through the same door as before, and the light of the candle framed it in the darkness and shot one single yellow beam across the gloom of the corridor. We shuffled cautiously towards it, trying every plank before we dared to put our whole weight upon it. We had taken the precaution of leaving our boots behind us, but, even so, the old boards snapped and creaked beneath our tread. Sometimes it seemed impossible that he should fail to hear our approach. However, the man is fortunately rather deaf, and he was entirely preoccupied in that which he was doing. When at last we reached the door and peeped through we found him crouching at the window, candle in hand, his white, intent face pressed against the pane, exactly as I had seen him two nights before.

段.文: 我们事先没定什么行动计划，可准男爵这个人，总觉得最直接的办法就是最自然的办法。他走进房间。他一进去，巴里摩尔就倒抽一口冷气，嘶的一声从窗前跳起来，脸色铁青，浑身发抖，站在我们面前。他那双黑眼睛从惨白如面具的脸上瞪着，充满了恐惧和惊愕，从亨利爵士看到我，又从我看到亨利爵士。
段.en: We had arranged no plan of campaign, but the baronet is a man to whom the most direct way is always the most natural. He walked into the room, and as he did so Barrymore sprang up from the window with a sharp hiss of his breath and stood, livid and trembling, before us. His dark eyes, glaring out of the white mask of his face, were full of horror and astonishment as he gazed from Sir Henry to me.

段.文: “巴里摩尔，你在这儿干什么？”
段.en: “What are you doing here, Barrymore?”

段.文: “没干什么，先生。”他慌得几乎说不出话来，蜡烛一抖，影子也跟着上下乱跳。“是窗户，先生。我夜里到处看看，看窗户是不是都关好了。”
段.en: “Nothing, sir.” His agitation was so great that he could hardly speak, and the shadows sprang up and down from the shaking of his candle. “It was the window, sir. I go round at night to see that they are fastened.”

段.文: “在三楼？”
段.en: “On the second floor?”

段.文: “是的，先生，所有的窗户。”
段.en: “Yes, sir, all the windows.”

段.文: “听着，巴里摩尔，”亨利爵士严厉地说，“我们已经下定决心要你说实话，所以你早说比晚说省事。来吧！别撒谎！你在那扇窗前干什么？”
段.en: “Look here, Barrymore,” said Sir Henry sternly, “we have made up our minds to have the truth out of you, so it will save you trouble to tell it sooner rather than later. Come, now! No lies! What were you doing at that window?”

段.文: 这家伙无可奈何地看着我们，绞着双手，就像一个疑虑重重、痛苦到了极点的人。
段.en: The fellow looked at us in a helpless way, and he wrung his hands together like one who is in the last extremity of doubt and misery.

段.文: “我没干坏事，先生。我只是拿着蜡烛对着窗户。”
段.en: “I was doing no harm, sir. I was holding a candle to the window.”

段.文: “那你为什么拿蜡烛对着窗户？”
段.en: “And why were you holding a candle to the window?”

段.文: “别问我，亨利爵士——别问我！我向您保证，先生，这不是我自己的秘密，我不能说。要是只关系到我一个人，我是不会瞒着您的。”
段.en: “Don’t ask me, Sir Henry—don’t ask me! I give you my word, sir, that it is not my secret, and that I cannot tell it. If it concerned no one but myself I would not try to keep it from you.”

段.文: 我突然想到一个主意，就从管家发抖的手里接过蜡烛。
段.en: A sudden idea occurred to me, and I took the candle from the trembling hand of the butler.

段.文: “他一定是拿它当信号，”我说，“我们看看有没有回应。”我像他那样举着蜡烛，凝视着窗外漆黑的夜。月亮躲在云后面，我只能隐约分辨出黑压压的一排树，和颜色稍浅的一片荒原。接着我欢呼了一声：一个针尖大的黄色光点忽然刺破了黑幕，在窗框围出的那块黑色方格中央，稳稳地亮着。
段.en: “He must have been holding it as a signal,” said I. “Let us see if there is any answer.” I held it as he had done, and stared out into the darkness of the night. Vaguely I could discern the black bank of the trees and the lighter expanse of the moor, for the moon was behind the clouds. And then I gave a cry of exultation, for a tiny pinpoint of yellow light had suddenly transfixed the dark veil, and glowed steadily in the centre of the black square framed by the window.

段.文: “在那儿！”我叫道。
段.en: “There it is!” I cried.

段.文: “不，不，先生，那没什么——根本没什么！”管家插嘴说，“我向您保证，先生——”
段.en: “No, no, sir, it is nothing—nothing at all!” the butler broke in; “I assure you, sir—”

段.文: “华生，把你的灯在窗前来回移动！”准男爵叫道，“看，那边的也动了！好啊，你这个混蛋，你还敢说这不是信号？来，说出来！外面那个同伙是谁？你们在搞什么阴谋？”
段.en: “Move your light across the window, Watson!” cried the baronet. “See, the other moves also! Now, you rascal, do you deny that it is a signal? Come, speak up! Who is your confederate out yonder, and what is this conspiracy that is going on?”

段.文: 那人的脸上露出了公然反抗的神色。“这是我的事，不是您的事。我不说。”
段.en: The man’s face became openly defiant. “It is my business, and not yours. I will not tell.”

段.文: “那你马上给我走人。”
段.en: “Then you leave my employment right away.”

段.文: “好的，先生。非走不可，那就走吧。”
段.en: “Very good, sir. If I must I must.”

段.文: “而且是不光彩地走。见鬼，你真该为自己感到羞耻。你家和我家在这个屋檐下一起生活了一百多年，可现在我却发现你深深卷进了什么对付我的阴谋。”
段.en: “And you go in disgrace. By thunder, you may well be ashamed of yourself. Your family has lived with mine for over a hundred years under this roof, and here I find you deep in some dark plot against me.”

段.文: “不，不，先生！不，不是对付您！”这是一个女人的声音。巴里摩尔太太站在门口，脸色比她丈夫还要苍白，神情更加惊恐。她身材臃肿，披着披肩，穿着裙子，要不是脸上那种强烈的感情，样子也许会有点滑稽。
段.en: “No, no, sir; no, not against you!” It was a woman’s voice, and Mrs. Barrymore, paler and more horror-struck than her husband, was standing at the door. Her bulky figure in a shawl and skirt might have been comic were it not for the intensity of feeling upon her face.

段.文: “我们得走了，伊丽莎。到头了。你去收拾东西吧。”管家说。
段.en: “We have to go, Eliza. This is the end of it. You can pack our things,” said the butler.

段.文: “哦，约翰，约翰，是我把你害到这一步的吗？亨利爵士，这都是我干的——全是我。他什么也没做，都是为了我，是我求他的。”
段.en: “Oh, John, John, have I brought you to this? It is my doing, Sir Henry—all mine. He has done nothing except for my sake and because I asked him.”

段.文: “那就说出来！这是怎么回事？”
段.en: “Speak out, then! What does it mean?”

段.文: “我那不幸的弟弟在荒原上快要饿死了。我们不能让他死在我们家门口。这灯光是告诉他，吃的东西已经准备好了；他在外面点的灯，是告诉我们把东西送到哪儿。”
段.en: “My unhappy brother is starving on the moor. We cannot let him perish at our very gates. The light is a signal to him that food is ready for him, and his light out yonder is to show the spot to which to bring it.”

段.文: “那么你弟弟是——”
段.en: “Then your brother is—”

段.文: “那个逃犯，先生——罪犯塞尔登。”
段.en: “The escaped convict, sir—Selden, the criminal.”

段.文: “这是实话，先生，”巴里摩尔说，“我说过这不是我的秘密，我不能告诉您。可现在您已经听到了，您会明白，即使有什么阴谋，也不是对付您的。”
段.en: “That’s the truth, sir,” said Barrymore. “I said that it was not my secret and that I could not tell it to you. But now you have heard it, and you will see that if there was a plot it was not against you.”

段.文: 原来，这就是夜里偷偷摸摸地出行、窗前亮灯的缘由。亨利爵士和我都惊讶地盯着这个女人。这样一个呆板而规矩体面的人，竟然和全国最臭名昭著的罪犯之一是一母同胞，这可能吗？
段.en: This, then, was the explanation of the stealthy expeditions at night and the light at the window. Sir Henry and I both stared at the woman in amazement. Was it possible that this stolidly respectable person was of the same blood as one of the most notorious criminals in the country?

段.文: “是的，先生，我娘家姓塞尔登，他是我弟弟。他小时候我们太娇惯他了，事事都由着他，结果他以为这世界是专为让他快活才造出来的，他想怎么样就可以怎么样。后来他长大了，交上了坏朋友，魔鬼钻进了他的心，他伤透了我母亲的心，把我们家的名声拖进了泥里。他犯了一桩罪又一桩罪，越陷越深，要不是上帝开恩，早就上了绞架。可是先生，在我眼里，他永远是那个我当姐姐的抱过、陪他玩过的卷头发小男孩。所以他才越狱的，先生。他知道我在这儿，知道我们不能不帮他。有一天夜里，他拖着身子来到这里，又累又饿，看守紧跟在后面追，我们能怎么办？我们收留了他，给他吃的，照顾他。后来您回来了，先生。我弟弟觉得，在风头过去之前，待在荒原上比待在哪儿都安全，所以他就躲在那里。不过每隔一晚，我们就在窗前放一盏灯，看他还在不在。要是有回应，我丈夫就给他送些面包和肉去。我们天天盼着他走了，可只要他还在那儿，我们就不能不管他。我是个诚实的基督徒，这就是全部的实情。您会明白，如果这件事有什么错，错不在我丈夫，而在我。他做的一切都是为了我。”
段.en: “Yes, sir, my name was Selden, and he is my younger brother. We humoured him too much when he was a lad and gave him his own way in everything until he came to think that the world was made for his pleasure, and that he could do what he liked in it. Then as he grew older he met wicked companions, and the devil entered into him until he broke my mother’s heart and dragged our name in the dirt. From crime to crime he sank lower and lower until it is only the mercy of God which has snatched him from the scaffold; but to me, sir, he was always the little curly-headed boy that I had nursed and played with as an elder sister would. That was why he broke prison, sir. He knew that I was here and that we could not refuse to help him. When he dragged himself here one night, weary and starving, with the warders hard at his heels, what could we do? We took him in and fed him and cared for him. Then you returned, sir, and my brother thought he would be safer on the moor than anywhere else until the hue and cry was over, so he lay in hiding there. But every second night we made sure if he was still there by putting a light in the window, and if there was an answer my husband took out some bread and meat to him. Every day we hoped that he was gone, but as long as he was there we could not desert him. That is the whole truth, as I am an honest Christian woman and you will see that if there is blame in the matter it does not lie with my husband but with me, for whose sake he has done all that he has.”

段.文: 这个女人说得极其恳切，让人不得不信。
段.en: The woman’s words came with an intense earnestness which carried conviction with them.

段.文: “这是真的吗，巴里摩尔？”
段.en: “Is this true, Barrymore?”

段.文: “是的，亨利爵士，句句是真。”
段.en: “Yes, Sir Henry. Every word of it.”

段.文: “好吧，你护着自己的妻子，我不能怪你。把我刚才说的话忘了吧。你们俩回房去，这件事明天早上再谈。”
段.en: “Well, I cannot blame you for standing by your own wife. Forget what I have said. Go to your room, you two, and we shall talk further about this matter in the morning.”

段.文: 他们走后，我们又朝窗外望去。亨利爵士把窗户一把推开，寒冷的夜风扑面而来。在远处漆黑的地方，那个小小的黄色光点还在亮着。
段.en: When they were gone we looked out of the window again. Sir Henry had flung it open, and the cold night wind beat in upon our faces. Far away in the black distance there still glowed that one tiny point of yellow light.

段.文: “真不知道他怎么敢这样。”亨利爵士说。
段.en: “I wonder he dares,” said Sir Henry.

段.文: “也许那灯放的位置很巧，只有从这里才看得见。”
段.en: “It may be so placed as to be only visible from here.”

段.文: “很可能。你看有多远？”
段.en: “Very likely. How far do you think it is?”

段.文: “我想是在裂岩那边。”
段.en: “Out by the Cleft Tor, I think.”

段.文: “不超过一两英里吧。”
段.en: “Not more than a mile or two off.”

段.文: “恐怕还不到。”
段.en: “Hardly that.”

段.文: “嗯，既然巴里摩尔得把吃的送过去，那就不会太远。这个恶棍正守在那根蜡烛旁边等着呢。见鬼，华生，我要出去抓住那个人！”
段.en: “Well, it cannot be far if Barrymore had to carry out the food to it. And he is waiting, this villain, beside that candle. By thunder, Watson, I am going out to take that man!”

段.文: 我心里也闪过了同样的念头。巴里摩尔夫妇并不是主动向我们吐露的，他们的秘密是被我们逼出来的。这个人对社会是个威胁，是个十足的恶棍，既不值得同情，也没有任何可以原谅的地方。我们趁这个机会把他送回到不能再害人的地方去，不过是尽我们的本分罢了。他生性残暴凶狠，要是我们袖手旁观，别人就得付出代价。比如说，我们的邻居斯台普顿一家随便哪天夜里都可能遭到他的袭击。也许正是想到这一点，亨利爵士才对这次冒险这么起劲。
段.en: The same thought had crossed my own mind. It was not as if the Barrymores had taken us into their confidence. Their secret had been forced from them. The man was a danger to the community, an unmitigated scoundrel for whom there was neither pity nor excuse. We were only doing our duty in taking this chance of putting him back where he could do no harm. With his brutal and violent nature, others would have to pay the price if we held our hands. Any night, for example, our neighbours the Stapletons might be attacked by him, and it may have been the thought of this which made Sir Henry so keen upon the adventure.

段.文: “我跟你去。”我说。
段.en: “I will come,” said I.

段.文: “那就去拿你的左轮手枪，穿上靴子。越早出发越好，那家伙说不定会把灯灭了溜掉。”
段.en: “Then get your revolver and put on your boots. The sooner we start the better, as the fellow may put out his light and be off.”

段.文: 五分钟后，我们已经出了门，开始了这次行动。我们匆匆穿过漆黑的灌木丛，秋风低沉地呜咽着，落叶沙沙作响。夜里的空气里弥漫着潮湿和腐烂的气味。月亮不时探出头来一下，可是乌云在天上飞驰。我们刚走上荒原，就下起了细雨。那点灯光仍在前方稳稳地亮着。
段.en: In five minutes we were outside the door, starting upon our expedition. We hurried through the dark shrubbery, amid the dull moaning of the autumn wind and the rustle of the falling leaves. The night air was heavy with the smell of damp and decay. Now and again the moon peeped out for an instant, but clouds were driving over the face of the sky, and just as we came out on the moor a thin rain began to fall. The light still burned steadily in front.

段.文: “你带武器了吗？”我问。
段.en: “Are you armed?” I asked.

段.文: “我带了一根猎鞭。”
段.en: “I have a hunting-crop.”

段.文: “我们得赶快逼近他，据说他是个亡命之徒。我们要出其不意，趁他还来不及反抗就把他制住。”
段.en: “We must close in on him rapidly, for he is said to be a desperate fellow. We shall take him by surprise and have him at our mercy before he can resist.”

段.文: “我说，华生，”准男爵说，“福尔摩斯会怎么说？那句什么在黑暗时刻、邪恶势力最猖獗的话，怎么说来着？”
段.en: “I say, Watson,” said the baronet, “what would Holmes say to this? How about that hour of darkness in which the power of evil is exalted?”
