段.文: 像是在回答他的话，荒原那无边的黑暗中突然响起了那种奇怪的叫声，就是我在格林彭大泥沼边上听到过的那种。它随着风穿过寂静的夜传来：先是长长的、低沉的咕哝，接着升成一声嚎叫，最后化为凄凉的呜咽，渐渐消失了。它一遍又一遍地响起，整个天地都随之震颤，尖利、狂野，充满威胁。准男爵一把抓住我的袖子，他的脸在黑暗中隐隐泛着白光。
段.en: As if in answer to his words there rose suddenly out of the vast gloom of the moor that strange cry which I had already heard upon the borders of the great Grimpen Mire. It came with the wind through the silence of the night, a long, deep mutter, then a rising howl, and then the sad moan in which it died away. Again and again it sounded, the whole air throbbing with it, strident, wild, and menacing. The baronet caught my sleeve and his face glimmered white through the darkness.

段.文: “天哪，那是什么，华生？”
段.en: “My God, what’s that, Watson?”

段.文: “我不知道。是荒原上的一种声音。我以前听到过一次。”
段.en: “I don’t know. It’s a sound they have on the moor. I heard it once before.”

段.文: 声音消失了，四周陷入一片死寂。我们竖起耳朵听着，却什么也没再听见。
段.en: It died away, and an absolute silence closed in upon us. We stood straining our ears, but nothing came.

段.文: “华生，”准男爵说，“那是猎犬的叫声。”
段.en: “Watson,” said the baronet, “it was the cry of a hound.”

段.文: 我浑身的血都凉了，因为他的声音发颤，说明他突然被一阵恐惧攫住了。
段.en: My blood ran cold in my veins, for there was a break in his voice which told of the sudden horror which had seized him.

段.文: “他们管这声音叫什么？”他问。
段.en: “What do they call this sound?” he asked.
“Who?”

段.文: “这一带的乡下人。”
段.en: “The folk on the countryside.”

段.文: “哦，他们都是些没知识的人。他们管它叫什么，你何必在意？”
段.en: “Oh, they are ignorant people. Why should you mind what they call it?”

段.文: “告诉我，华生。他们怎么说？”
段.en: “Tell me, Watson. What do they say of it?”

段.文: 我犹豫了一下，可还是躲不开这个问题。
段.en: I hesitated but could not escape the question.

段.文: “他们说，那是巴斯克维尔的猎犬在叫。”
段.en: “They say it is the cry of the Hound of the Baskervilles.”

段.文: 他呻吟了一声，沉默了一会儿。
段.en: He groaned and was silent for a few moments.

段.文: “是猎犬，”他终于说，“不过好像是从好几英里外传来的，我想是在那边。”
段.en: “A hound it was,” he said at last, “but it seemed to come from miles away, over yonder, I think.”

段.文: “很难说是从哪儿来的。”
段.en: “It was hard to say whence it came.”

段.文: “它随着风一高一低。那边不就是格林彭大泥沼的方向吗？”
段.en: “It rose and fell with the wind. Isn’t that the direction of the great Grimpen Mire?”

段.文: “是的。”
段.en: “Yes, it is.”

段.文: “嗯，就是在那边。说吧，华生，你自己难道不觉得那是猎犬的叫声吗？我又不是小孩子，你用不着怕说实话。”
段.en: “Well, it was up there. Come now, Watson, didn’t you think yourself that it was the cry of a hound? I am not a child. You need not fear to speak the truth.”

段.文: “我上次听到的时候，斯台普顿和我在一起。他说那可能是一种怪鸟在叫。”
段.en: “Stapleton was with me when I heard it last. He said that it might be the calling of a strange bird.”

段.文: “不，不，那是猎犬。天哪，难道那些故事里真有几分是真的？难道我真的面临着这么一种阴森的危险？你不信，对吧，华生？”
段.en: “No, no, it was a hound. My God, can there be some truth in all these stories? Is it possible that I am really in danger from so dark a cause? You don’t believe it, do you, Watson?”

段.文: “不信，不信。”
段.en: “No, no.”

段.文: “可是在伦敦拿它说笑是一回事，站在这黑漆漆的荒原上听到那样的叫声，又是另一回事。还有我伯父！他倒下的地方旁边就有猎犬的脚印。一切都对上了。华生，我不觉得自己是个胆小鬼，可那声音简直把我的血都冻住了。你摸摸我的手！”
段.en: “And yet it was one thing to laugh about it in London, and it is another to stand out here in the darkness of the moor and to hear such a cry as that. And my uncle! There was the footprint of the hound beside him as he lay. It all fits together. I don’t think that I am a coward, Watson, but that sound seemed to freeze my very blood. Feel my hand!”

段.文: 他的手冷得像一块大理石。
段.en: It was as cold as a block of marble.

段.文: “明天你就好了。”
段.en: “You’ll be all right tomorrow.”

段.文: “我看那叫声我是忘不掉了。你说我们现在怎么办？”
段.en: “I don’t think I’ll get that cry out of my head. What do you advise that we do now?”

段.文: “我们回去吧？”
段.en: “Shall we turn back?”

段.文: “不，见鬼。我们出来是要抓那个人的，就要抓到他。我们追逃犯，说不定还有一条地狱猎犬在追我们。走吧！就算地狱里的恶魔全都在荒原上乱跑，我们也要干到底。”
段.en: “No, by thunder; we have come out to get our man, and we will do it. We after the convict, and a hell-hound, as likely as not, after us. Come on! We’ll see it through if all the fiends of the pit were loose upon the moor.”

段.文: 我们在黑暗中跌跌撞撞地慢慢往前走，四周是嶙峋山丘黑黢黢的影子，前方那点黄色的灯光稳稳地亮着。在漆黑的夜里，最容易骗人的就是灯光的远近：有时候那点微光好像远在天边，有时候又好像离我们只有几码远。不过我们终于看清了它的来处，这才知道我们确实已经很近了。一根淌着蜡泪的蜡烛插在岩石缝里，两边都有岩石挡着，既能挡风，又能让它除了巴斯克维尔庄园那个方向以外，从别处都看不见。一块花岗岩巨石遮住了我们，我们蹲在它后面，从石头上方望着那盏信号灯。荒原中央就点着这么一根蜡烛，附近没有一点生命的迹象——只有那一道笔直的黄色火焰，和它两边岩石上的反光，看起来真是怪异。
段.en: We stumbled slowly along in the darkness, with the black loom of the craggy hills around us, and the yellow speck of light burning steadily in front. There is nothing so deceptive as the distance of a light upon a pitch-dark night, and sometimes the glimmer seemed to be far away upon the horizon and sometimes it might have been within a few yards of us. But at last we could see whence it came, and then we knew that we were indeed very close. A guttering candle was stuck in a crevice of the rocks which flanked it on each side so as to keep the wind from it and also to prevent it from being visible, save in the direction of Baskerville Hall. A boulder of granite concealed our approach, and crouching behind it we gazed over it at the signal light. It was strange to see this single candle burning there in the middle of the moor, with no sign of life near it—just the one straight yellow flame and the gleam of the rock on each side of it.

段.文: “我们现在怎么办？”亨利爵士小声问。
段.en: “What shall we do now?” whispered Sir Henry.

段.文: “在这儿等着。他一定就在灯附近。我们看看能不能瞥见他。”
段.en: “Wait here. He must be near his light. Let us see if we can get a glimpse of him.”

段.文: 我话音刚落，我们俩就都看见了他。在蜡烛所在的那道石缝上方，从岩石后面探出一张邪恶的黄脸，一张可怕的野兽般的脸，上面布满了种种邪念刻下的皱纹和沟壑。脸上糊满泥污，胡子乱蓬蓬地竖着，头发纠结成团地披挂下来，真像是古时候住在山坡洞穴里的野人。下面的烛光映在他那双狡猾的小眼睛里。那双眼睛凶狠地在黑暗中左右张望，就像一只狡诈凶猛的野兽听见了猎人的脚步声。
段.en: The words were hardly out of my mouth when we both saw him. Over the rocks, in the crevice of which the candle burned, there was thrust out an evil yellow face, a terrible animal face, all seamed and scored with vile passions. Foul with mire, with a bristling beard, and hung with matted hair, it might well have belonged to one of those old savages who dwelt in the burrows on the hillsides. The light beneath him was reflected in his small, cunning eyes which peered fiercely to right and left through the darkness like a crafty and savage animal who has heard the steps of the hunters.

段.文: 显然有什么东西引起了他的怀疑。也许巴里摩尔和他另有什么暗号，我们没有发出；也许这家伙另有什么理由觉得情况不对。总之我从他那张邪恶的脸上看出了恐惧。他随时都可能扑灭灯光，消失在黑暗中。于是我向前冲去，亨利爵士也冲了上去。就在这时，那逃犯冲我们尖声骂了一句，扔过来一块石头，砸在给我们作掩护的那块巨石上，碎成了好几块。他跳起身转身就跑，我瞥见了他那矮壮结实的身影。就在这时，真是运气好，月亮从云里钻了出来。我们冲过山顶，只见那家伙正飞快地顺着另一边山坡往下跑，像山羊一样敏捷地跳过路上的石头。要是我用左轮手枪碰运气远远开一枪，也许能打伤他。可我带枪只是为了在遭到袭击时自卫，不是为了朝一个正在逃跑、手无寸铁的人开枪。
段.en: Something had evidently aroused his suspicions. It may have been that Barrymore had some private signal which we had neglected to give, or the fellow may have had some other reason for thinking that all was not well, but I could read his fears upon his wicked face. Any instant he might dash out the light and vanish in the darkness. I sprang forward therefore, and Sir Henry did the same. At the same moment the convict screamed out a curse at us and hurled a rock which splintered up against the boulder which had sheltered us. I caught one glimpse of his short, squat, strongly built figure as he sprang to his feet and turned to run. At the same moment by a lucky chance the moon broke through the clouds. We rushed over the brow of the hill, and there was our man running with great speed down the other side, springing over the stones in his way with the activity of a mountain goat. A lucky long shot of my revolver might have crippled him, but I had brought it only to defend myself if attacked and not to shoot an unarmed man who was running away.

段.文: 我们俩都跑得很快，身体也算练得不错，可很快就发现根本没有希望追上他。在月光下，我们看了他很久，直到他变成一个小黑点，在远处一座山坡的巨石之间飞快地移动。我们跑啊跑，直到上气不接下气，可我们和他之间的距离却越拉越大。最后我们停了下来，坐在两块石头上喘气，眼睁睁地看着他消失在远方。
段.en: We were both swift runners and in fairly good training, but we soon found that we had no chance of overtaking him. We saw him for a long time in the moonlight until he was only a small speck moving swiftly among the boulders upon the side of a distant hill. We ran and ran until we were completely blown, but the space between us grew ever wider. Finally we stopped and sat panting on two rocks, while we watched him disappearing in the distance.

段.文: 就在这时，发生了一件极其奇怪、出乎意料的事。我们放弃了这场毫无希望的追赶，已经从石头上站起来，正转身要回家。月亮低低地挂在右边，一座花岗岩突岩那参差的尖顶，正好衬在银色月盘的下缘上。就在那里，在明亮的背景上，我看见突岩上站着一个人，轮廓漆黑，像一尊乌木雕像。福尔摩斯，别以为那是幻觉。我向你保证，我这辈子从没把什么东西看得这么清楚过。据我判断，那是个又高又瘦的男人。他两腿微微分开站着，双臂交叉，低着头，好像在沉思面前那片由泥炭和花岗岩构成的广袤荒野。他简直就像是那个可怕地方的精灵。那不是逃犯。这个人离逃犯消失的地方很远，而且个子要高得多。我惊叫一声，指给准男爵看。可就在我转身去抓他胳膊的一瞬间，那人不见了。那座花岗岩尖顶依然切着月亮的下缘，可顶上已经没有了那个沉默不动的身影。
段.en: And it was at this moment that there occurred a most strange and unexpected thing. We had risen from our rocks and were turning to go home, having abandoned the hopeless chase. The moon was low upon the right, and the jagged pinnacle of a granite tor stood up against the lower curve of its silver disc. There, outlined as black as an ebony statue on that shining background, I saw the figure of a man upon the tor. Do not think that it was a delusion, Holmes. I assure you that I have never in my life seen anything more clearly. As far as I could judge, the figure was that of a tall, thin man. He stood with his legs a little separated, his arms folded, his head bowed, as if he were brooding over that enormous wilderness of peat and granite which lay before him. He might have been the very spirit of that terrible place. It was not the convict. This man was far from the place where the latter had disappeared. Besides, he was a much taller man. With a cry of surprise I pointed him out to the baronet, but in the instant during which I had turned to grasp his arm the man was gone. There was the sharp pinnacle of granite still cutting the lower edge of the moon, but its peak bore no trace of that silent and motionless figure.

段.文: 我想往那个方向去，搜一搜那座突岩，可那里离得挺远。准男爵的神经还因为那声叫声在发颤——那声音让他想起了家族的阴暗故事——所以他已经没有心思再去冒险了。他没看见突岩上那个孤零零的人，也就体会不到那人奇异的出现和那种威严的姿态给我带来的震动。“肯定是个看守，”他说，“自从这家伙逃出来以后，荒原上到处都是看守。”嗯，也许他的解释是对的，不过我希望能有进一步的证据。今天我们打算通知普林斯敦那边，告诉他们该到哪里去找那个逃犯。只可惜我们没能亲手把他抓回去，尝尝那份胜利的滋味。这就是昨晚的经历。亲爱的福尔摩斯，你得承认，在写报告这件事上我很对得起你了。我告诉你的很多事无疑毫不相干，可我还是觉得，最好把所有的事实都告诉你，让你自己挑出那些最有助于你得出结论的。我们确实有了一些进展。就巴里摩尔夫妇来说，我们已经找到了他们行动的动机，这让局面清楚了许多。可是荒原和它的种种秘密、它那些奇怪的居民，依然和从前一样难以捉摸。也许下一封信里，我能把这方面也弄清楚一些。最好的办法是你能到我们这儿来。不管怎样，几天之内你还会收到我的信。
段.en: I wished to go in that direction and to search the tor, but it was some distance away. The baronet’s nerves were still quivering from that cry, which recalled the dark story of his family, and he was not in the mood for fresh adventures. He had not seen this lonely man upon the tor and could not feel the thrill which his strange presence and his commanding attitude had given to me. “A warder, no doubt,” said he. “The moor has been thick with them since this fellow escaped.” Well, perhaps his explanation may be the right one, but I should like to have some further proof of it. Today we mean to communicate to the Princetown people where they should look for their missing man, but it is hard lines that we have not actually had the triumph of bringing him back as our own prisoner. Such are the adventures of last night, and you must acknowledge, my dear Holmes, that I have done you very well in the matter of a report. Much of what I tell you is no doubt quite irrelevant, but still I feel that it is best that I should let you have all the facts and leave you to select for yourself those which will be of most service to you in helping you to your conclusions. We are certainly making some progress. So far as the Barrymores go we have found the motive of their actions, and that has cleared up the situation very much. But the moor with its mysteries and its strange inhabitants remains as inscrutable as ever. Perhaps in my next I may be able to throw some light upon this also. Best of all would it be if you could come down to us. In any case you will hear from me again in the course of the next few days.

章.原题: Extract from the Diary of Dr. Watson

段.文: 到这里为止，我都可以直接引用最初那些天寄给夏洛克·福尔摩斯的报告。但叙述到了这一步，我不得不放弃这个办法，重新依靠自己的回忆，再加上我当时记的日记。从日记里摘几段，就能把我带到后来那些场面——那些场面的每个细节都深深刻在我的记忆里，永远抹不掉。下面就从那天早上写起：头天夜里，我们追捕逃犯扑了个空，还在荒原上遇到了别的怪事。
段.en: So far I have been able to quote from the reports which I have forwarded during these early days to Sherlock Holmes. Now, however, I have arrived at a point in my narrative where I am compelled to abandon this method and to trust once more to my recollections, aided by the diary which I kept at the time. A few extracts from the latter will carry me on to those scenes which are indelibly fixed in every detail upon my memory. I proceed, then, from the morning which followed our abortive chase of the convict and our other strange experiences upon the moor.

段.文: 10月16日——天色阴沉，雾气弥漫，下着蒙蒙细雨。翻滚的云层把宅子团团围住，偶尔云层升起，露出荒原上凄凉起伏的轮廓。山坡上挂着一道道细细的银色水流，远处的巨石湿漉漉的，被光一照，闪闪发亮。屋外屋里都叫人郁闷。经过昨夜的刺激，准男爵情绪低落到了极点。我自己也觉得心头压着一块石头，总感到危险就要来临——这种危险时时都在，又说不清是什么，所以更加可怕。
段.en: October 16th.—A dull and foggy day with a drizzle of rain. The house is banked in with rolling clouds, which rise now and then to show the dreary curves of the moor, with thin, silver veins upon the sides of the hills, and the distant boulders gleaming where the light strikes upon their wet faces. It is melancholy outside and in. The baronet is in a black reaction after the excitements of the night. I am conscious myself of a weight at my heart and a feeling of impending danger—ever present danger, which is the more terrible because I am unable to define it.

段.文: 我有这种感觉，难道没有理由吗？想想这一连串的事情吧，桩桩件件都指向某种在我们周围作祟的邪恶力量。先是庄园的上一任主人死了，死的情形和家族传说里说的一模一样；又有农民一再说，在荒原上见过一只怪物。我也两次亲耳听到过那种声音，像是远处猎犬在嚎叫。说它真的超出了自然规律，那是难以置信、绝不可能的。一条鬼犬，既能留下实实在在的脚印，又能让嚎叫声响彻四野，这种事简直想都不用想。斯台普顿也许会相信这种迷信，莫蒂默也许也会；但如果说我这辈子有什么长处，那就是讲常识，什么也没法让我相信这种东西。信了它，我就跟这些可怜的农民一样了——他们光说是条魔犬还不满足，非得说它嘴里眼里都喷着地狱之火。福尔摩斯绝不会理会这种胡思乱想，而我是替他办事的人。可事实就是事实，我确实两次在荒原上听见过这种叫声。假如真有一条巨大的猎犬在荒原上乱跑，那几乎一切都能解释通了。可这样一条狗能藏在哪儿？它吃什么？它从哪儿来？为什么白天谁也没见过它？不得不承认，用自然原因来解释，碰到的难处几乎和另一种解释一样多。而且，就算撇开猎犬不谈，伦敦那边确实有人在暗中活动：马车里的那个人，还有那封警告亨利爵士别去荒原的信。这些至少是真的，不过它既可能出自一个想保护我们的朋友，也同样可能出自一个敌人。那个朋友或者敌人，现在在哪儿？他留在伦敦了，还是跟着我们来了这里？他会不会——会不会就是我在突岩上看到的那个陌生人？
段.en: And have I not cause for such a feeling? Consider the long sequence of incidents which have all pointed to some sinister influence which is at work around us. There is the death of the last occupant of the Hall, fulfilling so exactly the conditions of the family legend, and there are the repeated reports from peasants of the appearance of a strange creature upon the moor. Twice I have with my own ears heard the sound which resembled the distant baying of a hound. It is incredible, impossible, that it should really be outside the ordinary laws of nature. A spectral hound which leaves material footmarks and fills the air with its howling is surely not to be thought of. Stapleton may fall in with such a superstition, and Mortimer also, but if I have one quality upon earth it is common sense, and nothing will persuade me to believe in such a thing. To do so would be to descend to the level of these poor peasants, who are not content with a mere fiend dog but must needs describe him with hell-fire shooting from his mouth and eyes. Holmes would not listen to such fancies, and I am his agent. But facts are facts, and I have twice heard this crying upon the moor. Suppose that there were really some huge hound loose upon it; that would go far to explain everything. But where could such a hound lie concealed, where did it get its food, where did it come from, how was it that no one saw it by day? It must be confessed that the natural explanation offers almost as many difficulties as the other. And always, apart from the hound, there is the fact of the human agency in London, the man in the cab, and the letter which warned Sir Henry against the moor. This at least was real, but it might have been the work of a protecting friend as easily as of an enemy. Where is that friend or enemy now? Has he remained in London, or has he followed us down here? Could he—could he be the stranger whom I saw upon the tor?

段.文: 不错，我只看了他一眼，可有几点我敢发誓。他不是我在这里见过的任何人，而这一带的邻居我现在都已经见过了。那个身影比斯台普顿高得多，比弗兰克兰瘦得多。也有可能是巴里摩尔，可我们把他留在了身后，我敢肯定他不可能跟上来。这么说，仍然有个陌生人在跟踪我们，就像在伦敦时有个陌生人跟踪我们一样。我们从来没有甩掉过他。要是我能抓住这个人，我们的种种难题也许就终于到头了。从现在起，我要把全部精力都用在这件事上。
段.en: It is true that I have had only the one glance at him, and yet there are some things to which I am ready to swear. He is no one whom I have seen down here, and I have now met all the neighbours. The figure was far taller than that of Stapleton, far thinner than that of Frankland. Barrymore it might possibly have been, but we had left him behind us, and I am certain that he could not have followed us. A stranger then is still dogging us, just as a stranger dogged us in London. We have never shaken him off. If I could lay my hands upon that man, then at last we might find ourselves at the end of all our difficulties. To this one purpose I must now devote all my energies.

段.文: 我起初想把我的计划全都告诉亨利爵士。转念一想，更明智的做法是自己干自己的，跟谁都尽量少说。他沉默寡言，心神不定。荒原上那声嚎叫，让他的神经受了异乎寻常的震动。我不会说任何话来增加他的忧虑，但我要自己采取行动，达到自己的目的。
段.en: My first impulse was to tell Sir Henry all my plans. My second and wisest one is to play my own game and speak as little as possible to anyone. He is silent and distrait. His nerves have been strangely shaken by that sound upon the moor. I will say nothing to add to his anxieties, but I will take my own steps to attain my own end.

段.文: 今天早饭后，出了一场小风波。巴里摩尔请求和亨利爵士谈谈，两人在书房里关起门来谈了好一会儿。我坐在台球室里，不止一次听到他们提高了嗓门，也大致猜得出他们在争什么。过了一阵，准男爵打开门叫我过去。“巴里摩尔觉得受了委屈，”他说，“他认为，他是自愿把秘密告诉我们的，我们却去追捕他的小舅子，这不公道。”
段.en: We had a small scene this morning after breakfast. Barrymore asked leave to speak with Sir Henry, and they were closeted in his study some little time. Sitting in the billiard-room I more than once heard the sound of voices raised, and I had a pretty good idea what the point was which was under discussion. After a time the baronet opened his door and called for me. “Barrymore considers that he has a grievance,” he said. “He thinks that it was unfair on our part to hunt his brother-in-law down when he, of his own free will, had told us the secret.”

段.文: 管家站在我们面前，脸色十分苍白，神情却非常镇定。
段.en: The butler was standing very pale but very collected before us.

段.文: “我刚才话说得也许太冲了，先生，”他说，“如果是这样，我真心请您原谅。不过，今天早上听到你们两位先生回来，又得知你们是去追塞尔登了，我实在非常吃惊。这个可怜的家伙要对付的东西已经够多了，用不着我再给他添上追兵。”
段.en: “I may have spoken too warmly, sir,” said he, “and if I have, I am sure that I beg your pardon. At the same time, I was very much surprised when I heard you two gentlemen come back this morning and learned that you had been chasing Selden. The poor fellow has enough to fight against without my putting more upon his track.”

段.文: “要是你主动告诉我们，那就是另一回事了，”准男爵说，“可你是被逼得没办法了才说的，或者说，是你妻子才说的。”
段.en: “If you had told us of your own free will it would have been a different thing,” said the baronet, “you only told us, or rather your wife only told us, when it was forced from you and you could not help yourself.”

段.文: “我没想到您会利用这件事，亨利爵士——我真没想到。”
段.en: “I didn’t think you would have taken advantage of it, Sir Henry—indeed I didn’t.”

段.文: “这个人对大家都是个威胁。荒原上零零散散有好些孤零零的人家，而他是个什么都干得出来的家伙。你只要看他一眼就明白了。就拿斯台普顿先生家来说吧，除了他自己，没有别人能保护那个家。不把他关起来，谁都不安全。”
段.en: “The man is a public danger. There are lonely houses scattered over the moor, and he is a fellow who would stick at nothing. You only want to get a glimpse of his face to see that. Look at Mr. Stapleton’s house, for example, with no one but himself to defend it. There’s no safety for anyone until he is under lock and key.”

段.文: “他不会闯进哪户人家的，先生。这一点我可以郑重向您保证。而且他再也不会在这个国家给谁添麻烦了。我向您担保，亨利爵士，用不了几天，一切就都安排好了，他就会动身去南美洲。看在上帝的分上，先生，求您别让警察知道他还在荒原上。他们已经不在那一带搜捕了，他可以安安静静地躲着，等船准备好。您要是告发他，我和我妻子也会惹上麻烦。求求您，先生，什么也别跟警察说。”
段.en: “He’ll break into no house, sir. I give you my solemn word upon that. But he will never trouble anyone in this country again. I assure you, Sir Henry, that in a very few days the necessary arrangements will have been made and he will be on his way to South America. For God’s sake, sir, I beg of you not to let the police know that he is still on the moor. They have given up the chase there, and he can lie quiet until the ship is ready for him. You can’t tell on him without getting my wife and me into trouble. I beg you, sir, to say nothing to the police.”

段.文: “你怎么看，华生？”
段.en: “What do you say, Watson?”

段.文: 我耸了耸肩。“要是他能平安离开这个国家，纳税人倒是少了个负担。”
段.en: I shrugged my shoulders. “If he were safely out of the country it would relieve the tax-payer of a burden.”

段.文: “可是他走之前，会不会拦路抢劫谁呢？”
段.en: “But how about the chance of his holding someone up before he goes?”

段.文: “他不会干那么疯狂的事，先生。他需要的东西，我们都给他备齐了。犯一次案，就等于暴露了他藏在哪儿。”
段.en: “He would not do anything so mad, sir. We have provided him with all that he can want. To commit a crime would be to show where he was hiding.”

段.文: “这倒是真的，”亨利爵士说，“好吧，巴里摩尔——”
段.en: “That is true,” said Sir Henry. “Well, Barrymore—”

段.文: “上帝保佑您，先生，我从心底里感谢您！要是他再被抓回去，我那可怜的妻子会活不下去的。”
段.en: “God bless you, sir, and thank you from my heart! It would have killed my poor wife had he been taken again.”

段.文: “华生，我看咱们这是在包庇重罪犯了吧？不过，听了那些话以后，我觉得自己没法把这个人交出去，那就这么定了。好了，巴里摩尔，你可以走了。”
段.en: “I guess we are aiding and abetting a felony, Watson? But, after what we have heard I don’t feel as if I could give the man up, so there is an end of it. All right, Barrymore, you can go.”

段.文: 那人结结巴巴说了几句感激的话，转身要走，却又犹豫了一下，走了回来。
段.en: With a few broken words of gratitude the man turned, but he hesitated and then came back.

段.文: “您待我们这么好，先生，我也想尽力报答您。我知道一件事，亨利爵士，也许我早该说出来，可我是在验尸之后很久才发现的。这件事我还从没对任何人提过一个字。是关于可怜的查尔斯爵士的死。”
段.en: “You’ve been so kind to us, sir, that I should like to do the best I can for you in return. I know something, Sir Henry, and perhaps I should have said it before, but it was long after the inquest that I found it out. I’ve never breathed a word about it yet to mortal man. It’s about poor Sir Charles’s death.”

段.文: 准男爵和我都站了起来。“你知道他是怎么死的？”
段.en: The baronet and I were both upon our feet. “Do you know how he died?”

段.文: “不，先生，这个我不知道。”
段.en: “No, sir, I don’t know that.”

段.文: “那是什么事？”
段.en: “What then?”

段.文: “我知道他那个时候为什么会在那道门边。他是去见一个女人。”
段.en: “I know why he was at the gate at that hour. It was to meet a woman.”

段.文: “去见一个女人！他？”
段.en: “To meet a woman! He?”

段.文: “是的，先生。”
段.en: “Yes, sir.”

段.文: “那女人叫什么名字？”
段.en: “And the woman’s name?”

段.文: “名字我说不出来，先生，但我能告诉您她名字的缩写。她的缩写是L. L.。”
段.en: “I can’t give you the name, sir, but I can give you the initials. Her initials were L. L.”

段.文: “你是怎么知道的，巴里摩尔？”
段.en: “How do you know this, Barrymore?”

段.文: “是这样，亨利爵士，那天早上您伯父收到一封信。他平时信很多，因为他是个有名望的人，又是出了名的心肠好，谁遇上难处都愿意找他。可那天早上恰巧只有这一封信，所以我格外留意了一下。信是从库姆特雷西寄来的，信封上是女人的笔迹。”
段.en: “Well, Sir Henry, your uncle had a letter that morning. He had usually a great many letters, for he was a public man and well known for his kind heart, so that everyone who was in trouble was glad to turn to him. But that morning, as it chanced, there was only this one letter, so I took the more notice of it. It was from Coombe Tracey, and it was addressed in a woman’s hand.”

段.文: “后来呢？”
段.en: “Well?”

段.文: “后来，先生，我就没再想这件事，要不是我妻子，我也永远不会再想起来。就在几个星期前，她去打扫查尔斯爵士的书房——他死后那里从没动过——在壁炉里头发现了一封烧过的信的灰烬。信的大部分都烧成了碎片，只有一小条，是一页信的末尾，还连在一起，上面的字也还认得出来，只是黑底上的灰字。我们看那像是信末的附言，上面写着：‘求求您，求求您，您是位绅士，请把这封信烧掉，十点钟到那道门边来。’下面署着缩写L. L.。”
段.en: “Well, sir, I thought no more of the matter, and never would have done had it not been for my wife. Only a few weeks ago she was cleaning out Sir Charles’s study—it had never been touched since his death—and she found the ashes of a burned letter in the back of the grate. The greater part of it was charred to pieces, but one little slip, the end of a page, hung together, and the writing could still be read, though it was grey on a black ground. It seemed to us to be a postscript at the end of the letter and it said: ‘Please, please, as you are a gentleman, burn this letter, and be at the gate by ten o clock. Beneath it were signed the initials L. L.”

段.文: “那张纸条你还留着吗？”
段.en: “Have you got that slip?”

段.文: “没有，先生，我们一挪动，它就碎成了粉末。”
段.en: “No, sir, it crumbled all to bits after we moved it.”

段.文: “查尔斯爵士还收到过同样笔迹的别的信吗？”
段.en: “Had Sir Charles received any other letters in the same writing?”

段.文: “这个嘛，先生，我没特别留意他的信。这一封我本来也不会注意，只是碰巧它是单独来的。”
段.en: “Well, sir, I took no particular notice of his letters. I should not have noticed this one, only it happened to come alone.”

段.文: “你也不知道L. L.是谁？”
段.en: “And you have no idea who L. L. is?”

段.文: “不知道，先生。和您一样不知道。不过我想，要是能找到那位女士，我们对查尔斯爵士的死就会知道得更多。”
段.en: “No, sir. No more than you have. But I expect if we could lay our hands upon that lady we should know more about Sir Charles’s death.”

段.文: “巴里摩尔，我不明白，这么重要的情况，你怎么会瞒着不说。”
段.en: “I cannot understand, Barrymore, how you came to conceal this important information.”

段.文: “是这样，先生，那件事刚过，我们自家的麻烦就来了。再说，先生，我们俩都非常敬爱查尔斯爵士，想想他为我们做的一切，这也是应该的。把这件事翻出来，对我们可怜的主人也没有好处；而且事情牵涉到一位女士，还是小心点好。就算是最好的人也——”
段.en: “Well, sir, it was immediately after that our own trouble came to us. And then again, sir, we were both of us very fond of Sir Charles, as we well might be considering all that he has done for us. To rake this up couldn’t help our poor master, and it’s well to go carefully when there’s a lady in the case. Even the best of us—”

段.文: “你是怕这会损害他的名声？”
段.en: “You thought it might injure his reputation?”

段.文: “是的，先生，我觉得说出来不会有什么好处。可现在您待我们这么好，我觉得要是不把我知道的全告诉您，就太对不起您了。”
段.en: “Well, sir, I thought no good could come of it. But now you have been kind to us, and I feel as if it would be treating you unfairly not to tell you all that I know about the matter.”

段.文: “很好，巴里摩尔，你可以走了。”管家离开以后，亨利爵士转向我。“喂，华生，这条新线索你怎么看？”
段.en: “Very good, Barrymore; you can go.” When the butler had left us Sir Henry turned to me. “Well, Watson, what do you think of this new light?”

段.文: “它好像让原本的黑暗更黑了。”
段.en: “It seems to leave the darkness rather blacker than before.”

段.文: “我也这么想。不过只要能找到L. L.，整件事就该水落石出了。我们至少有了这点收获。我们知道有个人掌握着实情，只要能找到她就行。你看我们该怎么办？”
段.en: “So I think. But if we can only trace L. L. it should clear up the whole business. We have gained that much. We know that there is someone who has the facts if we can only find her. What do you think we should do?”

段.文: “马上把这些全告诉福尔摩斯。这正是他一直在找的线索。要是这还不能让他到这儿来，那就是我大错特错了。”
段.en: “Let Holmes know all about it at once. It will give him the clue for which he has been seeking. I am much mistaken if it does not bring him down.”

段.文: 我立刻回到房间，把早上这场谈话写成报告，准备寄给福尔摩斯。我看得出，他最近一定非常忙，因为我从贝克街收到的信很少，也很短，对我提供的情况不加评论，对我的任务也几乎只字不提。想必是那桩敲诈案占去了他的全部心思。可这个新情况一定能引起他的注意，重新唤起他的兴趣。我真希望他在这儿。
段.en: I went at once to my room and drew up my report of the morning’s conversation for Holmes. It was evident to me that he had been very busy of late, for the notes which I had from Baker Street were few and short, with no comments upon the information which I had supplied and hardly any reference to my mission. No doubt his blackmailing case is absorbing all his faculties. And yet this new factor must surely arrest his attention and renew his interest. I wish that he were here.

段.文: 10月17日——今天大雨下了一整天，打在常春藤上沙沙作响，从屋檐上滴滴答答往下淌。我想起了那个逃犯，他就在外面那片荒凉、寒冷、无遮无挡的荒原上。可怜的家伙！不管他犯过什么罪，他受的苦也算抵了一些了。接着我又想起了另一个人——马车里的那张脸，月光下的那个身影。他是不是也在这场大雨里——那个看不见的监视者，那个黑暗中的人？傍晚，我穿上雨衣，在泡透了水的荒原上走了很远，脑子里尽是些阴暗的念头，雨点打在脸上，风在耳边呼啸。愿上帝保佑这时候误入大泥沼的人吧，因为现在连坚实的高地都快成了沼泽。我找到了那座黑色的突岩，就是我看见那个孤零零的监视者的地方，我爬上它嶙峋的岩顶，自己也朝那片凄凉的丘陵望去。一阵阵急雨扫过赤褐色的坡面，厚重的石板色云层低低压在大地上，化成一缕缕灰色的云雾，沿着那些形状奇特的山坡拖曳下来。左边远处的洼地里，巴斯克维尔庄园的两座细高塔楼半隐在雾中，耸立在树林之上。除了山坡上密密麻麻的那些史前石屋，这就是我能看到的唯一的人烟了。两天前的夜里，我在同一个地方看见过那个孤零零的人，如今哪儿也找不到他的踪迹。
段.en: October 17th.—All day today the rain poured down, rustling on the ivy and dripping from the eaves. I thought of the convict out upon the bleak, cold, shelterless moor. Poor devil! Whatever his crimes, he has suffered something to atone for them. And then I thought of that other one—the face in the cab, the figure against the moon. Was he also out in that deluge—the unseen watcher, the man of darkness? In the evening I put on my waterproof and I walked far upon the sodden moor, full of dark imaginings, the rain beating upon my face and the wind whistling about my ears. God help those who wander into the great mire now, for even the firm uplands are becoming a morass. I found the black tor upon which I had seen the solitary watcher, and from its craggy summit I looked out myself across the melancholy downs. Rain squalls drifted across their russet face, and the heavy, slate-coloured clouds hung low over the landscape, trailing in grey wreaths down the sides of the fantastic hills. In the distant hollow on the left, half hidden by the mist, the two thin towers of Baskerville Hall rose above the trees. They were the only signs of human life which I could see, save only those prehistoric huts which lay thickly upon the slopes of the hills. Nowhere was there any trace of that lonely man whom I had seen on the same spot two nights before.

段.文: 往回走的时候，莫蒂默医生赶着他的轻便马车追上了我。他走的是一条崎岖的荒原小道，从偏远的福尔迈尔农庄那边过来。他对我们一直很关照，几乎没有哪天不到庄园来看看我们过得怎样。他一定要我上车，顺路把我送回家。我发现他正为他那条小长毛垂耳猎犬的失踪而十分苦恼。它跑到荒原上去了，再也没回来。我尽量安慰了他几句，可我想起了陷进格林彭大泥沼的那匹小马，觉得他恐怕再也见不到他的小狗了。
段.en: As I walked back I was overtaken by Dr. Mortimer driving in his dog-cart over a rough moorland track which led from the outlying farmhouse of Foulmire. He has been very attentive to us, and hardly a day has passed that he has not called at the Hall to see how we were getting on. He insisted upon my climbing into his dog-cart, and he gave me a lift homeward. I found him much troubled over the disappearance of his little spaniel. It had wandered on to the moor and had never come back. I gave him such consolation as I might, but I thought of the pony on the Grimpen Mire, and I do not fancy that he will see his little dog again.

段.文: “对了，莫蒂默，”我们在坎坷的路上颠簸着前进时，我说，“我想，住在这附近、坐车能到的人家，你不认识的大概没有几个吧？”
段.en: “By the way, Mortimer,” said I as we jolted along the rough road, “I suppose there are few people living within driving distance of this whom you do not know?”

段.文: “我想几乎没有。”
段.en: “Hardly any, I think.”

段.文: “那么，你能不能告诉我，有哪个女人名字的缩写是L. L.？”
段.en: “Can you, then, tell me the name of any woman whose initials are L. L.?”

段.文: 他想了几分钟。
段.en: He thought for a few minutes.

段.文: “没有，”他说，“有几个吉卜赛人和干活的人我说不准，可在农场主和乡绅里，没有谁是这个缩写。不过等等，”他停了一下又说，“有个劳拉·莱昂斯——她的缩写是L. L.——不过她住在库姆特雷西。”
段.en: “No,” said he. “There are a few gipsies and labouring folk for whom I can’t answer, but among the farmers or gentry there is no one whose initials are those. Wait a bit though,” he added after a pause. “There is Laura Lyons—her initials are L. L.—but she lives in Coombe Tracey.”

段.文: “她是什么人？”我问。
段.en: “Who is she?” I asked.

段.文: “她是弗兰克兰的女儿。”
段.en: “She is Frankland’s daughter.”

段.文: “什么！就是那个怪老头弗兰克兰？”
段.en: “What! Old Frankland the crank?”

段.文: “正是。她嫁给了一个姓莱昂斯的画家，那人到荒原上来写生。结果他是个无赖，把她抛弃了。据我听说，错处也许不全在一方。她父亲不肯再跟她来往，因为她没经他同意就结了婚，也许还有一两个别的原因。就这样，夹在老的和小的两个坏蛋中间，这姑娘的日子过得相当苦。”
段.en: “Exactly. She married an artist named Lyons, who came sketching on the moor. He proved to be a blackguard and deserted her. The fault from what I hear may not have been entirely on one side. Her father refused to have anything to do with her because she had married without his consent and perhaps for one or two other reasons as well. So, between the old sinner and the young one the girl has had a pretty bad time.”

段.文: “她靠什么过活？”
段.en: “How does she live?”

段.文: “我猜老弗兰克兰给她一点微薄的生活费，可也不可能更多了，因为他自己的经济也相当窘迫。不管她是不是自作自受，总不能眼看着她无可救药地堕落下去。她的事传开以后，这里有好几个人出了点力，让她能正正当当地谋生。斯台普顿算一个，查尔斯爵士也算一个。我自己也出了一点小钱。是帮她开了一家打字社。”
段.en: “I fancy old Frankland allows her a pittance, but it cannot be more, for his own affairs are considerably involved. Whatever she may have deserved one could not allow her to go hopelessly to the bad. Her story got about, and several of the people here did something to enable her to earn an honest living. Stapleton did for one, and Sir Charles for another. I gave a trifle myself. It was to set her up in a typewriting business.”

段.文: 他想知道我打听这些做什么，可我设法满足了他的好奇心，又没跟他说得太多，因为我们没有理由把秘密告诉任何人。明天上午我要设法去一趟库姆特雷西。要是能见到这位名声暧昧的劳拉·莱昂斯太太，那么在这一连串谜团里，就有一件事朝着弄清楚迈出了一大步。我的确越来越像蛇一样机灵了：莫蒂默追问得让我难以招架的时候，我随口问他弗兰克兰的头骨属于哪一类，结果一路上剩下的时间，我听到的全是颅骨学。我和夏洛克·福尔摩斯一起生活了这么多年，可不是白过的。
段.en: He wanted to know the object of my inquiries, but I managed to satisfy his curiosity without telling him too much, for there is no reason why we should take anyone into our confidence. Tomorrow morning I shall find my way to Coombe Tracey, and if I can see this Mrs. Laura Lyons, of equivocal reputation, a long step will have been made towards clearing one incident in this chain of mysteries. I am certainly developing the wisdom of the serpent, for when Mortimer pressed his questions to an inconvenient extent I asked him casually to what type Frankland’s skull belonged, and so heard nothing but craniology for the rest of our drive. I have not lived for years with Sherlock Holmes for nothing.

段.文: 在这个风雨交加、令人郁闷的日子里，我只剩一件事要记了。那就是刚才我和巴里摩尔的一番谈话，它又给了我一张好牌，到了适当的时候可以打出去。
段.en: I have only one other incident to record upon this tempestuous and melancholy day. This was my conversation with Barrymore just now, which gives me one more strong card which I can play in due time.

段.文: 莫蒂默留下来吃了晚饭，饭后他和准男爵玩起了埃卡泰纸牌。管家把咖啡端到书房给我，我趁机问了他几个问题。
段.en: Mortimer had stayed to dinner, and he and the baronet played écarté afterwards. The butler brought me my coffee into the library, and I took the chance to ask him a few questions.

段.文: “喂，”我说，“你那位宝贝亲戚走了没有，还是仍旧躲在那边？”
段.en: “Well,” said I, “has this precious relation of yours departed, or is he still lurking out yonder?”

段.文: “我不知道，先生。老天保佑他已经走了，他在这里除了惹麻烦什么也没带来！我最后一次给他放吃的以后，就再没有他的消息了，那是三天前的事。”
段.en: “I don’t know, sir. I hope to heaven that he has gone, for he has brought nothing but trouble here! I’ve not heard of him since I left out food for him last, and that was three days ago.”

段.文: “那次你见到他了吗？”
段.en: “Did you see him then?”

段.文: “没有，先生，可我下次再去那边的时候，吃的已经没了。”
段.en: “No, sir, but the food was gone when next I went that way.”

段.文: “那么他肯定在那儿了？”
段.en: “Then he was certainly there?”

段.文: “您会这么想，先生，除非是另一个人拿走的。”
段.en: “So you would think, sir, unless it was the other man who took it.”

段.文: 我端着咖啡杯，送到嘴边一半就停住了，瞪着巴里摩尔。
段.en: I sat with my coffee-cup halfway to my lips and stared at Barrymore.

段.文: “这么说，你知道还有另一个人？”
段.en: “You know that there is another man then?”

段.文: “是的，先生，荒原上还有另一个人。”
段.en: “Yes, sir; there is another man upon the moor.”

段.文: “你见过他吗？”
段.en: “Have you seen him?”

段.文: “没有，先生。”
段.en: “No, sir.”

段.文: “那你怎么知道有他？”
段.en: “How do you know of him then?”

段.文: “是塞尔登告诉我的，先生，一个多星期以前。他也躲着，不过据我看，他不是逃犯。我不喜欢这样，华生医生——我跟您直说吧，先生，我不喜欢这样。”他说这话时，突然变得十分激动而恳切。
段.en: “Selden told me of him, sir, a week ago or more. He’s in hiding, too, but he’s not a convict as far as I can make out. I don’t like it, Dr. Watson—I tell you straight, sir, that I don’t like it.” He spoke with a sudden passion of earnestness.

段.文: “好，你听我说，巴里摩尔！我关心这件事，只是为了你的主人。我到这里来，没有别的目的，就是要帮他。坦白告诉我，你不喜欢的到底是什么。”
段.en: “Now, listen to me, Barrymore! I have no interest in this matter but that of your master. I have come here with no object except to help him. Tell me, frankly, what it is that you don’t like.”

段.文: 巴里摩尔犹豫了一会儿，好像后悔自己刚才情绪失控，又好像难以用言语表达自己的感受。
段.en: Barrymore hesitated for a moment, as if he regretted his outburst or found it difficult to express his own feelings in words.

段.文: “就是这些事情，先生，”他终于嚷了起来，朝着面向荒原、被雨水抽打的窗户挥了挥手，“有人在什么地方搞鬼，正在酝酿一桩阴险的勾当，这一点我敢发誓！先生，我真巴不得看到亨利爵士回伦敦去！”
段.en: “It’s all these goings-on, sir,” he cried at last, waving his hand towards the rain-lashed window which faced the moor. “There’s foul play somewhere, and there’s black villainy brewing, to that I’ll swear! Very glad I should be, sir, to see Sir Henry on his way back to London again!”

段.文: “可到底是什么让你这么害怕？”
段.en: “But what is it that alarms you?”

段.文: “看看查尔斯爵士是怎么死的！不管验尸官怎么说，那都够糟的了。再听听夜里荒原上那些声音。太阳一落山，就算给钱也没人肯穿过荒原。再看看躲在那边的这个陌生人，他一直在监视、在等待！他在等什么？这是什么意思？对姓巴斯克维尔的人来说，这绝不是好事。等亨利爵士的新仆人能来接管庄园的那一天，我就能摆脱这一切了，那时我会非常高兴。”
段.en: “Look at Sir Charles’s death! That was bad enough, for all that the coroner said. Look at the noises on the moor at night. There’s not a man would cross it after sundown if he was paid for it. Look at this stranger hiding out yonder, and watching and waiting! What’s he waiting for? What does it mean? It means no good to anyone of the name of Baskerville, and very glad I shall be to be quit of it all on the day that Sir Henry’s new servants are ready to take over the Hall.”

段.文: “可是关于这个陌生人，”我说，“你能告诉我些什么吗？塞尔登是怎么说的？他有没有弄清那人藏在哪儿，或者在干什么？”
段.en: “But about this stranger,” said I. “Can you tell me anything about him? What did Selden say? Did he find out where he hid, or what he was doing?”

段.文: “他见过他一两次，可那人城府很深，什么也不露。起初他以为那人是警察，可很快就发现那人有自己的打算。照他看，那人像是个上等人，可到底在干什么，他就弄不明白了。”
段.en: “He saw him once or twice, but he is a deep one and gives nothing away. At first he thought that he was the police, but soon he found that he had some lay of his own. A kind of gentleman he was, as far as he could see, but what he was doing he could not make out.”

段.文: “那他说那人住在哪儿？”
段.en: “And where did he say that he lived?”

段.文: “在山坡上那些老房子里——就是古时候的人住过的那些石屋。”
段.en: “Among the old houses on the hillside—the stone huts where the old folk used to live.”

段.文: “那他吃什么呢？”
段.en: “But how about his food?”

段.文: “塞尔登发现，有个小伙子替他干活，给他送来所需的一切。我猜那小伙子是到库姆特雷西去买东西的。”
段.en: “Selden found out that he has got a lad who works for him and brings all he needs. I dare say he goes to Coombe Tracey for what he wants.”

段.文: “很好，巴里摩尔。这件事我们改天再谈。”管家走后，我走到漆黑的窗前，透过模糊的玻璃，望着奔涌的云层和狂风中摇摆的树影。待在屋里都觉得这是个狂野的夜晚，在荒原上的石屋里又该是什么光景呢？是怎样强烈的仇恨，能让一个人在这样的时候潜伏在那样的地方！他又怀着怎样深切而执着的目的，非要受这份罪不可！就在荒原上那间石屋里，似乎正藏着那个让我苦恼不已的问题的核心。我发誓，不出一天，我就要竭尽人力所能，去揭开这个谜的真相。
段.en: “Very good, Barrymore. We may talk further of this some other time.” When the butler had gone I walked over to the black window, and I looked through a blurred pane at the driving clouds and at the tossing outline of the wind-swept trees. It is a wild night indoors, and what must it be in a stone hut upon the moor. What passion of hatred can it be which leads a man to lurk in such a place at such a time! And what deep and earnest purpose can he have which calls for such a trial! There, in that hut upon the moor, seems to lie the very centre of that problem which has vexed me so sorely. I swear that another day shall not have passed before I have done all that man can do to reach the heart of the mystery.

段.文: 上一章是我私人日记的摘录，叙述已经到了10月18日。从这时起，这些离奇的事情开始迅速走向它们可怕的结局。接下来几天发生的事，深深刻在我的记忆里，不用翻看当时的笔记，我也能讲出来。我从那一天的第二天讲起。那一天，我弄清了两件非常重要的事：一是库姆特雷西的劳拉·莱昂斯太太曾写信给查尔斯·巴斯克维尔爵士，和他约定了见面，而约定的时间和地点，正是他送命的时间和地点；二是荒原上那个潜伏的人，可以在山坡上的石屋里找到。手里握着这两条事实，我觉得，要是还不能给这些黑暗的角落照进一点光亮，那不是我脑子不够用，就是我胆子不够大。
段.en: The extract from my private diary which forms the last chapter has brought my narrative up to the eighteenth of October, a time when these strange events began to move swiftly towards their terrible conclusion. The incidents of the next few days are indelibly graven upon my recollection, and I can tell them without reference to the notes made at the time. I start them from the day which succeeded that upon which I had established two facts of great importance, the one that Mrs. Laura Lyons of Coombe Tracey had written to Sir Charles Baskerville and made an appointment with him at the very place and hour that he met his death, the other that the lurking man upon the moor was to be found among the stone huts upon the hillside. With these two facts in my possession I felt that either my intelligence or my courage must be deficient if I could not throw some further light upon these dark places.

段.文: 前一天晚上，我没有机会把打听到的莱昂斯太太的事告诉准男爵，因为莫蒂默医生陪他打牌，一直打到很晚。不过吃早饭的时候，我把我的发现告诉了他，问他愿不愿意陪我去库姆特雷西。起初他很想去，可再一想，我们俩都觉得我一个人去效果也许更好。这次拜访越是正式，我们能得到的情况可能就越少。于是我把亨利爵士留在家里，心里不免有些过意不去，然后坐车出发，去追查这条新线索。
段.en: I had no opportunity to tell the baronet what I had learned about Mrs. Lyons upon the evening before, for Dr. Mortimer remained with him at cards until it was very late. At breakfast, however, I informed him about my discovery and asked him whether he would care to accompany me to Coombe Tracey. At first he was very eager to come, but on second thoughts it seemed to both of us that if I went alone the results might be better. The more formal we made the visit the less information we might obtain. I left Sir Henry behind, therefore, not without some prickings of conscience, and drove off upon my new quest.

段.文: 到了库姆特雷西，我叫珀金斯把马安顿好，然后打听我要来盘问的那位女士。她的住处不难找，位置在镇中心，陈设也很讲究。一个女仆没多客套就把我领了进去。我走进起居室，一位坐在雷明顿打字机前的女士跳了起来，脸上带着愉快的笑容表示欢迎。可是一看到我是个陌生人，她的脸色就沉了下来，又坐了回去，问我来有什么事。
段.en: When I reached Coombe Tracey I told Perkins to put up the horses, and I made inquiries for the lady whom I had come to interrogate. I had no difficulty in finding her rooms, which were central and well appointed. A maid showed me in without ceremony, and as I entered the sitting-room a lady, who was sitting before a Remington typewriter, sprang up with a pleasant smile of welcome. Her face fell, however, when she saw that I was a stranger, and she sat down again and asked me the object of my visit.

段.文: 莱昂斯太太给人的第一印象是非常美丽。她的眼睛和头发都是同样浓郁的榛褐色，脸颊上虽然有不少雀斑，却泛着深肤色女子特有的那种动人的红晕，像黄玫瑰花心里隐隐透出的那一抹淡淡的粉红。我再说一遍，第一印象是赞叹。可第二个印象就是挑剔了。这张脸上有种说不出的不对劲：表情有些粗俗，眼神也许有些冷硬，嘴唇有些松弛，破坏了它完美的美。当然，这些都是事后才想到的。当时我只意识到，我面前是一位非常漂亮的女人，她正在问我来访的原因。直到那一刻，我才真正明白我的任务有多么微妙。
段.en: The first impression left by Mrs. Lyons was one of extreme beauty. Her eyes and hair were of the same rich hazel colour, and her cheeks, though considerably freckled, were flushed with the exquisite bloom of the brunette, the dainty pink which lurks at the heart of the sulphur rose. Admiration was, I repeat, the first impression. But the second was criticism. There was something subtly wrong with the face, some coarseness of expression, some hardness, perhaps, of eye, some looseness of lip which marred its perfect beauty. But these, of course, are afterthoughts. At the moment I was simply conscious that I was in the presence of a very handsome woman, and that she was asking me the reasons for my visit. I had not quite understood until that instant how delicate my mission was.

段.文: “我有幸认识您的父亲。”我说。
段.en: “I have the pleasure,” said I, “of knowing your father.”

段.文: 这个开场白很笨拙，那位女士也让我感觉到了这一点。“我和我父亲之间没有任何共同之处，”她说，“我不欠他什么，他的朋友也不是我的朋友。要不是已故的查尔斯·巴斯克维尔爵士和另外几位好心人，就算我饿死了，我父亲也不会在乎。”
段.en: It was a clumsy introduction, and the lady made me feel it. “There is nothing in common between my father and me,” she said. “I owe him nothing, and his friends are not mine. If it were not for the late Sir Charles Baskerville and some other kind hearts I might have starved for all that my father cared.”

段.文: “我正是为了已故的查尔斯·巴斯克维尔爵士的事来见您的。”
段.en: “It was about the late Sir Charles Baskerville that I have come here to see you.”

段.文: 那位女士脸上的雀斑一下子显了出来。
段.en: The freckles started out on the lady’s face.

段.文: “关于他，我能告诉您什么呢？”她问，手指不安地在打字机的按键上拨弄着。
段.en: “What can I tell you about him?” she asked, and her fingers played nervously over the stops of her typewriter.

段.文: “您认识他，是吧？”
段.en: “You knew him, did you not?”

段.文: “我已经说过，我受了他很多恩惠。如果说我现在能自食其力，那很大程度上是因为他关心过我的不幸处境。”
段.en: “I have already said that I owe a great deal to his kindness. If I am able to support myself it is largely due to the interest which he took in my unhappy situation.”

段.文: “您和他通过信吗？”
段.en: “Did you correspond with him?”

段.文: 那位女士猛地抬起头来，榛褐色的眼睛里闪着怒火。
段.en: The lady looked quickly up with an angry gleam in her hazel eyes.

段.文: “您问这些是什么目的？”她尖锐地问。
段.en: “What is the object of these questions?” she asked sharply.

段.文: “目的是避免一场公开的丑闻。由我在这里问，总比让事情闹到我们控制不了的地步要好。”
段.en: “The object is to avoid a public scandal. It is better that I should ask them here than that the matter should pass outside our control.”

段.文: 她沉默了，脸色依然非常苍白。最后她抬起头来，神态里带着几分不顾一切的挑衅。
段.en: She was silent and her face was still very pale. At last she looked up with something reckless and defiant in her manner.

段.文: “好吧，我回答，”她说，“您要问什么？”
段.en: “Well, I’ll answer,” she said. “What are your questions?”

段.文: “您和查尔斯爵士通过信吗？”
段.en: “Did you correspond with Sir Charles?”

段.文: “我当然给他写过一两次信，感谢他的体贴和慷慨。”
段.en: “I certainly wrote to him once or twice to acknowledge his delicacy and his generosity.”

段.文: “那些信的日期您还记得吗？”
段.en: “Have you the dates of those letters?”

段.文: “不记得。”
段.en: “No.”

段.文: “您见过他吗？”
段.en: “Have you ever met him?”

段.文: “见过，一两次，是他到库姆特雷西来的时候。他是个很不爱抛头露面的人，做好事也喜欢悄悄地做。”
段.en: “Yes, once or twice, when he came into Coombe Tracey. He was a very retiring man, and he preferred to do good by stealth.”

段.文: “可是，既然您很少见他，也很少给他写信，他怎么会对您的情况了解得那么清楚，能像您说的那样帮助您呢？”
段.en: “But if you saw him so seldom and wrote so seldom, how did he know enough about your affairs to be able to help you, as you say that he has done?”

段.文: 我提出的难题，她应对得极其从容。
段.en: She met my difficulty with the utmost readiness.

段.文: “有好几位先生知道我不幸的遭遇，一起帮助过我。其中一位是斯台普顿先生，他是查尔斯爵士的邻居，也是他的密友。他待人非常好，查尔斯爵士就是通过他知道我的情况的。”
段.en: “There were several gentlemen who knew my sad history and united to help me. One was Mr. Stapleton, a neighbour and intimate friend of Sir Charles’s. He was exceedingly kind, and it was through him that Sir Charles learned about my affairs.”

段.文: 我早已知道，查尔斯·巴斯克维尔爵士有好几次请斯台普顿替他施舍救济，所以这位女士的话听起来确实可信。
段.en: I knew already that Sir Charles Baskerville had made Stapleton his almoner upon several occasions, so the lady’s statement bore the impress of truth upon it.

段.文: “您有没有写信给查尔斯爵士，约他见面？”我接着问。
段.en: “Did you ever write to Sir Charles asking him to meet you?” I continued.

段.文: 莱昂斯太太又气红了脸。“说真的，先生，这个问题太离奇了。”
段.en: Mrs. Lyons flushed with anger again. “Really, sir, this is a very extraordinary question.”

段.文: “很抱歉，夫人，可我必须再问一遍。”
段.en: “I am sorry, madam, but I must repeat it.”

段.文: “那我回答您：当然没有。”
段.en: “Then I answer, certainly not.”

段.文: “就在查尔斯爵士死的那一天，也没有吗？”
段.en: “Not on the very day of Sir Charles’s death?”

段.文: 她脸上的红晕一下子褪尽了，我面前是一张死人般惨白的脸。她干裂的嘴唇说不出那个“没有”，我是看出来的，而不是听出来的。
段.en: The flush had faded in an instant, and a deathly face was before me. Her dry lips could not speak the “No” which I saw rather than heard.

段.文: “您一定是记错了，”我说，“我甚至能背出您信里的一段话。那上面写着：‘求求您，求求您，您是位绅士，请把这封信烧掉，十点钟到那道门边来。’”
段.en: “Surely your memory deceives you,” said I. “I could even quote a passage of your letter. It ran ‘Please, please, as you are a gentleman, burn this letter, and be at the gate by ten o’clock.’”

段.文: 我以为她晕过去了，可她拼尽全力又镇定了下来。
段.en: I thought that she had fainted, but she recovered herself by a supreme effort.

段.文: “难道世上就没有真正的绅士吗？”她喘着气说。
段.en: “Is there no such thing as a gentleman?” she gasped.

段.文: “您冤枉查尔斯爵士了。他确实把信烧了。可有时候，一封信就算烧了，字也还认得出来。现在您承认这封信是您写的了？”
段.en: “You do Sir Charles an injustice. He did burn the letter. But sometimes a letter may be legible even when burned. You acknowledge now that you wrote it?”

段.文: “是的，是我写的，”她叫道，一股脑儿把心里话倾倒出来，“确实是我写的。我为什么要否认？我没有什么可羞愧的。我希望他帮助我。我相信，只要能当面谈一谈，我就能得到他的帮助，所以我约他见面。”
段.en: “Yes, I did write it,” she cried, pouring out her soul in a torrent of words. “I did write it. Why should I deny it? I have no reason to be ashamed of it. I wished him to help me. I believed that if I had an interview I could gain his help, so I asked him to meet me.”

段.文: “可为什么约在那个时候？”
段.en: “But why at such an hour?”

段.文: “因为我刚刚得知，他第二天就要去伦敦，可能一走就是几个月。而我有些原因，没法早点去。”
段.en: “Because I had only just learned that he was going to London next day and might be away for months. There were reasons why I could not get there earlier.”

段.文: “可为什么约在花园里见面，而不到宅子里去拜访？”
段.en: “But why a rendezvous in the garden instead of a visit to the house?”

段.文: “您以为一个女人能在那个时候独自到一个单身汉家里去吗？”
段.en: “Do you think a woman could go alone at that hour to a bachelor’s house?”

段.文: “好吧，那您到了那里以后，发生了什么事？”
段.en: “Well, what happened when you did get there?”

段.文: “我根本没去。”
段.en: “I never went.”

段.文: “莱昂斯太太！”
段.en: “Mrs. Lyons!”

段.文: “没去，我以我认为神圣的一切向您发誓。我根本没去。有件事插了进来，让我没能去成。”
段.en: “No, I swear it to you on all I hold sacred. I never went. Something intervened to prevent my going.”

段.文: “什么事？”
段.en: “What was that?”

段.文: “那是私事。我不能说。”
段.en: “That is a private matter. I cannot tell it.”

段.文: “这么说，您承认您和查尔斯爵士约在他送命的那个时间、那个地点见面，却否认您去赴了约。”
段.en: “You acknowledge then that you made an appointment with Sir Charles at the very hour and place at which he met his death, but you deny that you kept the appointment.”

段.文: “这是实话。”
段.en: “That is the truth.”

段.文: 我反复盘问她，可始终没能越过这一点。
段.en: Again and again I cross-questioned her, but I could never get past that point.

段.文: “莱昂斯太太，”这场冗长而没有结果的谈话结束时，我站起身来说，“您不把您知道的事彻底坦白出来，就是在承担一个非常重大的责任，也让自己处于非常不利的境地。如果我不得不请警察来帮忙，您就会知道自己牵连得有多深。如果您是清白的，那您起初为什么要否认那天给查尔斯爵士写过信？”
段.en: “Mrs. Lyons,” said I as I rose from this long and inconclusive interview, “you are taking a very great responsibility and putting yourself in a very false position by not making an absolutely clean breast of all that you know. If I have to call in the aid of the police you will find how seriously you are compromised. If your position is innocent, why did you in the first instance deny having written to Sir Charles upon that date?”

段.文: “因为我怕有人会因此得出错误的结论，怕自己卷进一场丑闻。”
段.en: “Because I feared that some false conclusion might be drawn from it and that I might find myself involved in a scandal.”

段.文: “那您为什么那样急切地要查尔斯爵士销毁您的信？”
段.en: “And why were you so pressing that Sir Charles should destroy your letter?”

段.文: “您要是读过那封信，就会知道了。”
段.en: “If you have read the letter you will know.”

段.文: “我没说我读过信的全文。”
段.en: “I did not say that I had read all the letter.”

段.文: “您引了信里的话。”
段.en: “You quoted some of it.”

段.文: “我引的是附言。我说过，那封信已经烧了，并不是全都认得出来。我再问您一遍：查尔斯爵士死的那天收到了这封信，您为什么那样急切地要他把它销毁？”
段.en: “I quoted the postscript. The letter had, as I said, been burned and it was not all legible. I ask you once again why it was that you were so pressing that Sir Charles should destroy this letter which he received on the day of his death.”

段.文: “这件事非常私密。”
段.en: “The matter is a very private one.”

段.文: “那您就更应该避免公开调查了。”
段.en: “The more reason why you should avoid a public investigation.”

段.文: “那我就告诉您吧。如果您听说过我不幸的经历，就会知道我草率地结了婚，后来又有理由后悔。”
段.en: “I will tell you, then. If you have heard anything of my unhappy history you will know that I made a rash marriage and had reason to regret it.”

段.文: “这些我听说了。”
段.en: “I have heard so much.”

段.文: “我的生活就是不停地遭受一个我痛恨的丈夫的迫害。法律站在他那一边，我每天都要面对这样的可能：他会强迫我回去跟他一起过。我给查尔斯爵士写这封信的时候，刚刚得知，只要能付得起某些费用，我就有希望重获自由。这对我意味着一切——心里的安宁、幸福、自尊——一切。我知道查尔斯爵士慷慨大方，我想，要是他听我亲口讲出这段经历，他会帮助我的。”
段.en: “My life has been one incessant persecution from a husband whom I abhor. The law is upon his side, and every day I am faced by the possibility that he may force me to live with him. At the time that I wrote this letter to Sir Charles I had learned that there was a prospect of my regaining my freedom if certain expenses could be met. It meant everything to me—peace of mind, happiness, self-respect—everything. I knew Sir Charles’s generosity, and I thought that if he heard the story from my own lips he would help me.”

段.文: “那您怎么又没去呢？”
段.en: “Then how is it that you did not go?”

段.文: “因为就在那段时间里，我从别处得到了帮助。”
段.en: “Because I received help in the interval from another source.”

段.文: “那您为什么不写信给查尔斯爵士，把这件事说明白？”
段.en: “Why then, did you not write to Sir Charles and explain this?”

段.文: “要不是第二天早上在报上看到他的死讯，我本来是会写的。”
段.en: “So I should have done had I not seen his death in the paper next morning.”

段.文: 这个女人的话前后连贯，我怎么问也动摇不了它。我只能去核实一下：在惨案发生前后，她是不是真的对丈夫提起了离婚诉讼。
段.en: The woman’s story hung coherently together, and all my questions were unable to shake it. I could only check it by finding if she had, indeed, instituted divorce proceedings against her husband at or about the time of the tragedy.

段.文: 如果她真去过巴斯克维尔庄园，她不大可能敢说自己没去过。因为她得坐一辆轻便马车去，而且要到第二天凌晨才能回到库姆特雷西。这样一趟出行是瞒不住人的。所以，她很可能说的是实话，至少是一部分实话。我离开的时候，既困惑又灰心。我又一次撞上了那堵死墙。我想尽办法要完成我的使命，可每条路上似乎都横着这样一堵墙。然而，我越是回想那位女士的脸色和神态，就越觉得她有什么事瞒着我。她为什么会脸色那么苍白？为什么每承认一件事，都要被逼得没办法了才肯说？惨案发生的时候，她为什么那样守口如瓶？这一切的解释，肯定不像她想让我相信的那么清白。眼下这个方向我已无法再往前走了，只好掉过头去，追查另一条线索，那条线索要到荒原上的石屋里去找。
段.en: It was unlikely that she would dare to say that she had not been to Baskerville Hall if she really had been, for a trap would be necessary to take her there, and could not have returned to Coombe Tracey until the early hours of the morning. Such an excursion could not be kept secret. The probability was, therefore, that she was telling the truth, or, at least, a part of the truth. I came away baffled and disheartened. Once again I had reached that dead wall which seemed to be built across every path by which I tried to get at the object of my mission. And yet the more I thought of the lady’s face and of her manner the more I felt that something was being held back from me. Why should she turn so pale? Why should she fight against every admission until it was forced from her? Why should she have been so reticent at the time of the tragedy? Surely the explanation of all this could not be as innocent as she would have me believe. For the moment I could proceed no farther in that direction, but must turn back to that other clue which was to be sought for among the stone huts upon the moor.

段.文: 而那是个极其模糊的方向。坐车回去的路上，我看到一座又一座山上都有古人留下的痕迹，这才意识到这一点。巴里摩尔唯一的提示，是那个陌生人住在一间废弃的石屋里，可这样的石屋在荒原上到处都是，成百上千。不过，我有自己的经历作向导，因为我亲眼见过那个人站在黑岩的顶上。那么，我就该以那里为中心展开搜索。从那里出发，我要把荒原上的石屋一间间查过去，直到找对为止。如果这人在屋里，我就要让他亲口说出他是谁，为什么跟踪了我们这么久，必要时就用左轮手枪逼他说。在摄政街的人群里，他也许能从我们手里溜走，可在这孤寂的荒原上，他想溜就难了。另一方面，如果我找到了石屋，屋主却不在里面，那我就得守在那里，不管守多久，直到他回来。福尔摩斯在伦敦让他跑了。要是我能在我的老师失手的地方把他逮住，那可真是我的一大胜利。
段.en: And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove back and noted how hill after hill showed traces of the ancient people. Barrymore’s only indication had been that the stranger lived in one of these abandoned huts, and many hundreds of them are scattered throughout the length and breadth of the moor. But I had my own experience for a guide since it had shown me the man himself standing upon the summit of the Black Tor. That, then, should be the centre of my search. From there I should explore every hut upon the moor until I lighted upon the right one. If this man were inside it I should find out from his own lips, at the point of my revolver if necessary, who he was and why he had dogged us so long. He might slip away from us in the crowd of Regent Street, but it would puzzle him to do so upon the lonely moor. On the other hand, if I should find the hut and its tenant should not be within it I must remain there, however long the vigil, until he returned. Holmes had missed him in London. It would indeed be a triumph for me if I could run him to earth where my master had failed.

段.文: 在这次调查中，运气一次又一次跟我们作对，可现在它终于来帮我了。而带来好运的不是别人，正是弗兰克兰先生。他站在自家花园的门外，花白的络腮胡子，红红的脸膛。他的花园门正对着我走的那条大路。
段.en: Luck had been against us again and again in this inquiry, but now at last it came to my aid. And the messenger of good fortune was none other than Mr. Frankland, who was standing, grey-whiskered and red-faced, outside the gate of his garden, which opened on to the highroad along which I travelled.

段.文: “您好，华生医生，”他嚷道，心情好得出奇，“您一定得让您的马歇一歇，进来喝杯酒，向我道个喜。”
段.en: “Good-day, Dr. Watson,” cried he with unwonted good humour, “you must really give your horses a rest and come in to have a glass of wine and to congratulate me.”

段.文: 听说了他怎样对待自己的女儿以后，我对他实在谈不上有什么好感。不过我正急着把珀金斯和马车打发回去，这是个好机会。我下了车，让人带话给亨利爵士，说我会走回去，赶得上吃晚饭。然后我跟着弗兰克兰进了他的餐厅。
段.en: My feelings towards him were very far from being friendly after what I had heard of his treatment of his daughter, but I was anxious to send Perkins and the wagonette home, and the opportunity was a good one. I alighted and sent a message to Sir Henry that I should walk over in time for dinner. Then I followed Frankland into his dining-room.

段.文: “今天对我来说是个了不起的日子，先生——是我一生中值得纪念的日子之一，”他嚷道，一边不住地咯咯笑，“我打赢了两场。我要让这一带的人知道，法律就是法律，这里有个人不怕诉诸法律。我已经确立了一条通行权，直穿老米德尔顿的园林中央，先生，就从正当中穿过去，离他家前门不到100码。您觉得怎么样？我们要让这些大人物知道，他们不能随意践踏平民的权利，该死的东西！我还封了那片林子，弗恩沃西的人以前常在那里野餐。这帮可恶的家伙好像以为没有什么财产权，可以带着他们的废纸和瓶子想去哪儿就去哪儿乱哄哄地挤。两个案子都判了，华生医生，两个都判我赢。自从我告约翰·莫兰爵士非法侵入——因为他在自己的养兔场里打猎——那一回以后，我还没有过这么痛快的日子。”
段.en: “It is a great day for me, sir—one of the red-letter days of my life,” he cried with many chuckles. “I have brought off a double event. I mean to teach them in these parts that law is law, and that there is a man here who does not fear to invoke it. I have established a right of way through the centre of old Middleton’s park, slap across it, sir, within a hundred yards of his own front door. What do you think of that? We’ll teach these magnates that they cannot ride roughshod over the rights of the commoners, confound them! And I’ve closed the wood where the Fernworthy folk used to picnic. These infernal people seem to think that there are no rights of property, and that they can swarm where they like with their papers and their bottles. Both cases decided, Dr. Watson, and both in my favour. I haven’t had such a day since I had Sir John Morland for trespass because he shot in his own warren.”

段.文: “您究竟是怎么做到的？”
段.en: “How on earth did you do that?”

段.文: “去查查案卷吧，先生。值得一读——弗兰克兰诉莫兰案，王座法院。花了我200镑，可我赢了判决。”
段.en: “Look it up in the books, sir. It will repay reading—Frankland v. Morland, Court of Queen’s Bench. It cost me £200, but I got my verdict.”

段.文: “这对您有什么好处吗？”
段.en: “Did it do you any good?”

段.文: “没有，先生，一点也没有。我可以自豪地说，这件事跟我没有任何利害关系。我完全是出于对公众的责任感才这样做的。比如说，我毫不怀疑，今晚弗恩沃西的人会烧我的模拟像。上次他们这么干的时候，我就告诉警察，他们应该制止这种可耻的把戏。郡警察局糟糕透顶，先生，我理应得到的保护，他们没有给我。弗兰克兰诉女王案会让公众注意到这件事。我对他们说过，他们会为这样对待我而后悔的，现在我的话已经应验了。”
段.en: “None, sir, none. I am proud to say that I had no interest in the matter. I act entirely from a sense of public duty. I have no doubt, for example, that the Fernworthy people will burn me in effigy tonight. I told the police last time they did it that they should stop these disgraceful exhibitions. The County Constabulary is in a scandalous state, sir, and it has not afforded me the protection to which I am entitled. The case of Frankland v. Regina will bring the matter before the attention of the public. I told them that they would have occasion to regret their treatment of me, and already my words have come true.”

段.文: “怎么说？”我问。
段.en: “How so?” I asked.

段.文: 老头摆出一副无所不知的神气。“因为他们做梦都想知道的事，我能告诉他们；可无论如何，我也不会帮这帮无赖任何忙。”
段.en: The old man put on a very knowing expression. “Because I could tell them what they are dying to know; but nothing would induce me to help the rascals in any way.”

段.文: 我本来一直在找借口，好从他的闲扯中脱身，可现在我开始想多听听了。这个老家伙的拧脾气我已经见识够了，明白只要我露出一点浓厚的兴趣，他准会闭口不说。
段.en: I had been casting round for some excuse by which I could get away from his gossip, but now I began to wish to hear more of it. I had seen enough of the contrary nature of the old sinner to understand that any strong sign of interest would be the surest way to stop his confidences.

段.文: “想必是什么偷猎案吧？”我装出一副漠不关心的样子说。
段.en: “Some poaching case, no doubt?” said I with an indifferent manner.

段.文: “哈哈，我的小伙子，比那重要得多！荒原上的那个逃犯怎么样？”
段.en: “Ha, ha, my boy, a very much more important matter than that! What about the convict on the moor?”

段.文: 我瞪大了眼睛。“您该不是说您知道他在哪儿吧？”我说。
段.en: I stared. “You don’t mean that you know where he is?” said I.

段.文: “我也许不确切知道他在哪儿，可我十分肯定，我能帮警察抓住他。您难道从没想过，抓那个人的办法就是弄清他从哪儿弄到吃的，顺藤摸瓜找到他？”
段.en: “I may not know exactly where he is, but I am quite sure that I could help the police to lay their hands on him. Has it never struck you that the way to catch that man was to find out where he got his food and so trace it to him?”

段.文: 他似乎确实已经离真相近得叫人不安了。“那当然，”我说，“可您怎么知道他还在荒原上呢？”
段.en: He certainly seemed to be getting uncomfortably near the truth. “No doubt,” said I; “but how do you know that he is anywhere upon the moor?”

段.文: “我知道，是因为我亲眼看见了给他送吃的人。”
段.en: “I know it because I have seen with my own eyes the messenger who takes him his food.”

段.文: 我不由得替巴里摩尔担心起来。落在这个心肠恶毒、爱管闲事的老头手里，可是件严重的事。可他接下来的话让我放下了心头的石头。
段.en: My heart sank for Barrymore. It was a serious thing to be in the power of this spiteful old busybody. But his next remark took a weight from my mind.

段.文: “您听了会吃惊的：给他送吃的是个孩子。我每天都用屋顶上的望远镜看见他。他总在同一个时候走同一条小路，他不是去找那个逃犯，还能去找谁？”
段.en: “You’ll be surprised to hear that his food is taken to him by a child. I see him every day through my telescope upon the roof. He passes along the same path at the same hour, and to whom should he be going except to the convict?”

段.文: 这可真是好运气！可我还是没有露出半点兴趣。一个孩子！巴里摩尔说过，给我们那个不明身份的人送东西的是个男孩。弗兰克兰偶然撞上的，是那个人的踪迹，而不是逃犯的。要是我能知道他知道的事，就可以省去一场漫长而辛苦的搜寻。不过显然，装作不信和不在乎才是我最好的牌。
段.en: Here was luck indeed! And yet I suppressed all appearance of interest. A child! Barrymore had said that our unknown was supplied by a boy. It was on his track, and not upon the convict’s, that Frankland had stumbled. If I could get his knowledge it might save me a long and weary hunt. But incredulity and indifference were evidently my strongest cards.

段.文: “依我看，更可能是荒原上哪个牧羊人的儿子在给他父亲送饭。”
段.en: “I should say that it was much more likely that it was the son of one of the moorland shepherds taking out his father’s dinner.”

段.文: 只要有一点点反对的意思，就能让这个老霸王冒出火来。他恶狠狠地瞪着我，花白的络腮胡子像发怒的猫一样竖了起来。
段.en: The least appearance of opposition struck fire out of the old autocrat. His eyes looked malignantly at me, and his grey whiskers bristled like those of an angry cat.

段.文: “是吗，先生！”他说着，指向辽阔的荒原，“您看见那边的黑岩了吗？好，您看见再远一点、长着荆棘丛的那座矮山了吗？那是整个荒原上石头最多的地方。牧羊人会到那种地方去放羊吗？先生，您的说法荒唐透顶。”
段.en: “Indeed, sir!” said he, pointing out over the wide-stretching moor. “Do you see that Black Tor over yonder? Well, do you see the low hill beyond with the thornbush upon it? It is the stoniest part of the whole moor. Is that a place where a shepherd would be likely to take his station? Your suggestion, sir, is a most absurd one.”

段.文: 我顺从地回答说，我是不了解全部情况才那么说的。我的服软让他很高兴，他便又对我说了些心里话。
段.en: I meekly answered that I had spoken without knowing all the facts. My submission pleased him and led him to further confidences.

段.文: “您可以放心，先生，我得出一个看法之前，总是有充分根据的。我一次又一次看见那男孩带着他的包袱。每天，有时一天两次，我都能——等一下，华生医生。是我眼花了，还是此刻那片山坡上真有什么东西在动？”
段.en: “You may be sure, sir, that I have very good grounds before I come to an opinion. I have seen the boy again and again with his bundle. Every day, and sometimes twice a day, I have been able—but wait a moment, Dr. Watson. Do my eyes deceive me, or is there at the present moment something moving upon that hillside?”

段.文: 那地方在几英里以外，可我清清楚楚地看到，在暗淡的绿色和灰色中间，有一个小黑点。
段.en: It was several miles off, but I could distinctly see a small dark dot against the dull green and grey.

段.文: “来，先生，快来！”弗兰克兰嚷着，冲上楼去，“您亲眼看看，自己判断吧。”
段.en: “Come, sir, come!” cried Frankland, rushing upstairs. “You will see with your own eyes and judge for yourself.”

段.文: 望远镜是个架在三脚架上的大家伙，摆在宅子平坦的铅皮屋顶上。弗兰克兰把眼睛贴上去，满意地叫了一声。
段.en: The telescope, a formidable instrument mounted upon a tripod, stood upon the flat leads of the house. Frankland clapped his eye to it and gave a cry of satisfaction.

段.文: “快，华生医生，快，趁他还没翻过山去！”
段.en: “Quick, Dr. Watson, quick, before he passes over the hill!”

段.文: 果然，他就在那里：一个小顽童，肩上扛着个小包袱，正慢吞吞地往山上爬。他爬到山顶时，我看见那个衣衫褴褛、样子粗野的身影，在寒冷的蓝天下映出了一瞬间的轮廓。他鬼鬼祟祟地四下张望，像是怕有人追赶。接着他就消失在山的那一边了。
段.en: There he was, sure enough, a small urchin with a little bundle upon his shoulder, toiling slowly up the hill. When he reached the crest I saw the ragged uncouth figure outlined for an instant against the cold blue sky. He looked round him with a furtive and stealthy air, as one who dreads pursuit. Then he vanished over the hill.

段.文: “怎么样！我说对了吧？”
段.en: “Well! Am I right?”

段.文: “的确，有个男孩，好像在办什么秘密差事。”
段.en: “Certainly, there is a boy who seems to have some secret errand.”

段.文: “至于是什么差事，连郡里的警察都猜得出来。可他们休想从我这里得到一个字，我也要您保守秘密，华生医生。一个字也别说！您明白吗！”
段.en: “And what the errand is even a county constable could guess. But not one word shall they have from me, and I bind you to secrecy also, Dr. Watson. Not a word! You understand!”

段.文: “就照您的意思办。”
段.en: “Just as you wish.”

段.文: “他们待我太可耻了——太可耻了。等弗兰克兰诉女王案的实情公之于众，我敢说全国都会激起一阵义愤。无论如何，我都不会帮警察任何忙。在他们看来，那帮无赖绑在火刑柱上烧的就算是我本人，而不是我的模拟像，也无所谓。您不是要走吧！您得帮我把这瓶酒喝光，庆祝这个伟大的日子！”
段.en: “They have treated me shamefully—shamefully. When the facts come out in Frankland v. Regina I venture to think that a thrill of indignation will run through the country. Nothing would induce me to help the police in any way. For all they cared it might have been me, instead of my effigy, which these rascals burned at the stake. Surely you are not going! You will help me to empty the decanter in honour of this great occasion!”

段.文: 可我谢绝了他的一再挽留，还劝住了他，没让他照他说的陪我走回去。只要他还看得见我，我就一直沿着大路走，然后才拐进荒原，朝那男孩消失的石头山走去。一切都对我有利。我发誓，命运送到我面前的这个机会，绝不能因为我不够卖力、不够坚持而错过。
段.en: But I resisted all his solicitations and succeeded in dissuading him from his announced intention of walking home with me. I kept the road as long as his eye was on me, and then I struck off across the moor and made for the stony hill over which the boy had disappeared. Everything was working in my favour, and I swore that it should not be through lack of energy or perseverance that I should miss the chance which fortune had thrown in my way.

段.文: 我爬到山顶时，太阳已经西沉，脚下长长的山坡一面是金绿色，一面是灰色的阴影。最远的天际线上低低地笼着一层薄雾，贝利弗岩和维克森岩奇特的形状从雾中突兀而出。广阔的原野上没有一点声音，也没有一点动静。一只灰色的大鸟，不知是海鸥还是杓鹬，在蓝天上高高翱翔。在巨大的天穹和它下面的荒漠之间，似乎只有它和我两个活物。荒凉的景色、孤独的感觉，加上我这项任务的神秘和紧迫，都让我心里发凉。那男孩已经不见踪影了。不过在我脚下的一道山谷里，有一圈古老的石屋，正中间的一间还留着足够的屋顶，可以遮风挡雨。一看到它，我的心就怦怦直跳。这一定就是那个陌生人藏身的窝。我终于踏上了他藏身之处的门槛——他的秘密已经快到我手里了。
段.en: The sun was already sinking when I reached the summit of the hill, and the long slopes beneath me were all golden-green on one side and grey shadow on the other. A haze lay low upon the farthest sky-line, out of which jutted the fantastic shapes of Belliver and Vixen Tor. Over the wide expanse there was no sound and no movement. One great grey bird, a gull or curlew, soared aloft in the blue heaven. He and I seemed to be the only living things between the huge arch of the sky and the desert beneath it. The barren scene, the sense of loneliness, and the mystery and urgency of my task all struck a chill into my heart. The boy was nowhere to be seen. But down beneath me in a cleft of the hills there was a circle of the old stone huts, and in the middle of them there was one which retained sufficient roof to act as a screen against the weather. My heart leaped within me as I saw it. This must be the burrow where the stranger lurked. At last my foot was on the threshold of his hiding place—his secret was within my grasp.

段.文: 我走近石屋，脚步小心翼翼，就像斯台普顿举着网、悄悄靠近停着的蝴蝶那样。我确认这地方的确有人住过。巨石之间有一条模模糊糊的小路，通向那个破败的、当作门用的缺口。屋里一片寂静。那个陌生人可能潜伏在里面，也可能正在荒原上游荡。冒险的感觉让我浑身的神经都紧绷起来。我扔掉香烟，一手握住左轮手枪的枪柄，快步走到门口，朝里面望去。屋里是空的。
段.en: As I approached the hut, walking as warily as Stapleton would do when with poised net he drew near the settled butterfly, I satisfied myself that the place had indeed been used as a habitation. A vague pathway among the boulders led to the dilapidated opening which served as a door. All was silent within. The unknown might be lurking there, or he might be prowling on the moor. My nerves tingled with the sense of adventure. Throwing aside my cigarette, I closed my hand upon the butt of my revolver and, walking swiftly up to the door, I looked in. The place was empty.

段.文: 可是有充分的迹象表明，我并没有找错。这里肯定是那个人住的地方。几条毯子裹在一件雨衣里，就放在新石器时代人曾经睡过的那块石板上。一个简陋的炉子里堆着柴火的灰烬。旁边放着几件炊具和半桶水。一堆空罐头盒说明，这地方已经有人住了一段时间。等我的眼睛适应了这斑驳的光线，我又看见角落里放着一只小铁杯和半瓶烈酒。石屋中间有块平平的石头当桌子，上面放着一个小布包——无疑就是我在望远镜里看到的、那男孩肩上扛的那个。里面有一条面包、一罐牛舌罐头和两罐桃子罐头。我查看完毕，把它放回原处，这时我的心猛地一跳：布包下面压着一张纸，上面写着字。我拿起来，只见上面用铅笔潦草地写着：“华生医生去了库姆特雷西。”
段.en: But there were ample signs that I had not come upon a false scent. This was certainly where the man lived. Some blankets rolled in a waterproof lay upon that very stone slab upon which Neolithic man had once slumbered. The ashes of a fire were heaped in a rude grate. Beside it lay some cooking utensils and a bucket half-full of water. A litter of empty tins showed that the place had been occupied for some time, and I saw, as my eyes became accustomed to the checkered light, a pannikin and a half-full bottle of spirits standing in the corner. In the middle of the hut a flat stone served the purpose of a table, and upon this stood a small cloth bundle—the same, no doubt, which I had seen through the telescope upon the shoulder of the boy. It contained a loaf of bread, a tinned tongue, and two tins of preserved peaches. As I set it down again, after having examined it, my heart leaped to see that beneath it there lay a sheet of paper with writing upon it. I raised it, and this was what I read, roughly scrawled in pencil: “Dr. Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey.”

段.文: 我拿着这张纸，站在那里足足一分钟，琢磨这条简短的消息是什么意思。这么说，这个神秘的人跟踪的是我，而不是亨利爵士。他没有亲自跟踪我，而是派了个帮手——也许就是那个男孩——盯着我，这就是他的报告。也许我到荒原以来走的每一步，都被人看在眼里、报告了上去。我总觉得有一股看不见的力量，像一张精巧细密的网，极其巧妙地罩在我们周围，罩得那么轻，只有到了某个紧要关头，人才会意识到自己确实已经陷在网里了。
段.en: For a minute I stood there with the paper in my hands thinking out the meaning of this curt message. It was I, then, and not Sir Henry, who was being dogged by this secret man. He had not followed me himself, but he had set an agent—the boy, perhaps—upon my track, and this was his report. Possibly I had taken no step since I had been upon the moor which had not been observed and reported. Always there was this feeling of an unseen force, a fine net drawn round us with infinite skill and delicacy, holding us so lightly that it was only at some supreme moment that one realised that one was indeed entangled in its meshes.

段.文: 既然有一份报告，也许还有别的，于是我在石屋里四处寻找。可是没有任何这类东西的踪迹，也找不到任何迹象，能说明住在这个奇特地方的人是什么性格、有什么意图。我只能看出，他一定过惯了斯巴达式的清苦生活，不怎么在乎舒适。想到那几场大雨，再看看这漏着大洞的屋顶，我明白了，他留在这么一个恶劣的住处，背后的目的一定非常坚定，不可动摇。他是我们的死敌，还是碰巧是我们的守护天使？我发誓，不弄清楚这一点，我就不离开这间石屋。
段.en: If there was one report there might be others, so I looked round the hut in search of them. There was no trace, however, of anything of the kind, nor could I discover any sign which might indicate the character or intentions of the man who lived in this singular place, save that he must be of Spartan habits and cared little for the comforts of life. When I thought of the heavy rains and looked at the gaping roof I understood how strong and immutable must be the purpose which had kept him in that inhospitable abode. Was he our malignant enemy, or was he by chance our guardian angel? I swore that I would not leave the hut until I knew.

段.文: 外面，太阳已经低低地沉下去，西天一片火红和金黄。格林彭大泥沼中远远近近的水塘，把霞光反射回来，映出一块块红斑。那边是巴斯克维尔庄园的两座塔楼，那边远处一片模糊的炊烟，标出了格林彭村的位置。两者之间，山的后面，就是斯台普顿家的宅子。在金色的暮光里，一切都那么柔和、甜美、安宁。可我望着这一切，心里却丝毫感受不到大自然的安宁，反而因为那场越来越近的会面而颤抖——那场会面会是什么样子，我一无所知，只觉得恐惧。我神经紧绷，但决心已定，坐在石屋幽暗的角落里，阴郁而耐心地等着屋主回来。
段.en: Outside the sun was sinking low and the west was blazing with scarlet and gold. Its reflection was shot back in ruddy patches by the distant pools which lay amid the great Grimpen Mire. There were the two towers of Baskerville Hall, and there a distant blur of smoke which marked the village of Grimpen. Between the two, behind the hill, was the house of the Stapletons. All was sweet and mellow and peaceful in the golden evening light, and yet as I looked at them my soul shared none of the peace of Nature but quivered at the vagueness and the terror of that interview which every instant was bringing nearer. With tingling nerves but a fixed purpose, I sat in the dark recess of the hut and waited with sombre patience for the coming of its tenant.

段.文: 终于，我听到他来了。远处传来靴子踩在石头上的清脆响声。接着又是一声，又是一声，越来越近。我缩进最暗的角落，在口袋里扳开了手枪的击锤，决定在看清这个陌生人之前不暴露自己。有好长一阵没有声音，看来他停住了。接着脚步声又走近了，一个影子落在了石屋门口。
段.en: And then at last I heard him. Far away came the sharp clink of a boot striking upon a stone. Then another and yet another, coming nearer and nearer. I shrank back into the darkest corner and cocked the pistol in my pocket, determined not to discover myself until I had an opportunity of seeing something of the stranger. There was a long pause which showed that he had stopped. Then once more the footsteps approached and a shadow fell across the opening of the hut.

段.文: “多美的傍晚啊，我亲爱的华生，”一个熟悉的声音说，“我真觉得，你待在外面会比待在里面舒服些。”
段.en: “It is a lovely evening, my dear Watson,” said a well-known voice. “I really think that you will be more comfortable outside than in.”

段.文: 有那么一两分钟，我坐在那里屏住了呼吸，简直不敢相信自己的耳朵。随后，我的知觉和声音都回来了，压在我心头的那副千斤重担，仿佛一下子卸了下来。那冷静、犀利、带着讥讽的声音，全世界只有一个人才有。
段.en: For a moment or two I sat breathless, hardly able to believe my ears. Then my senses and my voice came back to me, while a crushing weight of responsibility seemed in an instant to be lifted from my soul. That cold, incisive, ironical voice could belong to but one man in all the world.

段.文: “福尔摩斯！”我叫道，“福尔摩斯！”
段.en: “Holmes!” I cried—“Holmes!”

段.文: “出来吧，”他说，“请小心你那把左轮手枪。”
段.en: “Come out,” said he, “and please be careful with the revolver.”

段.文: 我弯腰钻出那道粗糙的门楣，只见他坐在外面一块石头上，看到我满脸惊愕，灰色的眼睛里闪着笑意。他又瘦又憔悴，可神志清醒，十分机警，那张敏锐的脸被太阳晒成了古铜色，又被风吹得粗糙了。他穿着粗花呢衣服，戴着布帽，看上去和荒原上别的游客没什么两样。他像猫一样爱干净，这是他的特点之一；他居然设法让自己的下巴刮得那么光，衬衫那么整洁，就跟待在贝克街一样。
段.en: I stooped under the rude lintel, and there he sat upon a stone outside, his grey eyes dancing with amusement as they fell upon my astonished features. He was thin and worn, but clear and alert, his keen face bronzed by the sun and roughened by the wind. In his tweed suit and cloth cap he looked like any other tourist upon the moor, and he had contrived, with that catlike love of personal cleanliness which was one of his characteristics, that his chin should be as smooth and his linen as perfect as if he were in Baker Street.

段.文: “我这辈子见到谁都没有这么高兴过。”我说着，紧紧握住他的手。
段.en: “I never was more glad to see anyone in my life,” said I as I wrung him by the hand.

段.文: “也没有这么吃惊过吧，嗯？”
段.en: “Or more astonished, eh?”

段.文: “嗯，这我得承认。”
段.en: “Well, I must confess to it.”

段.文: “我向你保证，吃惊的可不只你一个。我完全没想到你找到了我这个偶尔落脚的地方，更没想到你就在里面，直到我离门口不到20步才发觉。”
段.en: “The surprise was not all on one side, I assure you. I had no idea that you had found my occasional retreat, still less that you were inside it, until I was within twenty paces of the door.”

段.文: “我想是因为我的脚印吧？”
段.en: “My footprint, I presume?”

段.文: “不是，华生，世上有那么多脚印，我恐怕没本事认出哪一个是你的。你要是真想骗过我，就得换一家烟店。因为我一看见印着‘牛津街布拉德利’字样的烟头，就知道我的朋友华生就在附近。你会看到它就在小路边。毫无疑问，是你冲进这间空屋的那个紧要关头扔下的。”
段.en: “No, Watson, I fear that I could not undertake to recognize your footprint amid all the footprints of the world. If you seriously desire to deceive me you must change your tobacconist; for when I see the stub of a cigarette marked Bradley, Oxford Street, I know that my friend Watson is in the neighbourhood. You will see it there beside the path. You threw it down, no doubt, at that supreme moment when you charged into the empty hut.”

段.文: “正是。”
段.en: “Exactly.”

段.文: “我就是这么想的——而且我知道你那股令人钦佩的韧劲，所以我确信你正埋伏在里面，武器就在手边，等着屋主回来。这么说，你真以为我就是那个罪犯？”
段.en: “I thought as much—and knowing your admirable tenacity I was convinced that you were sitting in ambush, a weapon within reach, waiting for the tenant to return. So you actually thought that I was the criminal?”

段.文: “我不知道你是谁，可我下了决心要弄清楚。”
段.en: “I did not know who you were, but I was determined to find out.”

段.文: “好极了，华生！那你是怎么找到我的位置的？也许是在追捕逃犯的那天夜里看见了我？那次我太不小心，让月亮从我背后升了起来。”
段.en: “Excellent, Watson! And how did you localise me? You saw me, perhaps, on the night of the convict hunt, when I was so imprudent as to allow the moon to rise behind me?”

段.文: “对，那次我看见了你。”
段.en: “Yes, I saw you then.”

段.文: “然后你一定把石屋一间间都搜遍了，才找到这一间？”
段.en: “And have no doubt searched all the huts until you came to this one?”

段.文: “不是，有人看见了你那个男孩，这就给我指了路。”
段.en: “No, your boy had been observed, and that gave me a guide where to look.”

段.文: “一定是那个拿望远镜的老先生。我第一次看见镜片上闪光的时候，还弄不明白是怎么回事。”他站起身来，往石屋里瞧了瞧。“哈，我看卡特赖特送了些吃的来。这张纸是什么？这么说，你去过库姆特雷西了？”
段.en: “The old gentleman with the telescope, no doubt. I could not make it out when first I saw the light flashing upon the lens.” He rose and peeped into the hut. “Ha, I see that Cartwright has brought up some supplies. What’s this paper? So you have been to Coombe Tracey, have you?”

段.文: “是的。”
段.en: “Yes.”

段.文: “去见劳拉·莱昂斯太太？”
段.en: “To see Mrs. Laura Lyons?”

段.文: “正是。”
段.en: “Exactly.”

段.文: “干得好！显然我们的调查是沿着两条平行线进行的，等我们把结果合起来，我想对这个案子就能了解得相当全面了。”
段.en: “Well done! Our researches have evidently been running on parallel lines, and when we unite our results I expect we shall have a fairly full knowledge of the case.”

段.文: “说真的，你能来这儿，我打心底里高兴，因为那份责任和那些谜团，确实快让我的神经受不了了。可你到底是怎么跑到这儿来的？你一直在干什么？我还以为你在贝克街忙那桩敲诈案呢。”
段.en: “Well, I am glad from my heart that you are here, for indeed the responsibility and the mystery were both becoming too much for my nerves. But how in the name of wonder did you come here, and what have you been doing? I thought that you were in Baker Street working out that case of blackmailing.”

段.文: “我正是希望你这么想。”
段.en: “That was what I wished you to think.”

段.文: “这么说，你利用我，却又不信任我！”我有些心酸地叫道，“福尔摩斯，我觉得我不该受你这样的对待。”
段.en: “Then you use me, and yet do not trust me!” I cried with some bitterness. “I think that I have deserved better at your hands, Holmes.”

段.文: “我亲爱的朋友，在这个案子里，就像在许多别的案子里一样，你对我的帮助是无价的。如果我看起来像是捉弄了你，还请你原谅。说实话，我这样做一部分是为了你好。正是因为我意识到你所冒的危险，我才亲自来调查这件事。要是我和亨利爵士、和你待在一起，我的看法肯定会跟你的一样，而且我一露面，就会提醒我们那个非常厉害的对手提高警惕。现在这样，我就能到处活动，要是我住在庄园里，这是绝对做不到的。我在这件事里始终是个不为人知的因素，随时准备在关键时刻全力出击。”
段.en: “My dear fellow, you have been invaluable to me in this as in many other cases, and I beg that you will forgive me if I have seemed to play a trick upon you. In truth, it was partly for your own sake that I did it, and it was my appreciation of the danger which you ran which led me to come down and examine the matter for myself. Had I been with Sir Henry and you it is confident that my point of view would have been the same as yours, and my presence would have warned our very formidable opponents to be on their guard. As it is, I have been able to get about as I could not possibly have done had I been living in the Hall, and I remain an unknown factor in the business, ready to throw in all my weight at a critical moment.”

段.文: “可为什么要瞒着我呢？”
段.en: “But why keep me in the dark?”

段.文: “你知道了也帮不上我们的忙，反倒可能让我暴露。你会想告诉我点什么，或者出于好心，给我送点这样那样的东西来，让我舒服些，这样就会冒不必要的风险。我把卡特赖特带来了——你还记得送信公司的那个小家伙吧——他照料我简单的需要：一条面包，一条干净的领子。一个人还要什么呢？他给了我一双额外的眼睛，外加一双非常勤快的脚，这两样都无比宝贵。”
段.en: “For you to know could not have helped us and might possibly have led to my discovery. You would have wished to tell me something, or in your kindness you would have brought me out some comfort or other, and so an unnecessary risk would be run. I brought Cartwright down with me—you remember the little chap at the express office—and he has seen after my simple wants: a loaf of bread and a clean collar. What does man want more? He has given me an extra pair of eyes upon a very active pair of feet, and both have been invaluable.”

段.文: “这么说，我的报告全都白写了！”——想起我写那些报告时费了多少心血、又多么得意，我的声音都发抖了。
段.en: “Then my reports have all been wasted!”—My voice trembled as I recalled the pains and the pride with which I had composed them.

段.文: 福尔摩斯从口袋里掏出一叠纸。
段.en: Holmes took a bundle of papers from his pocket.

段.文: “这就是你的报告，我亲爱的朋友，我向你保证，都快被我翻烂了。我做了很周到的安排，它们在路上只耽搁一天。这个案子异常棘手，你在里面表现出的热忱和才智，我一定要大大称赞一番。”
段.en: “Here are your reports, my dear fellow, and very well thumbed, I assure you. I made excellent arrangements, and they are only delayed one day upon their way. I must compliment you exceedingly upon the zeal and the intelligence which you have shown over an extraordinarily difficult case.”

段.文: 被人这样蒙在鼓里，我心里仍然有点不是滋味，可福尔摩斯热情的赞扬驱散了我的怒气。我心里也觉得他说得对，为了我们的目标，我确实最好不知道他就在荒原上。
段.en: I was still rather raw over the deception which had been practised upon me, but the warmth of Holmes’s praise drove my anger from my mind. I felt also in my heart that he was right in what he said and that it was really best for our purpose that I should not have known that he was upon the moor.

段.文: “这就好多了，”他看到我脸上的阴云散去，说，“现在跟我说说你去见劳拉·莱昂斯太太的结果吧——我不难猜到你是去见她的，因为我早就知道，在库姆特雷西，她是唯一可能在这件事上帮得上我们的人。说实在的，要是你今天没去，我明天多半就会去了。”
段.en: “That’s better,” said he, seeing the shadow rise from my face. “And now tell me the result of your visit to Mrs. Laura Lyons—it was not difficult for me to guess that it was to see her that you had gone, for I am already aware that she is the one person in Coombe Tracey who might be of service to us in the matter. In fact, if you had not gone today it is exceedingly probable that I should have gone tomorrow.”

段.文: 太阳已经落山，暮色笼罩着荒原。空气变冷了，我们退回石屋里取暖。我们坐在暮色中，我把和那位女士的谈话告诉了福尔摩斯。他听得非常入神，有些话我得说上两遍他才满意。
段.en: The sun had set and dusk was settling over the moor. The air had turned chill and we withdrew into the hut for warmth. There, sitting together in the twilight, I told Holmes of my conversation with the lady. So interested was he that I had to repeat some of it twice before he was satisfied.

段.文: “这非常重要，”我讲完以后，他说，“这个案子错综复杂，其中有个缺口我一直没法填上，现在填上了。你也许知道，这位女士和那个斯台普顿关系非常亲密吧？”
段.en: “This is most important,” said he when I had concluded. “It fills up a gap which I had been unable to bridge in this most complex affair. You are aware, perhaps, that a close intimacy exists between this lady and the man Stapleton?”

段.文: “我不知道他们关系亲密。”
段.en: “I did not know of a close intimacy.”

段.文: “这是毫无疑问的。他们见面，他们通信，彼此心照不宣。这就给了我们一件非常有力的武器。只要我能用它离间他的妻子——”
