段.en: “There can be no doubt about the matter. They meet, they write, there is a complete understanding between them. Now, this puts a very powerful weapon into our hands. If I could only use it to detach his wife—”

段.文: “他的妻子？”
段.en: “His wife?”

段.文: “你给了我那么多情况，现在我也给你一些作为回报。在这里冒充斯台普顿小姐的那位女士，其实是他的妻子。”
段.en: “I am giving you some information now, in return for all that you have given me. The lady who has passed here as Miss Stapleton is in reality his wife.”

段.文: “天哪，福尔摩斯！你说的话有把握吗？那他怎么会让亨利爵士爱上她呢？”
段.en: “Good heavens, Holmes! Are you sure of what you say? How could he have permitted Sir Henry to fall in love with her?”

段.文: “亨利爵士爱上她，除了对亨利爵士自己以外，对谁都没有害处。你自己也看到了，他特别留心，不让亨利爵士向她求爱。我再说一遍，那位女士是他的妻子，不是他的妹妹。”
段.en: “Sir Henry’s falling in love could do no harm to anyone except Sir Henry. He took particular care that Sir Henry did not make love to her, as you have yourself observed. I repeat that the lady is his wife and not his sister.”

段.文: “可为什么要设这么一个精心的骗局呢？”
段.en: “But why this elaborate deception?”

段.文: “因为他预见到，她以自由女子的身份出现，对他会有用得多。”
段.en: “Because he foresaw that she would be very much more useful to him in the character of a free woman.”

段.文: 我那些没说出口的直觉、那些模糊的怀疑，一下子都有了形状，全都集中到了那位博物学者身上。那个戴草帽、拿捕蝶网、面无表情、平淡无奇的人，在我眼中似乎显出了某种可怕的东西——一个有着无穷耐心和狡诈的家伙，脸上带着笑，心里却藏着杀机。
段.en: All my unspoken instincts, my vague suspicions, suddenly took shape and centred upon the naturalist. In that impassive colourless man, with his straw hat and his butterfly-net, I seemed to see something terrible—a creature of infinite patience and craft, with a smiling face and a murderous heart.

段.文: “这么说，我们的敌人就是他——在伦敦跟踪我们的就是他？”
段.en: “It is he, then, who is our enemy—it is he who dogged us in London?”

段.文: “我是这样解这个谜的。”
段.en: “So I read the riddle.”

段.文: “那封警告信——一定是她寄的！”
段.en: “And the warning—it must have come from her!”

段.文: “正是。”
段.en: “Exactly.”

段.文: 长久以来笼罩着我的黑暗中，隐隐现出了一桩骇人罪行的轮廓，一半看得见，一半靠猜。
段.en: The shape of some monstrous villainy, half seen, half guessed, loomed through the darkness which had girt me so long.

段.文: “可你对这一点有把握吗，福尔摩斯？你怎么知道那女人是他的妻子？”
段.en: “But are you sure of this, Holmes? How do you know that the woman is his wife?”

段.文: “因为他第一次见到你的时候，一时大意，跟你讲了一段真实的身世，我敢说从那以后他后悔过不知多少次。他曾经在英格兰北部当过校长。要说追查谁的底细最容易，没有比校长更容易的了。有一些教育机构，凭它们就能查清任何干过这一行的人。我稍一调查就发现，有一所学校在极其恶劣的情况下垮了，学校的主人——名字不一样——带着妻子失踪了。相貌描述都对得上。等我得知那个失踪的人醉心于昆虫学，身份就完全确定了。”
段.en: “Because he so far forgot himself as to tell you a true piece of autobiography upon the occasion when he first met you, and I dare say he has many a time regretted it since. He was once a schoolmaster in the north of England. Now, there is no one more easy to trace than a schoolmaster. There are scholastic agencies by which one may identify any man who has been in the profession. A little investigation showed me that a school had come to grief under atrocious circumstances, and that the man who had owned it—the name was different—had disappeared with his wife. The descriptions agreed. When I learned that the missing man was devoted to entomology the identification was complete.”

段.文: 黑暗正在退去，可还有许多东西藏在阴影里。
段.en: The darkness was rising, but much was still hidden by the shadows.

段.文: “如果这个女人真是他的妻子，那劳拉·莱昂斯太太又是怎么回事呢？”我问。
段.en: “If this woman is in truth his wife, where does Mrs. Laura Lyons come in?” I asked.

段.文: “这正是你的调查照亮了的地方之一。你和那位女士的谈话，让情况清楚了很多。我原先不知道她和她丈夫打算离婚。既然这样，她把斯台普顿当成了未婚男子，无疑指望着成为他的妻子。”
段.en: “That is one of the points upon which your own researches have shed a light. Your interview with the lady has cleared the situation very much. I did not know about a projected divorce between herself and her husband. In that case, regarding Stapleton as an unmarried man, she counted no doubt upon becoming his wife.”

段.文: “等她发现自己受了骗呢？”
段.en: “And when she is undeceived?”

段.文: “哎，那时候这位女士也许就能帮上我们的忙了。我们首先要做的，就是明天去见她——我们两个一起去。华生，你不觉得你离开你要保护的人太久了吗？你应该待在巴斯克维尔庄园。”
段.en: “Why, then we may find the lady of service. It must be our first duty to see her—both of us—tomorrow. Don’t you think, Watson, that you are away from your charge rather long? Your place should be at Baskerville Hall.”

段.文: 西天最后几道红霞已经消失，夜色降临在荒原上。紫罗兰色的天空中，闪着几颗暗淡的星星。
段.en: The last red streaks had faded away in the west and night had settled upon the moor. A few faint stars were gleaming in a violet sky.

段.文: “最后一个问题，福尔摩斯，”我站起身来说，“你我之间当然用不着保密。这一切到底是什么意思？他到底想干什么？”
段.en: “One last question, Holmes,” I said as I rose. “Surely there is no need of secrecy between you and me. What is the meaning of it all? What is he after?”

段.文: 福尔摩斯回答时，压低了声音：
段.en: Holmes’s voice sank as he answered:

段.文: “是谋杀，华生——精心策划、冷酷无情、蓄意已久的谋杀。别问我细节。我的网正在向他收拢，就像他的网正在向亨利爵士收拢一样。有了你的帮助，他几乎已经落到我手里了。只有一种危险可能威胁到我们，那就是他抢在我们准备好之前先动手。再有一天——最多两天——我的证据就齐了。可在那之前，你要寸步不离地守着你要保护的人，就像慈爱的母亲守着生病的孩子那样。你今天这一趟没有白跑，可我几乎希望你没有离开他身边。听！”
段.en: “It is murder, Watson—refined, cold-blooded, deliberate murder. Do not ask me for particulars. My nets are closing upon him, even as his are upon Sir Henry, and with your help he is already almost at my mercy. There is but one danger which can threaten us. It is that he should strike before we are ready to do so. Another day—two at the most—and I have my case complete, but until then guard your charge as closely as ever a fond mother watched her ailing child. Your mission today has justified itself, and yet I could almost wish that you had not left his side. Hark!”

段.文: 一声可怕的尖叫——一声拖得长长的、充满恐惧和痛苦的嚎叫——划破了荒原的寂静。那骇人的叫声让我全身的血都凉透了。
段.en: A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst out of the silence of the moor. That frightful cry turned the blood to ice in my veins.

段.文: “哦，我的上帝！”我喘着气说，“那是什么？这是怎么回事？”
段.en: “Oh, my God!” I gasped. “What is it? What does it mean?”

段.文: 福尔摩斯已经一跃而起。我看见他矫健的黑色身影站在石屋门口，弯着肩，探着头，向黑暗中凝望。
段.en: Holmes had sprung to his feet, and I saw his dark, athletic outline at the door of the hut, his shoulders stooping, his head thrust forward, his face peering into the darkness.

段.文: “嘘！”他低声说，“嘘！”
段.en: “Hush!” he whispered. “Hush!”

段.文: 那叫声十分凄厉，所以听起来很响，其实是从阴暗的原野远处什么地方传来的。现在它又在我们耳边炸响，比刚才更近、更响、更急。
段.en: The cry had been loud on account of its vehemence, but it had pealed out from somewhere far off on the shadowy plain. Now it burst upon our ears, nearer, louder, more urgent than before.

段.文: “在哪儿？”福尔摩斯低声问。从他发颤的声音里我知道，连他这个铁打的人，也被震动到了灵魂深处。“在哪儿，华生？”
段.en: “Where is it?” Holmes whispered; and I knew from the thrill of his voice that he, the man of iron, was shaken to the soul. “Where is it, Watson?”

段.文: “我想是那边。”我指向黑暗中。
段.en: “There, I think.” I pointed into the darkness.

段.文: “不，是那边！”
段.en: “No, there!”

段.文: 那痛苦的叫声又一次掠过寂静的夜空，比任何一次都响，也近得多。这时又有一种新的声音混了进来，那是一种低沉的、含混的隆隆声，像音乐一样，却又带着威胁，忽高忽低，就像大海低沉而不停的呢喃。
段.en: Again the agonised cry swept through the silent night, louder and much nearer than ever. And a new sound mingled with it, a deep, muttered rumble, musical and yet menacing, rising and falling like the low, constant murmur of the sea.

段.文: “猎犬！”福尔摩斯叫道，“来，华生，快来！天哪，要是我们来晚了！”
段.en: “The hound!” cried Holmes. “Come, Watson, come! Great heavens, if we are too late!”

段.文: 他已经飞快地跑过荒原，我紧跟在他后面。可就在这时，从我们正前方那片崎岖不平的地方，传来了最后一声绝望的嚎叫，接着是沉重的一声闷响。我们停下来听。无风的夜晚一片死寂，再没有一点声音打破它。
段.en: He had started running swiftly over the moor, and I had followed at his heels. But now from somewhere among the broken ground immediately in front of us there came one last despairing yell, and then a dull, heavy thud. We halted and listened. Not another sound broke the heavy silence of the windless night.

段.文: 我看见福尔摩斯用手捂住额头，像个心神错乱的人。他用脚使劲跺着地。
段.en: I saw Holmes put his hand to his forehead like a man distracted. He stamped his feet upon the ground.

段.文: “他赢了我们，华生。我们来晚了。”
段.en: “He has beaten us, Watson. We are too late.”

段.文: “不，不，肯定不会的！”
段.en: “No, no, surely not!”

段.文: “我真蠢，一直按兵不动。还有你，华生，看看丢下你要保护的人会有什么结果！可是，老天在上，要是最坏的事已经发生了，我们一定要替他报仇！”
段.en: “Fool that I was to hold my hand. And you, Watson, see what comes of abandoning your charge! But, by Heaven, if the worst has happened we’ll avenge him!”

段.文: 我们在黑暗中盲目地奔跑，撞上巨石，从荆豆丛中硬挤过去，喘着气爬上山，又冲下坡，始终朝着那可怕的声音传来的方向。每到一处高地，福尔摩斯都急切地四下张望，可荒原上阴影浓重，凄凉的原野上什么也没有动。
段.en: Blindly we ran through the gloom, blundering against boulders, forcing our way through gorse bushes, panting up hills and rushing down slopes, heading always in the direction whence those dreadful sounds had come. At every rise Holmes looked eagerly round him, but the shadows were thick upon the moor, and nothing moved upon its dreary face.

段.文: “你看得见什么吗？”
段.en: “Can you see anything?”

段.文: “什么也看不见。”
段.en: “Nothing.”

段.文: “可是，听，那是什么？”
段.en: “But, hark, what is that?”

段.文: 一声低低的呻吟传进我们耳朵里。又来了，在我们左边！那一边有一道岩脊，尽头是一面陡峭的悬崖，下面是满是乱石的山坡。在参差不齐的岩面上，摊开着一个黑乎乎的、形状不规则的东西。我们朝它跑过去，那模糊的轮廓渐渐变成了一个清楚的形状。那是一个人，脸朝下扑倒在地上，头以一种可怕的角度折在身子底下，两肩拱起，身体缩成一团，像是正在翻跟头。那姿势太怪异了，我一时没意识到，刚才那声呻吟就是他咽下最后一口气。我们俯身看着这个黑乎乎的身体，现在它连一丝声息、一点动静都没有了。福尔摩斯把手放在他身上，又惊恐地叫了一声，把手举了起来。他划着一根火柴，火光照在他沾满凝血的手指上，照在一摊可怕的血泊上——血正从死者碎裂的头骨里慢慢往外淌，越淌越大。火光还照见了另一样东西，让我们的心一阵发紧、一阵发软——那是亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士的尸体！
段.en: A low moan had fallen upon our ears. There it was again upon our left! On that side a ridge of rocks ended in a sheer cliff which overlooked a stone-strewn slope. On its jagged face was spread-eagled some dark, irregular object. As we ran towards it the vague outline hardened into a definite shape. It was a prostrate man face downward upon the ground, the head doubled under him at a horrible angle, the shoulders rounded and the body hunched together as if in the act of throwing a somersault. So grotesque was the attitude that I could not for the instant realise that that moan had been the passing of his soul. Not a whisper, not a rustle, rose now from the dark figure over which we stooped. Holmes laid his hand upon him and held it up again with an exclamation of horror. The gleam of the match which he struck shone upon his clotted fingers and upon the ghastly pool which widened slowly from the crushed skull of the victim. And it shone upon something else which turned our hearts sick and faint within us—the body of Sir Henry Baskerville!

段.文: 我们俩谁都不会忘记那套特别的红色粗花呢衣服——正是我们第一次在贝克街见到他的那天早上，他穿的那一套。我们清清楚楚地看了一眼，接着火柴闪了闪就熄灭了，就像我们心中的希望熄灭了一样。福尔摩斯呻吟了一声，他的脸在黑暗中显得惨白。
段.en: There was no chance of either of us forgetting that peculiar ruddy tweed suit—the very one which he had worn on the first morning that we had seen him in Baker Street. We caught the one clear glimpse of it, and then the match flickered and went out, even as the hope had gone out of our souls. Holmes groaned, and his face glimmered white through the darkness.

段.文: “畜生！畜生！”我攥紧双拳叫道，“哦，福尔摩斯，我丢下他让他去送死，我永远也不会原谅自己。”
段.en: “The brute! The brute!” I cried with clenched hands. “Oh Holmes, I shall never forgive myself for having left him to his fate.”

段.文: “我比你更该受责备，华生。为了让我的证据圆满齐全，我断送了我委托人的性命。这是我一生中遭受的最大打击。可我怎么会知道——我怎么会知道——我再三警告过他，他还会冒着生命危险，独自跑到荒原上来？”
段.en: “I am more to blame than you, Watson. In order to have my case well rounded and complete, I have thrown away the life of my client. It is the greatest blow which has befallen me in my career. But how could I know—how could I know—that he would risk his life alone upon the moor in the face of all my warnings?”

段.文: “我们听见了他的尖叫——我的上帝，那尖叫声！——却没能救他！把他逼死的那条畜生一样的猎犬在哪儿？说不定这会儿它就潜伏在这些岩石中间。还有斯台普顿，他在哪儿？他要为这件事偿命。”
段.en: “That we should have heard his screams—my God, those screams!—and yet have been unable to save him! Where is this brute of a hound which drove him to his death? It may be lurking among these rocks at this instant. And Stapleton, where is he? He shall answer for this deed.”

段.文: “他会的。这件事交给我。叔侄二人都被谋杀了——一个是一看见那头他以为是超自然的野兽就吓死了，一个是为了逃命拼命狂奔，结果送了命。可现在我们得证明那个人和那头野兽之间的关系。除了我们听到的声音，我们甚至没法发誓说那头野兽确实存在，因为亨利爵士显然是摔死的。可是，老天在上，不管那家伙多么狡猾，不出一天，我就要叫他落到我手里！”
段.en: “He shall. I will see to that. Uncle and nephew have been murdered—the one frightened to death by the very sight of a beast which he thought to be supernatural, the other driven to his end in his wild flight to escape from it. But now we have to prove the connection between the man and the beast. Save from what we heard, we cannot even swear to the existence of the latter, since Sir Henry has evidently died from the fall. But, by heavens, cunning as he is, the fellow shall be in my power before another day is past!”

段.文: 我们心情沉痛，站在那具血肉模糊的尸体两边。这场突如其来、无法挽回的灾难让我们不知所措，我们长久以来的辛苦努力，竟落得这样一个凄惨的结局。后来月亮升起来了，我们爬上了我们可怜的朋友摔下来的那堆岩石的顶上，从那里眺望阴暗的荒原，一半银白，一半昏暗。远处，在几英里外格林彭的方向，有一点黄色的灯光，稳稳地亮着。那只可能是斯台普顿家那所孤零零的宅子。我望着它，狠狠地咒骂了一句，朝它挥了挥拳头。
段.en: We stood with bitter hearts on either side of the mangled body, overwhelmed by this sudden and irrevocable disaster which had brought all our long and weary labours to so piteous an end. Then as the moon rose we climbed to the top of the rocks over which our poor friend had fallen, and from the summit we gazed out over the shadowy moor, half silver and half gloom. Far away, miles off, in the direction of Grimpen, a single steady yellow light was shining. It could only come from the lonely abode of the Stapletons. With a bitter curse I shook my fist at it as I gazed.

段.文: “我们为什么不马上去抓他？”
段.en: “Why should we not seize him at once?”

段.文: “我们的证据还不齐全。那家伙极其警惕，极其狡猾。要紧的不是我们知道什么，而是我们能证明什么。我们只要走错一步，那个恶棍就可能逃掉。”
段.en: “Our case is not complete. The fellow is wary and cunning to the last degree. It is not what we know, but what we can prove. If we make one false move the villain may escape us yet.”

段.文: “那我们能做什么？”
段.en: “What can we do?”

段.文: “明天有的是事要做。今晚我们只能为我们可怜的朋友料理后事了。”
段.en: “There will be plenty for us to do tomorrow. Tonight we can only perform the last offices to our poor friend.”

段.文: 我们一起走下陡峭的山坡，走近那具尸体，它在银白色的石头上显得又黑又清楚。看着那扭曲的四肢所表现出的痛苦，我心里一阵剧痛，泪水模糊了双眼。
段.en: Together we made our way down the precipitous slope and approached the body, black and clear against the silvered stones. The agony of those contorted limbs struck me with a spasm of pain and blurred my eyes with tears.

段.文: “我们得去找人帮忙，福尔摩斯！我们没法一路把他抬回庄园去。天哪，你疯了吗？”
段.en: “We must send for help, Holmes! We cannot carry him all the way to the Hall. Good heavens, are you mad?”

段.文: 他叫了一声，俯身察看尸体。这时他又是跳又是笑，还使劲握我的手。这难道是我那位严峻而沉着的朋友吗？这可真是深藏不露的火焰啊！
段.en: He had uttered a cry and bent over the body. Now he was dancing and laughing and wringing my hand. Could this be my stern, self-contained friend? These were hidden fires, indeed!

段.文: “胡子！胡子！这人有胡子！”
段.en: “A beard! A beard! The man has a beard!”

段.文: “胡子？”
段.en: “A beard?”

段.文: “这不是准男爵——这是——哎呀，这是我的邻居，那个逃犯！”
段.en: “It is not the baronet—it is—why, it is my neighbour, the convict!”

段.文: 我们急不可耐地把尸体翻过来，那把湿淋淋的胡子朝上对着寒冷而明亮的月亮。那突出的前额、那深陷的野兽般的眼睛，是不会认错的。这确实就是那天晚上在烛光中从岩石后面瞪着我的那张脸——罪犯塞尔登的脸。
段.en: With feverish haste we had turned the body over, and that dripping beard was pointing up to the cold, clear moon. There could be no doubt about the beetling forehead, the sunken animal eyes. It was indeed the same face which had glared upon me in the light of the candle from over the rock—the face of Selden, the criminal.

段.文: 转眼之间，一切我都明白了。我想起准男爵跟我说过，他把自己的旧衣服给了巴里摩尔。巴里摩尔又转送了出去，好帮塞尔登逃走。靴子、衬衫、帽子——全是亨利爵士的。这场悲剧仍然够黑暗的，可按照这个国家的法律，这个人至少是罪该一死。我把事情的原委告诉了福尔摩斯，心里满是感激和喜悦。
段.en: Then in an instant it was all clear to me. I remembered how the baronet had told me that he had handed his old wardrobe to Barrymore. Barrymore had passed it on in order to help Selden in his escape. Boots, shirt, cap—it was all Sir Henry’s. The tragedy was still black enough, but this man had at least deserved death by the laws of his country. I told Holmes how the matter stood, my heart bubbling over with thankfulness and joy.

段.文: “这么说，是这些衣服要了这可怜虫的命，”他说，“很清楚，有人让猎犬闻了亨利爵士的什么东西——很可能就是在旅馆里被偷走的那只靴子——所以它追上了这个人。不过有一件事非常奇怪：塞尔登在黑暗中，怎么会知道猎犬在追他呢？”
段.en: “Then the clothes have been the poor devil’s death,” said he. “It is clear enough that the hound has been laid on from some article of Sir Henry’s—the boot which was abstracted in the hotel, in all probability—and so ran this man down. There is one very singular thing, however: How came Selden, in the darkness, to know that the hound was on his trail?”

段.文: “他听见了。”
段.en: “He heard him.”

段.文: “像这个逃犯这样的硬汉，在荒原上听见猎犬叫，不至于吓得魂飞魄散，不惜冒着再被抓住的危险，发疯似的大喊救命。从他的叫声判断，他知道那畜生在追他以后，一定跑了很长一段路。他是怎么知道的？”
段.en: “To hear a hound upon the moor would not work a hard man like this convict into such a paroxysm of terror that he would risk recapture by screaming wildly for help. By his cries he must have run a long way after he knew the animal was on his track. How did he know?”

段.文: “对我来说，更大的谜是，这条猎犬——假定我们的推测都对的话——”
段.en: “A greater mystery to me is why this hound, presuming that all our conjectures are correct—”

段.文: “我什么也不假定。”
段.en: “I presume nothing.”

段.文: “好吧，那就是，这条猎犬今晚为什么会放出来。我想它不会总在荒原上乱跑。除非斯台普顿有理由认为亨利爵士会在那里，否则他是不会把它放出来的。”
段.en: “Well, then, why this hound should be loose tonight. I suppose that it does not always run loose upon the moor. Stapleton would not let it go unless he had reason to think that Sir Henry would be there.”

段.文: “我的难题比你的更难对付，因为我想你的问题很快就会有答案，而我的也许永远是个谜。现在的问题是，这可怜虫的尸体怎么办？我们不能把它丢在这里喂狐狸和乌鸦。”
段.en: “My difficulty is the more formidable of the two, for I think that we shall very shortly get an explanation of yours, while mine may remain forever a mystery. The question now is, what shall we do with this poor wretch’s body? We cannot leave it here to the foxes and the ravens.”

段.文: “我建议先把它放进一间石屋里，等我们通知了警察再说。”
段.en: “I suggest that we put it in one of the huts until we can communicate with the police.”

段.文: “正是。我相信你和我能把它抬到那里。喂，华生，那是什么？真是奇了，好大的胆子，正是那个人自己！别露出你的怀疑——一个字也别说，否则我的计划就全完了。”
段.en: “Exactly. I have no doubt that you and I could carry it so far. Halloa, Watson, what’s this? It’s the man himself, by all that’s wonderful and audacious! Not a word to show your suspicions—not a word, or my plans crumble to the ground.”

段.文: 一个人影正穿过荒原朝我们走来，我看见了雪茄暗红的火光。月光照在他身上，我认出了那位博物学者整洁的身形和轻快的步态。他看见我们，停了一下，然后又走了过来。
段.en: A figure was approaching us over the moor, and I saw the dull red glow of a cigar. The moon shone upon him, and I could distinguish the dapper shape and jaunty walk of the naturalist. He stopped when he saw us, and then came on again.

段.文: “哎呀，华生医生，不是你吧？夜里这个时候，我最想不到会在荒原上碰见的就是你了。可是，天哪，这是怎么了？有人受伤了？不是——别告诉我是我们的朋友亨利爵士！”他匆匆从我身边走过，俯身去看死者。我听见他猛吸了一口气，雪茄从他指间掉了下去。
段.en: “Why, Dr. Watson, that’s not you, is it? You are the last man that I should have expected to see out on the moor at this time of night. But, dear me, what’s this? Somebody hurt? Not—don’t tell me that it is our friend Sir Henry!” He hurried past me and stooped over the dead man. I heard a sharp intake of his breath and the cigar fell from his fingers.

段.文: “这——这是谁？”他结结巴巴地说。
段.en: “Who—who’s this?” he stammered.

段.文: “是塞尔登，从普林斯敦逃出来的那个人。”
段.en: “It is Selden, the man who escaped from Princetown.”

段.文: 斯台普顿转过一张惨白的脸对着我们，可他拼尽全力，压住了自己的惊愕和失望。他目光锐利地从福尔摩斯看到我。“天哪！这事太骇人了！他是怎么死的？”
段.en: Stapleton turned a ghastly face upon us, but by a supreme effort he had overcome his amazement and his disappointment. He looked sharply from Holmes to me. “Dear me! What a very shocking affair! How did he die?”

段.文: “看样子是从这些岩石上摔下来，摔断了脖子。我的朋友和我正在荒原上散步，听见了一声叫喊。”
段.en: “He appears to have broken his neck by falling over these rocks. My friend and I were strolling on the moor when we heard a cry.”

段.文: “我也听见了叫喊。所以我才出来。我担心亨利爵士。”
段.en: “I heard a cry also. That was what brought me out. I was uneasy about Sir Henry.”

段.文: “为什么偏偏担心亨利爵士？”我忍不住问。
段.en: “Why about Sir Henry in particular?” I could not help asking.

段.文: “因为我请过他过来一趟。他没来，我很奇怪；听见荒原上有叫喊声，我自然就为他的安全担心了。对了，”——他的目光又从我脸上飞快地转到福尔摩斯脸上——“除了叫喊，你们还听见别的什么没有？”
段.en: “Because I had suggested that he should come over. When he did not come I was surprised, and I naturally became alarmed for his safety when I heard cries upon the moor. By the way”—his eyes darted again from my face to Holmes’s—“did you hear anything else besides a cry?”

段.文: “没有，”福尔摩斯说，“你呢？”
段.en: “No,” said Holmes; “did you?”

段.文: “没有。”
段.en: “No.”

段.文: “那你是什么意思？”
段.en: “What do you mean, then?”

段.文: “哦，你们知道农民们讲的那些故事，什么鬼犬之类的。据说夜里在荒原上能听到它叫。我在想，今晚有没有什么迹象说明有过这种声音。”
段.en: “Oh, you know the stories that the peasants tell about a phantom hound, and so on. It is said to be heard at night upon the moor. I was wondering if there were any evidence of such a sound tonight.”

段.文: “我们没听见那样的声音。”我说。
段.en: “We heard nothing of the kind,” said I.

段.文: “那这个可怜的家伙是怎么死的，你们怎么看？”
段.en: “And what is your theory of this poor fellow’s death?”

段.文: “我相信是焦虑和风吹雨淋让他精神失常了。他疯疯癫癫地在荒原上乱跑，最后从这里摔下去，摔断了脖子。”
段.en: “I have no doubt that anxiety and exposure have driven him off his head. He has rushed about the moor in a crazy state and eventually fallen over here and broken his neck.”

段.文: “这看来是最合理的解释了。”斯台普顿说着，叹了一口气，我觉得那是松了口气。“您怎么看，夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生？”
段.en: “That seems the most reasonable theory,” said Stapleton, and he gave a sigh which I took to indicate his relief. “What do you think about it, Mr. Sherlock Holmes?”

段.文: 我的朋友欠了欠身。“你认人倒是很快。”他说。
段.en: My friend bowed his compliments. “You are quick at identification,” said he.

段.文: “自从华生医生来了以后，我们就一直盼着您到这一带来。您来得正好，赶上了一场悲剧。”
段.en: “We have been expecting you in these parts since Dr. Watson came down. You are in time to see a tragedy.”

段.文: “是啊，的确如此。我相信我朋友的解释能说明一切事实。明天我要带着一段不愉快的回忆回伦敦去了。”
段.en: “Yes, indeed. I have no doubt that my friend’s explanation will cover the facts. I will take an unpleasant remembrance back to London with me tomorrow.”

段.文: “哦，您明天就回去？”
段.en: “Oh, you return tomorrow?”

段.文: “我是这么打算的。”
段.en: “That is my intention.”

段.文: “我希望您这次来，对那些让我们困惑的事情有所揭示吧？”
段.en: “I hope your visit has cast some light upon those occurrences which have puzzled us?”

段.文: 福尔摩斯耸了耸肩。
段.en: Holmes shrugged his shoulders.

段.文: “人不可能总是得偿所愿。侦查的人需要的是事实，而不是传说或谣言。这个案子办得不能令人满意。”
段.en: “One cannot always have the success for which one hopes. An investigator needs facts and not legends or rumours. It has not been a satisfactory case.”

段.文: 我的朋友说话的样子极其坦率，毫不在意。斯台普顿仍然紧紧盯着他。然后他转向我。
段.en: My friend spoke in his frankest and most unconcerned manner. Stapleton still looked hard at him. Then he turned to me.

段.文: “我本想把这个可怜的家伙抬到我家去，可那会把我妹妹吓坏的，我觉得不该这么做。我想，只要在他脸上盖点东西，到早上都不会有事的。”
段.en: “I would suggest carrying this poor fellow to my house, but it would give my sister such a fright that I do not feel justified in doing it. I think that if we put something over his face he will be safe until morning.”

段.文: 事情就这样定了。福尔摩斯和我谢绝了斯台普顿留宿的好意，动身回巴斯克维尔庄园，让博物学者独自回去。我们回头望去，只见那个身影在广阔的荒原上慢慢远去，他身后银白色的山坡上，有一块黑点，那就是那个死得那么惨的人躺着的地方。
段.en: And so it was arranged. Resisting Stapleton’s offer of hospitality, Holmes and I set off to Baskerville Hall, leaving the naturalist to return alone. Looking back we saw the figure moving slowly away over the broad moor, and behind him that one black smudge on the silvered slope which showed where the man was lying who had come so horribly to his end.

段.文: “我们终于短兵相接了，”我们一起穿过荒原时，福尔摩斯说，“这家伙的胆子真大！他发现落入圈套的竟是另一个人，那一定是让他浑身瘫软的打击，可他居然在这种打击面前稳住了自己。华生，我在伦敦就跟你说过，现在我再说一遍：我们从没遇到过这么值得一斗的对手。”
段.en: “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together across the moor. “What a nerve the fellow has! How he pulled himself together in the face of what must have been a paralyzing shock when he found that the wrong man had fallen a victim to his plot. I told you in London, Watson, and I tell you now again, that we have never had a foeman more worthy of our steel.”

段.文: “可惜让他看见你了。”
段.en: “I am sorry that he has seen you.”

段.文: “起初我也觉得可惜。可是避不开。”
段.en: “And so was I at first. But there was no getting out of it.”

段.文: “现在他知道你在这儿了，你看这对他的计划会有什么影响？”
段.en: “What effect do you think it will have upon his plans now that he knows you are here?”

段.文: “这可能让他更加小心，也可能逼得他马上铤而走险。像大多数聪明的罪犯一样，他也许太相信自己的聪明，以为已经把我们完全骗过去了。”
段.en: “It may cause him to be more cautious, or it may drive him to desperate measures at once. Like most clever criminals, he may be too confident in his own cleverness and imagine that he has completely deceived us.”

段.文: “我们为什么不马上逮捕他？”
段.en: “Why should we not arrest him at once?”

段.文: “我亲爱的华生，你生来就是个行动派。你的本能总是要干点什么有力的事。可是，就算我们今晚把他抓起来，那又对我们有什么好处呢？我们什么也证明不了他。这正是它狡猾得要命的地方！要是他通过一个人来作案，我们还能找到点证据；可就算我们把这条大狗拖到光天化日之下，也没法帮我们把绞索套到它主人的脖子上。”
段.en: “My dear Watson, you were born to be a man of action. Your instinct is always to do something energetic. But supposing, for argument’s sake, that we had him arrested tonight, what on earth the better off should we be for that? We could prove nothing against him. There’s the devilish cunning of it! If he were acting through a human agent we could get some evidence, but if we were to drag this great dog to the light of day it would not help us in putting a rope round the neck of its master.”

段.文: “我们当然有证据。”
段.en: “Surely we have a case.”

段.文: “连个影子都没有——只有推测和猜想。我们要是拿着这样的故事、这样的证据上法庭，会被人笑着轰出来的。”
段.en: “Not a shadow of one—only surmise and conjecture. We should be laughed out of court if we came with such a story and such evidence.”

段.文: “还有查尔斯爵士的死。”
段.en: “There is Sir Charles’s death.”

段.文: “他被发现时死了，身上没有一点伤痕。你和我都知道他纯粹是吓死的，也知道是什么吓死了他，可我们怎么才能让12个木头木脑的陪审员也知道呢？有什么迹象表明有猎犬？它的牙印在哪儿？当然，我们知道猎犬不会咬死尸，查尔斯爵士在那畜生追上他之前就已经死了。可这一切我们都得证明，而我们现在做不到。”
段.en: “Found dead without a mark upon him. You and I know that he died of sheer fright, and we know also what frightened him, but how are we to get twelve stolid jurymen to know it? What signs are there of a hound? Where are the marks of its fangs? Of course we know that a hound does not bite a dead body and that Sir Charles was dead before ever the brute overtook him. But we have to prove all this, and we are not in a position to do it.”

段.文: “那么，今晚的事呢？”
段.en: “Well, then, tonight?”

段.文: “今晚的事也好不了多少。同样，猎犬和这个人的死之间没有直接联系。我们从没见过那条猎犬。我们听见了它，可我们没法证明它是在追这个人。也完全找不出动机。不，我亲爱的朋友，我们必须接受这样一个事实：我们目前还没有证据，而为了取得证据，冒什么险都是值得的。”
段.en: “We are not much better off tonight. Again, there was no direct connection between the hound and the man’s death. We never saw the hound. We heard it, but we could not prove that it was running upon this man’s trail. There is a complete absence of motive. No, my dear fellow; we must reconcile ourselves to the fact that we have no case at present, and that it is worth our while to run any risk in order to establish one.”

段.文: “那你打算怎么做呢？”
段.en: “And how do you propose to do so?”

段.文: “等劳拉·莱昂斯太太明白了事情的真相，我对她能帮我们做的事寄予很大的希望。我自己也有一个计划。明天的难处明天再说吧；不过我希望，明天天黑之前，我们终于能占上风。”
段.en: “I have great hopes of what Mrs. Laura Lyons may do for us when the position of affairs is made clear to her. And I have my own plan as well. Sufficient for tomorrow is the evil thereof; but I hope before the day is past to have the upper hand at last.”

段.文: 我再也没能从他嘴里问出什么来。他陷入了沉思，一直走到巴斯克维尔庄园的大门口。
段.en: I could draw nothing further from him, and he walked, lost in thought, as far as the Baskerville gates.

段.文: “你要进去吗？”
段.en: “Are you coming up?”

段.文: “是的，我看没有理由再躲躲藏藏了。不过最后说一句，华生。关于猎犬的事，对亨利爵士一个字也别提。就让他以为塞尔登是像斯台普顿想让我们相信的那样死的。明天他要经受一场考验，这样他才能有更好的胆量去面对。要是我没记错你的报告，他明天要去和那家人一起吃晚饭。”
段.en: “Yes; I see no reason for further concealment. But one last word, Watson. Say nothing of the hound to Sir Henry. Let him think that Selden’s death was as Stapleton would have us believe. He will have a better nerve for the ordeal which he will have to undergo tomorrow, when he is engaged, if I remember your report aright, to dine with these people.”

段.文: “我也要去。”
段.en: “And so am I.”

段.文: “那你得找个借口推掉，让他一个人去。这很容易安排。好了，要是晚饭已经赶不上了，我想我们俩都该吃点夜宵了。”
段.en: “Then you must excuse yourself and he must go alone. That will be easily arranged. And now, if we are too late for dinner, I think that we are both ready for our suppers.”

段.文: 亨利爵士见到夏洛克·福尔摩斯，高兴多于意外。这些天他一直料想，最近出了这么多事，福尔摩斯迟早会从伦敦赶来。不过，发现我的朋友既没带行李，也不解释为什么没带，他还是扬了扬眉毛。我们俩很快帮福尔摩斯把缺的东西凑齐了。随后，在一顿迟到的晚饭上，我们把经历讲给准男爵听，只讲了看来适合让他知道的那部分。但在这之前，我得先去做一件不愉快的事：把消息告诉巴里摩尔和他的妻子。对巴里摩尔来说，这或许只是彻底的解脱；可他妻子却用围裙捂着脸，哭得很伤心。在世人眼里，那人是个凶徒，一半是野兽，一半是恶魔；可在她心里，他始终是她少女时代那个任性的小弟弟，那个紧紧抓着她手的孩子。一个人若是死了连一个为他哭的女人都没有，那才真是坏透了。
段.en: Sir Henry was more pleased than surprised to see Sherlock Holmes, for he had for some days been expecting that recent events would bring him down from London. He did raise his eyebrows, however, when he found that my friend had neither any luggage nor any explanations for its absence. Between us we soon supplied his wants, and then over a belated supper we explained to the baronet as much of our experience as it seemed desirable that he should know. But first I had the unpleasant duty of breaking the news to Barrymore and his wife. To him it may have been an unmitigated relief, but she wept bitterly in her apron. To all the world he was the man of violence, half animal and half demon; but to her he always remained the little wilful boy of her own girlhood, the child who had clung to her hand. Evil indeed is the man who has not one woman to mourn him.

段.文: “华生早上一走，我就在屋里闷了一整天。”准男爵说，“我想我该得点表扬，因为我守住了诺言。要不是发过誓不单独出门，我这个晚上本可以过得热闹些。斯台普顿捎信来，请我过去。”
段.en: “I’ve been moping in the house all day since Watson went off in the morning,” said the baronet. “I guess I should have some credit, for I have kept my promise. If I hadn’t sworn not to go about alone I might have had a more lively evening, for I had a message from Stapleton asking me over there.”

段.文: “我毫不怀疑，你这个晚上本来会过得更热闹。”福尔摩斯冷冷地说，“顺便说一句，你大概还不知道吧，我们刚才还在为你哀悼，以为你摔断了脖子。”
段.en: “I have no doubt that you would have had a more lively evening,” said Holmes drily. “By the way, I don’t suppose you appreciate that we have been mourning over you as having broken your neck?”

段.文: 亨利爵士睁大了眼睛。“这是怎么回事？”
段.en: Sir Henry opened his eyes. “How was that?”

段.文: “那个可怜虫穿的是你的衣服。恐怕把衣服给他的那位仆人，要跟警察惹上麻烦了。”
段.en: “This poor wretch was dressed in your clothes. I fear your servant who gave them to him may get into trouble with the police.”

段.文: “不大会。据我所知，那些衣服上都没有记号。”
段.en: “That is unlikely. There was no mark on any of them, as far as I know.”

段.文: “那算他走运。说实在的，你们大家都走运，因为在这件事上，你们全都站在了法律的对立面。作为一个尽职的侦探，我是不是该先把这一家子统统抓起来，我还真拿不准。华生的报告可是最有力的罪证。”
段.en: “That’s lucky for him—in fact, it’s lucky for all of you, since you are all on the wrong side of the law in this matter. I am not sure that as a conscientious detective my first duty is not to arrest the whole household. Watson’s reports are most incriminating documents.”

段.文: “可案子怎么样了？”准男爵问，“这团乱麻你理出点头绪没有？我和华生来了这么久，好像也没比当初明白多少。”
段.en: “But how about the case?” asked the baronet. “Have you made anything out of the tangle? I don’t know that Watson and I are much the wiser since we came down.”

段.文: “我想，过不了多久，我就能把情况给你讲得清楚些。这件事极其棘手，也极其复杂。还有几个地方我们没弄明白，不过亮光总会来的。”
段.en: “I think that I shall be in a position to make the situation rather more clear to you before long. It has been an exceedingly difficult and most complicated business. There are several points upon which we still want light—but it is coming all the same.”

段.文: “我们碰上过一回，华生一定跟你说了。我们在荒原上听到了猎犬的叫声，所以我敢发誓，这不全是无稽的迷信。我在西部那会儿跟狗打过些交道，一听就知道是不是狗叫。你要是能给那条狗戴上嘴套、拴上链子，我就发誓说你是有史以来最了不起的侦探。”
段.en: “We’ve had one experience, as Watson has no doubt told you. We heard the hound on the moor, so I can swear that it is not all empty superstition. I had something to do with dogs when I was out West, and I know one when I hear one. If you can muzzle that one and put him on a chain I’ll be ready to swear you are the greatest detective of all time.”

段.文: “只要你肯帮我，我想我准能给它戴上嘴套、拴上链子。”
段.en: “I think I will muzzle him and chain him all right if you will give me your help.”

段.文: “你让我做什么，我就做什么。”
段.en: “Whatever you tell me to do I will do.”

段.文: “很好。我还要请你照做的时候别多问，不要总问为什么。”
段.en: “Very good; and I will ask you also to do it blindly, without always asking the reason.”

段.文: “随你。”
段.en: “Just as you like.”

段.文: “只要你肯这样，我想我们这个小难题多半很快就能解决。我毫不怀疑……”
段.en: “If you will do this I think the chances are that our little problem will soon be solved. I have no doubt—”

段.文: 他忽然停住，目不转睛地盯着我头顶上方的半空。灯光照在他脸上，那张脸那样专注、那样一动不动，简直像一尊线条分明的古典雕像，是警觉和期待的化身。
段.en: He stopped suddenly and stared fixedly up over my head into the air. The lamp beat upon his face, and so intent was it and so still that it might have been that of a clear-cut classical statue, a personification of alertness and expectation.

段.文: “怎么了？”我们俩同时喊道。
段.en: “What is it?” we both cried.

段.文: 他低下头来的时候，我看得出他正压着心里的某种激动。他的神情依旧镇定，眼睛里却闪着得意又好笑的光。
段.en: I could see as he looked down that he was repressing some internal emotion. His features were still composed, but his eyes shone with amused exultation.

段.文: “请原谅一个鉴赏家的赞叹。”他说着，朝对面墙上那一排画像挥了挥手，“华生不承认我懂艺术，那纯粹是嫉妒，因为我们在这方面看法不同。说真的，这一组画像实在非常出色。”
段.en: “Excuse the admiration of a connoisseur,” said he as he waved his hand towards the line of portraits which covered the opposite wall. “Watson won’t allow that I know anything of art but that is mere jealousy because our views upon the subject differ. Now, these are a really very fine series of portraits.”

段.文: “哦，听你这么说我很高兴。”亨利爵士说着，有点惊讶地看了看我的朋友，“这些东西我不敢说懂，要论眼力，我看马看牛比看画强。我还不知道你有工夫研究这个。”
段.en: “Well, I’m glad to hear you say so,” said Sir Henry, glancing with some surprise at my friend. “I don’t pretend to know much about these things, and I’d be a better judge of a horse or a steer than of a picture. I didn’t know that you found time for such things.”

段.文: “好东西我一看就知道，现在我就看到了。那边穿蓝绸衣服的女士，我敢发誓是内勒画的；那位戴假发的胖绅士，应该是雷诺兹的手笔。我想，这些都是家族画像吧？”
段.en: “I know what is good when I see it, and I see it now. That’s a Kneller, I’ll swear, that lady in the blue silk over yonder, and the stout gentleman with the wig ought to be a Reynolds. They are all family portraits, I presume?”

段.文: “全都是。”
段.en: “Every one.”

段.文: “你知道他们的名字吗？”
段.en: “Do you know the names?”

段.文: “巴里摩尔一直在给我补课，我想这门功课我背得还算不错。”
段.en: “Barrymore has been coaching me in them, and I think I can say my lessons fairly well.”

段.文: “拿望远镜的那位绅士是谁？”
段.en: “Who is the gentleman with the telescope?”

段.文: “那是巴斯克维尔海军少将，在西印度群岛跟随罗德尼作过战。穿蓝外套、拿一卷纸的那位是威廉·巴斯克维尔爵士，皮特当政时做过下议院全院委员会主席。”
段.en: “That is Rear-Admiral Baskerville, who served under Rodney in the West Indies. The man with the blue coat and the roll of paper is Sir William Baskerville, who was Chairman of Committees of the House of Commons under Pitt.”

段.文: “我对面这位保王党人呢？穿黑天鹅绒、戴花边的那位？”
段.en: “And this Cavalier opposite to me—the one with the black velvet and the lace?”

段.文: “啊，他你可得知道。一切祸事都是从他起的，就是那个恶人雨果，巴斯克维尔的猎犬就是由他开的头。我们怕是忘不了他。”
段.en: “Ah, you have a right to know about him. That is the cause of all the mischief, the wicked Hugo, who started the Hound of the Baskervilles. We’re not likely to forget him.”

段.文: 我饶有兴趣地凝视着那幅画像，心里也有些意外。
段.en: I gazed with interest and some surprise upon the portrait.

段.文: “哎呀！”福尔摩斯说，“他看上去倒是个安静温和的人，不过我想，他眼睛里多半藏着一个魔鬼。我原先以为他会更粗壮、更像个恶棍。”
段.en: “Dear me!” said Holmes, “he seems a quiet, meek-mannered man enough, but I dare say that there was a lurking devil in his eyes. I had pictured him as a more robust and ruffianly person.”

段.文: “真假是没问题的，画布背面写着名字和年份：1647年。”
段.en: “There’s no doubt about the authenticity, for the name and the date, 1647, are on the back of the canvas.”

段.文: 福尔摩斯没再多说什么，可那个老浪荡子的画像似乎把他迷住了，吃晚饭时他的眼睛一直盯着它。直到后来亨利爵士回房去了，我才明白他在想什么。他手里拿着卧室的蜡烛，领我回到宴会厅，把蜡烛举起来，照着墙上那幅年深日久、颜色发暗的画像。
段.en: Holmes said little more, but the picture of the old roysterer seemed to have a fascination for him, and his eyes were continually fixed upon it during supper. It was not until later, when Sir Henry had gone to his room, that I was able to follow the trend of his thoughts. He led me back into the banqueting-hall, his bedroom candle in his hand, and he held it up against the time-stained portrait on the wall.

段.文: “你看出什么来没有？”
段.en: “Do you see anything there?”

段.文: 我看着那顶插着羽毛的宽边帽、那几绺卷曲的鬓发、那条白色的花边领子，还有夹在它们中间那张端正而严厉的脸。那张脸并不凶残，却古板、冷硬、严峻，嘴唇薄薄的，紧紧抿着，眼神冷漠，容不得人。
段.en: I looked at the broad plumed hat, the curling love-locks, the white lace collar, and the straight, severe face which was framed between them. It was not a brutal countenance, but it was prim, hard, and stern, with a firm-set, thin-lipped mouth, and a coldly intolerant eye.

段.文: “像不像你认识的什么人？”
段.en: “Is it like anyone you know?”

段.文: “下巴那儿有点像亨利爵士。”
段.en: “There is something of Sir Henry about the jaw.”

段.文: “也许有那么一点。不过你等一下！”他站到椅子上，左手举着蜡烛，右臂弯过来，遮住那顶宽边帽和那几绺长长的卷发。
段.en: “Just a suggestion, perhaps. But wait an instant!” He stood upon a chair, and, holding up the light in his left hand, he curved his right arm over the broad hat and round the long ringlets.

段.文: “天哪！”我惊叫起来。
段.en: “Good heavens!” I cried in amazement.

段.文: 斯台普顿的脸从画布上跳了出来。
段.en: The face of Stapleton had sprung out of the canvas.

段.文: “哈，你现在看出来了。我的眼睛受过训练，看的是脸，不是脸周围的装饰。一个刑事侦查员的第一项本事，就是能看穿伪装。”
段.en: “Ha, you see it now. My eyes have been trained to examine faces and not their trimmings. It is the first quality of a criminal investigator that he should see through a disguise.”

段.文: “可这太奇妙了。说是他的画像也行。”
段.en: “But this is marvellous. It might be his portrait.”

段.文: “是啊，这是返祖现象的一个有趣例子，看来外貌和精神都返了祖。研究一下家族画像，就足以让人相信转世轮回了。这家伙是巴斯克维尔家的人，这一点很明显。”
段.en: “Yes, it is an interesting instance of a throwback, which appears to be both physical and spiritual. A study of family portraits is enough to convert a man to the doctrine of reincarnation. The fellow is a Baskerville—that is evident.”

段.文: “而且打着继承家产的主意。”
段.en: “With designs upon the succession.”

段.文: “正是。这幅画碰巧给我们补上了一个最明显的缺环。我们抓住他了，华生，我们抓住他了。我敢发誓，不到明天晚上，他就会在我们的网里扑腾，跟他自己捉的蝴蝶一样无可奈何。一根针、一块软木、一张卡片，我们就把他收进贝克街的标本集里！”他转身离开画像时，突然大笑起来。他难得这样笑。我很少听到他笑，而每次他这样笑，总有人要倒霉。
段.en: “Exactly. This chance of the picture has supplied us with one of our most obvious missing links. We have him, Watson, we have him, and I dare swear that before tomorrow night he will be fluttering in our net as helpless as one of his own butterflies. A pin, a cork, and a card, and we add him to the Baker Street collection!” He burst into one of his rare fits of laughter as he turned away from the picture. I have not heard him laugh often, and it has always boded ill to somebody.

段.文: 第二天早上我起得很早，可福尔摩斯起得更早。我穿衣服的时候，就看见他已经沿着车道走回来了。
段.en: I was up betimes in the morning, but Holmes was afoot earlier still, for I saw him as I dressed, coming up the drive.

段.文: “对，今天会是忙碌的一天。”他说着，搓着双手，满是要行动的兴奋，“网都撒好了，马上就要收网。今天天黑以前我们就会知道，是捉住了那条下巴瘦长的大狗鱼，还是让它从网眼里溜掉了。”
段.en: “Yes, we should have a full day today,” he remarked, and he rubbed his hands with the joy of action. “The nets are all in place, and the drag is about to begin. We’ll know before the day is out whether we have caught our big, lean-jawed pike, or whether he has got through the meshes.”

段.文: “你已经去过荒原了？”
段.en: “Have you been on the moor already?”

段.文: “我从格林彭给普林斯敦送了一份报告，讲塞尔登的死。我想我可以保证，这件事不会给你们任何人添麻烦。我还跟我忠实的卡特赖特联系了一下。要是我不让他对我的安全放心，他准会守在我那间石屋门口，像狗守着主人的坟那样，一直憔悴下去。”
段.en: “I have sent a report from Grimpen to Princetown as to the death of Selden. I think I can promise that none of you will be troubled in the matter. And I have also communicated with my faithful Cartwright, who would certainly have pined away at the door of my hut, as a dog does at his master’s grave, if I had not set his mind at rest about my safety.”

段.文: “下一步做什么？”
段.en: “What is the next move?”

段.文: “去见亨利爵士。啊，他来了！”
段.en: “To see Sir Henry. Ah, here he is!”

段.文: “早上好，福尔摩斯。”准男爵说，“你看上去就像一位将军，正在跟参谋长商量怎么打仗。”
段.en: “Good-morning, Holmes,” said the baronet. “You look like a general who is planning a battle with his chief of the staff.”

段.文: “情形正是这样。华生正在向我请示命令。”
段.en: “That is the exact situation. Watson was asking for orders.”

段.文: “我也一样。”
段.en: “And so do I.”

段.文: “很好。据我所知，你今晚约好了去我们的朋友斯台普顿家吃饭。”
段.en: “Very good. You are engaged, as I understand, to dine with our friends the Stapletons tonight.”

段.文: “我希望你也去。他们非常好客，我相信他们见到你一定会很高兴。”
段.en: “I hope that you will come also. They are very hospitable people, and I am sure that they would be very glad to see you.”

段.文: “恐怕我和华生得回伦敦去。”
段.en: “I fear that Watson and I must go to London.”

段.文: “回伦敦？”
段.en: “To London?”

段.文: “是的，我想眼下我们在那边更能派上用场。”
段.en: “Yes, I think that we should be more useful there at the present juncture.”

段.文: 准男爵的脸明显地拉长了。
段.en: The baronet’s face perceptibly lengthened.

段.文: “我还以为你们会帮我把这件事撑到底呢。一个人待着的时候，庄园也好，荒原也好，都不是什么叫人舒服的地方。”
段.en: “I hoped that you were going to see me through this business. The Hall and the moor are not very pleasant places when one is alone.”

段.文: “我亲爱的朋友，你必须绝对信任我，完全照我说的去做。你可以告诉你的朋友们，我们本来很乐意跟你一起去，可是有急事，必须回城里。我们希望很快就回德文郡来。你会记得把这话转告他们吧？”
段.en: “My dear fellow, you must trust me implicitly and do exactly what I tell you. You can tell your friends that we should have been happy to have come with you, but that urgent business required us to be in town. We hope very soon to return to Devonshire. Will you remember to give them that message?”

段.文: “既然你坚持的话。”
段.en: “If you insist upon it.”

段.文: “我向你保证，没有别的办法。”
段.en: “There is no alternative, I assure you.”

段.文: 从准男爵阴沉的眉头上，我看出他深深受了伤害。在他看来，我们这是要丢下他不管了。
段.en: I saw by the baronet’s clouded brow that he was deeply hurt by what he regarded as our desertion.

段.文: “你们打算什么时候走？”他冷冷地问。
段.en: “When do you desire to go?” he asked coldly.

段.文: “吃过早饭马上就走。我们坐车去库姆特雷西，不过华生会把他的东西留下，作为他一定回来的保证。华生，你给斯台普顿写张便条，说你很抱歉不能去了。”
段.en: “Immediately after breakfast. We will drive in to Coombe Tracey, but Watson will leave his things as a pledge that he will come back to you. Watson, you will send a note to Stapleton to tell him that you regret that you cannot come.”

段.文: “我真想跟你们一起去伦敦。”准男爵说，“我凭什么一个人待在这儿？”
段.en: “I have a good mind to go to London with you,” said the baronet. “Why should I stay here alone?”

段.文: “因为这是你的岗位。因为你答应过我，要照吩咐去做，而我吩咐你留下。”
段.en: “Because it is your post of duty. Because you gave me your word that you would do as you were told, and I tell you to stay.”

段.文: “好吧，那我就留下。”
段.en: “All right, then, I’ll stay.”

段.文: “还有一条指示！我希望你坐车去梅里皮特宅。不过，到了以后把马车打发回来，让他们知道你打算走回家。”
段.en: “One more direction! I wish you to drive to Merripit House. Send back your trap, however, and let them know that you intend to walk home.”

段.文: “穿过荒原走回来？”
段.en: “To walk across the moor?”
“Yes.”

段.文: “可你一次又一次提醒我，千万不能这么做。”
段.en: “But that is the very thing which you have so often cautioned me not to do.”

段.文: “这一回你可以放心去做。要不是我对你的胆量和勇气十分有信心，我也不会这样提议。但你一定得这么做。”
段.en: “This time you may do it with safety. If I had not every confidence in your nerve and courage I would not suggest it, but it is essential that you should do it.”

段.文: “那我就这么做。”
段.en: “Then I will do it.”

段.文: “还有，你要是爱惜自己的性命，穿过荒原时就千万别往别的方向走，只能沿着那条从梅里皮特宅通到格林彭路的直路走。那本来也是你回家该走的路。”
段.en: “And as you value your life do not go across the moor in any direction save along the straight path which leads from Merripit House to the Grimpen Road, and is your natural way home.”

段.文: “我一定完全照你说的做。”
段.en: “I will do just what you say.”

段.文: “很好。我希望吃过早饭尽快动身，好在下午赶到伦敦。”
段.en: “Very good. I should be glad to get away as soon after breakfast as possible, so as to reach London in the afternoon.”

段.文: 这个安排让我大吃一惊。不过我记起来，福尔摩斯头天晚上对斯台普顿说过，他第二天就结束这次拜访。可我万万没想到，他会要我跟他一起走；他自己都说眼下是紧要关头，我们俩怎么能同时离开，我也想不通。然而，除了绝对服从，别无他法。于是我们向闷闷不乐的朋友道了别。两个小时以后，我们到了库姆特雷西车站，把马车打发了回去。站台上有个小男孩在等着。
段.en: I was much astounded by this programme, though I remembered that Holmes had said to Stapleton on the night before that his visit would terminate next day. It had not crossed my mind however, that he would wish me to go with him, nor could I understand how we could both be absent at a moment which he himself declared to be critical. There was nothing for it, however, but implicit obedience; so we bade good-bye to our rueful friend, and a couple of hours afterwards we were at the station of Coombe Tracey and had dispatched the trap upon its return journey. A small boy was waiting upon the platform.

段.文: “有什么吩咐吗，先生？”
段.en: “Any orders, sir?”

段.文: “卡特赖特，你坐这趟火车回城里。一到那儿，就以我的名义给亨利·巴斯克维尔爵士发一封电报，说如果他找到我丢下的那个笔记本，请用挂号信寄到贝克街。”
段.en: “You will take this train to town, Cartwright. The moment you arrive you will send a wire to Sir Henry Baskerville, in my name, to say that if he finds the pocketbook which I have dropped he is to send it by registered post to Baker Street.”

段.文: “是，先生。”
段.en: “Yes, sir.”

段.文: “再去车站办公室问问，有没有给我的消息。”
段.en: “And ask at the station office if there is a message for me.”

段.文: 男孩拿回来一封电报，福尔摩斯递给了我。上面写着：
段.en: The boy returned with a telegram, which Holmes handed to me. It ran:

段.文: 电报收到。带空白逮捕令前来。五点四十分到。雷斯垂德。
段.en: Wire received. Coming down with unsigned warrant. Arrive five-forty. Lestrade.

段.文: “这是回复我今天早上那封电报的。我认为他是职业警探里最出色的一个，我们也许需要他帮忙。好了，华生，我想现在最好的安排，就是去拜访你认识的那位劳拉·莱昂斯太太。”
段.en: “That is in answer to mine of this morning. He is the best of the professionals, I think, and we may need his assistance. Now, Watson, I think that we cannot employ our time better than by calling upon your acquaintance, Mrs. Laura Lyons.”

段.文: 他的作战计划渐渐清楚了。他要借准男爵之口让斯台普顿一家相信我们真的走了，而实际上，一到需要我们的时候，我们就会赶回来。伦敦来的那封电报，只要亨利爵士在斯台普顿一家面前提一句，就一定能打消他们最后的疑虑。我仿佛已经看见，我们的网正朝那条下巴瘦长的狗鱼一点点收紧。
段.en: His plan of campaign was beginning to be evident. He would use the baronet in order to convince the Stapletons that we were really gone, while we should actually return at the instant when we were likely to be needed. That telegram from London, if mentioned by Sir Henry to the Stapletons, must remove the last suspicions from their minds. Already I seemed to see our nets drawing closer around that lean-jawed pike.

段.文: 劳拉·莱昂斯太太正在她的办公室里。夏洛克·福尔摩斯一开口就直截了当、毫不掩饰，让她相当吃惊。
段.en: Mrs. Laura Lyons was in her office, and Sherlock Holmes opened his interview with a frankness and directness which considerably amazed her.

段.文: “我正在调查已故的查尔斯·巴斯克维尔爵士之死的前后经过。”他说，“我这位朋友华生医生已经告诉我，在这件事上你说了些什么，又隐瞒了些什么。”
段.en: “I am investigating the circumstances which attended the death of the late Sir Charles Baskerville,” said he. “My friend here, Dr. Watson, has informed me of what you have communicated, and also of what you have withheld in connection with that matter.”

段.文: “我隐瞒了什么？”她挑衅地问。
段.en: “What have I withheld?” she asked defiantly.

段.文: “你已经承认，你请查尔斯爵士十点钟到那扇门边去。我们知道，那正是他死去的地点和时间。你隐瞒的，是这两件事之间有什么联系。”
段.en: “You have confessed that you asked Sir Charles to be at the gate at ten o’clock. We know that that was the place and hour of his death. You have withheld what the connection is between these events.”

段.文: “没有什么联系。”
段.en: “There is no connection.”

段.文: “那这个巧合可真是太不寻常了。不过我想，我们终究能把这种联系找出来。莱昂斯太太，我想对你完全坦白。我们认为这是一桩谋杀案，证据可能不只牵连你的朋友斯台普顿先生，还会牵连到他的妻子。”
段.en: “In that case the coincidence must indeed be an extraordinary one. But I think that we shall succeed in establishing a connection, after all. I wish to be perfectly frank with you, Mrs. Lyons. We regard this case as one of murder, and the evidence may implicate not only your friend Mr. Stapleton but his wife as well.”

段.文: 那位太太从椅子上跳了起来。
段.en: The lady sprang from her chair.

段.文: “他的妻子！”她喊道。
段.en: “His wife!” she cried.

段.文: “这已经不是秘密了。那个冒充他妹妹的人，其实是他的妻子。”
段.en: “The fact is no longer a secret. The person who has passed for his sister is really his wife.”

段.文: 莱昂斯太太又坐了下来。她的双手紧紧抓着椅子扶手，我看到她那粉红的指甲因为用力而发白了。
段.en: Mrs. Lyons had resumed her seat. Her hands were grasping the arms of her chair, and I saw that the pink nails had turned white with the pressure of her grip.

段.文: “他的妻子！”她又说了一遍，“他的妻子！他没结过婚。”
段.en: “His wife!” she said again. “His wife! He is not a married man.”

段.文: 夏洛克·福尔摩斯耸了耸肩。
段.en: Sherlock Holmes shrugged his shoulders.

段.文: “拿证据给我看！拿证据给我看！要是你拿得出来……！”
段.en: “Prove it to me! Prove it to me! And if you can do so—!”

段.文: 她眼里那道凶狠的光，比任何话都说得更多。
段.en: The fierce flash of her eyes said more than any words.

段.文: “我就是有备而来的。”福尔摩斯说着，从口袋里掏出几张纸，“这是四年前在约克给这对夫妇拍的一张照片，背面写着‘范德勒夫妇’。不过你一眼就能认出他来；如果你见过她，也认得出她。这里是三份书面描述，出自可靠的证人，讲的是范德勒夫妇，他们当时办着一所私立学校，叫圣奥利弗学校。你看一看，看你还能不能怀疑这两个人是谁。”
段.en: “I have come prepared to do so,” said Holmes, drawing several papers from his pocket. “Here is a photograph of the couple taken in York four years ago. It is indorsed ‘Mr. and Mrs. Vandeleur,’ but you will have no difficulty in recognizing him, and her also, if you know her by sight. Here are three written descriptions by trustworthy witnesses of Mr. and Mrs. Vandeleur, who at that time kept St. Oliver’s private school. Read them and see if you can doubt the identity of these people.”

段.文: 她扫了一眼，然后抬头看着我们，脸绷得紧紧的，像个走投无路的女人。
段.en: She glanced at them, and then looked up at us with the set, rigid face of a desperate woman.

段.文: “福尔摩斯先生，”她说，“这个人向我求过婚，条件是我能跟我丈夫离婚。这个恶棍，用尽了一切办法骗我。他从来没对我说过一句真话。为什么？为什么？我还以为这一切都是为了我。现在我才明白，我从头到尾不过是他手里的一件工具。他从来没对我守过信，我为什么还要对他守信？他自己干了坏事，我为什么还要替他遮掩？你想问什么就问吧，我什么都不会瞒着。有一件事我可以向你发誓：我写那封信的时候，做梦也没想到会害了那位老先生。他一直是待我最好的朋友。”
段.en: “Mr. Holmes,” she said, “this man had offered me marriage on condition that I could get a divorce from my husband. He has lied to me, the villain, in every conceivable way. Not one word of truth has he ever told me. And why—why? I imagined that all was for my own sake. But now I see that I was never anything but a tool in his hands. Why should I preserve faith with him who never kept any with me? Why should I try to shield him from the consequences of his own wicked acts? Ask me what you like, and there is nothing which I shall hold back. One thing I swear to you, and that is that when I wrote the letter I never dreamed of any harm to the old gentleman, who had been my kindest friend.”

段.文: “我完全相信你，太太。”夏洛克·福尔摩斯说，“要你把这些事讲出来，一定很痛苦。也许由我来说说经过，会让你好受些。如果我有什么要紧的地方说错了，你可以纠正我。寄这封信，是斯台普顿给你出的主意吧？”
段.en: “I entirely believe you, madam,” said Sherlock Holmes. “The recital of these events must be very painful to you, and perhaps it will make it easier if I tell you what occurred, and you can check me if I make any material mistake. The sending of this letter was suggested to you by Stapleton?”

段.文: “信是他口述的。”
段.en: “He dictated it.”

段.文: “我猜，他给你的理由是，查尔斯爵士会资助你打离婚官司的费用？”
段.en: “I presume that the reason he gave was that you would receive help from Sir Charles for the legal expenses connected with your divorce?”

段.文: “正是这样。”
段.en: “Exactly.”

段.文: “然后，等你把信寄出去以后，他又劝你别去赴约？”
段.en: “And then after you had sent the letter he dissuaded you from keeping the appointment?”

段.文: “他对我说，为这种事让别的男人出钱，会伤他的自尊；他自己虽然穷，也愿意拿出最后一个便士，扫清把我们隔开的障碍。”
段.en: “He told me that it would hurt his self-respect that any other man should find the money for such an object, and that though he was a poor man himself he would devote his last penny to removing the obstacles which divided us.”

段.文: “看来他这个人倒是前后一贯。后来你就什么都没听说，直到在报上读到查尔斯爵士的死讯？”
段.en: “He appears to be a very consistent character. And then you heard nothing until you read the reports of the death in the paper?”

段.文: “是的。”
段.en: “No.”

段.文: “他还让你发誓，绝不提你跟查尔斯爵士约会的事？”
段.en: “And he made you swear to say nothing about your appointment with Sir Charles?”

段.文: “是的。他说那件死亡非常蹊跷，要是事情传出去，我一定会被怀疑。他吓唬我，让我闭口不言。”
段.en: “He did. He said that the death was a very mysterious one, and that I should certainly be suspected if the facts came out. He frightened me into remaining silent.”

段.文: “原来如此。可你心里起了疑？”
段.en: “Quite so. But you had your suspicions?”

段.文: 她犹豫了一下，低下头去。
段.en: She hesitated and looked down.

段.文: “我了解他。”她说，“可是只要他对我守信，我也会一直对他守信。”
段.en: “I knew him,” she said. “But if he had kept faith with me I should always have done so with him.”

段.文: “我认为，总的来说，你算是侥幸逃过了一劫。”夏洛克·福尔摩斯说，“你手里握着他的把柄，他也知道，可你还活着。这几个月来，你一直走在悬崖边上。莱昂斯太太，我们现在得告辞了。很可能，你不久就会再听到我们的消息。”
段.en: “I think that on the whole you have had a fortunate escape,” said Sherlock Holmes. “You have had him in your power and he knew it, and yet you are alive. You have been walking for some months very near to the edge of a precipice. We must wish you good-morning now, Mrs. Lyons, and it is probable that you will very shortly hear from us again.”

段.文: “我们的案子渐渐圆满了，难题一个接一个在我们面前消散。”我们站在站台上等伦敦来的快车时，福尔摩斯说，“我很快就能把这桩现代最离奇、最耸人听闻的罪案，连成一篇完整的故事讲出来。研究犯罪学的人会记得，1866年在小俄罗斯的戈德诺发生过类似的事，当然还有北卡罗来纳的安德森谋杀案。不过这个案子有几处特点完全是它独有的。就是到现在，我们手里也还没有能定这个狡猾家伙罪的确凿证据。可要是今晚睡觉之前还不够确凿，那我就太意外了。”
段.en: “Our case becomes rounded off, and difficulty after difficulty thins away in front of us,” said Holmes as we stood waiting for the arrival of the express from town. “I shall soon be in the position of being able to put into a single connected narrative one of the most singular and sensational crimes of modern times. Students of criminology will remember the analogous incidents in Godno, in Little Russia, in the year ’66, and of course there are the Anderson murders in North Carolina, but this case possesses some features which are entirely its own. Even now we have no clear case against this very wily man. But I shall be very much surprised if it is not clear enough before we go to bed this night.”

段.文: 伦敦来的快车轰隆隆地开进站来，一个矮小精悍、像斗牛犬一样的人从头等车厢里跳了下来。我们三个人握了手。我一眼就从雷斯垂德望着我同伴时那副恭敬的样子看出来，自从他们第一次合作以来，他已经长了不少见识。我还清楚地记得，当年这位推理家的种种理论，总是引来这位讲究实际的人的嘲笑。
段.en: The London express came roaring into the station, and a small, wiry bulldog of a man had sprung from a first-class carriage. We all three shook hands, and I saw at once from the reverential way in which Lestrade gazed at my companion that he had learned a good deal since the days when they had first worked together. I could well remember the scorn which the theories of the reasoner used then to excite in the practical man.

段.文: “有什么好买卖吗？”他问。
段.en: “Anything good?” he asked.

段.文: “这几年来最大的一桩。”福尔摩斯说，“我们还有两个小时才需要考虑动身。我想可以利用这段时间吃顿饭。然后，雷斯垂德，我们带你去呼吸一下达特穆尔夜里的清新空气，把伦敦的雾从你嗓子里清出去。从来没去过？啊，好吧，我想你这第一次去，是不会忘记的。”
段.en: “The biggest thing for years,” said Holmes. “We have two hours before we need think of starting. I think we might employ it in getting some dinner and then, Lestrade, we will take the London fog out of your throat by giving you a breath of the pure night air of Dartmoor. Never been there? Ah, well, I don’t suppose you will forget your first visit.”

段.文: 夏洛克·福尔摩斯有个毛病（如果这真能算毛病的话）：不到计划实现的那一刻，他极不愿意把全盘打算告诉任何人。这一半无疑出于他好强的天性，他喜欢掌控局面，喜欢让身边的人吃惊；一半也出于职业上的谨慎，他从不肯冒一点险。可这样一来，替他跑腿、给他帮忙的人就很难熬了。我常常为此吃苦头，但没有哪一次比那天夜里在黑暗中长途坐车更难受。重大的考验就在眼前，我们终于要做最后一搏了，可福尔摩斯什么也没说，我只能猜测他打算怎么做。后来，冷风扑在脸上，窄路两旁是黑洞洞的空旷，我知道我们又回到了荒原上，不由得浑身紧张，满怀期待。马每迈一步，车轮每转一圈，都把我们带得离那场最大的冒险更近一些。
段.en: One of Sherlock Holmes’s defects—if, indeed, one may call it a defect—was that he was exceedingly loath to communicate his full plans to any other person until the instant of their fulfilment. Partly it came no doubt from his own masterful nature, which loved to dominate and surprise those who were around him. Partly also from his professional caution, which urged him never to take any chances. The result, however, was very trying for those who were acting as his agents and assistants. I had often suffered under it, but never more so than during that long drive in the darkness. The great ordeal was in front of us; at last we were about to make our final effort, and yet Holmes had said nothing, and I could only surmise what his course of action would be. My nerves thrilled with anticipation when at last the cold wind upon our faces and the dark, void spaces on either side of the narrow road told me that we were back upon the moor once again. Every stride of the horses and every turn of the wheels was taking us nearer to our supreme adventure.

段.文: 租来的马车上有车夫在，我们说话不方便。心里明明又激动又紧张，嘴上却只能聊些琐碎的事。这样不自然地憋了一路，等到终于经过弗兰克兰的宅子，知道离庄园、离行动的地点越来越近时，我才松了口气。我们没有把车赶到庄园门口，而是在林荫道的大门附近下了车。付了车钱，吩咐车夫马上回库姆特雷西去，我们三人便动身朝梅里皮特宅走去。
段.en: Our conversation was hampered by the presence of the driver of the hired wagonette, so that we were forced to talk of trivial matters when our nerves were tense with emotion and anticipation. It was a relief to me, after that unnatural restraint, when we at last passed Frankland’s house and knew that we were drawing near to the Hall and to the scene of action. We did not drive up to the door but got down near the gate of the avenue. The wagonette was paid off and ordered to return to Coombe Tracey forthwith, while we started to walk to Merripit House.

段.文: “你带枪了吗，雷斯垂德？”
段.en: “Are you armed, Lestrade?”

段.文: 小个子侦探笑了笑。“只要我还穿着裤子，就有后兜；只要我有后兜，里面就总揣着点东西。”
段.en: The little detective smiled. “As long as I have my trousers I have a hip-pocket, and as long as I have my hip-pocket I have something in it.”

段.文: “好！我和我的朋友也做好了应急的准备。”
段.en: “Good! My friend and I are also ready for emergencies.”

段.文: “这件事你嘴可真紧，福尔摩斯先生。现在要干什么？”
段.en: “You’re mighty close about this affair, Mr. Holmes. What’s the game now?”
“A waiting game.”

段.文: “我的天，这地方可真叫人高兴不起来。”侦探打了个寒战，环顾着周围阴森的山坡，还有笼罩在格林彭大泥沼上那一大片湖水似的浓雾，“我看见前面有座房子亮着灯。”
段.en: “My word, it does not seem a very cheerful place,” said the detective with a shiver, glancing round him at the gloomy slopes of the hill and at the huge lake of fog which lay over the Grimpen Mire. “I see the lights of a house ahead of us.”

段.文: “那就是梅里皮特宅，我们这趟路的终点。我得请你们踮着脚走，说话只能小声。”
段.en: “That is Merripit House and the end of our journey. I must request you to walk on tiptoe and not to talk above a whisper.”

段.文: 我们沿着小路小心翼翼地往前走，好像要去那座房子似的。可是离房子大约还有两百码时，福尔摩斯让我们停了下来。
段.en: We moved cautiously along the track as if we were bound for the house, but Holmes halted us when we were about two hundred yards from it.

段.文: “就这儿吧。”他说，“右边这些石头是绝好的掩护。”
段.en: “This will do,” said he. “These rocks upon the right make an admirable screen.”

段.文: “我们就在这儿等？”
段.en: “We are to wait here?”

段.文: “对，我们就在这儿设个小小的埋伏。雷斯垂德，你躲进这个坑里。华生，你进过这座房子，是不是？你能说说各个房间的位置吗？这一头那几扇格子窗是什么房间？”
段.en: “Yes, we shall make our little ambush here. Get into this hollow, Lestrade. You have been inside the house, have you not, Watson? Can you tell the position of the rooms? What are those latticed windows at this end?”

段.文: “我想是厨房的窗户。”
段.en: “I think they are the kitchen windows.”

段.文: “再过去那扇，亮得很的那扇呢？”
段.en: “And the one beyond, which shines so brightly?”

段.文: “那肯定是餐厅。”
段.en: “That is certainly the dining-room.”

段.文: “百叶窗是拉起来的。这儿的地形你最熟。悄悄爬过去，看看他们在干什么。可看在老天的分上，千万别让他们发现有人在盯着！”
段.en: “The blinds are up. You know the lie of the land best. Creep forward quietly and see what they are doing—but for heaven’s sake don’t let them know that they are watched!”

段.文: 我踮着脚走下小路，弯腰躲到一道矮墙后面，墙里围着一片长得矮小的果园。我借着墙影往前爬，爬到一个地方，正好能透过那扇没挂窗帘的窗户把里面看得清清楚楚。
段.en: I tiptoed down the path and stooped behind the low wall which surrounded the stunted orchard. Creeping in its shadow I reached a point whence I could look straight through the uncurtained window.

段.文: 屋里只有两个人：亨利爵士和斯台普顿。他们分坐在圆桌两边，侧脸对着我。两人都抽着雪茄，面前摆着咖啡和酒。斯台普顿谈得眉飞色舞，准男爵却脸色苍白，心不在焉。也许他一想到待会儿要独自穿过那片不祥的荒原，心里就沉甸甸的。
段.en: There were only two men in the room, Sir Henry and Stapleton. They sat with their profiles towards me on either side of the round table. Both of them were smoking cigars, and coffee and wine were in front of them. Stapleton was talking with animation, but the baronet looked pale and distrait. Perhaps the thought of that lonely walk across the ill-omened moor was weighing heavily upon his mind.

段.文: 我正看着，斯台普顿站起身走出了房间。亨利爵士又给自己斟满一杯，往椅背上一靠，吸着雪茄。我听见吱呀一声开门，接着是靴子踩在碎石上的清脆声响。脚步声沿着小路，从我蹲着的那道墙的另一边经过。我探头一看，只见那位博物学者在果园角落一间外屋门口停了下来。钥匙在锁里一转，他走进去时，里面传出一阵奇怪的扭打般的响动。他在里面只待了一分钟左右，接着我又听见钥匙转动的声音，他从我身边走过，回到了房子里。我看他回到客人身边，便悄悄爬回同伴们等着的地方，把看到的情形告诉他们。
段.en: As I watched them Stapleton rose and left the room, while Sir Henry filled his glass again and leaned back in his chair, puffing at his cigar. I heard the creak of a door and the crisp sound of boots upon gravel. The steps passed along the path on the other side of the wall under which I crouched. Looking over, I saw the naturalist pause at the door of an out-house in the corner of the orchard. A key turned in a lock, and as he passed in there was a curious scuffling noise from within. He was only a minute or so inside, and then I heard the key turn once more and he passed me and reentered the house. I saw him rejoin his guest, and I crept quietly back to where my companions were waiting to tell them what I had seen.

段.文: “华生，你是说那位女士不在屋里？”我报告完以后，福尔摩斯问道。
段.en: “You say, Watson, that the lady is not there?” Holmes asked when I had finished my report.

段.文: “不在。”
段.en: “No.”

段.文: “那她会在哪儿呢？除了厨房，别的房间都没亮灯。”
段.en: “Where can she be, then, since there is no light in any other room except the kitchen?”

段.文: “我想不出她会在哪儿。”
段.en: “I cannot think where she is.”

段.文: 前面说过，格林彭大泥沼上空笼着一片浓浓的白雾。这时它正慢慢朝我们这边飘来，在我们那一侧堆起一道墙，不高，但很厚，轮廓分明。月光照在雾上，看去就像一大片闪闪发亮的冰原，远处突岩的顶端好比冰面上托着的岩石。福尔摩斯脸朝着那片雾，看着它慢吞吞地飘移，不耐烦地低声嘀咕着。
段.en: I have said that over the great Grimpen Mire there hung a dense, white fog. It was drifting slowly in our direction and banked itself up like a wall on that side of us, low but thick and well defined. The moon shone on it, and it looked like a great shimmering ice-field, with the heads of the distant tors as rocks borne upon its surface. Holmes’s face was turned towards it, and he muttered impatiently as he watched its sluggish drift.

段.文: “它正朝我们这边移过来，华生。”
段.en: “It’s moving towards us, Watson.”

段.文: “这很严重吗？”
段.en: “Is that serious?”

段.文: “确实非常严重。世上只有这一样东西能打乱我的计划。他不会待太久了，现在已经十点了。我们能不能成功，甚至他能不能活命，也许就看他能不能在雾漫过小路之前出来。”
段.en: “Very serious, indeed—the one thing upon earth which could have disarranged my plans. He can’t be very long, now. It is already ten o’clock. Our success and even his life may depend upon his coming out before the fog is over the path.”

段.文: 我们头顶上的夜空晴朗美好。星星闪着清冷明亮的光，半个月亮给整片景色洒下一层柔和而朦胧的光。我们面前是那座房子黑黢黢的轮廓，锯齿般的屋顶和林立的烟囱，在缀满银星的天幕上勾出清晰的线条。楼下窗户里射出几道宽宽的金色光带，横过果园，一直铺到荒原上。忽然，其中一道熄灭了。仆人们离开了厨房。只剩下餐厅里那盏灯还亮着，那两个人，一个是杀气腾腾的主人，一个是蒙在鼓里的客人，仍在抽着雪茄闲谈。
段.en: The night was clear and fine above us. The stars shone cold and bright, while a half-moon bathed the whole scene in a soft, uncertain light. Before us lay the dark bulk of the house, its serrated roof and bristling chimneys hard outlined against the silver-spangled sky. Broad bars of golden light from the lower windows stretched across the orchard and the moor. One of them was suddenly shut off. The servants had left the kitchen. There only remained the lamp in the dining-room where the two men, the murderous host and the unconscious guest, still chatted over their cigars.

段.文: 那片盖住了半个荒原的白茫茫的羊毛般的平原，每一分钟都在朝房子逼近。最早的几缕薄雾已经在那扇亮灯窗户的金色方框前打着卷儿。果园远处的那道墙已经看不见了，树木像是从一团翻卷的白色水汽里冒出来的。我们看着看着，一圈圈的雾绕过房子的两角爬过来，慢慢滚成一道浓厚的雾堤。房子的楼上和屋顶浮在上面，像一艘奇怪的船漂在幽暗的海上。福尔摩斯焦躁地用手猛拍面前的岩石，不耐烦地直跺脚。
段.en: Every minute that white woolly plain which covered one-half of the moor was drifting closer and closer to the house. Already the first thin wisps of it were curling across the golden square of the lighted window. The farther wall of the orchard was already invisible, and the trees were standing out of a swirl of white vapour. As we watched it the fog-wreaths came crawling round both corners of the house and rolled slowly into one dense bank on which the upper floor and the roof floated like a strange ship upon a shadowy sea. Holmes struck his hand passionately upon the rock in front of us and stamped his feet in his impatience.

段.文: “他要是一刻钟之内还不出来，小路就会被雾盖住。再过半个小时，我们连自己的手都看不见了。”
段.en: “If he isn’t out in a quarter of an hour the path will be covered. In half an hour we won’t be able to see our hands in front of us.”

段.文: “我们要不要往后退，退到高一点的地方去？”
段.en: “Shall we move farther back upon higher ground?”

段.文: “好，我想这样也好。”
段.en: “Yes, I think it would be as well.”

段.文: 于是雾堤往前漫，我们就往后退，一直退到离房子半英里远的地方。可那片浓浓的白色雾海，上沿镀着月亮的银光，仍旧缓慢而无情地向前推进。
段.en: So as the fog-bank flowed onward we fell back before it until we were half a mile from the house, and still that dense white sea, with the moon silvering its upper edge, swept slowly and inexorably on.

段.文: “我们退得太远了。”福尔摩斯说，“他可能还没走到我们这儿就被追上，这个险我们冒不起。无论如何，我们都得在这儿守住。”他跪下去，把耳朵贴在地上。“谢天谢地，我想我听到他来了。”
段.en: “We are going too far,” said Holmes. “We dare not take the chance of his being overtaken before he can reach us. At all costs we must hold our ground where we are.” He dropped on his knees and clapped his ear to the ground. “Thank God, I think that I hear him coming.”

段.文: 一阵急促的脚步声打破了荒原的寂静。我们蹲在石头中间，紧紧盯着面前那道顶端泛着银光的雾堤。脚步声越来越响，我们等着的那个人穿过浓雾走了出来，就像穿过一道帘幕。他走进晴朗的星夜里，惊讶地朝四周看了看，然后沿着小路快步走来，从我们藏身的地方近旁经过，继续往我们身后那道长坡上走去。他一边走，一边不住地左右回头张望，像个心神不宁的人。
段.en: A sound of quick steps broke the silence of the moor. Crouching among the stones we stared intently at the silver-tipped bank in front of us. The steps grew louder, and through the fog, as through a curtain, there stepped the man whom we were awaiting. He looked round him in surprise as he emerged into the clear, starlit night. Then he came swiftly along the path, passed close to where we lay, and went on up the long slope behind us. As he walked he glanced continually over either shoulder, like a man who is ill at ease.

段.文: “嘘！”福尔摩斯低声喝道，我听见手枪扳起击锤时清脆的咔嗒一声，“当心！它来了！”
段.en: “Hist!” cried Holmes, and I heard the sharp click of a cocking pistol. “Look out! It’s coming!”

段.文: 从那道蠕动的雾堤深处，不知什么地方传来一阵细碎、清脆、连续不断的嗒嗒声。雾团离我们藏身的地方不到五十码了，我们三个人都瞪大眼睛盯着它，不知道会有什么可怕的东西从里面冲出来。我就在福尔摩斯身旁，朝他脸上瞥了一眼。他脸色苍白，却满是得意，眼睛在月光下闪闪发亮。可是突然间，他的眼睛直直地瞪了出去，僵住不动，嘴唇也惊愕地张开了。就在同一刻，雷斯垂德惊恐地大叫一声，扑倒在地，脸朝下趴着。我一跃而起，手无力地攥着手枪，脑子都被那个从雾影里扑向我们的可怕东西吓僵了。那是一条猎犬，一条煤一般漆黑的巨大猎犬，可绝不是凡人见过的那种猎犬。它张开的嘴里喷着火，眼睛闪着阴燃般的凶光，口鼻、颈毛和喉下的垂肉都勾着一圈跳动的火焰。就是一个神志错乱的人在最狂乱的梦里，也想象不出比这更凶残、更骇人、更像来自地狱的东西了，那黑色的身影和狰狞的脸，就这样从雾墙里冲到了我们面前。
段.en: There was a thin, crisp, continuous patter from somewhere in the heart of that crawling bank. The cloud was within fifty yards of where we lay, and we glared at it, all three, uncertain what horror was about to break from the heart of it. I was at Holmes’s elbow, and I glanced for an instant at his face. It was pale and exultant, his eyes shining brightly in the moonlight. But suddenly they started forward in a rigid, fixed stare, and his lips parted in amazement. At the same instant Lestrade gave a yell of terror and threw himself face downward upon the ground. I sprang to my feet, my inert hand grasping my pistol, my mind paralyzed by the dreadful shape which had sprung out upon us from the shadows of the fog. A hound it was, an enormous coal-black hound, but not such a hound as mortal eyes have ever seen. Fire burst from its open mouth, its eyes glowed with a smouldering glare, its muzzle and hackles and dewlap were outlined in flickering flame. Never in the delirious dream of a disordered brain could anything more savage, more appalling, more hellish be conceived than that dark form and savage face which broke upon us out of the wall of fog.

段.文: 那只巨大的黑色怪物一跳老远，顺着小路蹿下去，紧紧追着我们那位朋友的脚步。我们被这个怪影吓呆了，直到它从面前过去才回过神来。接着，福尔摩斯和我同时开了枪，那怪物发出一声可怕的嚎叫，说明至少有一枪打中了。可它并没有停下，仍旧往前蹿去。我们看见远远的小路上，亨利爵士正回头张望，脸在月光下一片惨白，双手惊恐地举着，无助地瞪着那个正在追捕他的可怕东西。可是猎犬那一声痛叫，把我们的恐惧一扫而空。它会受伤，就是血肉之躯；我们能打伤它，就能打死它。我从没见过有谁像福尔摩斯那天夜里跑得那样快。人家都说我腿脚快，可他把我甩下的距离，跟我把那个小个子职业警探甩下的一样远。我们顺着小路飞奔，听见前面传来亨利爵士一声接一声的惨叫，还有猎犬低沉的咆哮。我赶到时，正好看见那畜生扑向它的猎物，把他扑倒在地，咬向他的喉咙。可就在下一刻，福尔摩斯已经把左轮手枪里的五发子弹全打进了那怪物的侧腹。它发出最后一声痛苦的嚎叫，凶狠地朝空中咬了一口，便仰面翻倒，四只脚疯狂地乱蹬，接着瘫软地侧倒在地。我气喘吁吁地弯下腰，把手枪抵在那颗闪着微光的可怕脑袋上，可已经用不着扣扳机了。那条巨大的猎犬死了。
段.en: With long bounds the huge black creature was leaping down the track, following hard upon the footsteps of our friend. So paralyzed were we by the apparition that we allowed him to pass before we had recovered our nerve. Then Holmes and I both fired together, and the creature gave a hideous howl, which showed that one at least had hit him. He did not pause, however, but bounded onward. Far away on the path we saw Sir Henry looking back, his face white in the moonlight, his hands raised in horror, glaring helplessly at the frightful thing which was hunting him down. But that cry of pain from the hound had blown all our fears to the winds. If he was vulnerable he was mortal, and if we could wound him we could kill him. Never have I seen a man run as Holmes ran that night. I am reckoned fleet of foot, but he outpaced me as much as I outpaced the little professional. In front of us as we flew up the track we heard scream after scream from Sir Henry and the deep roar of the hound. I was in time to see the beast spring upon its victim, hurl him to the ground, and worry at his throat. But the next instant Holmes had emptied five barrels of his revolver into the creature’s flank. With a last howl of agony and a vicious snap in the air, it rolled upon its back, four feet pawing furiously, and then fell limp upon its side. I stooped, panting, and pressed my pistol to the dreadful, shimmering head, but it was useless to press the trigger. The giant hound was dead.

段.文: 亨利爵士倒在原地，不省人事。我们扯开他的领子，看到他身上没有伤痕，救援来得及时，福尔摩斯低声念了一句感恩的祷告。我们的朋友眼皮已经在颤动，他微微挣扎着想动一动。雷斯垂德把白兰地酒瓶塞到准男爵牙缝里，一双惊恐的眼睛便抬起来望着我们。
段.en: Sir Henry lay insensible where he had fallen. We tore away his collar, and Holmes breathed a prayer of gratitude when we saw that there was no sign of a wound and that the rescue had been in time. Already our friend’s eyelids shivered and he made a feeble effort to move. Lestrade thrust his brandy-flask between the baronet’s teeth, and two frightened eyes were looking up at us.

段.文: “我的上帝！”他低声说，“那是什么？老天爷，那到底是什么？”
段.en: “My God!” he whispered. “What was it? What, in heaven’s name, was it?”

段.文: “不管是什么，它已经死了。”福尔摩斯说，“我们把你们家族的鬼魂彻底镇住了。”
段.en: “It’s dead, whatever it is,” said Holmes. “We’ve laid the family ghost once and forever.”

段.文: 单论体型和力气，躺在我们面前的这东西就已经够吓人了。它既不是纯种的寻血猎犬，也不是纯种的獒犬，看来是两者杂交的，瘦骨嶙峋，凶猛异常，个头有一头小母狮那么大。即使此刻已经死去，一动不动，那张巨大的嘴似乎仍在滴着蓝幽幽的火焰，那双深陷的、凶残的小眼睛周围还环着一圈火光。我把手放在它发光的口鼻上，抬起手来一看，我自己的手指在黑暗中也隐隐发亮。
段.en: In mere size and strength it was a terrible creature which was lying stretched before us. It was not a pure bloodhound and it was not a pure mastiff; but it appeared to be a combination of the two—gaunt, savage, and as large as a small lioness. Even now in the stillness of death, the huge jaws seemed to be dripping with a bluish flame and the small, deep-set, cruel eyes were ringed with fire. I placed my hand upon the glowing muzzle, and as I held them up my own fingers smouldered and gleamed in the darkness.

段.文: “是磷。”我说。
段.en: “Phosphorus,” I said.

段.文: “是精心调配过的磷。”福尔摩斯说着，凑近闻了闻那只死去的畜生，“没有一点气味，不会妨碍它的嗅觉。亨利爵士，让你受了这么大的惊吓，我们实在对不住你。我料到会有一条猎犬，却没料到是这样一个怪物。再加上这场雾，我们几乎来不及迎击它。”
段.en: “A cunning preparation of it,” said Holmes, sniffing at the dead animal. “There is no smell which might have interfered with his power of scent. We owe you a deep apology, Sir Henry, for having exposed you to this fright. I was prepared for a hound, but not for such a creature as this. And the fog gave us little time to receive him.”

段.文: “你救了我的命。”
段.en: “You have saved my life.”

段.文: “可也是我先让你的命陷入险境的。你还有力气站起来吗？”
段.en: “Having first endangered it. Are you strong enough to stand?”

段.文: “再给我喝一口白兰地，我就什么都应付得了。好了！现在请扶我起来。你们打算怎么办？”
段.en: “Give me another mouthful of that brandy and I shall be ready for anything. So! Now, if you will help me up. What do you propose to do?”

段.文: “把你留在这儿。你今晚经不起再冒险了。你要是愿意等一等，我们当中会有一个人陪你回庄园去。”
段.en: “To leave you here. You are not fit for further adventures tonight. If you will wait, one or other of us will go back with you to the Hall.”

段.文: 他想挣扎着站起来，可脸色仍然惨白，四肢都在发抖。我们扶他到一块石头上坐下，他坐在那里，双手捂着脸，浑身哆嗦。
段.en: He tried to stagger to his feet; but he was still ghastly pale and trembling in every limb. We helped him to a rock, where he sat shivering with his face buried in his hands.

段.文: “我们现在得离开你了。”福尔摩斯说，“剩下的事必须做完，每一刻都很要紧。证据我们已经有了，现在只差把人抓住。
段.en: “We must leave you now,” said Holmes. “The rest of our work must be done, and every moment is of importance. We have our case, and now we only want our man.

段.文: “要在那座房子里找到他，希望只有千分之一。”我们沿着小路快步往回走时，他接着说，“那几声枪响一定让他知道，这场把戏已经完了。”
段.en: “It’s a thousand to one against our finding him at the house,” he continued as we retraced our steps swiftly down the path. “Those shots must have told him that the game was up.”

段.文: “我们离得挺远，这场雾也许把枪声闷住了。”
段.en: “We were some distance off, and this fog may have deadened them.”

段.文: “他一定跟在猎犬后面，好把它唤回去，这一点你可以肯定。不，不，这会儿他早跑了！不过我们还是要搜一搜房子，弄个明白。”
段.en: “He followed the hound to call him off—of that you may be certain. No, no, he’s gone by this time! But we’ll search the house and make sure.”

段.文: 前门开着，我们冲了进去，一间一间地匆匆搜查。一个老态龙钟的男仆在过道里迎面碰见我们，惊得目瞪口呆。除了餐厅，别处都没有灯，福尔摩斯便抓起那盏灯，把房子的每个角落都搜遍了。我们要追的那个人，一点踪影也没有。不过在楼上，有一间卧室的门锁着。
段.en: The front door was open, so we rushed in and hurried from room to room to the amazement of a doddering old manservant, who met us in the passage. There was no light save in the dining-room, but Holmes caught up the lamp and left no corner of the house unexplored. No sign could we see of the man whom we were chasing. On the upper floor, however, one of the bedroom doors was locked.

段.文: “这里面有人！”雷斯垂德喊道，“我听见有动静。开门！”
段.en: “There’s someone in here,” cried Lestrade. “I can hear a movement. Open this door!”

段.文: 里面传出微弱的呻吟声和窸窣声。福尔摩斯抬起脚，用脚掌对准门锁上方一踹，门一下子开了。我们三个人手里握着枪，冲进屋去。
段.en: A faint moaning and rustling came from within. Holmes struck the door just over the lock with the flat of his foot and it flew open. Pistol in hand, we all three rushed into the room.

段.文: 可屋里并没有我们以为会见到的那个铤而走险、负隅顽抗的恶棍。我们面前出现的，是一样那么奇怪、那么出人意料的东西，让我们一时间站在那里，惊愕地盯着它。
段.en: But there was no sign within it of that desperate and defiant villain whom we expected to see. Instead we were faced by an object so strange and so unexpected that we stood for a moment staring at it in amazement.

段.文: 这个房间被布置成了一个小小的博物馆，四面墙边排着许多玻璃面的柜子，里面装满了蝴蝶和蛾子的标本。收集这些标本，是这个复杂而危险的人的消遣。房间中央立着一根柱子，是不知什么时候竖起来撑住横过屋顶的那根被虫蛀了的旧梁木的。柱子上绑着一个人，被用来捆绑的床单层层裹住，一时竟看不出是男是女。一条毛巾绕过喉咙，系在柱子后面；另一条蒙住了脸的下半部分，毛巾上方，一双黑眼睛回望着我们，那眼里满是悲痛、羞耻和一种可怕的询问。不到一分钟，我们就扯掉了堵嘴的毛巾，解开了捆绑，斯台普顿太太瘫倒在我们面前的地板上。她那美丽的头垂到胸前时，我看见她脖子上有一道清清楚楚的红色鞭痕。
段.en: The room had been fashioned into a small museum, and the walls were lined by a number of glass-topped cases full of that collection of butterflies and moths the formation of which had been the relaxation of this complex and dangerous man. In the centre of this room there was an upright beam, which had been placed at some period as a support for the old worm-eaten baulk of timber which spanned the roof. To this post a figure was tied, so swathed and muffled in the sheets which had been used to secure it that one could not for the moment tell whether it was that of a man or a woman. One towel passed round the throat and was secured at the back of the pillar. Another covered the lower part of the face, and over it two dark eyes—eyes full of grief and shame and a dreadful questioning—stared back at us. In a minute we had torn off the gag, unswathed the bonds, and Mrs. Stapleton sank upon the floor in front of us. As her beautiful head fell upon her chest I saw the clear red weal of a whiplash across her neck.

段.文: “这个畜生！”福尔摩斯喊道，“快，雷斯垂德，你的白兰地！把她扶到椅子上！她受了虐待，又累坏了，晕过去了。”
段.en: “The brute!” cried Holmes. “Here, Lestrade, your brandy-bottle! Put her in the chair! She has fainted from ill-usage and exhaustion.”

段.文: 她又睁开了眼睛。
段.en: She opened her eyes again.

段.文: “他安全吗？”她问，“他逃掉了吗？”
段.en: “Is he safe?” she asked. “Has he escaped?”

段.文: “他逃不出我们的手掌，太太。”
段.en: “He cannot escape us, madam.”

段.文: “不，不，我说的不是我丈夫。亨利爵士呢？他安全吗？”
段.en: “No, no, I did not mean my husband. Sir Henry? Is he safe?”

段.文: “安全。”
段.en: “Yes.”

段.文: “那条猎犬呢？”
段.en: “And the hound?”

段.文: “死了。”
段.en: “It is dead.”

段.文: 她长长地舒了一口气，如释重负。
段.en: She gave a long sigh of satisfaction.

段.文: “谢天谢地！谢天谢地！噢，这个恶棍！看他是怎么对待我的！”她把双臂从袖子里伸出来，我们惊恐地看到，那上面全是一块块青紫的伤痕。“可这算不了什么，算不了什么！他折磨、玷污的是我的心灵和灵魂。虐待也好，孤独也好，一辈子活在欺骗里也好，所有这一切我都能忍受，只要我还能抱着一线希望，相信他是爱我的。可现在我知道了，在这件事上，我也只是被他愚弄的人，是他的工具。”她说着，失声痛哭起来。
段.en: “Thank God! Thank God! Oh, this villain! See how he has treated me!” She shot her arms out from her sleeves, and we saw with horror that they were all mottled with bruises. “But this is nothing—nothing! It is my mind and soul that he has tortured and defiled. I could endure it all, ill-usage, solitude, a life of deception, everything, as long as I could still cling to the hope that I had his love, but now I know that in this also I have been his dupe and his tool.” She broke into passionate sobbing as she spoke.

段.文: “你对他已经没有什么情分了，太太。”福尔摩斯说，“那就告诉我们，到哪儿能找到他。如果你曾经帮他作过恶，那就现在帮帮我们，将功补过吧。”
段.en: “You bear him no good will, madam,” said Holmes. “Tell us then where we shall find him. If you have ever aided him in evil, help us now and so atone.”

段.文: “他只可能逃到一个地方去。”她回答，“泥沼中央有个小岛，岛上有一座废弃的锡矿。他就是在那儿养那条猎犬的，还在那儿做了准备，好有个藏身之处。他一定会逃到那儿去。”
段.en: “There is but one place where he can have fled,” she answered. “There is an old tin mine on an island in the heart of the mire. It was there that he kept his hound and there also he had made preparations so that he might have a refuge. That is where he would fly.”

段.文: 雾堤像一团白羊毛似的贴在窗户上。福尔摩斯把灯朝窗户举了举。
段.en: The fog-bank lay like white wool against the window. Holmes held the lamp towards it.

段.文: “你看，”他说，“今晚谁也别想找到路进格林彭大泥沼。”
段.en: “See,” said he. “No one could find his way into the Grimpen Mire tonight.”

段.文: 她笑了起来，拍着手，眼睛和牙齿都闪着凶狠的快意。
段.en: She laughed and clapped her hands. Her eyes and teeth gleamed with fierce merriment.

段.文: “他也许找得到路进去，可永远别想出来。”她喊道，“今晚他怎么看得见那些引路的标杆？那是我和他一起插的，用来标出穿过泥沼的路。噢，要是我今天能把它们拔掉就好了。那样的话，他就真的任凭你们处置了！”
段.en: “He may find his way in, but never out,” she cried. “How can he see the guiding wands tonight? We planted them together, he and I, to mark the pathway through the mire. Oh, if I could only have plucked them out today. Then indeed you would have had him at your mercy!”

段.文: 我们很清楚，雾散之前，怎么追都是白费力气。于是我们留下雷斯垂德看守那座房子，福尔摩斯和我陪准男爵回了巴斯克维尔庄园。斯台普顿一家的事再也瞒不住他了。得知他所爱的那个女人的真相时，他勇敢地承受住了这个打击。可是这一夜的惊险把他的神经彻底击垮了，天亮之前，他就发起高烧，说起了胡话，由莫蒂默医生照料着。后来，他们两人结伴去周游世界，亨利爵士这才重新变回从前那个健壮爽朗的人，就像他成为那片不祥庄园的主人之前那样。
段.en: It was evident to us that all pursuit was in vain until the fog had lifted. Meanwhile we left Lestrade in possession of the house while Holmes and I went back with the baronet to Baskerville Hall. The story of the Stapletons could no longer be withheld from him, but he took the blow bravely when he learned the truth about the woman whom he had loved. But the shock of the night’s adventures had shattered his nerves, and before morning he lay delirious in a high fever under the care of Dr. Mortimer. The two of them were destined to travel together round the world before Sir Henry had become once more the hale, hearty man that he had been before he became master of that ill-omened estate.

段.文: 现在，我很快就要讲到这个离奇故事的结尾了。我一直想让读者也体会到那些阴暗的恐惧和模糊的猜测，它们在我们的生活上笼罩了那么久，最后以那样悲惨的方式收场。猎犬死后的第二天早上，雾散了，斯台普顿太太领我们来到他们在沼地里找到路径的地方。看到她把我们引上她丈夫的踪迹时那种急切和欢喜，我们才明白这个女人过的是怎样可怕的日子。我们让她留在一条狭长的半岛上，那里是坚实的泥炭土，越往前越窄，伸进一望无际的沼地。从半岛尽头起，到处零零星星插着细细的标杆，标出那条小路如何在一丛丛灯心草之间曲折穿行。四周是浮着绿沫的水坑和污秽的泥潭，挡住了陌生人的去路。茂密的芦苇和肥厚黏滑的水草，把一股腐烂的气味和浓重的瘴气扑到我们脸上。有好几次，我们一脚踩空，陷进黑乎乎、颤动着的泥沼里，一直没到大腿，脚边几码之内的泥浆都随之软软地起伏。我们走路时，泥沼死死地扯着我们的脚后跟；一陷进去，就好像有一只恶毒的手在把我们往那肮脏的深处拽，它抓得那么狠，那么有意。只有一次，我们看到了有人在我们之前走过这条险路的痕迹。一丛羊胡子草把一样黑乎乎的东西托出了烂泥，那东西就从草丛中间露出来。福尔摩斯离开小路去抓它，一下子陷到了腰部，要不是我们在旁边把他拉出来，他就再也踏不上坚实的土地了。他把一只旧的黑皮靴举在空中，靴子里面的皮子上印着“多伦多迈耶斯鞋店”。
段.en: And now I come rapidly to the conclusion of this singular narrative, in which I have tried to make the reader share those dark fears and vague surmises which clouded our lives so long and ended in so tragic a manner. On the morning after the death of the hound the fog had lifted and we were guided by Mrs. Stapleton to the point where they had found a pathway through the bog. It helped us to realise the horror of this woman’s life when we saw the eagerness and joy with which she laid us on her husband’s track. We left her standing upon the thin peninsula of firm, peaty soil which tapered out into the widespread bog. From the end of it a small wand planted here and there showed where the path zigzagged from tuft to tuft of rushes among those green-scummed pits and foul quagmires which barred the way to the stranger. Rank reeds and lush, slimy water-plants sent an odour of decay and a heavy miasmatic vapour onto our faces, while a false step plunged us more than once thigh-deep into the dark, quivering mire, which shook for yards in soft undulations around our feet. Its tenacious grip plucked at our heels as we walked, and when we sank into it it was as if some malignant hand was tugging us down into those obscene depths, so grim and purposeful was the clutch in which it held us. Once only we saw a trace that someone had passed that perilous way before us. From amid a tuft of cotton grass which bore it up out of the slime some dark thing was projecting. Holmes sank to his waist as he stepped from the path to seize it, and had we not been there to drag him out he could never have set his foot upon firm land again. He held an old black boot in the air. “Meyers, Toronto,” was printed on the leather inside.

段.文: “洗这一回泥浆澡值得。”他说，“这是我们的朋友亨利爵士丢的那只靴子。”
段.en: “It is worth a mud bath,” said he. “It is our friend Sir Henry’s missing boot.”

段.文: “是斯台普顿逃跑时扔在这儿的。”
段.en: “Thrown there by Stapleton in his flight.”

段.文: “正是。他用这只靴子让猎犬认准了气味，之后一直拿在手里。他知道把戏败露了，逃跑时还攥着它，逃到这儿才把它扔掉。至少我们知道，他平安地走到了这里。”
段.en: “Exactly. He retained it in his hand after using it to set the hound upon the track. He fled when he knew the game was up, still clutching it. And he hurled it away at this point of his flight. We know at least that he came so far in safety.”

段.文: 可是再多的，我们就永远无从知道了，虽然有许多事可以推测。要在泥沼里找脚印是不可能的，因为泥浆很快就涌上来把脚印填满了。不过等我们终于走过泥潭，到了比较坚实的地面上，大家都急切地寻找他的脚印，却连一丝痕迹也没看到。如果大地说的是实话，那么在那最后一夜，斯台普顿在雾里挣扎着朝那座避难的小岛走去，却始终没有走到。在格林彭大泥沼中央的某个地方，在那片吞没了他的巨大泥潭的污泥深处，这个冷酷无情的人永远地埋葬了。
段.en: But more than that we were never destined to know, though there was much which we might surmise. There was no chance of finding footsteps in the mire, for the rising mud oozed swiftly in upon them, but as we at last reached firmer ground beyond the morass we all looked eagerly for them.
